title: Professional Ethics & Liabilities of Auditors
description: CA Final – Auditing and Assurance | Advanced MCQ practice bank on the ICAI Code of Ethics, NOCLAR, membership and certificate of practice, misconduct under the First and Second Schedules, Council General Guidelines (networking, corporate form of practice, assignment limits), ethical decisions of the Ethical Standards Board and the disciplinary machinery. Analytical, case-study and application-based questions.

questions.question:
Match the following:

Column I (Category of threat)
A. Self-interest threat
B. Self-review threat
C. Advocacy threat
D. Familiarity threat
E. Intimidation threat

Column II (Circumstance given in the Code)
1. Issuing a report on the effectiveness of systems after having implemented those systems
2. Being threatened with dismissal by the client
3. Holding a direct financial interest in, or having a close business relationship with, a client
4. Manipulating information in a prospectus in order to obtain favourable financing
5. Long association with the individuals who influence the client's business decisions

Which of the following is the correct matching?
questions.explanation: A self-interest threat exists where a financial or other interest could influence the accountant's judgment or behaviour; the Code's illustrations are a direct financial interest or close business relationship with a client, and holding a financial interest in or receiving a loan from the employing organisation. A self-review threat is failure to evaluate appropriately the result of a previous judgment or activity of the accountant, illustrated by reporting on the effectiveness of systems after implementing them and by fixing the accounting treatment for a business combination after doing the supporting feasibility study. Advocacy is promoting the client's or employer's position till objectivity is compromised, illustrated by acting as advocate for an assurance client in litigation or disputes and by manipulating prospectus information to obtain favourable financing. Familiarity is undue sympathy arising from a long or close relationship, illustrated by a close family relationship or long association with the client and long association with individuals influencing business decisions. Intimidation is being deterred from objectivity by actual or perceived pressure, illustrated by threat of dismissal by the client and threat of dismissal or replacement by the employing organisation. The other combinations either transpose the self-review and advocacy illustrations or attach the client-dismissal illustration to the wrong category.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the fundamental principle of integrity:

1. A professional accountant shall not knowingly be associated with information which, in his belief, contains statements or information provided negligently, even if no single statement in that information is materially false or misleading.
2. Where such information is nevertheless involved, the accountant is not treated as being in breach if he provides a modified report in respect of that matter.
3. If he has already become associated with such information, recording his disagreement in the engagement file discharges his obligation under integrity.
4. The relief of providing a modified report is available only where the objection is that the information omits required information, and not where it contains a materially false or misleading statement.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Integrity requires the accountant to be straightforward and honest in all relationships, and prohibits knowing association with information he believes (i) contains a materially false or misleading statement, (ii) contains statements or information provided negligently, or (iii) omits required information. Statement 1 is therefore correct, because negligent provision is a head of breach in its own right and does not require the underlying statement to be false. Statement 2 is correct: the Code expressly says he will not be considered in breach if he provides a modified report in respect of the matter. Statement 3 is wrong, because where he has become associated with such information he must take steps to be disassociated from it; a file note leaves him associated with it. Statement 4 is wrong, because the modified-report relief is expressed in respect of 'the above matter', that is, all three heads, and not merely the omission head.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Deepa Nair, a chartered accountant in practice, discovers while signing a certificate that the expenditure statement annexed to it has been put together carelessly by the client's clerk and includes three duplicated items. She neither gets the annexure corrected nor modifies her certificate, and the certificate is issued. She is in breach of integrity even though she honestly believed that nobody reading it would be misled.

Reason (R): Integrity is breached only where the accountant intends to mislead the user of the report.

In the light of the above, choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: The decisive fact is that Deepa became aware of the position before the certificate went out, so her continued association with the information was knowing. The integrity principle bars knowing association with information the accountant believes contains a materially false or misleading statement, or statements or information provided negligently, or which omits required information; careless compilation by the clerk squarely engages the 'provided negligently' head, which requires no intention to deceive. Reason R is therefore false, since the test is the accountant's belief about the quality of the information, not his motive or any intent to mislead. Nor did she avail herself of the relief the Code allows, namely providing a modified report in respect of the matter, nor did she take steps to be disassociated from the information. An assertion built on the opposite premise, that she is not liable because she meant no harm, would fail for the same reason.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on the fundamental principle of confidentiality:

1. The obligation extends to information acquired as a result of professional as well as employment relationships.
2. Where a disclosure is permitted by law, that fact by itself is a complete answer and nothing further is needed.
3. Disclosure is permissible where there is a professional duty or right to disclose, for instance to protect the accountant's own interest in legal proceedings or to comply with technical and professional standards.
4. Where an inquiry or investigation is being conducted by a regulatory body, the accountant may disclose only if the client also consents.

Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are accurate: confidentiality covers information acquired through professional and employment relationships, and the third situation recognised by the Code is a professional duty or right to disclose, which the Code illustrates by Peer or Quality Review of ICAI, inquiry or investigation by a regulatory body, protecting his own interest in legal proceedings, and complying with technical and professional standards. Statement 2 is not correct because the second situation is compound: the disclosure must be permitted by law and also authorised by the client or the employing organisation; permission of law alone does not supply the client's or employer's authority. Statement 4 is not correct because a response to a regulatory inquiry or investigation is placed by the Code in the professional duty or right category and is not conditioned on client consent. The common error in both wrong statements is treating one limb of a disclosure route as if it were the whole route, or adding a consent requirement that the Code does not impose.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about addressing threats to compliance with the fundamental principles:

1. The obligation to address a threat arises when the accountant determines that the identified threats are not at an acceptable level.
2. If the threat cannot be eliminated, and safeguards do not bring it down to an acceptable level, declining or ending the specific professional activity is a course the Code contemplates.
3. Since the Code illustrates safeguards for every category of threat, applying an appropriate reviewer disposes of the matter and the accountant need not consider eliminating the interests or relationships that created the threat.
4. Once any threat is identified, the accountant must withdraw from the entire client relationship.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: The trigger in the Code is the accountant's determination that the identified threats are not at an acceptable level; only then must he address them, so statement 1 is correct. The Code then offers three alternative routes, namely eliminating the circumstances including the interests or relationships creating the threat, applying safeguards to reduce the threats to an acceptable level, or declining or ending the specific professional activity, and statement 2 correctly identifies the third as an alternative where the first two do not work. Statement 3 is wrong because safeguards and elimination are independent routes, and safeguards are not represented as available or adequate for every threat; where the circumstance itself can be eliminated, that route remains live. Statement 4 is wrong because it converts the narrow route of declining or ending the specific professional activity into a blanket duty to resign from the client relationship, which the Code does not impose.

questions.question:
Match the following situations with the illustrations of safeguards given in the Code:

Column I (Situation)
A. The partners who audit an assurance client also wish to render a non-assurance service to that same client
B. Work done on a sensitive valuation must be checked by someone who did not take part in performing it
C. Persons holding information obtained for one client are also serving another client whose interests run counter to the first
D. The team doubts whether it can look at a critical procedure it itself performed at an earlier stage of the same engagement with fresh objectivity

Column II (Safeguard)
1. Having an appropriate reviewer, who was not a member of the team, review the work performed
2. Using different partners and teams for provision of non-assurance services to an assurance client
3. Involving another firm to perform or re-perform part of the engagement
4. Separating teams when dealing with matters of a confidential nature

Which of the following is the correct matching?
questions.explanation: Situation A is the classic case for using different partners and teams for the non-assurance work rendered to an assurance client, so that the people auditing are not the people who performed the service. Situation B calls for an appropriate reviewer who was not a member of the team, which is a review of work already done rather than re-performance of it. Situation C concerns information of a confidential nature, which is addressed by separating teams when dealing with such matters. Situation D differs from B because the object is to have the procedure itself performed or re-performed by someone outside the firm's team, which the Code illustrates by involving another firm to perform or re-perform part of the engagement. The combinations that swap C with D, or B with D, fail precisely on the distinction between reviewing work and re-performing part of the engagement.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on the fundamental principle of professional behaviour:

1. The accountant must comply with relevant laws and regulations and avoid any conduct that might discredit the profession.
2. Indirect measures of publicity fall outside this principle, since only direct advertisement is contemplated.
3. While promoting himself, an accountant may draw a comparison with the work of other firms so long as he does not name any of them.
4. When promoting himself and his work, the accountant shall not bring the profession into disrepute.

Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 4 restate the principle as the Code frames it, and are correct. Statement 2 is not correct because the Code bars exaggerated claims for services, qualifications or experience, disparaging references or unsubstantiated comparisons with the work of others, and any direct or indirect measures to advertise in violation of the Advertisement Guidelines; the word 'indirect' is expressly used, so a publicity device that stops short of a formal advertisement is still caught. Statement 3 is not correct because the objection is to a disparaging reference or an unsubstantiated comparison, and anonymity of the competitor neither removes the disparagement nor supplies the substantiation the principle requires. The trap in statement 3 is treating a naming requirement as the test, when the Code's tests are disparagement and substantiation.

questions.question: In each of the following situations the conduct of a chartered accountant is called in question. In which one is the primary failure that of objectivity, as distinguished from the other fundamental principles?
options: A member accepts an assignment to verify a physical stock worth ₹ 58 crore although he has never attended such a count and is unfamiliar with the count methodology, and he nevertheless signs the report.

A member settles the provision for doubtful debts not on the evidence but because the finance director insists that a lower provision is what everyone in the industry does, and he does not resist that influence.
A member issues a valuation report drafted entirely by an intern whose file he has never opened, the intern having received no training whatever in valuation.
A member signs a certificate along with an expenditure schedule which he believes to have been put together carelessly and to contain duplicated items, and modifies nothing in it.
questions.explanation: Objectivity requires the accountant not to compromise professional judgment because of bias, conflict of interest or the undue influence of others; in option 2 the conclusion is dictated by the finance director's insistence, which is undue influence of others and therefore an objectivity failure. Option 1 is a professional competence matter, since competence requires attaining and maintaining professional knowledge and acting diligently in accordance with technical and professional standards. Option 3 engages the separate limb of competence and due care requiring the accountant to take reasonable steps to ensure that those working under his authority have appropriate training and supervision. Option 4 engages integrity, because he knowingly allowed himself to be associated with information he believed contained statements provided negligently, without modifying the report or disassociating himself. The distinguishing point is that objectivity is about the inputs to judgment being corrupted, not about the absence of skill or about the honesty of what is certified.

questions.question:
Anil Shah, a chartered accountant in practice at Indore, was appointed auditor of a textile exporter for the year ended 31 March 2026. He had last studied the export incentive scheme in 2018 and did not update himself. He entrusted verification of an export incentive receivable of ₹ 1.86 crore to a second-year articled assistant, gave no instructions, and never looked at the working papers; the assistant's check covered 4 shipping bills out of 612. Anil knew by April 2026 that the file was incomplete yet issued an unmodified report on 30 July 2026.

Which of the following best describes the position under the fundamental principle of professional competence and due care?
options: Only the competence limb is breached, because the duty as to training and supervision is owed in respect of employees and not in respect of articled assistants.
Only the due care limb is breached, because a member is entitled to rely on the work of those under his authority once he has himself signed and dated the report.
Neither limb is breached, because the only failure that can be measured is the delay in issuing the report, and that engages professional behaviour.

Both limbs are breached, since competence requires continuing awareness of technical and professional developments, and those working under his authority must be given appropriate training and supervision.
questions.explanation: Two separate duties in the same principle are offended here. Maintaining professional competence requires continuing awareness and understanding of technical and professional developments, and relying on knowledge of a scheme last studied in 2018 for a 2025-26 audit fails that duty; the principle also requires diligence in accordance with technical and professional standards and the exercise of sound judgment in applying knowledge and skill. The further duty to take reasonable steps to ensure that those working under his authority have appropriate training and supervision is breached by handing a ₹ 1.86 crore verification to an uninstructed assistant on 4 of 612 items and never reviewing the file; an articled assistant plainly works under his authority, so option 1's employee-only reading is untenable. Option 2 inverts the rule, since supervision is the member's own obligation and signing cannot convert reliance into compliance. Option 3 mistakes the chronology, because the incomplete file was known in April, well before the July issue date.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about a situation where complying with one fundamental principle appears to conflict with compliance with another:

1. The accountant may consult others within his organisation, those charged with governance, ICAI or legal counsel.
2. If he obtains a considered opinion from legal counsel, he is relieved of the responsibility to exercise his own professional judgment to resolve the conflict.
3. Having consulted ICAI, the accountant need not concern himself with disassociating from the matter creating the conflict.
4. Those charged with governance are one of the persons whose views the accountant may seek in such a situation.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: The Code names four consultative avenues for an apparent conflict between fundamental principles, namely others within the organisation, those charged with governance, ICAI and legal counsel, which makes statements 1 and 4 correct. It then adds that consultation does not relieve the accountant of the responsibility to exercise professional judgment to resolve the conflict, or to disassociate himself from the matter creating the conflict; statement 2 fails on the first of these and statement 3 on the second. The common error in statements 2 and 3 is treating an external opinion as a transfer of responsibility, whereas the Code treats consultation as an input to, and not a substitute for, the accountant's own decision. The identity of the person consulted is immaterial; legal counsel and ICAI stand in the same position in this respect.

questions.question:
Rajat Iyer is the Chief Financial Officer of a listed company. On 3 February 2026 the Managing Director asked him to release a provision of ₹ 220 crore carried for a pending customer claim and told him, in writing, that his role and his emoluments would be 'reviewed' if he persisted with the present treatment. Rajat is not being asked to certify anything for a third party and holds no shares in the company.

Which one of the following correctly identifies the threat and the courses the Code contemplates?
options: Self-interest threat, since what is in issue is his emoluments and not his objectivity; and declining or ending the professional activity is not a course the Code offers to an accountant in service.
Advocacy threat, since he is being pressed to adopt management's position on the provision; the only remedy the Code contemplates in such a case is a reviewer who is not a member of the team.

Intimidation threat, arising from pressure by the employing organisation; the Code's courses are eliminating the circumstances creating the threat, applying safeguards to reduce it to an acceptable level, or declining or ending the specific professional activity.
Intimidation threat, but the Code requires him in every such case to disclose the matter to a regulatory body or to ICAI, that being one of the three routes it gives for addressing threats.
questions.explanation: The Code's intimidation illustration is being threatened with dismissal by a client, or facing a threat of dismissal or replacement by the employing organisation; a written warning that his role and emoluments will be 'reviewed' if he resists is pressure from the employing organisation which deters him from acting objectively, so this is an intimidation threat. The three routes for addressing a threat that is not at an acceptable level are eliminating the circumstances including the interests or relationships creating it, applying safeguards, or declining or ending the specific professional activity, and option 3 lists them truly. Option 1 mislabels the threat and wrongly suggests the third route is unavailable to an accountant in service. Option 2 confuses advocacy, which involves the accountant promoting the client's or employer's position to the point his objectivity is compromised, with being subjected to pressure, and wrongly presents one safeguard as the sole remedy. Option 4 imports the confidentiality disclosure provisions into the framework for addressing threats, where they do not belong.

questions.question:
Case: Nikhil Mehta & Associates (NMA), a chartered accountants' firm in Ahmedabad, is the statutory auditor of Shivalik Alloys Limited for the year ended 31 March 2026. On 12 May 2025 NMA was engaged by Shivalik's Chief Financial Officer, for a fee of ₹ 28 lakh, to design and roll out a goods-issue-note and warehouse-verification module in the company's ERP; the module went live on 1 September 2025 and generates the 'quantity dispatched' figure from which the company's closing inventory of ₹ 214 crore is derived. Nikhil Mehta, the engagement partner for the audit, personally supervised the go-live, has been the engagement partner on this account for eleven consecutive years, and his brother-in-law Anil Shah is a Whole-time Director of Shivalik who decides inventory holding policy. In December 2025 a different partner of NMA, Priya Doshi, appeared before the sales-tax authorities and argued Shivalik's contested position on a demand of ₹ 6 crore, and NMA has also filed the company's monthly GST returns since 2019 through a third partner, Imran Qureshi. On 20 January 2026 the CFO telephoned Nikhil and said that if inventory was reported as misstated, NMA would be moved at the next annual general meeting, at which Anil Shah is also a director. Nikhil has drafted an unmodified audit report dated 5 February 2026 and has not discussed the inventory matter with anyone. NMA's total fee from Shivalik for the year is ₹ 62 lakh.

Which of the following threats to compliance with the fundamental principles arise on these facts?

1. Self-review threat, because the firm implemented the module which produces the inventory figure it must now audit.
2. Familiarity threat, because of the eleven consecutive years and the close family relationship with a person who influences business decisions.
3. Intimidation threat, because the CFO's telephone statement threatens the firm with being moved.
4. Advocacy threat, because NMA has been filing Shivalik's monthly GST returns since 2019.
5. Advocacy threat, because a partner of NMA appeared before the sales-tax authorities and argued the company's contested position on a ₹ 6 crore demand.
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is a self-review threat in its purest form: the Code's illustration is issuing a report after having implemented the systems, and here the module generating 'quantity dispatched' was designed and rolled out by the audit firm itself. Statement 2 is familiarity, the Code covering both a close family relationship or long association with the client and long association with individuals influencing business decisions; the brother-in-law who sets inventory holding policy and the eleven-year run fall under these. Statement 3 is intimidation, since the Code expressly lists being threatened with dismissal by the client, and a threat to have the firm moved at the AGM is the same thing. Statement 5 is advocacy because acting as advocate on behalf of an assurance client in litigation or disputes is the Code's illustration, and appearing to argue a contested demand before the sales-tax authorities is exactly that. Statement 4 is not advocacy, because filing periodic returns is a routine compliance service and does not involve promoting the client's position to the point that objectivity is compromised; the GST work and the ₹ 62 lakh fee aggregate are the facts that do not change the analysis.

questions.question:
Case: Nikhil Mehta & Associates (NMA), a chartered accountants' firm in Ahmedabad, is the statutory auditor of Shivalik Alloys Limited for the year ended 31 March 2026. On 12 May 2025 NMA was engaged by Shivalik's Chief Financial Officer, for a fee of ₹ 28 lakh, to design and roll out a goods-issue-note and warehouse-verification module in the company's ERP; the module went live on 1 September 2025 and generates the 'quantity dispatched' figure from which the company's closing inventory of ₹ 214 crore is derived. Nikhil Mehta, the engagement partner for the audit, personally supervised the go-live, has been the engagement partner on this account for eleven consecutive years, and his brother-in-law Anil Shah is a Whole-time Director of Shivalik who decides inventory holding policy. In December 2025 a different partner of NMA, Priya Doshi, appeared before the sales-tax authorities and argued Shivalik's contested position on a demand of ₹ 6 crore, and NMA has also filed the company's monthly GST returns since 2019 through a third partner, Imran Qureshi. On 20 January 2026 the CFO telephoned Nikhil and said that if inventory was reported as misstated, NMA would be moved at the next annual general meeting, at which Anil Shah is also a director. Nikhil has drafted an unmodified audit report dated 5 February 2026 and has not discussed the inventory matter with anyone. NMA's total fee from Shivalik for the year is ₹ 62 lakh.

With reference to the self-review element created by the ERP module work, which one of the following states the safeguard illustrated in the Code that is directed at it, together with its correct limitation?
options: Using different partners and teams for the non-assurance work done for Shivalik, which completely cures the position because the GST returns are already handled by a different partner of the firm.
Involving another firm to perform or re-perform the whole of the statutory audit, since the Code does not contemplate re-performance of a part only of an engagement.
Separating the teams when dealing with matters of a confidential nature, because the dispatched-quantity data generated by the module is commercially sensitive.

Having an appropriate reviewer who was not a member of the team review the inventory work, which reduces the threat without removing the circumstance that the firm implemented the module whose output it audits.
questions.explanation: The safeguard the Code illustrates for work already performed is an appropriate reviewer who was not a member of the team, and it operates as a safeguard, that is, as an action to reduce a threat to an acceptable level; it does not eliminate the underlying circumstance that the firm built the module generating the inventory figure. Option 1 is wrong on two counts, because allocating work among different partners addresses non-assurance services generally and is anyway directed at a different threat, and because the GST returns were never the source of the self-review. Option 2 misstates the Code, which permits involving another firm to perform or re-perform part of the engagement and does not require the whole audit to be handed over. Option 3 is a real safeguard in the Code but is aimed at confidential information held across competing clients, not at evaluating a previous activity of the accountant. The decisive point is the distinction between reducing a threat and eliminating the circumstances creating it.

questions.question:
Case: Nikhil Mehta & Associates (NMA), a chartered accountants' firm in Ahmedabad, is the statutory auditor of Shivalik Alloys Limited for the year ended 31 March 2026. On 12 May 2025 NMA was engaged by Shivalik's Chief Financial Officer, for a fee of ₹ 28 lakh, to design and roll out a goods-issue-note and warehouse-verification module in the company's ERP; the module went live on 1 September 2025 and generates the 'quantity dispatched' figure from which the company's closing inventory of ₹ 214 crore is derived. Nikhil Mehta, the engagement partner for the audit, personally supervised the go-live, has been the engagement partner on this account for eleven consecutive years, and his brother-in-law Anil Shah is a Whole-time Director of Shivalik who decides inventory holding policy. In December 2025 a different partner of NMA, Priya Doshi, appeared before the sales-tax authorities and argued Shivalik's contested position on a demand of ₹ 6 crore, and NMA has also filed the company's monthly GST returns since 2019 through a third partner, Imran Qureshi. On 20 January 2026 the CFO telephoned Nikhil and said that if inventory was reported as misstated, NMA would be moved at the next annual general meeting, at which Anil Shah is also a director. Nikhil has drafted an unmodified audit report dated 5 February 2026 and has not discussed the inventory matter with anyone. NMA's total fee from Shivalik for the year is ₹ 62 lakh.

Nikhil determines that the threats are not at an acceptable level. Which combination of actions is consistent with the routes the Code contemplates for addressing them?

1. Eliminating the circumstances, including the interests and relationships creating the threats, for example by not reporting on the inventory balances produced by a module the firm itself implemented and by removing Nikhil from the engagement.
2. Applying safeguards, such as having an appropriate reviewer who is not a member of the team review the inventory work and using different partners and teams for the non-assurance services rendered to this assurance client.
3. Declining or ending the specific professional activity if the threats can neither be eliminated nor reduced to an acceptable level by safeguards.
4. Issuing the unmodified report and recording in the file that the threats had been considered, since considering a threat is itself a route prescribed for addressing it.
questions.explanation: Once the accountant determines that identified threats are not at an acceptable level, the Code gives him three routes: eliminate the circumstances including the interests or relationships creating the threat, apply safeguards to reduce the threat to an acceptable level, or decline or end the specific professional activity. Actions 1, 2 and 3 map onto these three routes respectively, and they are alternatives, so nothing prevents the firm from eliminating part of a threat and safeguarding the residue. Action 4 is not one of the routes; the file note records a determination but does not eliminate, reduce or avoid anything, and on these facts it also leaves untouched the intimidation created by the CFO's telephone call and the familiarity arising from eleven years and a brother-in-law who decides inventory policy. Note that the Code requires the threat to be addressed, not merely weighed, so the answer that includes 4 substitutes documentation for action.

questions.question:
Case: Nikhil Mehta & Associates (NMA), a chartered accountants' firm in Ahmedabad, is the statutory auditor of Shivalik Alloys Limited for the year ended 31 March 2026. On 12 May 2025 NMA was engaged by Shivalik's Chief Financial Officer, for a fee of ₹ 28 lakh, to design and roll out a goods-issue-note and warehouse-verification module in the company's ERP; the module went live on 1 September 2025 and generates the 'quantity dispatched' figure from which the company's closing inventory of ₹ 214 crore is derived. Nikhil Mehta, the engagement partner for the audit, personally supervised the go-live, has been the engagement partner on this account for eleven consecutive years, and his brother-in-law Anil Shah is a Whole-time Director of Shivalik who decides inventory holding policy. In December 2025 a different partner of NMA, Priya Doshi, appeared before the sales-tax authorities and argued Shivalik's contested position on a demand of ₹ 6 crore, and NMA has also filed the company's monthly GST returns since 2019 through a third partner, Imran Qureshi. On 20 January 2026 the CFO telephoned Nikhil and said that if inventory was reported as misstated, NMA would be moved at the next annual general meeting, at which Anil Shah is also a director. Nikhil has drafted an unmodified audit report dated 5 February 2026 and has not discussed the inventory matter with anyone. NMA's total fee from Shivalik for the year is ₹ 62 lakh.

Assume the facts are altered so that the module is implemented by an unrelated software vendor and NMA only advised on the specification document. Which of the following best describes the effect on the threat analysis?
options: Nothing changes, because advising on a specification document before implementation is the circumstance expressly given as an example of self-review in the Code.
The self-review element remains and the intimidation threat converts into advocacy, because NMA would then be promoting the company's choice of ERP to the authorities.
The self-review element falls away in this respect, since NMA would no longer be evaluating its own previous activity, while the familiarity and intimidation threats remain untouched.
All the threats identified fall away, because each of them is traceable to the implementation engagement and to nothing else on these facts.
The self-review element is replaced by a self-interest threat, because the ₹ 28 lakh would then be earned by the software vendor instead of by NMA.
questions.explanation: A self-review threat arises because the accountant will not appropriately evaluate the results of a previous judgment made or activity performed by him, and the Code's illustration is issuing a report on the effectiveness of systems after implementing those systems; if the implementation is by an unrelated vendor, that specific ground disappears. It does not matter for this limb that NMA wrote the specification, because the Code's example is the implementation of the system, and option 1 overstates the illustration. The familiarity threat is independent, resting on eleven years as engagement partner and a brother-in-law who decides inventory holding policy, and the intimidation threat is independent too, resting on the CFO's threat to have the firm moved at the annual general meeting. Option 4 wrongly treats every threat on these facts as a by-product of the ERP work, and option 5 invents a self-interest threat from money that the firm no longer receives; the option suggesting conversion into advocacy misreads advocacy, which requires NMA to be promoting the client's position, as Priya Doshi did before the sales-tax authorities.

questions.question:
Case: Suresh Rao, a chartered accountant in practice at Bengaluru, is the statutory auditor of Kaaveri Pharmaceuticals Limited for the year ended 31 March 2026. From the company's contract research notes he learns that a drug candidate representing 62% of the projected pipeline value has failed its safety trial; management has not recorded the fact, has not placed it before the board's risk committee and has omitted it from the annual report, and the working papers show the trial report reached the company on 8 August 2025. On 2 March 2026 a journalist friend asks him at a private dinner whether Kaaveri's pipeline is 'as strong as it claims'. On 4 March 2026 he receives a letter from a regulatory body seeking the trial-related audit documentation for the purposes of an investigation already commenced. On 10 March 2026 the Institute writes to him seeking the same working papers for a Peer Review. Rao proposes to answer the journalist in general terms without naming the company, to send the regulator two working papers without recording why he selected those two, and to refuse the Institute because he regards Peer Review as optional; he has not satisfied himself that every fact he intends to describe is substantiated.

Which of the following observations on Rao's proposals are correct?

1. The Institute's Peer Review request falls within the professional duty or right to disclose, so treating Peer Review as optional is not supported.
2. Disclosure to a regulator investigating a matter is a recognised ground, but the extent and mode of what is sent still call for the points the Code says should be considered before deciding whether to disclose.
3. Answering the journalist is covered by the professional duty or right to disclose, because an enquiry about a listed company is a matter of public interest.
4. It is unnecessary to record the reasons for what is sent and to whom, because the points to be considered before disclosure deal only with whether the information is substantiated.
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the Code lists compliance with the requirements of Peer or Quality Review of ICAI as one of the situations in which there is a professional duty or right to disclose, so the request is covered and the refusal has no basis. Statement 2 is correct: responding to an inquiry or investigation by a regulatory body is another recognised situation, but the Code separately requires the accountant, when deciding whether to disclose, to consider whether all relevant information is known and substantiated, the proposed type of communication and to whom it is addressed, and whether the parties addressed are appropriate recipients, all of which bear on how much documentation goes to the regulator. Statement 3 is wrong because a journalist's enquiry is none of the three situations, namely disclosure required by law, disclosure permitted by law and authorised by the client or employing organisation, and a professional duty or right to disclose; public curiosity about a listed entity does not create a duty or right. Statement 4 is wrong because two of the three considerations are directed at the communication and its recipients and not only at substantiation, which is exactly what Rao's unexplained selection of two working papers ignores.

questions.question:
Case: Suresh Rao, a chartered accountant in practice at Bengaluru, is the statutory auditor of Kaaveri Pharmaceuticals Limited for the year ended 31 March 2026. From the company's contract research notes he learns that a drug candidate representing 62% of the projected pipeline value has failed its safety trial; management has not recorded the fact, has not placed it before the board's risk committee and has omitted it from the annual report, and the working papers show the trial report reached the company on 8 August 2025. On 2 March 2026 a journalist friend asks him at a private dinner whether Kaaveri's pipeline is 'as strong as it claims'. On 4 March 2026 he receives a letter from a regulatory body seeking the trial-related audit documentation for the purposes of an investigation already commenced. On 10 March 2026 the Institute writes to him seeking the same working papers for a Peer Review. Rao proposes to answer the journalist in general terms without naming the company, to send the regulator two working papers without recording why he selected those two, and to refuse the Institute because he regards Peer Review as optional; he has not satisfied himself that every fact he intends to describe is substantiated.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate course in dealing with the journalist's enquiry?
options: Decline to answer, because the enquiry falls within none of the situations the Code recognises, that is, required by law, permitted by law and authorised by the client, or a professional duty or right to disclose.
Answer in general terms, because a communication that does not name the client cannot amount to a disclosure of information acquired through the professional relationship.
Answer, because the limb permitting disclosure to comply with technical and professional standards extends to correcting a wrong impression held by the market about an audited entity.
Answer, because the limb permitting disclosure to protect his own interest in legal proceedings is engaged by the risk that the journalist will publish an adverse story about him.
questions.explanation: Confidentiality covers information acquired as a result of professional and employment relationships, and the Code permits or requires disclosure only in three situations. A journalist's dinner-time question is not required by law, is not permitted by law and authorised by Kaaveri, and is not within the four illustrations of a professional duty or right to disclose, which are Peer or Quality Review of ICAI, an inquiry or investigation by a regulatory body, protecting his own interest in legal proceedings and complying with technical and professional standards. Option 2 is wrong because removing the client's name does not change the nature of the information; the pipeline failure is precisely what the audit brought to his knowledge. Option 3 misreads the technical and professional standards limb, which concerns the accountant's own compliance with such standards and not the correction of market impressions about a client. Option 4 is wrong because the legal-proceedings limb presupposes proceedings in which he protects his own interest, not a threatened adverse story about the client, and in any event Rao has not satisfied himself that the facts he would repeat are known and substantiated.

questions.question:
Case: Suresh Rao, a chartered accountant in practice at Bengaluru, is the statutory auditor of Kaaveri Pharmaceuticals Limited for the year ended 31 March 2026. From the company's contract research notes he learns that a drug candidate representing 62% of the projected pipeline value has failed its safety trial; management has not recorded the fact, has not placed it before the board's risk committee and has omitted it from the annual report, and the working papers show the trial report reached the company on 8 August 2025. On 2 March 2026 a journalist friend asks him at a private dinner whether Kaaveri's pipeline is 'as strong as it claims'. On 4 March 2026 he receives a letter from a regulatory body seeking the trial-related audit documentation for the purposes of an investigation already commenced. On 10 March 2026 the Institute writes to him seeking the same working papers for a Peer Review. Rao proposes to answer the journalist in general terms without naming the company, to send the regulator two working papers without recording why he selected those two, and to refuse the Institute because he regards Peer Review as optional; he has not satisfied himself that every fact he intends to describe is substantiated.

Assume instead that on 4 March 2026 Kaaveri's board passed a resolution authorising Rao in writing to discuss the pipeline with named industry analysts, and that a specific provision of law permits such a discussion. Which of the following is correct?
options: It becomes a disclosure required by law, because a duly passed board resolution operates for the same purpose as an obligation imposed by statute on the accountant.
Client authorisation by itself is sufficient, the Code not requiring in addition that the disclosure be permitted by law rather than merely not prohibited.

It falls within disclosure permitted by law and authorised by the client, which is distinct from disclosure required by law, and the three points to be considered before deciding whether to disclose still apply.
It becomes a disclosure under the professional duty to comply with technical and professional standards, the client's authorisation being irrelevant to that limb of the Code.
questions.explanation: The second situation in the Code is compound, requiring both that the disclosure be permitted by law and that it be authorised by the client or the employing organisation; both limbs are now satisfied, so the disclosure falls within that situation. It is not disclosure required by law, which is the first situation and operates where the law compels the disclosure irrespective of the client's wishes, so option 1 conflates the two. Option 2 removes the conjunctive element and is therefore wrong, as a client cannot authorise what the law does not permit. Option 3 is not applicable because the technical and professional standards limb is a separate head of professional duty or right to disclose and is not the route opened up by a board resolution. The pre-disclosure considerations, whether all relevant information is known and substantiated, the proposed type of communication and to whom it is addressed, and whether the recipients are appropriate, are directed to the decision whether to disclose in any case and are not displaced by the client's authority, though the named analysts now make the recipient test easier to satisfy.

questions.question:
Case: Rekha Joshi, a chartered accountant in practice at Nagpur, is engaged by Bharat Spintex Limited to certify a statement of export turnover of ₹ 96.40 crore for a government incentive scheme. On 17 March 2026 she notices that Annexure II has been compiled by the company's export clerk by lifting figures from a shipping status report prepared for internal purposes, that three invoices of ₹ 4.10 crore each appear twice, and that the summary omits the freight and insurance columns required by the scheme's format. She tells the CFO the same day that the annexure 'looks sloppy' and, on 18 March 2026, issues the certificate in the prescribed proforma, which admits of no qualification or other modification, without the annexure having been corrected. She records her observations in the engagement file and adds a note to the client that the figures 'may require revision'. Her engagement letter dated 4 February 2026 fixes a fee of ₹ 1.10 lakh and requires the certificate by 20 March 2026.

Which of the following statements about the position under integrity are NOT correct?

1. The certificate as issued associates Rekha with information she believes was provided negligently, with a materially false figure arising from the duplication, and with the omission of information required by the format.
2. Because the prescribed proforma admits of no modification, the modified-report relief is unavailable and she had instead to take steps to be disassociated from the information.
3. Her file note recording the observations brings her within the relief of providing a modified report.
4. The three grounds cannot co-exist in a single document, so only the duplication ground is attracted.
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is a correct application: lifting figures from an internal-use report is information provided negligently, the duplicated ₹ 12.30 crore makes the turnover overstated and so materially false, and the missing freight and insurance columns are omitted required information. Statement 2 is also correct, since the Code excuses the accountant where he provides a modified report in respect of the matter and, where that route is closed by the prescribed form, the remaining obligation is to take steps to be disassociated from the information, which a covering note to the client saying the figures 'may require revision' does not achieve. Statement 3 is not correct because a file note is neither a modified report nor a disassociation. Statement 4 is not correct because the three grounds are separate and cumulative descriptions of the information, not mutually exclusive categories, and any one of them suffices.

questions.question:
Case: Rekha Joshi, a chartered accountant in practice at Nagpur, is engaged by Bharat Spintex Limited to certify a statement of export turnover of ₹ 96.40 crore for a government incentive scheme. On 17 March 2026 she notices that Annexure II has been compiled by the company's export clerk by lifting figures from a shipping status report prepared for internal purposes, that three invoices of ₹ 4.10 crore each appear twice, and that the summary omits the freight and insurance columns required by the scheme's format. She tells the CFO the same day that the annexure 'looks sloppy' and, on 18 March 2026, issues the certificate in the prescribed proforma, which admits of no qualification or other modification, without the annexure having been corrected. She records her observations in the engagement file and adds a note to the client that the figures 'may require revision'. Her engagement letter dated 4 February 2026 fixes a fee of ₹ 1.10 lakh and requires the certificate by 20 March 2026.

Which one of the following was the most appropriate course open to Rekha on 17 March 2026?
options: Have the annexure corrected and re-verified before she certifies it, and if that is refused, decline to issue the certificate and take steps to be disassociated from the statement.
Issue the certificate with her file note and the covering letter to the client, since a letter saying the figures 'may require revision' is a modified report in substance.
Issue the certificate and then write to the incentive department, since disclosure to protect his own interest in legal proceedings permits correcting the record with the authority.

Issue the certificate unmodified, because integrity is attracted only where the accountant believes the information contains a materially false or misleading statement and the duplicated amount is a small fraction of the ₹ 96.40 crore certified.
questions.explanation: Integrity bars knowing association with information believed to be materially false, negligently provided or omitting required information; the first remedy is to have the defect cured so that the information ceases to be objectionable. If the client refuses, the modified-report relief cannot be used because the prescribed proforma admits of no qualification or modification, so the only route left by the Code is to take steps to be disassociated from that information, in practice by not issuing the certificate. Option 2 treats an unqualified external document and an internal file note as equivalent to a modified report, which they are not. Option 3 borrows a confidentiality limb that presupposes legal proceedings in which he protects his own interest, and it does not cure the association that has already arisen. Option 4 is the most tempting error, since material falsity is only one of the three grounds; compilation lifted from an internal status report engages the negligent-provision ground and the absent freight and insurance columns engage the omission ground, neither of which depends on the size of the duplication.

questions.question:
Case: Vikram Sethi & Co., a two-partner chartered accountants' firm in Kolkata, opened a second office on 1 January 2026. Its launch brochure states that the firm is 'the only firm in Eastern India to have delivered a zero-qualification audit report for fourteen consecutive years to a listed company', a claim founded on the record of one partner at a firm he left in 2011. The brochure also carries a paragraph noting that 'several competitors have been issued show-cause notices by the Institute', without naming them, and a coupon allowing 15% off audit fees to students enrolled at a coaching centre run by one partner's wife. Separately, in an interview carried by a trade monthly on 20 January 2026, Vikram Sethi said his firm 'outperforms the Big Four on every parameter that matters to a mid-cap board'. The brochure was printed in December 2025 and the firm's fee income for the year is ₹ 3.4 crore of which ₹ 2.1 crore is audit fee.

Which of the following observations on the professional behaviour principle are correct?

1. The fourteen-year claim is an exaggerated claim as to services, qualifications or experience, since the record belongs to a firm the partner left in 2011 and is presented as the firm's own.
2. The paragraph about show-cause notices is unobjectionable because the statements are verifiable and no competitor is named.
3. The trade monthly remark is objectionable as a disparaging reference or an unsubstantiated comparison with the work of others.
4. The fee-discount coupon is not a professional behaviour matter, because it concerns price and not publicity.
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: an accountant must be honest and truthful and must not make exaggerated claims for services, qualifications or experience, and attributing another firm's fourteen-year record to the present firm, in a superlative form, is such a claim. Statement 3 is correct, since the Code bars disparaging references or unsubstantiated comparisons to the work of others, and 'outperforms the Big Four on every parameter' is both disparaging and unsupported. Statement 2 is wrong because the objection to a disparaging reference or an unsubstantiated comparison does not depend on naming the competitor, and verifiability of the fact asserted does not make the comparison substantiated as to the work of others. Statement 4 is wrong because the Code catches any direct or indirect measures to advertise in violation of the Advertisement Guidelines, and a discount coupon distributed to a defined audience through a brochure is an indirect device for publicity and not merely a price decision. The printing date and the ₹ 3.4 crore fee split are the facts that do not bear on the analysis.

Case: Vikram Sethi & Co., a two-partner chartered accountants' firm in Kolkata, opened a second office on 1 January 2026. Its launch brochure states that the firm is 'the only firm in Eastern India to have delivered a zero-qualification audit report for fourteen consecutive years to a listed company', a claim founded on the record of one partner at a firm he left in 2011. The brochure also carries a paragraph noting that 'several competitors have been issued show-cause notices by the Institute', without naming them, and a coupon allowing 15% off audit fees to students enrolled at a coaching centre run by one partner's wife. Separately, in an interview carried by a trade monthly on 20 January 2026, Vikram Sethi said his firm 'outperforms the Big Four on every parameter that matters to a mid-cap board'. The brochure was printed in December 2025 and the firm's fee income for the year is ₹ 3.4 crore of which ₹ 2.1 crore is audit fee.

The offending paragraph was drafted by an assistant and was released without any partner reading it. Which one of the following states an additional limb of the fundamental principles separately engaged, and the reason for it?
options: Confidentiality, because the assistant had access to information about the other firms acquired in the course of professional and employment relationships.

Professional competence and due care, because a member must take reasonable steps to see that those working under his authority have appropriate training and supervision, and the draft went out unreviewed.
Objectivity, because releasing a draft written by a subordinate is itself an instance of the undue influence of others on the accountant's professional judgment.
Integrity, because a document prepared by a person working under his authority is information with which the member is deemed to be knowingly associated.
questions.explanation: The principle of professional competence and due care carries a distinct duty to take reasonable steps to ensure that those working under the accountant's authority have appropriate training and supervision; releasing an assistant's externally circulated draft without reading it is a failure of supervision quite apart from the professional behaviour breach the paragraph itself causes. Option 2 is not engaged on these facts, since nothing shows the assistant using client information for another client, and the paragraph refers to nothing personal or confidential. Option 3 misapplies objectivity, which concerns bias, conflict of interest or undue influence of others corrupting the accountant's judgment, and not a failure to check a subordinate's work. Option 4 states a deeming rule that integrity does not contain; the integrity bar operates where the accountant knowingly associates himself with information he believes to be materially false, negligently provided or omitting required information, and on the stated facts he had not read the draft and so held no such belief. The decisive fact is the complete absence of review, not the content of the draft.

questions.question:
Consider the following four situations, each involving an act contrary to a prevailing law or regulation, which come to the notice of a professional accountant:
(i) The Finance Manager of the audit client omits to withhold tax at the notified rate on professional fees paid to consultants, the omission arising from inadvertence rather than from design.
(ii) A non-executive director on the board of the professional accountant's employing organisation supports a decision to retain customer data beyond the period permitted by the data protection law.
(iii) A store clerk employed by the audit client falsifies consignment notes so that a statutory transport levy is not paid.
(iv) The principal supplier of the audit client, a separate business, fails to deduct tax at source on salaries payable to its own workers.
In which of the above does the non-compliance fall within the meaning of non-compliance with laws and regulations as addressed by NOCLAR?
questions.explanation: NOCLAR means acts of omission or commission, intentional or unintentional, contrary to prevailing laws or regulations, committed by the client or the professional accountant's employing organisation, by the TCWG of either, by the management of either, or by other individuals working for either. In (i) the Finance Manager is management of the client and the act is an omission; inadvertence is irrelevant because unintentional acts are expressly included. In (ii) the non-executive director forms part of the TCWG of the employing organisation, and in (iii) the store clerk is an individual working for the client. (iv) falls outside, because the supplier is a party other than those listed in the definition of NOCLAR, and non-compliance by such other parties is not addressed. Note that the data protection and tax fields mentioned in (i), (ii) and (iv) are all within the illustrative examples, so the subject matter of the law is not what excludes (iv).

questions.question: CA Anuja Sawant is a member of the Institute and is the Financial Controller of Vikram Metals Limited, a listed entity in India; she is key managerial personnel of the company. In the course of her work she learns of the following four matters. Which one of these is NOT excluded from the scope of NOCLAR, so that she must respond to it under the NOCLAR framework?
options: The Chief Executive Officer has, in his personal capacity and wholly unconnected with the company's business, raised an extra floor on his residence without the permission that the municipal bye-laws require.
The company's principal customer, a separate listed company, has failed to deduct tax at source on salaries payable to its own employees.
The personnel function of the company has, for the last six months, failed to deposit ₹ 1.85 crores of provident fund contributions deducted from employees' salaries.
Two trustees of a family settlement of the Chief Executive Officer have not obtained the registration required of that settlement under the State trusts Act.
questions.explanation: NOCLAR excludes two categories: personal misconduct unrelated to the business of the client or of the professional accountant's employing organisation, and non-compliance by parties other than those listed in its definition. Non-payment of provident fund contributions already deducted from employees' salaries is non-compliance by Anuja's own employing organisation, it is expressly within the illustrative example of tax and pension liabilities and payments, and it harms employees, who are among the persons whose interests NOCLAR addresses; it is therefore not excluded. The CEO's residential construction is by a member of management but is personal misconduct unrelated to the company's business, so the exclusion applies despite the identity of the wrongdoer. The customer's default is the default of a party outside the listed persons, and the trustees' default concerns a private family settlement, so both are excluded. Anuja, being a senior professional accountant in service who is key managerial personnel and an employee of a listed entity, is within the applicability of the responding framework, which prescribes no net worth condition for accountants in service.

questions.question:
Match the following situations noticed in a professional accountant's files with the illustrative category of non-compliance expressly listed under NOCLAR:
Column I
(A) A client has failed to remit tax deducted at source on consultant fees for eleven months.
(B) A client's plant has continued production although its air emission authorisation stands lapsed.
(C) A client has routed ₹ 90 lakhs through layering entities to disguise its criminal origin.
(D) A client's officer has traded in the company's shares on unpublished price sensitive information.
Column II
(1) Money laundering, terrorist financing and proceeds of crime
(2) Securities markets and trading
(3) Environmental protection
(4) Tax and pension liabilities and payments
Select the correct option:
questions.explanation: Non-remittance of tax deducted at source is a failure in respect of tax liabilities and payments, so A pairs with 4, which already eliminates the two options that pair A with 1. Continued operation on a lapsed air emission authorisation is environmental harm, so B pairs with 3, and layering to disguise the criminal origin of money is money laundering and proceeds of crime, so C pairs with 1. Trading by an officer on unpublished price sensitive information is a matter of securities markets and trading, so D pairs with 2. The pairing turns on the nature of the regulated interest breached and not on the department that committed the act, which is why the swapped pairings are wrong. The listed examples additionally cover fraud, corruption and bribery and public health and safety, neither of which appears above.

questions.question:
Vardhman Synthetics Limited (VSL), a listed entity in India, has a net worth of ₹ 412 crores as at 31 March 2025. M/s Kalyani & Associates is the statutory auditor of VSL for the year ended 31 March 2025. During the audit, the engagement partner CA Kalyani Menon finds that Mr. Rakesh Bhandari, Head of Compliance at VSL, has authorised payments of ₹ 3.20 crores to two overseas agents so that VSL's Panaji plant keeps operating without renewal of its consent to establish, and that untreated effluent from the plant has already contaminated the drinking-water sources of three nearby villages. The Whole-Time Director (Finance) tells CA Menon that nothing needs to be reported because the ₹ 3.20 crores has been recorded in the books and is not material to the financial statements. The environmental regulator is due to inspect the plant on 15 April 2025 and a prosecution expected to result in closure of the plant will follow immediately after the inspection. VSL's previous auditor resigned in July 2024 citing ill health and an unpaid fee dispute, and the Chief Operating Officer was convicted in 2019 of an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with imprisonment but was subsequently granted a pardon. CA Menon has completed obtaining an understanding of the matter and has addressed the matter with management and those charged with governance of VSL, without result.

Consider the following statements:
(i) The NOCLAR responding framework applies to M/s Kalyani & Associates because the assignment is an audit engagement of a listed entity in India whose net worth is ₹ 250 crores or more.
(ii) The framework is not available because the harm is to villagers and to the environment rather than to the financial statements, and the amount stands recorded in the books.
(iii) Both the payments to the overseas agents to keep the plant running without consent and the discharge of untreated effluent fall within the illustrative matters covered by NOCLAR.
(iv) Mr. Bhandari's conduct cannot be treated as NOCLAR because he is only an employee of VSL and not the client, its management or those charged with governance.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: For a professional accountant in practice, responding to NOCLAR in India is applicable to audit engagements of listed entities in India having net worth of ₹ 250 crores or more, and VSL's ₹ 412 crores satisfies that condition, so (i) is correct. (ii) fails because NOCLAR covers non-compliance that causes substantial harm in financial or non-financial terms; accounting or immateriality defences do not take the matter outside its scope, which is precisely where it differs from SA 250's concern with laws having a direct effect on the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. (iii) is correct because fraud, corruption and bribery, environmental protection and public health and safety are all expressly among the examples covered by NOCLAR. (iv) is wrong because the definition extends to acts of commission by other individuals working for the client, and the Head of Compliance is such an individual. The COO's pardoned conviction and the previous auditor's resignation are irrelevant to the applicability of NOCLAR to this engagement.

questions.question:
Vardhman Synthetics Limited (VSL), a listed entity in India, has a net worth of ₹ 412 crores as at 31 March 2025. M/s Kalyani & Associates is the statutory auditor of VSL for the year ended 31 March 2025. During the audit, the engagement partner CA Kalyani Menon finds that Mr. Rakesh Bhandari, Head of Compliance at VSL, has authorised payments of ₹ 3.20 crores to two overseas agents so that VSL's Panaji plant keeps operating without renewal of its consent to establish, and that untreated effluent from the plant has already contaminated the drinking-water sources of three nearby villages. The Whole-Time Director (Finance) tells CA Menon that nothing needs to be reported because the ₹ 3.20 crores has been recorded in the books and is not material to the financial statements. The environmental regulator is due to inspect the plant on 15 April 2025 and a prosecution expected to result in closure of the plant will follow immediately after the inspection. VSL's previous auditor resigned in July 2024 citing ill health and an unpaid fee dispute, and the Chief Operating Officer was convicted in 2019 of an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with imprisonment but was subsequently granted a pardon. CA Menon has completed obtaining an understanding of the matter and has addressed the matter with management and those charged with governance of VSL, without result.

Two of the seven prescribed steps stand completed on these facts, and the last of them is not yet reached. Which of the following correctly sets out the remaining steps for responding to NOCLAR, in the order in which they are to be taken?
options: Determining whether further action is needed, then seeking advice, then imminent breach, then documentation, then determining whether to disclose the matter to an Appropriate Authority.
Seeking advice, then imminent breach, then documentation, then determining whether further action is needed, then determining whether to disclose the matter to an Appropriate Authority.
Imminent breach, then seeking advice, then determining whether further action is needed, then documentation, then determining whether to disclose the matter to an Appropriate Authority.
Seeking advice, then determining whether further action is needed, then imminent breach, then determining whether to disclose the matter to an Appropriate Authority, then documentation.
questions.explanation: The prescribed order is: obtaining an understanding of the matter, addressing the matter, seeking advice, determining whether further action is needed, imminent breach, determining whether to disclose the matter to an Appropriate Authority, and documentation. Since the first two steps are complete, the next step is seeking advice, and documentation is the terminal step because the accountant can only document a course of action once the decisions on further action and disclosure have been reached. Option placing documentation before the disclosure decision is therefore wrong, as is any option that treats determining whether further action is needed as preceding seeking advice. The imminent breach consideration is a distinct intermediate step that sits after determining whether further action is needed and before the disclosure decision, not at the start of the sequence. The order matters here because CA Menon cannot reach the disclosure decision on the 15 April 2025 inspection without first having determined whether further action is needed.

questions.question:
Vardhman Synthetics Limited (VSL), a listed entity in India, has a net worth of ₹ 412 crores as at 31 March 2025. M/s Kalyani & Associates is the statutory auditor of VSL for the year ended 31 March 2025. During the audit, the engagement partner CA Kalyani Menon finds that Mr. Rakesh Bhandari, Head of Compliance at VSL, has authorised payments of ₹ 3.20 crores to two overseas agents so that VSL's Panaji plant keeps operating without renewal of its consent to establish, and that untreated effluent from the plant has already contaminated the drinking-water sources of three nearby villages. The Whole-Time Director (Finance) tells CA Menon that nothing needs to be reported because the ₹ 3.20 crores has been recorded in the books and is not material to the financial statements. The environmental regulator is due to inspect the plant on 15 April 2025 and a prosecution expected to result in closure of the plant will follow immediately after the inspection. VSL's previous auditor resigned in July 2024 citing ill health and an unpaid fee dispute, and the Chief Operating Officer was convicted in 2019 of an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with imprisonment but was subsequently granted a pardon. CA Menon has completed obtaining an understanding of the matter and has addressed the matter with management and those charged with governance of VSL, without result.

Having regard to the regulator's inspection scheduled for 15 April 2025 and the prosecution expected to follow, which of the following is the MOST appropriate action for CA Menon?
options: Wait for the regulator's inspection on 15 April 2025 to conclude and then consider further action, because the consequences of the breach, including the prosecution and the closure of the plant, will crystallise only after the inspection has been completed.

Qualify the audit report for the year ended 31 March 2025 in respect of the recorded amount and take no other step, because communication to those charged with governance and a reporting outcome together discharge the whole of the auditor's responsibility.

Determine whether the breach is imminent and, if so, whether it should be disclosed immediately to the Appropriate Authority to prevent or mitigate its consequences, and document the course of action considered and the judgements and decisions taken.

Resign from the audit of VSL and decline to act further, because no step remains available to the accountant once management and those charged with governance have refused to act on the matter put before them, and disassociation is the only remedy left to him.
questions.explanation: Where the professional accountant becomes aware of an imminent breach of a law or regulation, he is required to determine whether to disclose it immediately to the Appropriate Authority so as to prevent or mitigate the consequences of that imminent breach. The scheduled inspection and the prosecution that will follow, which is expected to shut down the plant, are the facts that make the breach imminent and that give the disclosure its point, since disclosure after the inspection would achieve nothing that the framework contemplates. Waiting for the inspection misreads the requirement, which is directed at a breach that has not yet run its course. Reporting through the audit report alone is insufficient, because SA 250 contains no provision for imminent breach and addresses only the audit, whereas NOCLAR addresses the effect of the non-compliance on investors, creditors, employees and the general public, which here means the villagers. Resignation is not the response prescribed at this step; determining whether to disclose to the Appropriate Authority is, and the judgements and decisions must then be documented.

questions.question:
Vardhman Synthetics Limited (VSL), a listed entity in India, has a net worth of ₹ 412 crores as at 31 March 2025. M/s Kalyani & Associates is the statutory auditor of VSL for the year ended 31 March 2025. During the audit, the engagement partner CA Kalyani Menon finds that Mr. Rakesh Bhandari, Head of Compliance at VSL, has authorised payments of ₹ 3.20 crores to two overseas agents so that VSL's Panaji plant keeps operating without renewal of its consent to establish, and that untreated effluent from the plant has already contaminated the drinking-water sources of three nearby villages. The Whole-Time Director (Finance) tells CA Menon that nothing needs to be reported because the ₹ 3.20 crores has been recorded in the books and is not material to the financial statements. The environmental regulator is due to inspect the plant on 15 April 2025 and a prosecution expected to result in closure of the plant will follow immediately after the inspection. VSL's previous auditor resigned in July 2024 citing ill health and an unpaid fee dispute, and the Chief Operating Officer was convicted in 2019 of an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with imprisonment but was subsequently granted a pardon. CA Menon has completed obtaining an understanding of the matter and has addressed the matter with management and those charged with governance of VSL, without result.

Which of the following must CA Menon bring into her documentation under the documentation requirements of NOCLAR?
(i) How management and those charged with governance of VSL have responded to the matter.
(ii) The course of action considered by CA Menon, the judgements made and the decisions taken.
(iii) How CA Menon is satisfied that the responsibility of public interest has been fulfilled.
(iv) The reasons for the resignation of VSL's previous auditor in July 2024.
questions.explanation: The documentation prescribed for NOCLAR comprises three matters: how management or those charged with governance have responded to the matter, the course of action considered by the accountant together with the judgements made and decisions taken, and how the accountant is satisfied that the responsibility of public interest has been fulfilled. Items (i), (ii) and (iii) correspond exactly to those three, and the third is particularly pointed on these facts because the public interested in the effluent contamination is the villagers as part of the general public. (iv) is not a NOCLAR documentation item; the previous auditor's resignation over ill health and a fee dispute is unconnected with the non-compliance and does not become examinable merely because it appears in the file. This documentation is additional to, and not a substitute for, the documentation requirements under the Standards on Auditing, so complying with SA documentation would not by itself discharge the NOCLAR requirement.

The environmental regulator is due to inspect the plant on 15 April 2025 and a prosecution expected to result in closure of the plant will follow immediately after the inspection. VSL's previous auditor resigned in July 2024 citing ill health and an unpaid fee dispute, and the Chief Operating Officer was convicted in 2019 of an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with imprisonment but was subsequently granted a pardon. CA Menon has completed obtaining an understanding of the matter and has addressed the matter with management and those charged with governance of VSL, without result.

Assume instead that VSL's net worth as at 31 March 2025 is ₹ 249 crores, its shares continuing to be listed and every other fact remaining unchanged. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
options: The NOCLAR responding framework ceases to apply to the audit engagement, because for a professional accountant in practice it is attracted only where the listed entity has a net worth of ₹ 250 crores or more.
The framework continues to apply, because the ₹ 250 crore condition is tested at the date of the auditor's appointment and VSL's net worth exceeded ₹ 250 crores on that date.
The framework continues to apply, because the harm threatened is non-financial, and the net worth condition is not required to be satisfied where the harm is non-financial.

The framework ceases to apply to the audit engagement, and in consequence M/s Kalyani & Associates is also relieved of its responsibilities under SA 250 for laws having a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures in the financial statements.
questions.explanation: The applicability of responding to NOCLAR in India for professional accountants in practice is expressed by reference to audit engagements of listed entities in India having net worth of ₹ 250 crores or more, so a net worth of ₹ 249 crores falls short of the condition by one crore and the framework is not attracted. The condition is a stated monetary threshold and the framework does not create an exception where the threatened harm is non-financial, even though NOCLAR's coverage of non-compliance extends to substantial harm in financial or non-financial terms; coverage and applicability are different questions. Nor does the framework turn on the date of appointment of the auditor, which is a reading the threshold language does not support. Finally, the two regimes operate independently, so failing the NOCLAR applicability condition leaves SA 250 untouched on an audit. The decisive fact is therefore the net worth figure alone, since listing, the audit nature of the engagement and the identity of the wrongdoer are all unchanged.

questions.question:
Meera Iyer, aged 19 years, passed all groups of the CA Final examination in April 2025 and seeks entry of her name in the Register of Members of the Institute; her father is a Fellow Member.
