Arvind Nair, aged 44 years, was adjudged an insolvent in January 2021 and was discharged by the court in November 2024, and he has neither applied for nor obtained any certificate from the court as to the cause of his insolvency; he seeks entry in the Register in July 2025. Deep Chauhan, aged 38 years, was convicted by a competent Court in 2019 of an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with imprisonment; he has served the sentence and committed no further offence, he has not been granted a pardon and the Central Government has not removed the disability; he seeks entry in the Register. Fatima Qureshi has been an Associate Member since 2010; she was in continuous practice in India from 2010 to 2013, was employed in Dubai from 2013 to 2019, and has been in continuous practice in India again from 2019 to 2025; she applies for transfer to the Fellowship and relies only on the length of her practice. Har Gobind, an Associate Member, has not paid the prescribed membership fee for three consecutive years, his name has been removed from the Register, and he now seeks restoration. Nandita Bose is an Associate Member who does not hold a certificate of practice but represents to clients that she is in practice; she was convicted of this for the first time in March 2025. J. S. Kulkarni is not a member of the Institute but prints visiting cards describing himself as 'J. S. Kulkarni, CA - Business Advisor'; he was convicted on the first occasion in 2022 and has now been convicted again in 2025 for the same conduct.

Consider the following statements:
(i) Meera cannot have her name entered in the Register, because she has not attained the age of 21 years, and her father's Fellowship is beside the point.
(ii) Arvind cannot have his name entered in the Register, because being a discharged insolvent he has not obtained a certificate from the court that his insolvency was caused by misfortune without any misconduct on his part.
(iii) Deep cannot have his name entered in the Register, because the conviction attracts the disability unless a pardon has been granted or the Central Government has removed the disability, and service of the sentence achieves neither.
(iv) Meera can have her name entered in the Register, because she has passed the CA Final examination and the age condition is tested when the Council decides her application and not when she applies.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A person is debarred from having his name entered in the Register of Members if he has not attained the age of 21 years, if he is of unsound mind, if he is an undischarged insolvent, if he is a discharged insolvent without the required court certificate, or if he has been convicted by a competent Court of an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with transportation or imprisonment unless pardoned or the disability has been removed by the Central Government. Meera at 19 fails the age condition, and descent from a Fellow Member is not a ground of eligibility or of exception, so (i) is correct and (iv) is wrong because it invents a date-of-decision test that the disability provision does not contain. Arvind is a discharged insolvent and the disability for a discharged insolvent bites precisely because he has not obtained the certificate stating that the insolvency was caused by misfortune without any misconduct on his part, so (ii) is correct; discharge by itself does not remove it. Deep's conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with imprisonment engages the fifth disability, and the only two exits are a pardon or removal of the disability by the Central Government, neither of which he has, so (iii) is correct. Serving the sentence and subsequent good conduct are not among those exits.

questions.question:
Meera Iyer, aged 19 years, passed all groups of the CA Final examination in April 2025 and seeks entry of her name in the Register of Members of the Institute; her father is a Fellow Member. Arvind Nair, aged 44 years, was adjudged an insolvent in January 2021 and was discharged by the court in November 2024, and he has neither applied for nor obtained any certificate from the court as to the cause of his insolvency; he seeks entry in the Register in July 2025. Deep Chauhan, aged 38 years, was convicted by a competent Court in 2019 of an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with imprisonment; he has served the sentence and committed no further offence, he has not been granted a pardon and the Central Government has not removed the disability; he seeks entry in the Register. Fatima Qureshi has been an Associate Member since 2010; she was in continuous practice in India from 2010 to 2013, was employed in Dubai from 2013 to 2019, and has been in continuous practice in India again from 2019 to 2025; she applies for transfer to the Fellowship and relies only on the length of her practice. Har Gobind, an Associate Member, has not paid the prescribed membership fee for three consecutive years, his name has been removed from the Register, and he now seeks restoration. Nandita Bose is an Associate Member who does not hold a certificate of practice but represents to clients that she is in practice; she was convicted of this for the first time in March 2025. J. S. Kulkarni is not a member of the Institute but prints visiting cards describing himself as 'J. S. Kulkarni, CA - Business Advisor'; he was convicted on the first occasion in 2022 and has now been convicted again in 2025 for the same conduct.

Which of the following is the MOST appropriate conclusion on Fatima Qureshi's application for transfer to the Fellowship?
options: She is not eligible, because the 2010 to 2013 and 2019 to 2025 stretches of practice in India are separated by her Dubai employment and cannot be aggregated into a continuous period.
She is not eligible, because the Fellowship requires an Associate Member to possess qualifications equivalent to five years of continuous practice in addition to having practised for that period.
She is eligible, because the practice from 2019 to 2025 is itself a period of at least five years of continuous practice in India, and no aggregation with the earlier stretch is needed.
She is not eligible, because only an Associate Member in continuous practice in India for five years immediately preceding the application may be designated a Fellow Member.
questions.explanation: A Fellow Member is an Associate member who has been in continuous practice in India for at least five years, or an Associate member who possesses qualifications equivalent to five years of continuous practice, the two limbs being alternatives. Fatima's practice from 2019 to 2025 is six continuous years of practice in India and therefore satisfies the first limb on its own, which is why the interruption caused by her 2013 to 2019 Dubai employment and the length of her Associate membership since 2010 are both immaterial. The first option is wrong because it assumes that the five years must be built up by aggregating the two stretches; nothing turns on the 2010 to 2013 period once a single continuous stretch of five years in India exists. The second option is wrong because it converts the alternative equivalence limb into an additional requirement. The fourth option adds an immediacy condition, requiring practice to be current up to the date of application, which the Fellowship condition does not impose.

questions.question:
Meera Iyer, aged 19 years, passed all groups of the CA Final examination in April 2025 and seeks entry of her name in the Register of Members of the Institute; her father is a Fellow Member. Arvind Nair, aged 44 years, was adjudged an insolvent in January 2021 and was discharged by the court in November 2024, and he has neither applied for nor obtained any certificate from the court as to the cause of his insolvency; he seeks entry in the Register in July 2025. Deep Chauhan, aged 38 years, was convicted by a competent Court in 2019 of an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with imprisonment; he has served the sentence and committed no further offence, he has not been granted a pardon and the Central Government has not removed the disability; he seeks entry in the Register. Fatima Qureshi has been an Associate Member since 2010; she was in continuous practice in India from 2010 to 2013, was employed in Dubai from 2013 to 2019, and has been in continuous practice in India again from 2019 to 2025; she applies for transfer to the Fellowship and relies only on the length of her practice. Har Gobind, an Associate Member, has not paid the prescribed membership fee for three consecutive years, his name has been removed from the Register, and he now seeks restoration. Nandita Bose is an Associate Member who does not hold a certificate of practice but represents to clients that she is in practice; she was convicted of this for the first time in March 2025. J. S. Kulkarni is not a member of the Institute but prints visiting cards describing himself as 'J. S. Kulkarni, CA - Business Advisor'; he was convicted on the first occasion in 2022 and has now been convicted again in 2025 for the same conduct.

Match the situations in Column I with the consequences in Column II:
Column I
(A) Har Gobind seeks to have his name entered again in the Register.
(B) An Associate Member's name was removed after the Disciplinary Committee so ordered.
(C) The Council strikes off a member who, since his admission, has been found to be of unsound mind.
(D) The Council strikes off a member who had intimated in writing that he did not wish to continue as a member.
Column II
(1) Restoration is to be only in accordance with the order concerned.
(2) Name may be entered again on payment of the arrears of fee along with additional fee.
(3) Removal is open to the Council because the member is from whom a request has been received to that effect.
(4) Removal is open to the Council because the member is found to have one of the disabilities for the purpose of membership.
Select the correct option:
questions.explanation: Har Gobind's name was removed for non-payment of the prescribed fee, and in that case alone the name may be entered again on payment of the arrears of fee along with additional fee, so A pairs with 2. Where removal is due to the orders of the Board of Discipline, the Disciplinary Committee, the Appellate Authority or the High Court, restoration shall be only in accordance with those orders, so B pairs with 1 and not with the arrears-and-additional-fee route, which presupposes a fee default. Unsound mind is one of the five disabilities for the purpose of membership, and the Council may remove a name where a member is found to have any of those disabilities, so C pairs with 4. A member who has intimated that he does not wish to continue is a member from whom a request has been received to that effect, which is the second removal case, so D pairs with 3. The pairings that assign the fee-based restoration to the disciplinary removal are the ones that ignore which removal ground was operative.

questions.question:
Meera Iyer, aged 19 years, passed all groups of the CA Final examination in April 2025 and seeks entry of her name in the Register of Members of the Institute; her father is a Fellow Member. Arvind Nair, aged 44 years, was adjudged an insolvent in January 2021 and was discharged by the court in November 2024, and he has neither applied for nor obtained any certificate from the court as to the cause of his insolvency; he seeks entry in the Register in July 2025. Deep Chauhan, aged 38 years, was convicted by a competent Court in 2019 of an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with imprisonment; he has served the sentence and committed no further offence, he has not been granted a pardon and the Central Government has not removed the disability; he seeks entry in the Register. Fatima Qureshi has been an Associate Member since 2010; she was in continuous practice in India from 2010 to 2013, was employed in Dubai from 2013 to 2019, and has been in continuous practice in India again from 2019 to 2025; she applies for transfer to the Fellowship and relies only on the length of her practice. Har Gobind, an Associate Member, has not paid the prescribed membership fee for three consecutive years, his name has been removed from the Register, and he now seeks restoration. Nandita Bose is an Associate Member who does not hold a certificate of practice but represents to clients that she is in practice; she was convicted of this for the first time in March 2025. J. S. Kulkarni is not a member of the Institute but prints visiting cards describing himself as 'J. S. Kulkarni, CA - Business Advisor'; he was convicted on the first occasion in 2022 and has now been convicted again in 2025 for the same conduct.

Consider the following statements:
(i) Nandita Bose, being a member who does not hold a certificate of practice but who has represented that she is in practice, is punishable, and on first conviction she is liable to a fine up to ₹ 1,000.
(ii) J. S. Kulkarni, not being a member, has represented that he is a member and used the designation CA, and his 2025 conviction being a subsequent one, he is liable to imprisonment up to 6 months or a fine up to ₹ 5,000, or to both.
(iii) Kulkarni escapes liability because the description 'Business Advisor' on his visiting card shows that he did not hold himself out exclusively as a chartered accountant.
(iv) Nandita escapes liability because the penalty provision is directed only at persons who are not members of the Institute.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: The penalty provision strikes at two distinct persons: one who, not being a member of the Institute, represents that he is a member or uses the designation CA, and one who, being a member but not holding a certificate of practice, represents that he is in practice. Nandita falls in the second category, so (iv) is wrong, and her March 2025 conviction being her first, the punishment is a fine up to ₹ 1,000, imprisonment not being available on a first conviction. Kulkarni falls in the first category, and because he was convicted on a first occasion in 2022 and again in 2025, the sentence for a subsequent conviction applies, which is imprisonment up to 6 months or fine up to ₹ 5,000, or both. (iii) fails because the offence is complete once a non-member represents that he is a member or uses the designation CA, and adding another description to the card does not withdraw that representation. The decisive facts are membership and certificate of practice on the one hand, and whether the conviction is the first or a subsequent one on the other.

questions.question:
Meera Iyer, aged 19 years, passed all groups of the CA Final examination in April 2025 and seeks entry of her name in the Register of Members of the Institute; her father is a Fellow Member. Arvind Nair, aged 44 years, was adjudged an insolvent in January 2021 and was discharged by the court in November 2024, and he has neither applied for nor obtained any certificate from the court as to the cause of his insolvency; he seeks entry in the Register in July 2025. Deep Chauhan, aged 38 years, was convicted by a competent Court in 2019 of an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with imprisonment; he has served the sentence and committed no further offence, he has not been granted a pardon and the Central Government has not removed the disability; he seeks entry in the Register. Fatima Qureshi has been an Associate Member since 2010; she was in continuous practice in India from 2010 to 2013, was employed in Dubai from 2013 to 2019, and has been in continuous practice in India again from 2019 to 2025; she applies for transfer to the Fellowship and relies only on the length of her practice. Har Gobind, an Associate Member, has not paid the prescribed membership fee for three consecutive years, his name has been removed from the Register, and he now seeks restoration. Nandita Bose is an Associate Member who does not hold a certificate of practice but represents to clients that she is in practice; she was convicted of this for the first time in March 2025. J. S. Kulkarni is not a member of the Institute but prints visiting cards describing himself as 'J. S. Kulkarni, CA - Business Advisor'; he was convicted on the first occasion in 2022 and has now been convicted again in 2025 for the same conduct.

Assume that Arvind Nair obtained in December 2024 a certificate from the court stating that his insolvency was caused by misfortune without any misconduct on his part, and that Deep Chauhan has been granted a pardon. Every other fact remains unchanged. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
options: Neither can have his name entered in the Register, because once insolvency has been adjudged and once a conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude has been recorded, the disabilities flowing from them are permanent and cannot be cured by anything done afterwards.

Arvind is no longer disabled, but Deep continues to be disabled, because the disability arising from such a conviction can be removed only by the Central Government and a pardon is ineffective for the purpose.

Arvind continues to be disabled, because the court certificate contemplated by that disability can be granted only at the time of discharge and not afterwards, while Deep is no longer disabled, because a pardon stands on the same footing as removal of the disability by the Central Government.

So far as these two disabilities are concerned, both may have their names entered in the Register, because the insolvency disability presupposes the absence of the court certificate and the conviction disability does not operate where a pardon has been granted.
questions.explanation: The insolvency disability is framed not against discharge as such but against a discharged insolvent who has not obtained a certificate from the court stating that the insolvency was caused by misfortune without any misconduct on his part; once that certificate is held, the condition of the disability is no longer satisfied. The conviction disability for an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with transportation or imprisonment expressly admits of two alternatives, namely that a pardon has been granted or that the Central Government has removed the disability, so a pardon is as effective for this purpose as action by the Central Government and the second option is wrong for reading the alternative out of the provision. The third option is wrong because it imposes a timing condition on the certificate which the disability does not require, even though its statement about the footing on which a pardon stands is correct. The conclusion is confined to the two disabilities whose operative facts have changed, and no other disability of Arvind or Deep is in issue on these facts.

questions.category: NOCLAR - Applicability to accountants in service
questions.question:
CA Shantanu Vaidya is a member of the Institute and is the Chief Financial Officer of Nadella Bearings Limited, a listed entity in India with a net worth of ₹ 118 crores; he is key managerial personnel of the company and is not in practice. In February 2025 he discovers that a whole-time director of the company, acting in collusion with the Head of its sales division, has been inflating the reported price of the company's shares by routing purchases through six benami accounts belonging to relatives, in defiance of the prohibitions on such dealings, so that the company raised ₹ 260 crores from the market at an inflated price. When CA Vaidya points this out, the director replies that the dealings have nothing to do with the determination of amounts in the financial statements. Separately, CA Vaidya's wife, who runs a textile business in Kolhapur independently of him, has failed to file her GST returns for two quarters.

Consider the following statements:
(i) The requirement to respond to NOCLAR applies to CA Vaidya, because he is a senior professional accountant in service, being key managerial personnel and an employee of a listed entity.
(ii) The manipulation of the share price through the benami accounts is within the illustrative matters covered by NOCLAR, as it concerns securities markets and trading.
(iii) The requirement does not apply to CA Vaidya, because the net worth of his employing organisation is below ₹ 250 crores and he is not engaged in an audit engagement.
(iv) The wife's un-filed GST returns are governed by NOCLAR, because tax and pension liabilities and payments are expressly listed as an example.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: For professional accountants in service, responding to NOCLAR in India is applicable to senior professional accountants in service who are employees of listed entities, and senior professional accountants means key managerial personnel, that is, directors, officers or senior employees; CA Vaidya as Chief Financial Officer and key managerial personnel of a listed entity is within that description, so (i) is correct. (iii) is wrong because the net worth of ₹ 250 crores or more and the audit engagement qualification are the conditions prescribed for professional accountants in practice and are not imported into the case of an accountant in service, which is why the company's ₹ 118 crores of net worth is not decisive. Securities markets and trading is one of the illustrative matters covered by NOCLAR, and the director's observation that the dealings do not affect the financial statements is irrelevant, because NOCLAR covers non-compliance causing substantial harm in financial or non-financial terms. (iv) fails because NOCLAR does not address personal misconduct unrelated to the business of the employing organisation, nor non-compliance by parties other than those listed in its definition, and the wife is neither an employee nor an individual working for the company.

questions.category: NOCLAR - Course of action for accountant in service
questions.question:
CA Shantanu Vaidya is a member of the Institute and is the Chief Financial Officer of Nadella Bearings Limited, a listed entity in India with a net worth of ₹ 118 crores; he is key managerial personnel of the company and is not in practice. In February 2025 he discovers that a whole-time director of the company, acting in collusion with the Head of its sales division, has been inflating the reported price of the company's shares by routing purchases through six benami accounts belonging to relatives, in defiance of the prohibitions on such dealings, so that the company raised ₹ 260 crores from the market at an inflated price. When CA Vaidya points this out, the director replies that the dealings have nothing to do with the determination of amounts in the financial statements. Separately, CA Vaidya's wife, who runs a textile business in Kolhapur independently of him, has failed to file her GST returns for two quarters.

Which of the following combinations of action is fully appropriate for CA Vaidya?
options: Take no further action beyond recording the director's explanation in the file, because the manipulation was carried out by a whole-time director and by the Head of the sales division and not by the company as such, and NOCLAR addresses only the client or the professional accountant's employing organisation.

Obtain an understanding of the matter, address the matter, seek advice, determine whether further action is needed, consider imminent breach and whether to disclose to an Appropriate Authority, and document the course of action considered, the judgements made and the decisions taken, such documentation being in addition to that required under the Standards on Auditing.

Address the matter with those charged with governance, then determine whether further action is needed, then obtain an understanding of the matter, and treat the NOCLAR documentation as replacing the documentation otherwise required under the Standards on Auditing.

Disclose the matter immediately to the market regulator in every case, because the price of the shares of a listed company affects investors, creditors, employees and the general public, and any non-compliance which affects them is for that reason to be treated as an imminent breach attracting immediate disclosure.
questions.explanation: The framework prescribes a sequence, beginning with obtaining an understanding of the matter and addressing it, followed by seeking advice, determining whether further action is needed, considering imminent breach, and determining whether to disclose to an Appropriate Authority, and it closes with documentation of how management or those charged with governance responded, of the course of action considered with the judgements and decisions, and of how the accountant is satisfied that the responsibility of public interest has been fulfilled. That documentation is in addition to the documentation required under the Standards on Auditing, so it neither replaces nor duplicates away the SA requirements. The first option misreads the covered persons, because non-compliance by management and by other individuals working for the employing organisation, as well as by its TCWG, is within NOCLAR, and the director and the Head of the sales division fall there. The third option reverses the sequence by placing understanding of the matter after the decision on further action and wrongly treats the documentation as substitute. The fourth option treats disclosure as automatic, whereas the accountant is required to determine whether to disclose, and an imminent breach is a separate question from the mere fact that investors and the general public are affected.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A professional accountant who becomes aware of an imminent breach of a law or regulation has to determine whether to disclose it immediately to the Appropriate Authority so as to prevent or mitigate its consequences, whereas an auditor whose responsibilities are governed only by SA 250 has no such provision.
Reason (R): SA 250 is applicable only on audit and not on other assurance engagements, whereas the NOCLAR provisions are applicable to professional accountants in service as well as in practice.
In the context of the above, which of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is true because NOCLAR requires the accountant, on becoming aware of an imminent breach, to determine whether to disclose it immediately to the Appropriate Authority to prevent or mitigate the consequences, while SA 250 contains no provision for imminent breach. R is also true, since SA 250 is applicable only on audit and not on other assurance engagements, whereas NOCLAR extends to professional accountants both in service and in practice. R nonetheless does not explain A: the difference in the persons and engagements to which the two frameworks apply does not account for the absence of an imminent breach mechanism in SA 250, which is a separate difference between them. Indeed NOCLAR itself applies to the audit of a listed entity, so an accountant can be inside both frameworks and still face the imminent breach question that only one of them addresses. The true explanation of A lies in the fact that SA 250 is confined to compliance with laws affecting the financial statements and the operating aspect of the business, and not in the range of engagements it covers.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements comparing NOCLAR with SA 250:
(i) SA 250 is applicable to all assurance engagements, whereas NOCLAR is applicable only to professional accountants in practice.
(ii) SA 250 covers laws having a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures in the financial statements, and other laws whose compliance is fundamental to the operating aspect of the business, whereas NOCLAR covers non-compliance causing substantial harm in financial or non-financial terms.
(iii) SA 250 defines stakeholders as investors, creditors, employees and the general public, whereas NOCLAR does not define stakeholders.
(iv) SA 250 contains no provision for an imminent breach, whereas NOCLAR requires the accountant to determine whether to disclose an imminent breach immediately to the Appropriate Authority to prevent or mitigate its consequences.
Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
questions.explanation: SA 250 is applicable only on audit and not on other assurance engagements, and NOCLAR is applicable to professional accountants in service as well as in practice, so (i) reverses and overstates both halves and is not correct. The contrast drawn in (iii) is also reversed: it is SA 250 that does not define stakeholders, while NOCLAR is concerned with the effect of non-compliance on investors, creditors, employees and the general public. Statements (ii) and (iv) correctly reproduce two further distinctions, namely that SA 250 is organised around direct-effect laws and laws fundamental to the operating aspect of the business while NOCLAR is organised around substantial harm in financial or non-financial terms, and that the imminent breach mechanism exists only in NOCLAR. The practical consequence of (iii) is that a shareholder or a villager affected by an effluent discharge is not a stakeholder identified by SA 250, even though NOCLAR addresses that effect.

questions.question: CA Vikram Deshpande has been in continuous practice in India since 2014, a period of eleven years, and holds a certificate of practice. He was adjudged an insolvent in 2016 and discharged by the court in 2017, but he never applied for or obtained a certificate from the court stating that the insolvency was caused by misfortune without any misconduct on his part. He has not paid the prescribed membership fee for the last two years. He has also failed to furnish information called for by the Council, which failure has now come to the Council's notice. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
options: He is entitled to be designated a Fellow Member, because his eleven years of continuous practice in India satisfy the Fellowship condition, and a member who has stood discharged from insolvency for more than five years is not subject to any disability for the purpose of membership.

His name may be removed only for non-payment of the prescribed membership fee, because the disability relating to a discharged insolvent operates solely at the time of first entry in the Register and cannot be invoked afresh against a member whose name is already there.

The Council may remove his name from the Register for non-payment of the prescribed fee and, separately, on the ground that he is found to have a disability, since a discharged insolvent without the required court certificate is debarred from membership; his eleven years of continuous practice does not cure that, and restoration on the fee ground would require payment of the arrears along with additional fee.

His name is liable to removal because he has not paid the prescribed fee, and once removed on that ground it can be restored only if the Board of Discipline or the Disciplinary Committee so orders in accordance with the terms of its order.
questions.explanation: The Council may remove a name from the Register where the member has not paid the prescribed fee required to be paid by him, and also where the member is found to have any of the disabilities prescribed for the purpose of membership, which is a ground independent of the fee default. A discharged insolvent who has not obtained the court certificate regarding the cause of the insolvency is subject to that disability, and because removal is available for a member found to have any of those disabilities, the disability is not confined to the moment of first entry, so the second option is wrong. Length of continuous practice in India bears only on eligibility for the Fellowship, which presupposes that the person's name is and remains in the Register, and it cannot displace a disability or a removal ground, so the first option is wrong. The fourth option applies the wrong restoration route, since restoration in accordance with the orders of the Board of Discipline, the Disciplinary Committee, the Appellate Authority or the High Court is prescribed for removals made on account of such orders, whereas removal for non-payment of fee is cured by payment of the arrears along with additional fee. Failure to supply information called for by the Council is not itself one of the four removal cases.

questions.question: An Associate Member of the Institute died on 12 January 2025. A Second Member, aged 63 years, retired from professional activity in 2024 and now lives entirely on a pension from a former employer. A Third Member, convicted in 2023 of an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with imprisonment, has neither been granted a pardon nor obtained removal of the disability from the Central Government. A Fourth Member has not paid the prescribed membership fee required to be paid by him. In how many of these four situations is the Council empowered to remove the member's name from the Register under the removal provisions?
questions.explanation: The Council may remove a name from the Register in four cases, namely where the member is dead, where a request has been received from him to that effect, where he has not paid the prescribed fee, and where he is found to have any of the disabilities prescribed for the purpose of membership. The death and the non-payment of the prescribed fee are therefore squarely within those cases. The conviction also is, because a conviction by a competent Court for an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with transportation or imprisonment, absent a pardon or removal of the disability by the Central Government, is one of the disabilities, and a member found to have such a disability is removable. Retirement at 63 and cessation of professional activity are not among the four cases and are not disabilities, so that situation alone does not support removal, which is why the answer is three and not four. The trap in counting four is to treat discontinuance of practice as if it were a ground for striking off, whereas it is a ground relevant to cancellation of a certificate of practice and not to the Register.

questions.question:
M/s Trivedi & Ghai is the statutory auditor of Surakshit Pharma Limited, a listed entity in India with a net worth of ₹ 1,120 crores, for the year ended 31 March 2025. The engagement partner concludes as follows:
Statement 1: SA 250 governs this audit and it also covers the non-compliance causing substantial non-financial harm to the general public, so nothing further is required of him.
Statement 2: The NOCLAR framework applies to this engagement because it is an audit engagement of a listed entity in India having net worth of ₹ 250 crores or more, and its documentation requirements operate in addition to the documentation required under SA 250.
Statement 3: Because SA 250 has no provision for imminent breach, he need not consider whether an imminent breach of law, if identified, should be disclosed immediately to anyone outside the company.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement 2 is correct on both limbs: the engagement is an audit engagement of a listed entity in India whose net worth far exceeds ₹ 250 crores, so responding to NOCLAR is applicable to the firm as professional accountants in practice, and the NOCLAR documentation is to be maintained in addition to the documentation required under the Standards on Auditing. Statement 1 is wrong because SA 250 addresses laws having a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures in the financial statements and other laws whose compliance is fundamental to the operating aspect of the business, whereas non-compliance causing substantial harm in non-financial terms, including its effect on investors, creditors, employees and the general public, is the province of NOCLAR; SA 250 also does not define stakeholders. Statement 3 draws the wrong conclusion from a correct premise, since the absence of an imminent breach provision in SA 250 does not eliminate the requirement, which arises under NOCLAR, to determine whether an imminent breach should be disclosed immediately to the Appropriate Authority to prevent or mitigate its consequences. The two frameworks therefore coexist on this audit rather than one substituting for the other.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements relating to the significance of a Certificate of Practice (CoP):

1. No member of the Institute is entitled to practise unless he has obtained a CoP.
2. A member who is not in practice may accept an engagement to render a service prescribed for a chartered accountant, provided that no special qualification is required for that particular service.
3. A member of the Institute can occupy, alongside his capacity to practise as a member, another separable capacity in which he may take up such practice.
4. A member who has been punished by suspension from practice may contend that, since he continues to be a member of the Institute, he is entitled to practise in some other capacity.

Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Statement 1 alone is a faithful statement of the rule that no member is entitled to practise without a CoP; the other three invert the position. A member not in practice is precluded from accepting an engagement to render any service prescribed for a chartered accountant even where the service needs no special qualification, so statement 2 is wrong. A member can have no capacity separable from his capacity as a member of the Institute in which to take up such practice, because once he becomes a member he is bound by the CA Act and its Regulations, so statement 3 is wrong. The corollary drawn in the source is that a member punished by suspension from practice cannot contend that he may practise in another capacity, so statement 4 is wrong. Hence the set of statements which are not correct is 2, 3 and 4.

questions.question:
CA Dinesh Rao has been a member of the Institute since 2009 and has held a Certificate of Practice (CoP) since 2016. He runs a proprietary practice, D. Rao & Co, at Nagpur. The following events are relevant: (a) In 2021, his CoP was cancelled after it was found to have been issued on the basis of incorrect and misleading information, and a fresh CoP was later issued to him. (b) In 2023, his name was removed from the Register of Members because a prescribed fee due from him had not been paid, and his CoP was cancelled in consequence. (c) For the current year he did not pay the annual fee for his CoP till 1 October of that year, and his CoP was treated as liable for cancellation; on 12 December of the same year he filed an application for restoration along with the fee, and that application was received by the Secretary. (d) During the gap period in (c), Rao appeared before the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal as an authorised representative for two of his assessees, taking the position that appearance before the Tribunal required no special qualification and was therefore being undertaken by him in a capacity separable from his capacity as a member of the Institute. (e) In 2019, Rao had been punished by suspension from practice.

What is the MOST appropriate conclusion on the effect of the restoration of the CoP cancelled in event (c)?
options: Restoration can operate only from the date of the Council's order, since the annual fee was paid after 30 September

Restoration can be made with effect from the date on which the CoP was cancelled, the default being non-payment of the annual fee and the application with fee having reached the Secretary before the expiry of the relevant year
Restoration is unavailable, the relevant year having already expired when the fee was paid on 1 October
Restoration with retrospective effect is available because Rao appeared before the Tribunal in his capacity as a chartered accountant and not in any other capacity
questions.explanation: Non-payment of the annual fee for the CoP up to 30 September of the relevant year only makes the CoP liable for cancellation; it does not close the door on retrospective restoration. The Council may restore a CoP cancelled for non-payment of the annual fee with effect from the date of cancellation where the application along with the fee is received by the Secretary before expiry of the relevant year. The decisive facts are that the cancellation in (c) was on the annual-fee ground and that the application reached the Secretary on 12 December, within the same year, so restoration can be back-dated to the date of cancellation. The first option wrongly treats 30 September as the cut-off for restoration, the second-last wrongly assumes the year had expired, and the last option imports the unrelated Tribunal issue in (d), which affects the characterisation of his appearance and not the restoration timetable.

questions.question:
CA Dinesh Rao has been a member of the Institute since 2009 and has held a Certificate of Practice (CoP) since 2016. He runs a proprietary practice, D. Rao & Co, at Nagpur. The following events are relevant: (a) In 2021, his CoP was cancelled after it was found to have been issued on the basis of incorrect and misleading information, and a fresh CoP was later issued to him. (b) In 2023, his name was removed from the Register of Members because a prescribed fee due from him had not been paid, and his CoP was cancelled in consequence. (c) For the current year he did not pay the annual fee for his CoP till 1 October of that year, and his CoP was treated as liable for cancellation; on 12 December of the same year he filed an application for restoration along with the fee, and that application was received by the Secretary. (d) During the gap period in (c), Rao appeared before the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal as an authorised representative for two of his assessees, taking the position that appearance before the Tribunal required no special qualification and was therefore being undertaken by him in a capacity separable from his capacity as a member of the Institute. (e) In 2019, Rao had been punished by suspension from practice.

Consider the following statements on the plea taken by Rao in event (d):

1. Since no special qualification is needed for appearance before the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal, a member may make such an appearance in a capacity other than that of a chartered accountant.
2. Once a person becomes a member of the Institute he is bound by the provisions of the CA Act and its Regulations, and appearing before the Tribunal after becoming a member could be only in his capacity as a chartered accountant and member of the Institute.
3. The earlier punishment by suspension in 2019 is the decisive factor in deciding whether Rao can appear before the Tribunal at all.
4. A member who is not in practice is precluded from accepting an engagement to render any service prescribed for a chartered accountant, even where the service does not require any special qualification.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: The illustration in the source is precisely about the Income-tax Tribunal: after becoming a member, a person is bound by the CA Act and its Regulations, so he can appear only in his capacity as a chartered accountant and member of the Institute, which makes statement 2 correct and statement 1 wrong. Statement 4 states the express preclusion of a member who is not in practice from accepting an engagement to render a prescribed service notwithstanding that no special qualification is needed. Statement 3 is not correct as the ground of decision: the suspension fact is relevant to the separate proposition that a suspended member cannot claim to practise in another capacity, but the absence of any separable capacity follows from membership itself, not from the pendency of a disciplinary punishment. The absence of separability is what defeats Rao's plea in (d).

questions.question:
CA Dinesh Rao has been a member of the Institute since 2009 and has held a Certificate of Practice (CoP) since 2016. He runs a proprietary practice, D. Rao & Co, at Nagpur. The following events are relevant: (a) In 2021, his CoP was cancelled after it was found to have been issued on the basis of incorrect and misleading information, and a fresh CoP was later issued to him. (b) In 2023, his name was removed from the Register of Members because a prescribed fee due from him had not been paid, and his CoP was cancelled in consequence. (c) For the current year he did not pay the annual fee for his CoP till 1 October of that year, and his CoP was treated as liable for cancellation; on 12 December of the same year he filed an application for restoration along with the fee, and that application was received by the Secretary. (d) During the gap period in (c), Rao appeared before the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal as an authorised representative for two of his assessees, taking the position that appearance before the Tribunal required no special qualification and was therefore being undertaken by him in a capacity separable from his capacity as a member of the Institute. (e) In 2019, Rao had been punished by suspension from practice.

Consider the following statements on the events above:

1. The cancellation in event (c) is capable of restoration by the Council with effect from the date of cancellation, on an application with fee received by the Secretary before the expiry of the relevant year.
2. The cancellation in event (b) is capable of restoration on the same terms as statement 1, once Rao pays the arrears of the prescribed fee before the expiry of the relevant year.
3. The cancellation in event (a) is not capable of restoration on the terms described in statement 1.
4. Event (c) does not expose the CoP to cancellation at all, because payment on 1 October cured the default.
5. If Rao had, during the year, ceased to practise, that circumstance by itself would not make his CoP liable for cancellation.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: The four grounds on which a CoP is liable for cancellation are removal of the holder's name from the Register, issue of the CoP on incorrect, misleading or false information or by mistake, the member ceasing to practise, and non-payment of the annual fee for the CoP up to 30 September of the relevant year. Events (a), (b) and (c) therefore all attract cancellation, which is why statement 4 fails, payment on 1 October being itself proof that the fee remained unpaid up to 30 September, and why statement 5 also fails, cessation of practice being an independent ground. The retrospective restoration rule is, however, confined to a CoP cancelled for non-payment of the annual fee where the application along with the fee reaches the Secretary before the expiry of the relevant year, so it covers event (c) but not events (a) or (b). Statement 2 wrongly transplants that concession to a cancellation arising from removal of the name from the Register.

questions.question:
CA Farida Contractor holds a CoP and practises as the proprietor of F. Contractor & Co at Pune. During the financial year 2024-25 she accepted the following six assignments: (I) Valuation, as a Registered Valuer under the Companies Act, of the plant and machinery of Bharat Steels Ltd., for a fee of ₹ 40 lakh, this being the largest fee the firm billed in the year. (II) Acting as advisor to the public issue of Venus Organics Ltd., her work covering drafting of the prospectus and the memorandum, filing of documents with SEBI, preparation of the publicity budget and advice regarding the selection of brokers and underwriters, for a fee of ₹ 55 lakh. (III) Underwriting ₹ 5 crore of the Venus Organics issue and, in addition, managing the investment portfolios of two clients of the firm. (IV) Acting as registrar to the Venus Organics issue and as registrar for the transfer of securities. (V) Insurance Financial Advisory Services under the IRDA Act, including insurance brokerage. (VI) Performing the functions of a GST practitioner for Trims & Co, being the word processing, preparation and submission of its GST forms and returns.

Which one of the following combinations of assignments is fully permissible for Farida as a chartered accountant in practice?
options: I, II, IV and V only
II, III, IV and VI only
II, IV, V and VI only
I, II, III and VI only
questions.explanation: Assignments II, IV, V and VI all fall inside the range of Management Consultancy and Other Services permitted by the Council: advising or consulting to an issue (including drafting the prospectus and memorandum, filing with SEBI, publicity budget and advice on selection of brokers and underwriters), acting as registrar to an issue and for transfer of securities, Insurance Financial Advisory Services under the IRDA Act including insurance brokerage, and administrative services such as word processing and preparing and submitting forms, which involve routine or mechanical work requiring little or no professional judgement. Assignment I fails because a CA may act as a Registered Valuer only for valuation of securities or financial assets and not for plant and machinery. Assignment III fails because broking, underwriting and portfolio management services are expressly outside what a CA in practice may undertake, notwithstanding that advising on the selection of underwriters is permitted. That the valuation fee was the firm's largest, and that the assignments were accepted in the same year as audit work, does not alter the analysis.

questions.question:
CA Farida Contractor holds a CoP and practises as the proprietor of F. Contractor & Co at Pune. During the financial year 2024-25 she accepted the following six assignments: (I) Valuation, as a Registered Valuer under the Companies Act, of the plant and machinery of Bharat Steels Ltd., for a fee of ₹ 40 lakh, this being the largest fee the firm billed in the year. (II) Acting as advisor to the public issue of Venus Organics Ltd., her work covering drafting of the prospectus and the memorandum, filing of documents with SEBI, preparation of the publicity budget and advice regarding the selection of brokers and underwriters, for a fee of ₹ 55 lakh. (III) Underwriting ₹ 5 crore of the Venus Organics issue and, in addition, managing the investment portfolios of two clients of the firm. (IV) Acting as registrar to the Venus Organics issue and as registrar for the transfer of securities. (V) Insurance Financial Advisory Services under the IRDA Act, including insurance brokerage. (VI) Performing the functions of a GST practitioner for Trims & Co, being the word processing, preparation and submission of its GST forms and returns.

Assignment I is re-scoped by the client. Farida is now asked, as a Registered Valuer, to value (a) the debentures issued by Bharat Steels Ltd. and (b) a specified plant and machinery item of the same company, the aggregate fee remaining ₹ 40 lakh. What is the correct position on the re-scoped engagement?
options: Both (a) and (b) are permissible, because it is the registration as a valuer and not the subject matter of the valuation that fixes what a CA may value
Neither (a) nor (b) is permissible, because a valuation assignment is outside the permitted range unless it is bundled with advice regarding amalgamation or merger
Both are permissible, because valuation of shares and of a business is expressly permitted and plant and machinery is only one of the inputs to the value of a business
(a) is permissible as valuation of securities; (b) remains impermissible, the permitted subject matter being securities or financial assets and not plant and machinery
questions.explanation: The Council's permission to act as a Registered Valuer under the Companies Act is expressly limited to valuation of securities or financial assets, and plant and machinery is specifically outside that scope. Debentures are securities, so limb (a) is within the permission; the machinery item in limb (b) is tangible movable property and not a security or financial asset, so limb (b) remains impermissible notwithstanding that the two are covered by one engagement letter and one fee. The fee quantum and the fact that both valuations are for the same company are not decisive. The third option mistakes the separate permission for valuation of shares and of a business for a permission to value every asset of that business.

questions.question:
CA Farida Contractor holds a CoP and practises as the proprietor of F. Contractor & Co at Pune. During the financial year 2024-25 she accepted the following six assignments: (I) Valuation, as a Registered Valuer under the Companies Act, of the plant and machinery of Bharat Steels Ltd., for a fee of ₹ 40 lakh, this being the largest fee the firm billed in the year. (II) Acting as advisor to the public issue of Venus Organics Ltd., her work covering drafting of the prospectus and the memorandum, filing of documents with SEBI, preparation of the publicity budget and advice regarding the selection of brokers and underwriters, for a fee of ₹ 55 lakh. (III) Underwriting ₹ 5 crore of the Venus Organics issue and, in addition, managing the investment portfolios of two clients of the firm. (IV) Acting as registrar to the Venus Organics issue and as registrar for the transfer of securities. (V) Insurance Financial Advisory Services under the IRDA Act, including insurance brokerage. (VI) Performing the functions of a GST practitioner for Trims & Co, being the word processing, preparation and submission of its GST forms and returns.

Which one of the following positions is LEAST appropriate to the above assignments?
options: Farida may advise on the selection of underwriters while consulting to the issue, yet may not herself underwrite it
Farida may value plant and machinery under assignment I, since valuation of shares and of a business is permitted and plant and machinery is only an input to the value of a business
Farida may undertake insurance brokerage under assignment V, yet may not carry on broking in securities
Farida's work on GST forms under assignment VI is administrative in character, being routine and requiring little or no professional judgement
questions.explanation: The permission to act as a Registered Valuer is confined to valuation of securities or financial assets and expressly excludes plant and machinery, so the second position is not correct even though valuation of shares and of a business is separately permitted as a Management Consultancy and Other Service. The first position is correct because advising on the selection of brokers and underwriters is part of issue consultancy while underwriting itself is one of the three activities, along with broking and portfolio management services, that a CA in practice may not undertake. The third position is correct because Insurance Financial Advisory Services under the IRDA Act, including insurance brokerage, are permitted, whereas securities broking is not. The fourth position correctly characterises preparing and submitting forms and the functions of a GST practitioner as administrative services.

questions.question:
Match the following activities of a member holding a CoP with the status applicable to each.

Column I
A. Underwriting a public issue of a client
B. Valuation of shares, as a Registered Valuer under the Companies Act
C. Preparing and submitting GST forms and returns for a client
D. Acting as an Insolvency Professional under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code

Column II
1. Permitted as an item in the range of Management Consultancy and Other Services allowed by the Council
2. Permitted as an administrative service involving routine or mechanical work requiring little or no professional judgement
3. Not permitted to a chartered accountant in practice
4. Permitted as a Registered Valuer, the subject matter being securities or financial assets
questions.explanation: Underwriting is one of the activities, with broking and portfolio management services, that a CA in practice is not permitted to undertake, so A pairs with 3. Valuation of shares is within the Registered Valuer permission because shares are securities, so B pairs with 4; the same assignment covering plant and machinery would fall outside it. Preparing and submitting forms is administrative service work, clerical in nature and requiring little or no professional judgement, so C pairs with 2, and not with 1. Acting as an Insolvency Professional under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code is one of the specifically enumerated items in the Council's permitted range, so D pairs with 1.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A member of the Institute who is not in practice cannot accept an engagement to render a service prescribed for a chartered accountant, even where that particular service can also be performed by persons who hold no special qualification.

Reason (R): A member of the Institute can have no capacity in which he can take up such practice separable from his capacity to practise as a member of the Institute, because once a person becomes a member he is bound by the provisions of the CA Act and its Regulations.

In the light of the above, choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
questions.explanation: Both statements reproduce the provisions on the significance of the CoP: no member may practise without a CoP, a member not in practice is precluded from accepting an engagement to render a prescribed service even where no special qualification is needed, and there is no separable capacity outside membership. The reason is not merely consistent with the assertion but is the ground for it: the absence of any alternative capacity is exactly why the member cannot escape the bar by pointing to the service being one open to non-qualified persons. The illustration in the source confirms this, since appearance before the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal after becoming a member could be only in the capacity of a chartered accountant. The second option therefore understates the connection between the two statements.

questions.question:
CA Tenzing Bhutia is a member in practice established at Gangtok, a hill area, under the name Bhutia & Co. Clients of the firm migrate to the plains in winter, so he opened an office at Siliguri, a city in the plains, on 1 November and kept it functioning till 15 February, a period of three and a half months, his regular office at Gangtok continuing to remain open throughout. He installed at Siliguri a name board reading 'Bhutia & Co, Chartered Accountants' on 1 November and removed it only on 15 February. He printed the Siliguri address on the firm's letterheads and on his visiting cards with effect from 1 November. On 20 January, after winter had set in, he wrote to the Institute informing it that he had opened the Siliguri office. He also resides at Gangtok, where he caused to be fixed at the entrance of his residence a name board reading 'Bhutia & Co, Chartered Accountants'.

Consider the following statements:

1. The Siliguri office functioned for a period beyond the maximum permitted to a hill-area member's temporary office in a city in the plains.
2. Because the regular office at Gangtok was not required to be closed, no breach arises from the length of the Siliguri period.
3. The Siliguri address could be shown in the letterheads and visiting cards for so long as that office actually functioned.
4. Intimation to the Institute was obligatory before the commencement of every winter, and the letter written on 20 January does not satisfy that requirement.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A member practising in a hill area may open a temporary office in a city in the plains for a maximum of three months in a year; three and a half months is outside that limit, so statement 1 is correct. The immunity that the regular office need not be closed during that period is a separate concession and cannot cure the excess in duration, so statement 2 is wrong. The temporary office must not appear in letterheads, visiting cards or any other document as a place of business, irrespective of whether it was functioning, so statement 3 is wrong. Intimation to the Institute before the commencement of every winter is obligatory and a letter written once winter has set in does not meet it, so statement 4 is correct.

questions.question:
CA Tenzing Bhutia is a member in practice established at Gangtok, a hill area, under the name Bhutia & Co. Clients of the firm migrate to the plains in winter, so he opened an office at Siliguri, a city in the plains, on 1 November and kept it functioning till 15 February, a period of three and a half months, his regular office at Gangtok continuing to remain open throughout. He installed at Siliguri a name board reading 'Bhutia & Co, Chartered Accountants' on 1 November and removed it only on 15 February. He printed the Siliguri address on the firm's letterheads and on his visiting cards with effect from 1 November. On 20 January, after winter had set in, he wrote to the Institute informing it that he had opened the Siliguri office. He also resides at Gangtok, where he caused to be fixed at the entrance of his residence a name board reading 'Bhutia & Co, Chartered Accountants'.

Which one of the following positions is NOT correct?
options: The name board at Siliguri could be displayed only during the period for which that office was permitted to function
A board at the member's place of residence with the designation Chartered Accountant is permissible if it is the name plate or name board of an individual member and not of the firm
The residential board at Gangtok is unobjectionable, because the residence is in the same city as the member's regular office
The maximum period for which a temporary office in a city in the plains may function is three months in a year, and the regular office need not be closed for that period
questions.explanation: The permission regarding a name board at the place of residence is expressly conditioned on the board being that of an individual member and not of the firm; a board reading 'Bhutia & Co, Chartered Accountants' is the firm's board, and the fact that the residence is in the same city as the regular office does not remove that condition. The first position states the rule that the firm's name board at a temporary office may not be displayed other than during the period the office is permitted to function, which here also limits the display to the permitted three months rather than to 15 February. The fourth position correctly combines the three month ceiling with the concession that the regular office need not be closed.

questions.question:
CA Tenzing Bhutia is a member in practice established at Gangtok, a hill area, under the name Bhutia & Co. Clients of the firm migrate to the plains in winter, so he opened an office at Siliguri, a city in the plains, on 1 November and kept it functioning till 15 February, a period of three and a half months, his regular office at Gangtok continuing to remain open throughout. He installed at Siliguri a name board reading 'Bhutia & Co, Chartered Accountants' on 1 November and removed it only on 15 February. He printed the Siliguri address on the firm's letterheads and on his visiting cards with effect from 1 November. On 20 January, after winter had set in, he wrote to the Institute informing it that he had opened the Siliguri office. He also resides at Gangtok, where he caused to be fixed at the entrance of his residence a name board reading 'Bhutia & Co, Chartered Accountants'.

Assume the geography is reversed: Bhutia's regular office is at Siliguri, a city in the plains, and he proposes to open an office at Gangtok, a hill area, for three months each summer, keeping the Siliguri office open and intimating the Institute before the summer begins. Which is the MOST appropriate advice?
options: The exemption does not cover this arrangement, because it is available to members practising in hill areas for temporary offices in a city in the plains; the Siliguri and Gangtok offices are in different cities and beyond 50 km from each other, so the Gangtok office must be in the separate charge of a member of the Institute
The exemption operates both ways, so the Gangtok office may function for three months without a member in separate charge, provided the Institute is intimated before the summer begins
The arrangement is permissible because Bhutia himself, being the proprietor, is necessarily the member in charge of every office of his firm
The arrangement is permissible, because the only condition for a second office without separate charge is that the member should attend it for at least 182 days in the year
questions.explanation: The hill-area exemption is drafted in one direction only: a member practising in a hill area may open a temporary office in a city in the plains for a maximum of three months in a year; a plains-based member opening an office in a hill area is outside it. Neither of the other exemptions assists him either, since Gangtok is not the same premises as, nor the same city as, Siliguri, and the two are more than 50 km from the municipal limits of the city in which the first office is located. More than one office must accordingly be in the separate charge of a member of the Institute, and failure in this regard is professional misconduct. The last option inverts the rule, because the 182 day expectation attaches to the CA in charge of a branch, not to the test for being relieved of having a separate member in charge.

questions.question:
CA Kavita Deshmukh holds a CoP and has her first office at Bhubaneswar. She proposes to open three more offices in the same year: Office A at Cuttack, which is 28 km from the municipal limits of the city of Bhubaneswar; Office B at a place which is 62 km from the municipal limits of the city of Bhubaneswar; and Office C on the third floor of the same building in which her first office at Bhubaneswar is situated, having a separate entrance and its own sign board. Kavita proposes to place all three offices in the charge of CA Salil Nadkarni, a member of the Institute who is associated with her firm as a paid assistant in whole-time employment. Nadkarni attended Office A for 174 days and Office B for 40 days during the year, the two attendances together totalling 214 days; he did not attend Office C, which Kavita herself visited whenever she was in Bhubaneswar. Kavita intends to state Cuttack as her professional address in her dealings with the Institute while describing Bhubaneswar as her main office.

Which offices are exempt from the requirement that the office be in the separate charge of a member of the Institute?
options: Office A and Office B only
Office A and Office C only
Office B and Office C only
questions.explanation: A second office may be held without separate charge of a member of the Institute if it is in the same premises as the first office, or in the same city, or within 50 km of the municipal limits of the city in which the first office is located. Office A at 28 km from the municipal limits of Bhubaneswar and Office C in the same building as the first office both satisfy that test, so neither needs a member in separate charge. Office B at 62 km fails the distance test and is outside the two other limbs as well, so it must be in the separate charge of a member of the Institute, and a member in charge must be associated as a partner or as a paid assistant in whole-time employment and attend that office for at least 182 days. The separate entrance and sign board of Office C do not take it out of the same premises exemption.

questions.question:
CA Kavita Deshmukh holds a CoP and has her first office at Bhubaneswar. She proposes to open three more offices in the same year: Office A at Cuttack, which is 28 km from the municipal limits of the city of Bhubaneswar; Office B at a place which is 62 km from the municipal limits of the city of Bhubaneswar; and Office C on the third floor of the same building in which her first office at Bhubaneswar is situated, having a separate entrance and its own sign board. Kavita proposes to place all three offices in the charge of CA Salil Nadkarni, a member of the Institute who is associated with her firm as a paid assistant in whole-time employment. Nadkarni attended Office A for 174 days and Office B for 40 days during the year, the two attendances together totalling 214 days; he did not attend Office C, which Kavita herself visited whenever she was in Bhubaneswar. Kavita intends to state Cuttack as her professional address in her dealings with the Institute while describing Bhubaneswar as her main office.

Which of the following is the correct position regarding Office B?
options: Only a partner of the firm, and not a paid assistant, can be the member in charge of a branch office
The aggregate of 214 days across Offices A and B satisfies the 182 day minimum for Office B, the requirement being referable to the member and not to the office
Because Office B is more than 50 km from the municipal limits of Bhubaneswar, the 182 day attendance requirement does not apply to it
Nadkarni's 40 days at Office B falls short of the minimum of 182 days, and his attendance at Office A cannot be added to make it up
questions.explanation: Office B at 62 km from the municipal limits of the city in which the first office is located does not qualify for the second-office exemption, so it must be in the separate charge of a member of the Institute. The member in charge must be associated with the member or firm as a partner or as a paid assistant in whole-time employment and must attend that office for at least 182 days, so Nadkarni's status is not the problem; 40 days of attendance is. The 182 day expectation is measured office-wise for the office which requires a member in charge, and days spent at Office A cannot be aggregated with it. The third option confuses the trigger for the exemption with the content of the requirement, and the first wrongly excludes paid assistants in whole-time employment.

questions.question:
CA Kavita Deshmukh holds a CoP and has her first office at Bhubaneswar. She proposes to open three more offices in the same year: Office A at Cuttack, which is 28 km from the municipal limits of the city of Bhubaneswar; Office B at a place which is 62 km from the municipal limits of the city of Bhubaneswar; and Office C on the third floor of the same building in which her first office at Bhubaneswar is situated, having a separate entrance and its own sign board. Kavita proposes to place all three offices in the charge of CA Salil Nadkarni, a member of the Institute who is associated with her firm as a paid assistant in whole-time employment. Nadkarni attended Office A for 174 days and Office B for 40 days during the year, the two attendances together totalling 214 days; he did not attend Office C, which Kavita herself visited whenever she was in Bhubaneswar. Kavita intends to state Cuttack as her professional address in her dealings with the Institute while describing Bhubaneswar as her main office.

Consider the following statements:

1. Where a CA in practice or a firm has more than one office in India, each office must be in the separate charge of a member of the Institute, and failure in this regard constitutes professional misconduct.
2. Of the two offices falling within the same-premises or 50 km exemption, Kavita must declare which is her main office, and that office constitutes her professional address.
3. Kavita's stated intention, of describing Bhubaneswar as her main office while disclosing Cuttack as her professional address, is not consistent with the declaration rule.
4. Because Office C has a separate entrance and its own sign board, it must be in the separate charge of a member of the Institute.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement 1 states the general rule for more than one office in India and the consequence of failure, namely professional misconduct. A member having two offices of the exempted type must declare which of the two is his main office, and the office so declared is what constitutes his professional address, so statements 2 and 3 are both correct; on the declared facts Kavita cannot treat Bhubaneswar as main and Cuttack as her professional address simultaneously. Statement 4 is not correct because Office C is on the same premises as the first office, and the exemption for a second office located in the same premises does not turn on a separate entrance or a separate sign board.

questions.question:
M/s Razak Sons LLP holds the statutory audit of Kokan Pharma Ltd for 2024-25. In the same year the firm takes up the following work: (a) design and implementation of a new financial information system for Kokan Pharma Ltd, for a fee of ₹ 90 lakh; (b) internal audit of the Nagpur warehouse of Kokan Pharma Ltd, for a fee of ₹ 25 lakh; (c) accounting and book-keeping services for Sundar Holdings Ltd, which holds 61 per cent of the equity share capital of Kokan Pharma Ltd; (d) investment advisory services for Girija Intermediaries Ltd, a company which is neither the holding nor a subsidiary company of Kokan Pharma Ltd; (e) actuarial services for Kokan Bio Ltd, a wholly owned subsidiary of Kokan Pharma Ltd; and (f) management services for Kokan Pharma Ltd, for an aggregate fee of ₹ 15 lakh, which is less than the statutory audit fee of ₹ 22 lakh for the same year.

Which combination of assignments is barred to Razak Sons LLP by section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013?
questions.explanation: Section 144, as extracted, bars the company auditor from providing accounting and book-keeping, internal audit, design and implementation of any financial information system, actuarial services, investment advisory services, investment banking services, outsourced financial services, management services and any other prescribed services to the company or its holding or subsidiary company. Assignments (a), (b) and (f) are barred in relation to Kokan Pharma Ltd, (c) is barred because Sundar Holdings Ltd is the holding company and (e) because Kokan Bio Ltd is a subsidiary; the size of the fee relative to the audit fee is not a condition of the bar. Assignment (d) is not caught, because Girija Intermediaries Ltd is neither the auditee nor its holding or subsidiary company. The second option omits (f) and the third omits (a), each on the irrelevant footing that a small fee or an internal assignment escapes the list.

questions.question:
M/s Razak Sons LLP holds the statutory audit of Kokan Pharma Ltd for 2024-25. In the same year the firm takes up the following work: (a) design and implementation of a new financial information system for Kokan Pharma Ltd, for a fee of ₹ 90 lakh; (b) internal audit of the Nagpur warehouse of Kokan Pharma Ltd, for a fee of ₹ 25 lakh; (c) accounting and book-keeping services for Sundar Holdings Ltd, which holds 61 per cent of the equity share capital of Kokan Pharma Ltd; (d) investment advisory services for Girija Intermediaries Ltd, a company which is neither the holding nor a subsidiary company of Kokan Pharma Ltd; (e) actuarial services for Kokan Bio Ltd, a wholly owned subsidiary of Kokan Pharma Ltd; and (f) management services for Kokan Pharma Ltd, for an aggregate fee of ₹ 15 lakh, which is less than the statutory audit fee of ₹ 22 lakh for the same year.

Two facts are now changed. In (b), what the firm undertakes at the Nagpur warehouse is a management and operational audit together with a quality audit, instead of an internal audit. In (d), Girija Intermediaries Ltd is taken over wholly by Kokan Pharma Ltd and becomes its subsidiary, the investment advisory work continuing. What is the correct consequence of these changes?
options: Neither assignment falls within the bar, since management, operational and quality audit work is in the Council's permitted range and Girija, being a separate legal entity, is outside section 144 in any event

The changed work in (b) is not among the services specifically barred, the barred item being internal audit while management and operational audit and quality audit are services permitted by the Council; the changed work in (d) is barred, since the bar covers the company and its holding or subsidiary company
Both assignments are now barred, because every kind of audit other than the statutory audit is prohibited to the company auditor
The change in (b) makes no difference, a quality audit being a form of internal audit, while the change in (d) takes the advisory outside the bar because the firm audits only Kokan Pharma Ltd
questions.explanation: Section 144 as extracted names internal audit among the barred services, whereas management and operational audit and quality audit appear in the range of Management Consultancy and Other Services which the Council has permitted, so the re-scoped warehouse work is not the barred item. The change in (d) pulls the investment advisory services inside the bar, because the bar reaches services rendered to the company or to its holding or subsidiary company and Girija has now become a subsidiary; the fact that the firm's statutory audit is of the parent does not help, since the bar expressly runs to the subsidiary. The first option ignores the extension of the bar to a subsidiary and the third over-reads the provision as prohibiting all audit-like work. The fourth wrongly equates a quality audit with internal audit.

questions.question:
Consider the following activities undertaken by a member holding a CoP, in relation to clients for which he is not the statutory auditor:

1. Preparing project reports and feasibility studies, financial management planning and financial policy determination, capital structure planning and advice regarding raising finance.
2. Setting up executive incentive plans and wage incentive plans, and personnel recruitment and selection including development of human resources and the design and conduct of training programmes.
3. Market research and demand studies, business policy and corporate planning, and advice regarding the selection of advertisement media, of centres for holding conferences of brokers, of bankers to an issue and of collection centres and other agencies connected with an issue and post-issue activities.
4. Carrying on broking and underwriting, where these are done as an integral part of an assignment on which the member advises a client regarding an issue.
5. Working capital management, cost management and decision making, and preparation of budgets and profitability statements.
6. Acting as a Recovery Consultant in the banking sector, and undertaking environment audit and energy audit assignments.

Which of the above are NOT within the range of Management Consultancy and Other Services permitted by the Council?
