questions.explanation: Items 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 are each drawn from the range the Council has permitted under the residuary limb which deems a member to be in practice when he renders such other services as, in the opinion of the Council, are rendered by a chartered accountant in practice: project reports and feasibility studies, financial management planning and financial policy determination, capital structure planning and advice on raising finance, executive and wage incentive plans, personnel recruitment and selection including training programmes, market research and demand studies together with business policy and corporate planning, advice on advertisement media and on centres for conferences of brokers, bankers to the issue and collection centres, working capital and cost management, budgets and profitability statements, recovery consultancy in the banking sector, and environment and energy audit work. Item 4 is not, because broking, underwriting and portfolio management services are expressly outside what a CA in practice may undertake. The connection of the activity to a permitted issue consultancy assignment does not convert it into a permitted service, since advising on the selection of brokers and underwriters is permitted while acting as broker or underwriter is not.

questions.question:
Consider the following activities of a member holding a CoP.

A. Investment advisory services rendered to a company whose statutory audit the member holds
B. Systems analysis and design, computer related services and services relating to EDP, rendered to a client other than his audit client
C. Investment counselling in respect of securities, rendered to a client other than his audit client
D. Design and implementation of a financial information system rendered to a company whose statutory audit the member holds

Column II
1. Permitted as a service in the range of Management Consultancy and Other Services allowed by the Council
2. Barred by section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013

Choose the correct pairing.
questions.explanation: Investment advisory services and the design and implementation of any financial information system are expressly among the services a company auditor may not provide to the company or its holding or subsidiary company, so A and D pair with 2. Investment counselling in respect of securities, and systems analysis and design with computer and EDP related services, are items in the range the Council has permitted to a CA in practice, so B and C pair with 1. The permitted character of these two services is not lost merely because the member also audits other companies; what matters for section 144 is that the recipient is his audit client or that client's holding or subsidiary company. The pairing therefore turns on the identity of the recipient, not on the subject matter being similar in form.

questions.category: Companies not to Engage in Accountancy
questions.question:
Two entities offer professional services in the market. The first, Anand Kulkarni Consultancy Services Private Limited, is registered as a company, describes itself as a firm of chartered accountants offering audit, assurance and taxation services under a published tariff, and has CA Anand, who holds a CoP, as its whole-time director and CA Kulkarni, a member who has not obtained a CoP, as its managing director. The second, Kulkarni Anand LLP, has as its partners Vertex Holdings Private Limited, a company, and CA Renu Bhatia, a member holding a CoP; the LLP signs engagement letters for the statutory audit of two private companies in the name of the LLP.

Consider the following statements:

1. Anand Kulkarni Consultancy Services Private Limited cannot offer audit and assurance services in its own name, because no company shall practise as a chartered accountant.
2. Kulkarni Anand LLP is outside the restriction, because an LLP is a body corporate distinct from a company.
3. The presence of CA Anand, a member holding a CoP, as whole-time director removes the objection to the company describing itself as a firm of chartered accountants.
4. CA Kulkarni, being a member without a CoP, is precluded from accepting an engagement to render a service prescribed for a chartered accountant, even where that service requires no special qualification.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement 1 applies the rule that no company shall practise as a chartered accountant, which is what a company does when it offers audit, assurance and taxation services in its own name. Statement 2 is not correct, because for this purpose company includes any LLP which has a company as its partner, and Vertex Holdings Private Limited is such a partner of Kulkarni Anand LLP. Statement 3 is not correct, because the bar attaches to the company as such and is not lifted by employing or appointing a member who holds a CoP. Statement 4 correctly states the consequence of holding no CoP, namely preclusion from accepting an engagement to render a service prescribed for a chartered accountant, notwithstanding that no special qualification is required for the service.

questions.category: Companies not to Engage in Accountancy
questions.question:
Two entities offer professional services in the market. The first, Anand Kulkarni Consultancy Services Private Limited, is registered as a company, describes itself as a firm of chartered accountants offering audit, assurance and taxation services under a published tariff, and has CA Anand, who holds a CoP, as its whole-time director and CA Kulkarni, a member who has not obtained a CoP, as its managing director. The second, Kulkarni Anand LLP, has as its partners Vertex Holdings Private Limited, a company, and CA Renu Bhatia, a member holding a CoP; the LLP signs engagement letters for the statutory audit of two private companies in the name of the LLP.

On 1 April, Vertex Holdings Private Limited retires from Kulkarni Anand LLP and is replaced as partner by an individual member of the Institute who holds a CoP, so that the LLP's only partners are individual members holding CoPs. What change, if any, does this make to the position of the LLP under the provision that no company shall practise as a chartered accountant?
options: The LLP no longer has a company as its partner, so the extended meaning of company for this purpose is no longer attracted, and that particular provision does not by itself reach the LLP
Nothing changes, because every LLP is a company for the purposes of the provision that no company shall practise as a chartered accountant
Nothing changes, because an LLP cannot have an individual chartered accountant holding a CoP as its partner
The position is worsened, because the LLP's earlier engagement letters must now be re-signed by the incoming individual partner
questions.explanation: The provision bars a company from practising as a chartered accountant and, for this purpose, company includes any LLP which has a company as its partner. The deeming limb is satisfied only so long as a company is a partner, so the replacement of Vertex Holdings Private Limited by individual members holding CoPs removes the basis on which the LLP was caught by this particular provision. The second option treats the inclusion as absolute rather than conditional on a company being a partner. The third invents a bar on an individual CoP holder being a partner in an LLP, which is not to be found in the provision, and the fourth addresses the mechanics of the earlier engagements rather than the question asked.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on the use of designations by members of the Institute:

1. A member in practice may use any other description he considers appropriate alongside the designation Chartered Accountant, provided he does not use it on professional documents or letterheads.
2. A member in practice may not use any designation other than Chartered Accountant, and may not use any title, letters or initials indicating membership of another professional body.
3. A member who is not in practice may use another description only if he is in the whole-time employment of a single employer.
4. A member in practice cannot use a designation other than Chartered Accountant, but use of titles, letters or initials such as C.A., C.S. or C.M.A. is permitted; a member who is not in practice and who does not use the designation Chartered Accountant may use another description.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement 4 correctly states both limbs of the rule: a member in practice is confined to the designation Chartered Accountant, yet the use of titles, letters or initials such as C.A., C.S. or C.M.A. is permitted, and a member not in practice who does not use the designation Chartered Accountant may use another description. Statement 1 is wrong because the prohibition on another designation applies to the member in practice and is not disapplied by keeping the description off professional documents. Statement 2 is right in its first half but wrong in its second, since titles, letters and initials indicating membership of other bodies are expressly allowed. Statement 3 superadds a whole-time employment condition that the rule does not contain.

questions.category: KYC Norms for CA in Practice
questions.question:
CA Ishita Bose is appointed statutory auditor of Meridian Textiles Pvt Ltd, a subsidiary of Meridian Global Ltd, of a partnership firm called Bose Traders, and of Mr Vikram Sethi, an individual carrying on business. Her articles clerk proposes the following for the KYC files: (1) to obtain the name of the parent company for all three clients; (2) to obtain the Company Identification Number, the names and addresses of the directors and the Directors' Identification Numbers for Meridian Textiles Pvt Ltd; (3) to obtain the copy of the last audited financial statements only from Meridian Textiles Pvt Ltd, on the ground that a partnership firm and an individual may not have audited financial statements; (4) to record the description of business and the type of engagement for all three clients.

Which of these proposals correctly apply the KYC norms approved by the Council of ICAI?
questions.explanation: Regulatory Information, comprising the Company Identification Number, the directors' names and addresses and the Directors' Identification Number, is required only in the case of a company, so proposal 2 is correctly directed to Meridian Textiles Pvt Ltd. Type of engagement is the whole of Engagement Information and, being required for every client, must be recorded for all three, while description of business is General Information along with the name and address of the individual, partner or entity and the copy of PAN, and is likewise to be obtained for a firm and an individual, so proposal 4 is correct. The name of the parent company in the case of a subsidiary is tagged in the norms as applicable only to a company, so extending it to a firm and an individual in proposal 1 is wrong. Copy of the last audited financial statements is General Information along with the name and address of the individual, partner or entity and the copy of PAN, and is not confined to companies, so proposal 3 is wrong.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on who is a chartered accountant in practice:

1. The expression covers a member of the Institute holding a CoP and also members who are deemed to be in practice.
2. A member is deemed to be in practice during the period he renders service with the armed forces.
3. The entire range of Management Consultancy and Other Services has been permitted by the Council pursuant to the limb which deems a member to be in practice when he engages himself in the practice of accountancy.
4. A member is deemed to be in practice where he merely offers to perform, as well as where he actually performs, a service involving the auditing or verification of financial transactions, books, accounts or records.

Which of the above statements is/are NOT correct?
questions.explanation: A practising chartered accountant is a member of the Institute holding a CoP, and the expression includes members deemed to be in practice, so statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 correctly reproduces the rule that a member is deemed to be in practice during the period he renders service with the armed forces. Statement 3 misidentifies the limb: the range of Management Consultancy and Other Services has been permitted by the Council pursuant to the residuary limb under which a member is deemed to be in practice when he renders such other services as, in the opinion of the Council, are rendered by a chartered accountant in practice, and not the limb relating to the practice of accountancy. Statement 4 is correct, because the relevant limb covers offering to perform as well as performing such services, and extends to preparation, verification or certification of financial accounting and holding out to the public as an accountant.

questions.question:
CA Vikram Sinha holds a CoP at Ranchi and is the statutory auditor of Tansen Steels Ltd for 2025-26. In the same year he does the following: (1) designs and implements a new financial information system for Tansen Steels Ltd for a fee of ₹ 60 lakh; (2) accepts a fee of ₹ 1.2 crore for acting as a Registered Valuer for the plant and machinery of an unrelated client; (3) opens an office at a place 70 km from the municipal limits of the city of Ranchi and keeps it in the charge of Mr D. K. Banerjee, a retired bank officer who is not a member of the Institute and who attends that office for 250 days in the year; (4) causes a name plate carrying only his own name with the designation Chartered Accountant to be fixed at his residence, his firm's board being displayed only at his office.

In how many and which of the above matters has Vikram contravened the provisions governing chartered accountants in practice?
questions.explanation: Item 1 is barred by section 144, which prohibits the company auditor from designing and implementing any financial information system for the company or its holding or subsidiary company. Item 2 is outside the permitted range, because the Registered Valuer permission covers valuation of securities or financial assets and not plant and machinery, and the size of the fee does not lend it legitimacy. Item 3 offends the requirement that each of more than one office in India be in the separate charge of a member of the Institute, the office being 70 km from the municipal limits of Ranchi and therefore outside the 50 km exemption, and being 250 days of attendance irrelevant because Mr Banerjee is not a member of the Institute at all. Item 4 is permissible, since there is no bar on a name board or name plate at the place of residence bearing the designation Chartered Accountant, provided it is that of an individual member and not of the firm.

questions.question:
CA Shalini Kale holds a CoP but has not signed a single audit report during the year. In that year she: (a) prepared and verified the books and accounts of two proprietary concerns for fees aggregating ₹ 3.4 lakh; (b) rendered assistance relating to the presentation and certification of financial facts and data to a third client; and (c) served with the armed forces for five months, during which she billed no professional fee. Her husband, CA Nitin Kale, is a member of the Institute who has not obtained a CoP and who has been asked by a business house to compile and certify its accounts, the work being one for which the business house would not require any special qualification.

Which is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
options: Shalini is in practice only for (a), since (b) is assistance rather than a service and (c) involves no client
Shalini is not in practice at all, because practice requires the actual signing of an audit report, and Nitin may accept the work since it needs no special qualification
Shalini holds a CoP and is in any event deemed to be in practice in respect of (a), (b) and (c)
Shalini is deemed to be in practice for (a) and (c), but not for (b), which is an administrative service requiring little or no professional judgement
questions.explanation: A chartered accountant in practice is a member of the Institute holding a CoP and includes members deemed to be in practice, so Shalini is in practice independently of whether she signed any audit report during the year. Work (a) falls within the limb covering offering to perform or performing services involving verification of financial transactions, books, accounts or records and the preparation or verification of financial accounting, and work (b) falls within the limb for professional services or assistance relating to the presentation or certification of financial facts or data. The deeming also extends to the period during which a member renders service with the armed forces, so the absence of billing in (c) is immaterial. Nitin's position is the opposite: a member without a CoP is precluded from accepting an engagement to render a service prescribed for a chartered accountant even where no special qualification is required.

questions.category: Schedules to the CA Act - Structure
questions.question:
Match each Part of the Schedules to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 given in Column I with its applicability, the number of clauses it contains and the type of misconduct it deals with, as set out in the table of Schedules to the Act in Column II, and select the correct answer.

Column I
A. First Schedule, Part I
B. First Schedule, Part IV
C. Second Schedule, Part II
D. Second Schedule, Part III

Column II
1. All chartered accountants; 2 clauses; Other misconduct
2. Chartered accountants in practice; 12 clauses; Professional misconduct
3. All chartered accountants; 5 clauses; Professional misconduct
4. All chartered accountants; 1 clause; Other misconduct
5. Chartered accountants in service; 2 clauses; Professional misconduct
questions.explanation: The Schedule table shows First Schedule Part I (CA in practice, 12 clauses, professional misconduct), Part II (CA in service, 2 clauses, professional), Part III (all CA, 3 clauses, professional) and Part IV (all CA, 2 clauses, other misconduct); Second Schedule Part I (CA in practice, 10 clauses, professional), Part II (all CA, 5 clauses, professional) and Part III (all CA, 1 clause, other misconduct). Hence A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4 is the only fully correct pairing. Item 5 in Column II describes First Schedule Part II, which is not called for in Column I, and the alternatives that use it are therefore wrong. The combination A-2/B-1/C-4/D-3 fails because Second Schedule Part II has 5 clauses of professional misconduct, not 1 clause of other misconduct. Note also that Part IV of the First Schedule and Part III of the Second Schedule are the only two Parts dealing with other misconduct.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements relating to the types of misconduct under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949:
I. Professional misconduct has been defined in Parts I, II and III of the First Schedule and in Parts I and II of the Second Schedule.
II. Other misconduct has been defined in Part IV of the First Schedule and in Part III of the Second Schedule.
III. A member can be inquired into and proceeded against only for misconduct arising out of his professional work, since the Schedules are confined to the practice of accountancy.
IV. A member is liable to disciplinary action under section 21 of the Chartered Accountants Act if he is found guilty of any professional or other misconduct.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I, II and IV reproduce the position exactly: professional misconduct occupies Parts I, II and III of the First Schedule and Parts I and II of the Second Schedule, other misconduct occupies Part IV of the First Schedule and Part III of the Second Schedule, and the consequence of being found guilty of either variety is disciplinary action under section 21. Statement III is the one that fails, because it denies the very reason for which the category of other misconduct was created. The other-misconduct provisions empower the Council to inquire into any misconduct of a member even if it does not arise out of his professional work, on the footing that a chartered accountant must maintain the highest standards of integrity even in his personal affairs. Any option that includes statement III is therefore wrong, however well the other statements in it are chosen.

questions.question:
Direction: In the questions below, an Assertion (A) is followed by a Reason (R). Mark the correct option.
(A): A chartered accountant who is in service and has no connection with practice can still be inquired into and held guilty under the disciplinary provisions of the Act in respect of an act wholly unconnected with his professional work.
(R): Other misconduct is defined in Part IV of the First Schedule and Part III of the Second Schedule, and these provisions apply only to members in practice, because only a member in practice comes into contact with the public.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
questions.explanation: The assertion is true: the other-misconduct provisions exist precisely so that the Council may inquire into misconduct even where it does not arise out of professional work, because a chartered accountant is expected to maintain the highest standards of integrity in his personal affairs as well. The reason, however, is false in a material particular. Part IV of the First Schedule and Part III of the Second Schedule are expressed to apply to a member of the Institute 'whether in practice or not', i.e., to members generally, and not only to members in practice. It is this general applicability, read with the disrepute rationale, that supports the assertion; the reason as framed contradicts the assertion it purports to explain. The first two options fail because R is untrue, and the last two fail because A is true and is explained by the general applicability of the other-misconduct provisions, not by the restricted statement made in R.

questions.question:
CA Giridhar Menon holds a certificate of practice and carries on a sole proprietary practice at Kochi. His childhood friend Mr. Ashok Pillai is a commerce graduate who has cleared six papers of the intermediate course; he holds no certificate of practice, is not a member of the Institute, and is neither a partner in nor an employee of Giridhar's firm. Ashok had for years been doing income-tax work in the locality on his own. In January 2024 Giridhar fell ill and, to keep the practice running, allowed Ashok to attend client meetings, to issue letters to clients and to put up a board outside the office describing the concern as 'G. Menon & Co., Chartered Accountants', while Giridhar himself continued to sign the audit reports. During the same period Giridhar also engaged Mr. Rajiv Shenoy, the legal representative of a deceased partner of another firm at Chennai, as a whole-time employee and paid him a monthly salary.
Which of the following is the MOST appropriate conclusion with reference to clause (1) of Part I of the First Schedule?
options: There is no contravention, because Giridhar himself continued to sign every audit report and Ashok merely carried on routine correspondence and attended client meetings on his behalf.
There is no contravention, because Ashok had been independently doing income-tax work in the locality for years before this arrangement, and the board merely reflected that established practice.

There is a contravention of clause (1) only on account of the engagement of Mr. Rajiv Shenoy as a whole-time employee, a legal representative of a deceased partner not being eligible to be employed by another chartered accountant.
There is a contravention of clause (1), since Ashok is neither a chartered accountant in practice nor a partner in or employee of the firm, yet he is allowed to practise in Giridhar's name.
There is a contravention of clause (1), because only a fellow of the Institute may be allowed to practise in a member's name and Ashok is at best an intermediate student.
questions.explanation: Clause (1) of Part I of the First Schedule permits a member to allow another person to practise in his name as a chartered accountant only if that person is himself a chartered accountant in practice and is in partnership with or employed by the first-mentioned member. Ashok fails both limbs - he is not a chartered accountant in practice and is not a partner in or employee of Giridhar's firm - and the name board and client correspondence amount to allowing him to practise in Giridhar's name. The fact that Giridhar signed the audit reports is not decisive, because the clause bites on allowing the person to practise in the member's name, not merely on signing. Ashok's earlier independent tax practice and the employment of Mr. Rajiv Shenoy are red herrings; employing a member's legal representative as a whole-time employee does not attract clause (1), and clause (1) says nothing about fellows - the fellow/associate distinction appears in clause (1) of Part III of the First Schedule.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I - Death of Sole Proprietor
questions.question:
CA Anant Krishnan (FCA) carried on a sole proprietary practice at Pune under the name 'A. Krishnan & Co.'. He died on 14 August 2023. His widow Smt. Meena Krishnan, a Company Secretary who does not hold a certificate of practice, and his brother are the legal heirs. On 2 September 2023, CA Sunita Balan, a sole practitioner at Mumbai, agreed to purchase the goodwill of 'A. Krishnan & Co.' for Rs. 18,00,000, the agreement providing for payment in six equal six-monthly instalments. On 20 October 2023, before the sale was completed, Meena and CA Sunita Balan shared the audit fees of four of Anant's former clients between themselves in the ratio 40:60. On 5 January 2024 a dispute arose between Meena and Anant's brother as to who was the rightful legal heir; the dispute was settled by a competent court on 10 February 2025. The goodwill sale in favour of CA Sunita Balan was ultimately completed on 25 July 2024.
Consider the following statements:
I. The sharing of audit fees between Meena and CA Sunita Balan on 20 October 2023 is permissible, because the legal representative of a deceased proprietor stands in the same position as the legal representative of a deceased partner.
II. Payment of the Rs. 18,00,000 goodwill consideration in six equal instalments is permissible, since the sale agreement provides for it.
III. The goodwill could be sold or transferred to CA Sunita Balan only if the sale was completed within one year of Anant's death, and on these facts the sale completed on 25 July 2024 is within time.
IV. Meena, as legal heir, had to obtain the permission of the Council within one year of the death of the proprietor.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements II, III and IV are correct. There is no sharing of fees between the legal representative and the purchaser of the goodwill on the death of a sole proprietor, so the 20 October 2023 division of audit fees is impermissible and statement I is wrong; the proprietorship case is deliberately kept distinct from the partnership case, in which the legal representative of a deceased partner may continue to receive a share only where the partnership deed so provides. The instalment feature is protected, because goodwill payment may be made in instalments if the sale agreement so provides. The sale was completed on 25 July 2024, within one year of the death on 14 August 2023, so the transfer to another chartered accountant is validly made, and the legal heir had to obtain the Council's permission within one year of the proprietor's death. The decisive fact for statement I is therefore the identity of the transferee as purchaser of goodwill, not the widow's qualification as a Company Secretary.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I - Death of Sole Proprietor
questions.question:
CA Anant Krishnan (FCA) carried on a sole proprietary practice at Pune under the name 'A. Krishnan & Co.'. He died on 14 August 2023. His widow Smt. Meena Krishnan, a Company Secretary who does not hold a certificate of practice, and his brother are the legal heirs. On 2 September 2023, CA Sunita Balan, a sole practitioner at Mumbai, agreed to purchase the goodwill of 'A. Krishnan & Co.' for Rs. 18,00,000, the agreement providing for payment in six equal six-monthly instalments. On 20 October 2023, before the sale was completed, Meena and CA Sunita Balan shared the audit fees of four of Anant's former clients between themselves in the ratio 40:60. On 5 January 2024 a dispute arose between Meena and Anant's brother as to who was the rightful legal heir; the dispute was settled by a competent court on 10 February 2025. The goodwill sale in favour of CA Sunita Balan was ultimately completed on 25 July 2024.
Which of the following statements correctly describes the period up to which the name of the concern 'A. Krishnan & Co.' may be kept in abeyance, that is, not removed?
options: Up to one year from 20 October 2023, being the date on which the audit fees were shared between the legal heir and the purchaser of goodwill.
Up to one year from 25 July 2024, being the date on which the sale of goodwill was completed.
Up to one year from 14 August 2023 only, because the period of one year invariably runs from the date of the proprietor's death irrespective of any dispute between the persons claiming to be heirs.
Indefinitely, so long as the legal heir continues to receive a share in the fees of the practice.
Up to one year from 14 August 2023; but where there is a dispute regarding the legal heir, one year from settlement of the dispute, that is, from 10 February 2025.
questions.explanation: The name of the concern is kept in abeyance, and not removed, only up to one year from the death of the proprietor; where, however, there is a dispute regarding the legal heir, the period of one year runs from the settlement of the dispute, which on these facts is 10 February 2025. The dates of fee sharing and of completion of the goodwill sale are irrelevant to this particular period, so the first two options are wrong. The option which insists that the period must always run from the date of death ignores the express dispute carve-out, and the option permitting indefinite abeyance fails twice over, because the protection is limited to one year and because the sharing of fees between the legal representative and the purchaser of goodwill is itself impermissible. Note the contrast: the Council's permission and the completion of the sale of goodwill are measured from the date of death, and not from settlement of the dispute.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I - Fee and Profit Sharing
questions.question:
CA Anant Krishnan (FCA) carried on a sole proprietary practice at Pune under the name 'A. Krishnan & Co.'. He died on 14 August 2023. His widow Smt. Meena Krishnan, a Company Secretary who does not hold a certificate of practice, and his brother are the legal heirs. On 2 September 2023, CA Sunita Balan, a sole practitioner at Mumbai, agreed to purchase the goodwill of 'A. Krishnan & Co.' for Rs. 18,00,000, the agreement providing for payment in six equal six-monthly instalments. On 20 October 2023, before the sale was completed, Meena and CA Sunita Balan shared the audit fees of four of Anant's former clients between themselves in the ratio 40:60. On 5 January 2024 a dispute arose between Meena and Anant's brother as to who was the rightful legal heir; the dispute was settled by a competent court on 10 February 2025. The goodwill sale in favour of CA Sunita Balan was ultimately completed on 25 July 2024.
Assume now that instead of being a sole proprietor, Anant Krishnan had been a partner in the three-partner firm 'Krishnan, Desai & Co.', and that the firm's partnership deed was entirely silent as to the rights of the legal representatives of a deceased partner. On Anant's death Meena continues to receive a 25% share in the profits of the firm for two years, and no part of the fees of the firm's professional business is paid to any outsider.
Which of the following is the MOST appropriate conclusion on this modified fact?
options: Meena may continue to receive the share, because the legal representative of a deceased partner is in every case entitled to a share of the firm for one year from the date of the partner's death.
Meena may not receive any share, because a share in the profits of professional business may be paid only to a member of the Institute who holds a certificate of practice.
Meena may continue to receive the share only if the partnership deed contains a provision enabling this; the deed being silent, the exception is unavailable and the sharing is not supported.
Meena may continue to receive the share, because a Company Secretary is one of the members of other professional bodies prescribed under Regulation 53A.
Meena may not receive any share, because profit sharing with the legal representative of a deceased partner is permitted only where the deceased was a sole proprietor.
questions.explanation: Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule lists the legal representative of a deceased partner among the persons to whom a share in the fees or profits of professional business may be paid, but the study position adds the condition that in a partnership firm the legal representative of a deceased partner can continue to receive a share of the firm only if the deed contains such a provision. A silent deed therefore defeats the continuation, which is the decisive fact in the modified question. The first option invents a uniform one-year entitlement; the one-year periods in the source belong to the proprietorship case (Council permission, completion of the goodwill sale and keeping the name in abeyance) and not to a partner's legal representative. The option which confines payment to members holding a certificate of practice misstates the permitted class, and the option founded on Meena's Company Secretary qualification misapplies Regulation 53A, because the legal representative of a deceased partner is permitted in his or her own right and not by reason of any professional qualification, no professional service being rendered by her. The last option reverses the position, since it is the proprietorship case that prohibits sharing between the legal representative and the purchaser of goodwill.

questions.question:
CA Deepa Nair holds a certificate of practice and runs a sole proprietary practice at Bengaluru. During 2023-24 the following five arrangements were in place.
(i) She received Rs. 75,000 from CA Harish Rao, a member in practice at Mangaluru, for having referred the statutory audit of a mining company to him.
(ii) She paid 12% of the fees of one assignment to Mr. Vikram Shetty, a Fellow of the Institute of Actuaries of India, who worked with her in designing an actuarial valuation model for a client.
(iii) She paid 8% of the fees of a management consultancy assignment to Mrs. Rukmini Iyer, who holds an MBA degree from a university established by law and who assisted her in preparing a project report.
(iv) She paid 10% of the fees of a GST assignment to Mr. Salim Bhai, a property dealer who is not a member of any professional body, for having procured the client for her.
(v) In the audit of a State Co-operative Society she shared a portion of the audit fee of Rs. 3,60,000 with the State treasury, as provided in the relevant State enactment.
Which of the above arrangements contravene clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949?
questions.explanation: Clause (2) prohibits paying, allowing or agreeing to pay, directly or indirectly, any share, commission or brokerage in the fees or profits of the professional business to anyone other than a member of the Institute, a partner, a retired partner, the legal representative of a deceased partner, or a member of another professional body or other person having a prescribed qualification. Mr. Salim Bhai falls in none of these classes, so arrangement (iv) alone contravenes the clause. An Actuary (Institute of Actuaries of India) and an MBA from a university established or recognised by law are both on the Regulation 53A list, so (ii) and (iii) are protected. Sharing or payment of audit fees with the State treasury in the audit of State Cooperative Societies is expressly allowed, so (v) is protected. Arrangement (i) is a receipt, not a payment, and the charging of referral fees, that is, fees obtained by a member in practice from another member in practice for referring a client to him, is not prohibited.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I - Clauses (2) and (3)
questions.question:
CA Deepa Nair holds a certificate of practice and runs a sole proprietary practice at Bengaluru. During 2023-24 the following five arrangements were in place.
(i) She received Rs. 75,000 from CA Harish Rao, a member in practice at Mangaluru, for having referred the statutory audit of a mining company to him.
(ii) She paid 12% of the fees of one assignment to Mr. Vikram Shetty, a Fellow of the Institute of Actuaries of India, who worked with her in designing an actuarial valuation model for a client.
(iii) She paid 8% of the fees of a management consultancy assignment to Mrs. Rukmini Iyer, who holds an MBA degree from a university established by law and who assisted her in preparing a project report.
(iv) She paid 10% of the fees of a GST assignment to Mr. Salim Bhai, a property dealer who is not a member of any professional body, for having procured the client for her.
(v) In the audit of a State Co-operative Society she shared a portion of the audit fee of Rs. 3,60,000 with the State treasury, as provided in the relevant State enactment.
Consider the following statements:
Statement 1: Arrangement (i) is not prohibited, because charging of referral fees, that is, fees obtained by a member in practice from another member in practice in relation to referring a client to him, is not prohibited.
Statement 2: Had CA Harish Rao not been a member of the Institute, the Rs. 75,000 received in (i) would attract clause (3) of Part I of the First Schedule, and could be supported by its proviso only if Harish Rao were a member of such professional body or other person having the qualifications referred to in clause (2).
Statement 3: Arrangement (iii) is permissible, because an MBA degree from a university established or recognised by law is one of the qualifications prescribed under Regulation 53A.
Statement 4: Arrangement (ii) is impermissible, because an Actuary is recognised for the purposes of partnership under Regulation 53B alone and not for the purposes of sharing fees under Regulation 53A.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Referral fees obtained by a member in practice from another member in practice are expressly stated not to be prohibited, which disposes of statement 1. Clause (3) prohibits accepting or agreeing to accept any part of the profits of professional work of a person who is not a member of the Institute, and its only relief is the proviso permitting profit-sharing or similar arrangements, including receiving a share, commission or brokerage in the fees, with a member of such professional body or other person having the qualifications referred to in clause (2); hence statement 2 is a correct statement of the mechanism. Regulation 53A does include an MBA from a university or institution established or recognised by law, so statement 3 is correct. Statement 4 fails because the Institute of Actuaries of India appears in both Regulation 53A and Regulation 53B lists, so an Actuary is eligible both to be paid a share in fees and to be taken into partnership.

questions.question:
CA Deepa Nair holds a certificate of practice and runs a sole proprietary practice at Bengaluru. During 2023-24 the following five arrangements were in place.
(i) She received Rs. 75,000 from CA Harish Rao, a member in practice at Mangaluru, for having referred the statutory audit of a mining company to him.
(ii) She paid 12% of the fees of one assignment to Mr. Vikram Shetty, a Fellow of the Institute of Actuaries of India, who worked with her in designing an actuarial valuation model for a client.
(iii) She paid 8% of the fees of a management consultancy assignment to Mrs. Rukmini Iyer, who holds an MBA degree from a university established by law and who assisted her in preparing a project report.
(iv) She paid 10% of the fees of a GST assignment to Mr. Salim Bhai, a property dealer who is not a member of any professional body, for having procured the client for her.
(v) In the audit of a State Co-operative Society she shared a portion of the audit fee of Rs. 3,60,000 with the State treasury, as provided in the relevant State enactment.
A colleague complains that Deepa has contravened clause (5) of Part I of the First Schedule in respect of arrangements (ii), (iii) and (iv). Which of the following is the MOST appropriate conclusion on the complaint?
options: Clause (5) is contravened by (ii), (iii) and (iv) alike, because each of those assignments involved the services of a person who was neither Deepa's employee nor her partner at the relevant time.
Clause (5) is contravened by (iv) alone, because the proviso to clause (5) does not prohibit any agreement permitted in items (2), (3) and (4) of Part I, and (ii) and (iii) are such agreements.
Clause (5) is contravened by (iv) and (v), because the State treasury is neither a member of the Institute nor a partner of Deepa and is therefore a person falling outside the permitted class.
Clause (5) is contravened by none of them, because that clause operates only where professional business is secured through the services of another chartered accountant in practice.
Clause (5) is not contravened by (iv), because a payment which is already dealt with by clause (2) of Part I cannot simultaneously fall within clause (5) of Part I.
questions.explanation: Clause (5) prohibits securing professional business either through the services of a person who is not an employee of the chartered accountant or not his partner, or by means which are not open to a chartered accountant, subject to the proviso that nothing in it prohibits any agreement permitted in items (2), (3) and (4) of Part I. Arrangements (ii) and (iii) are agreements permitted by item (2), because an Actuary and an MBA from a university established by law are on the Regulation 53A list, and are therefore protected by the proviso. Arrangement (iv) is not so protected, since a property dealer who is not a member of any professional body is outside clause (2), and the GST assignment was secured through his services; clause (5) is accordingly attracted. The complaint does not extend to arrangement (v), which in any event involves sharing of audit fees with the State treasury in the audit of a State Cooperative Society, an arrangement expressly allowed. The last option is wrong because the same set of facts can contravene both clause (2) and clause (5).

questions.category: First Schedule Part II - Members in Service
questions.question:
CA Naveen Verma is employed as Group Finance Controller of Vardhman Spinning Mills Ltd. and does not hold a certificate of practice. The following are facts of the year 2023-24.
(a) He agreed to pay 15% of his monthly emoluments of Rs. 2,60,000 to Mr. J. P. Gupta, a retired banker who was a director on the board that approved his appointment, as a mark of thanks for having helped him secure the job.
(b) He transfers Rs. 45,000 every month to his aged parents and Rs. 20,000 every month to his younger brother; neither amount is a consideration for procuring the job nor is it paid on account of any retainership.
(c) He received Rs. 1,50,000 by way of commission from the stock broker engaged by the company, for facilitating the company's commercial paper issue.
(d) He received Rs. 60,000 by way of gratification from a purchasing agent of the company at the time of renewal of the company's coal supply contract.
(e) He agreed to pay 5% of his emoluments to CA Seema Joshi, a member in practice engaged as an advisor to the company, for having introduced him to a part-time lectureship.
Which of the above facts constitute professional misconduct under Part II of the First Schedule of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949?
options: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only, on the footing that a regular monthly transfer to a brother's account is a payment of a share in emoluments to a person.
(c) and (d) only, since clause (1) of Part II reaches only payments actually made and not an agreement to pay a share of future emoluments.
(a), (b) and (e) only, because commission received from a broker engaged by the company is outside clause (2) of Part II.
(a), (c) and (d) only, since the agreement with CA Seema Joshi related to a lectureship and not to the employment undertaken by Naveen.
questions.explanation: Part II of the First Schedule applies to a member of the Institute other than a member in practice who is an employee of a company, firm or person. Clause (1) prohibits paying, allowing or agreeing to pay, directly or indirectly, to any person any share in the emoluments of the employment undertaken by him, which covers (a) and (e), the payments being made to persons who are neither relatives nor dependants and being linked to the procurement of the job or of the lectureship. Clause (2) prohibits accepting or agreeing to accept any part of fees, profits or gains from a lawyer, a chartered accountant or a broker engaged by such company, firm or person, or an agent or customer of such company, firm or person, by way of commission or gratification, which covers (c) and (d). Fact (b) is outside the prohibition, because the additional point under clause (1) expressly does not restrict sharing among relatives, dependants or friends where the payment is not a consideration for job procurement or retainership. Any option that drops (e) overlooks that a share in emoluments paid to a member in practice is still a share in emoluments.

questions.category: First Schedule Parts I and II - Applicability
questions.question:
CA Naveen Verma is employed as Group Finance Controller of Vardhman Spinning Mills Ltd. and does not hold a certificate of practice. During 2023-24 he agreed to pay 15% of his monthly emoluments of Rs. 2,60,000 to Mr. J. P. Gupta, a retired banker who was a director on the board that approved his appointment, as a mark of thanks for having helped him secure the job. In April 2024 Naveen obtains a certificate of practice, resigns from the company and starts practice at Indore. He nonetheless continues to pay Mr. J. P. Gupta 15% of the fees of his professional business, Gupta having by then retired from all activity and rendered no service of any description to Naveen.
Which of the following is the MOST appropriate analysis of Naveen's position in his new capacity?
options: Clause (2) of Part I is contravened, since a member in practice paying a share in the fees or profits of his professional business to a person outside the permitted class falls squarely within that clause.

Clause (1) of Part II of the First Schedule continues to apply, because Part II governs every member of the Institute whether in practice or not and does not turn on the holding of a certificate of practice.
No clause is contravened, because Gupta having ceased to be a director of the company, the payment can no longer be characterised as a consideration for the procurement of any job or engagement.
Part IV of the First Schedule alone is attracted, because a payment made to a person wholly outside the profession cannot amount to professional misconduct and can only amount to other misconduct.

Clause (2) of Part II of the First Schedule is contravened, since Gupta must be treated as an agent of the person who earlier engaged Naveen, and payments made to such an agent are within that clause.
questions.explanation: Once Naveen holds a certificate of practice and is in practice, Part II of the First Schedule, which is expressly directed to a member other than a member in practice, no longer governs him; the applicable provision is clause (2) of Part I. Mr. J. P. Gupta is not a member of the Institute, not a partner or retired partner of Naveen's firm, not the legal representative of a deceased partner, and is not shown to be a member of any of the professional bodies or to hold any qualification prescribed under Regulation 53A, so the payment of 15% of professional fees is squarely within the prohibition. The alternative founded on clause (1) of Part II misreads the scope of that Part, and the alternative founded on clause (2) of Part II fails for the same reason and also because Gupta was never an agent of the employer. The cessation-of-directorship argument is irrelevant once the payment is of professional fees and is governed by Part I, and Part IV cannot be invoked to excuse conduct expressly covered as professional misconduct by clause (2) of Part I.

questions.category: First Schedule Part III - Members Generally
questions.question:
CA Prem Subramaniam obtained his certificate of practice in 2021 and has been in continuous practice at Hyderabad since then; he became an Associate member of the Institute in 2018 and is not a Fellow. The following are separate and independent facts about him.
P. He prints 'FCA' before his name on his visiting cards and letter heads.
Q. In February 2024 the Regional Council of the Institute wrote to him seeking confirmation of the date on which he had left his employment with a manufacturing company; he did not reply for eleven months and no cause was shown for the delay.
R. While applying for his certificate of practice he left un-filled the columns relating to his engagement in other business, although the information was required to be submitted online within the stipulated time.
S. While responding to a tender floated by a State Public Financial Institution for its statutory audit, he stated that his firm had completed 46 audit assignments when he knew the correct number to be 14.
T. In 2025 a criminal court held him guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of three months, and imposed only a fine on him.
U. In the same month he withdrew Rs. 4,50,000 from a bank account at Secunderabad, being money which did not belong to him.
Which of the following correctly identifies the provision(s) of the First Schedule contravened by facts P, Q and S respectively?
options: P - Part III clause (3); Q - Part III clause (2); S - Part IV clause (2)
P - Part III clause (1); Q - Part IV clause (2); S - Part III clause (3)
P - Part II clause (1); Q - Part III clause (2); S - Part IV clause (1)
P - Part III clause (1); Q - Part III clause (2); S - Part III clause (3)
P - Part III clause (1); Q - Part III clause (3); S - Part III clause (2)
questions.explanation: All three of P, Q and S fall in Part III of the First Schedule, which deals with members of the Institute generally, whether in practice or not. Clause (1) of Part III covers not being a fellow of the Institute and yet acting as a fellow, which is what printing 'FCA' amounts to; clause (2) covers not supplying information called for, or not complying with requirements asked for, by the Institute, Council or any of its Committees, the Director (Discipline), the Board of Discipline, the Disciplinary Committee, the Quality Review Board or the Appellate Authority, and failure to reply to letters of the Institute asking the member to confirm the date of leaving service is one of the worked illustrations; clause (3) covers giving information knowing it to be false while responding to tenders or enquiries. The trap in the second option is Q: non-reply to a letter from public authorities, as opposed to a letter from the Institute or its organs, is illustrated as other misconduct under Part IV clause (2), so it is the identity of the addressee that decides between clause (2) of Part III and clause (2) of Part IV. Fact R, on similar reasoning, is clause (2) of Part III and not Part IV.

questions.category: First Schedule Part IV - Other Misconduct
questions.question:
CA Prem Subramaniam obtained his certificate of practice in 2021 and has been in continuous practice at Hyderabad since then; he became an Associate member of the Institute in 2018 and is not a Fellow. The following are separate and independent facts about him.
P. He prints 'FCA' before his name on his visiting cards and letter heads.
Q. In February 2024 the Regional Council of the Institute wrote to him seeking confirmation of the date on which he had left his employment with a manufacturing company; he did not reply for eleven months and no cause was shown for the delay.
R. While applying for his certificate of practice he left un-filled the columns relating to his engagement in other business, although the information was required to be submitted online within the stipulated time.
S. While responding to a tender floated by a State Public Financial Institution for its statutory audit, he stated that his firm had completed 46 audit assignments when he knew the correct number to be 14.
T. In 2025 a criminal court held him guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of three months, and imposed only a fine on him.
U. In the same month he withdrew Rs. 4,50,000 from a bank account at Secunderabad, being money which did not belong to him.
Which of the following is the MOST appropriate classification of facts T and U?
options: T is professional misconduct under Part III of the First Schedule, and U is other misconduct under clause (2) of Part IV of the First Schedule.
T is other misconduct under clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule, because the court awarded a fine and not imprisonment; U is other misconduct under clause (2) of Part IV.
Both T and U are other misconduct under clause (1) of Part IV of the First Schedule, because neither of the two acts has any connection with his professional work.
T is professional misconduct, an offence of this nature not being contemplated by Part IV at all; U is other misconduct under clause (2) of Part IV.
T is other misconduct under clause (1) of Part IV, the test being the term of imprisonment with which the offence is punishable; U is other misconduct under clause (2) of Part IV.
questions.explanation: Clause (1) of Part IV of the First Schedule covers a member being held guilty by any civil or criminal court of an offence which is punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months. The offence in T is punishable with three months' imprisonment, which is within that ceiling, and the clause attaches to the nature of the offence and to the fact of being held guilty, not to whether imprisonment was in fact awarded, so the fine-only sentence is a red herring. Clause (2) of Part IV covers conduct which in the opinion of the Council brings disrepute to the profession or the Institute as a result of an action whether or not related to professional work, and withdrawing money from a bank which does not belong to the member is one of the illustrations given under it, which is why U is clause (2) and not clause (1). Had the offence in T been punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months, it would have been other misconduct under clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule instead. Nothing in Part III of the First Schedule makes T professional misconduct, since that Part is confined to acting as a fellow, non-compliance with calls for information, and giving false information while inviting work or responding to tenders.

questions.category: First Schedule Part IV - Other Misconduct
questions.question:
CA Prem Subramaniam obtained his certificate of practice in 2021 and has been in continuous practice at Hyderabad since then; he became an Associate member of the Institute in 2018 and is not a Fellow. The following are separate and independent facts about him.
P. He prints 'FCA' before his name on his visiting cards and letter heads.
Q. In February 2024 the Regional Council of the Institute wrote to him seeking confirmation of the date on which he had left his employment with a manufacturing company; he did not reply for eleven months and no cause was shown for the delay.
R. While applying for his certificate of practice he left un-filled the columns relating to his engagement in other business, although the information was required to be submitted online within the stipulated time.
S. While responding to a tender floated by a State Public Financial Institution for its statutory audit, he stated that his firm had completed 46 audit assignments when he knew the correct number to be 14.
T. In 2025 a criminal court held him guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of three months, and imposed only a fine on him.
U. In the same month he withdrew Rs. 4,50,000 from a bank account at Secunderabad, being money which did not belong to him.
Consider the following further statements about Prem:
Statement 1: Fact U is an illustration of conduct bringing disrepute under clause (2) of Part IV of the First Schedule, and it is immaterial that the act has nothing to do with his professional work.
Statement 2: Had Prem, being an auditor, used his position to obtain funds from a bank and failed to repay the same, the conduct would be professional misconduct under Part I of the First Schedule and not other misconduct.
Statement 3: Had Prem retained a client's books and documents and failed to return them on request without any cause, that would fall within clause (2) of Part IV of the First Schedule.
Statement 4: Had Prem failed to reply within a reasonable time and without any cause to a letter from public authorities, that would fall within clause (2) of Part III of the First Schedule.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is correct because clause (2) of Part IV of the First Schedule brands as other misconduct any action of a member which in the opinion of the Council brings disrepute to the profession or the Institute, whether or not the action is related to his professional work, and withdrawing money from a bank which does not belong to him is one of the listed illustrations. Statement 3 is likewise correct, since retaining a client's books and documents and failing to return them on request without any cause is also one of the listed illustrations under the same clause. Statement 2 is wrong because an auditor using his position to obtain funds and failing to repay them to the bank is itself enumerated as an illustration of other misconduct under clause (2) of Part IV, not as professional misconduct in Part I. Statement 4 is wrong on the identity of the correspondent: failure to reply to a letter from public authorities within a reasonable time and without cause is an illustration under clause (2) of Part IV, whereas clause (2) of Part III takes non-compliance with information called for by the Institute, Council, its Committees, Director (Discipline), Board of Discipline, Disciplinary Committee, Quality Review Board or the Appellate Authority.

questions.question:
CA Meenal Deshpande (FCA), practising at Nagpur, proposes to constitute a new firm with effect from 1 April 2024. Four proposals are before her.
Proposal 1: A partnership with Mr. K. Raghu, a Company Secretary (ICSI), and Ms. Sneha Kulkarni, an Advocate enrolled with the Bar Council of India.
Proposal 2: A partnership with Mr. Aditya Rao, who holds an MBA (Marketing) degree from a university established by law and who heads the proposed firm's business-development function.
Proposal 3: A partnership with Mr. Ganesh Iyengar, a mechanical Engineer, and Mr. Praveen Menon, an Actuary of the Institute of Actuaries of India.
Proposal 4: A partnership with Mr. Sameer Qureshi, a resident of India living and working in Dubai who, but for his residence abroad, would have been entitled to be registered as a member under section 4(1)(v) of the Act.
Which of these proposals for partnership are permissible under clause (4) of Part I of the First Schedule read with the prescribed list in Regulation 53B?
questions.explanation: Clause (4) of Part I of the First Schedule prohibits a chartered accountant in practice from entering into partnership, in or outside India, with any person other than a chartered accountant in practice or a member of another professional body having such qualifications as may be prescribed, and expressly includes a resident who but for his residence abroad would be entitled to be registered as a member under section 4(1)(v) or whose qualifications are recognised by the Central Government or the Council. The Regulation 53B list is CS (ICSI), CMA (ICMAI), Advocate (Bar Council of India), Architect (Indian Institute of Architects), Actuary (Institute of Actuaries of India) and Engineer, so Proposals 1 and 3 are covered and Proposal 4 is covered by the express inclusion for the NRI resident. Proposal 2 fails because an MBA is not in the Regulation 53B list; an MBA is recognised only under Regulation 53A, which governs sharing of fees and not partnership. The contrast between the two lists is the decisive point in this question.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I - Clauses (2), (4) and (5)
questions.question:
CA Meenal Deshpande (FCA), practising at Nagpur, is advised that Mr. Aditya Rao, who holds an MBA (Marketing) degree from a university established by law, cannot be taken as her partner. She therefore drops that proposal and instead enters into an arrangement with Mr. Aditya Rao under which he is paid 9% of the fees of assignments on which he assists in preparing project reports and feasibility studies. Separately, Meenal secures the statutory audit of a large textile exporter through the services of Mr. Vithal, a retired bank officer who is neither her employee nor her partner, and pays him 15% of the first year's fees.
Which of the following is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
options: Both arrangements are permissible, because Regulation 53A and Regulation 53B prescribe the same set of professional bodies and qualifications for both purposes.

Both arrangements are impermissible, because a share in the fees of professional business may be paid only to a member of the Institute, a partner, a retired partner or the legal representative of a deceased partner.

The arrangement with Mr. Aditya Rao is permissible under Regulation 53A, which recognises an MBA from a university established or recognised by law for sharing of fees, while the payment to Mr. Vithal is not, and clause (5) is additionally attracted.
The arrangement with Mr. Aditya Rao is impermissible, since an MBA is recognised for the purposes of partnership under Regulation 53B but not for the purposes of sharing of fees under Regulation 53A.
The arrangement with Mr. Vithal is permissible, because the proviso to clause (5) saves any agreement entered into by a member for the purpose of securing professional business for his firm.
questions.explanation: Regulation 53A, which supports sharing of fees or profits of professional business under clause (2) of Part I, includes an MBA and a Bachelor in Engineering, Technology or Law from a university or institution established or recognised by law, whereas Regulation 53B, which governs partnership under clause (4), lists CS, CMA, Advocate, Architect, Actuary and Engineer and does not include an MBA. Mr. Aditya Rao is therefore a permissible recipient of a share in fees but an impermissible partner, which is exactly why the partnership proposal was dropped. Mr. Vithal is outside both lists, so the payment of 15% of fees to him contravenes clause (2), and because the audit business was secured through his services, clause (5) is independently attracted. The last option misreads the proviso to clause (5), which protects only agreements permitted in items (2), (3) and (4) of Part I and not agreements for securing business generally. The second option omits the class of members of other professional bodies and persons with prescribed qualifications, and the fourth reverses the two Regulation lists.

questions.category: First Schedule Part IV - Other Misconduct
questions.question: All of the following have been illustrated in the study material as conduct bringing disrepute to the profession or the Institute under clause (2) of Part IV of the First Schedule, EXCEPT:
options: A member's cheques being dishonoured due to insufficiency of funds.
A member, not being a fellow of the Institute, acting as a fellow of the Institute.
Personal benefit taken by a council member of the Institute.
A member advising an unethical practice to his client.
A member retaining the books and documents of a client and failing to return them on request without any cause.
questions.explanation: Clause (2) of Part IV of the First Schedule, which deals with other misconduct arising from conduct bringing disrepute to the profession or the Institute whether or not related to professional work, is illustrated in the source by an auditor using his position to obtain funds and failing to repay them to the bank, cheques dishonoured for insufficiency of funds, withdrawing money from a bank which does not belong to the member, retaining a client's books and documents and failing to return them on request without cause, personal benefit taken by a council member of the Institute, not replying within a reasonable time and without cause to a letter from public authorities, and advising an unethical practice to the client. Not being a fellow of the Institute and yet acting as a fellow is not one of them: it is clause (1) of Part III of the First Schedule and is therefore professional misconduct, not other misconduct. This is the only option in the list whose characterisation as professional rather than other misconduct changes, which is why it is the correct exception. Note that the retention of client's books appears in Part IV as other misconduct even though it arises directly out of a professional assignment, because clause (2) reaches acts whether or not related to professional work.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I - Clauses (1) to (4)
questions.question:
Match the provisions in Column I with the correct statement of the clause or its exception in Column II and select the correct answer.

Column I
A. Clause (1) of Part I of the First Schedule
B. Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule
C. Clause (3) of Part I of the First Schedule
D. Clause (4) of Part I of the First Schedule

Column II
1. Prohibits accepting or agreeing to accept any part of the profits of professional work of a person who is not a member of the Institute, subject to a proviso permitting profit sharing or similar arrangements, including receiving a share, commission or brokerage in the fees, with a member of such professional body or other person having the qualifications referred to in clause (2).
2. Prohibits allowing any person to practise in the chartered accountant's name as a chartered accountant, unless that person is also a chartered accountant in practice and is in partnership with or employed by him.
3. Prohibits entering into partnership, in or outside India, with any person other than a chartered accountant in practice or a member of any other professional body having such qualifications as may be prescribed, including a resident who but for his residence abroad would be entitled to be registered as a member under section 4(1)(v).
4. Prohibits paying or allowing, or agreeing to pay or allow, directly or indirectly, any share, commission or brokerage in the fees or profits of the professional business to any person other than a member of the Institute, a partner, a retired partner, the legal representative of a deceased partner, or a member of another professional body or other person having prescribed qualifications.
5. Prohibits securing professional business either through the services of a person who is not an employee or not a partner of the chartered accountant, or by means which are not open to a chartered accountant.
questions.explanation: Clause (1) is about allowing a person to practise in the member's name; clause (2) is the outgoing side of money, that is, paying or allowing a share, commission or brokerage in the fees or profits of professional business; clause (3) is the incoming side, accepting part of the profits of professional work of a non-member, with its proviso aligned to the class permitted by clause (2); and clause (4) is partnership, which expressly includes the resident who but for residence abroad would be entitled to be registered under section 4(1)(v). Item 5 in Column II describes clause (5) of Part I, which is not called for in Column I, and any combination using it is wrong. The frequent error visible in the distractors is interchanging statements 1 and 4, that is, treating the clause which prohibits paying out as the one which prohibits receiving; the direction of payment is the decisive test.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the professional bodies and qualifications prescribed under Regulation 53A and Regulation 53B is NOT correct?
options: Regulation 53A prescribes CS (ICSI), CMA (ICMAI), Advocate (Bar Council of India), Architect (Indian Institute of Architects), Actuary (Institute of Actuaries of India), MBA, and Bachelor in Engineering, Technology or Law from a university or institution established or recognised by law.
Regulation 53B prescribes CS (ICSI), CMA (ICMAI), Advocate (Bar Council of India), Architect (Indian Institute of Architects), Actuary (Institute of Actuaries of India) and Engineer.
The distinction between the two lists is that Regulation 53A additionally recognises an Engineer, while Regulation 53B additionally recognises an MBA and a Bachelor in Engineering, Technology or Law.
A Fellow of the Institute of Actuaries of India is eligible both to be paid a share in the fees or profits of professional business and to be taken as a partner by a chartered accountant in practice.

A person holding an MBA degree from a university established by law may be paid a share in the fees of professional business, but cannot on that qualification alone be taken as a partner by a chartered accountant in practice.
questions.explanation: The third statement reverses the two lists. Regulation 53A, which supports the sharing of fees or profits under clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule, is the wider academic list and includes MBA and Bachelor in Engineering, Technology or Law from a university or institution established or recognised by law, while Regulation 53B, which governs partnership under clause (4), substitutes Engineer for those academic qualifications and omits MBA. The remaining statements follow from this: the Actuary appears in both lists and is therefore eligible for both purposes, and an MBA is eligible for fee sharing but not for partnership on that qualification alone. The question asks for the statement which is not correct, so the true descriptions of the two lists are the wrong answers here. The single decisive fact to retain is that 53A contains MBA and the Bachelor's degrees while 53B contains Engineer and no MBA.

questions.category: First Schedule Part III - Members Generally
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about clause (2) of Part III of the First Schedule of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949:
I. The clause is contravened where a member does not supply the information called for, or does not comply with the requirements asked for, by the Institute, the Council or any of its Committees, the Director (Discipline), the Board of Discipline, the Disciplinary Committee, the Quality Review Board or the Appellate Authority.
II. Failure to furnish information required by the Institute to be submitted online within the stipulated time is an instance of misconduct under this clause.
III. Not replying within a reasonable time and without any cause to a letter received from public authorities is an instance of misconduct under this clause.
IV. Failure to reply to letters of the Institute asking the member to confirm the date of his appointment or the date of leaving service as an employee is an instance of misconduct under this clause.
V. The study material appends the reference 'SACHIN & ATUL AGARWAL (AIR 1)' against Part III of the First Schedule.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: I, II, III and IV only
I, II, IV and V only
II, III, IV and V only
I, II, III, IV and V
questions.explanation: Clause (2) of Part III of the First Schedule obliges a member, whether in practice or not, to supply information called for and comply with requirements asked for by the enumerated authorities, namely the Institute, the Council or any of its Committees, the Director (Discipline), the Board of Discipline, the Disciplinary Committee, the Quality Review Board and the Appellate Authority. The two illustrations worked out in the source under this clause are failure to reply to letters of the Institute asking the member to confirm the date of appointment or of leaving service as an employee, and failure to furnish within the stipulated time information required to be submitted online, including not filling in the columns about engagement in other business while applying for a certificate of practice. Statement III is misplaced, because not replying within a reasonable time and without cause to a letter from public authorities is an illustration of other misconduct under clause (2) of Part IV, not professional misconduct under Part III. Statement V correctly records the citation appended by the material against this Part, the point being that the reference is attached to Part III and not to Part IV.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I - Clauses (2), (3) and (5)
questions.question:
Match each situation in Column I with its correct consequence in Column II and select the right answer.

Column I
A. A member in practice receives a share in fees from another member in practice for having referred a client to him.
B. A member in practice accepts a part of the profits of professional work of a person who is not a member of the Institute and who possesses none of the qualifications referred to in clause (2), no arrangement within the proviso being available.
C. A member in practice allows a retired partner of his firm to continue to receive a share in the profits of the firm's professional business.
D. A member in practice secures professional business through the services of a person who is neither his employee nor his partner, otherwise than under an agreement permitted by items (2), (3) or (4) of Part I.

Column II
1. No misconduct is attracted, because charging referral fees, that is, fees obtained by a member in practice from another member in practice in relation to referring a client to him, is not prohibited.
2. Professional misconduct under clause (3) of Part I of the First Schedule.
3. No misconduct is attracted, because a retired partner is expressly outside the prohibition in clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule.
4. Professional misconduct under clause (5) of Part I of the First Schedule.
5. Other misconduct under clause (2) of Part IV of the First Schedule, because the act is not connected with professional work.
questions.explanation: Situation A is a referral fee received from a fellow member in practice and is expressly stated not to be prohibited, so it pairs with 1 and not with clause (3), which is concerned with the profits of professional work of a person who is not a member of the Institute. Situation B is the core of clause (3), since without the support of the proviso the receipt of profits of a non-member's professional work is professional misconduct. Situation C is outside clause (2), which permits paying or allowing a share in the fees or profits of professional business to, among others, a partner or a retired partner. Situation D is clause (5), and the proviso to clause (5) does not save it because that proviso protects only agreements permitted in items (2), (3) and (4) of Part I. Item 5 is the trap: other misconduct under clause (2) of Part IV is reserved for conduct bringing disrepute and cannot be used to characterise conduct that the Schedules already treat as professional misconduct.

questions.category: Part IV versus Second Schedule Part III
questions.question: A member of the Institute who is in service and not in practice was in 2024 held guilty by a criminal court of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of nine months. He contends that no disciplinary proceeding can be founded on this, first, because the offence has nothing to do with his professional work, and secondly, because the court suspended the sentence of imprisonment. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate response?
options: The contention is valid, because the Schedules to the Act are directed only at conduct arising out of professional work and not at the personal affairs of a member.

The contention is invalid; the case is other misconduct under clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule, which covers an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months and applies to members whether or not the act relates to professional work.
The contention is invalid; the case is other misconduct under clause (1) of Part IV of the First Schedule, since the offence is one which is punishable with imprisonment of some description.
The contention is valid, because only the Council and not a criminal court is competent to hold a member guilty of professional or other misconduct.

The contention is invalid; the case is professional misconduct under clause (1) of Part II of the First Schedule, which applies to every employee of a company who happens to be a member of the Institute.
questions.explanation: Two thresholds have to be kept apart. Clause (1) of Part IV of the First Schedule covers a member being held guilty by a civil or criminal court of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, while clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule covers an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months. Nine months exceeds six months, so the member's case falls in the Second Schedule Part III clause (1), which is still other misconduct, and any option placing it in Part IV of the First Schedule applies the wrong ceiling. The plea that the act was unconnected with professional work fails, because the other-misconduct provisions exist precisely to let the Council inquire into such conduct in view of the standards of integrity expected of a chartered accountant in his personal affairs as well, and Part III of the Second Schedule applies to members generally. The suspension of the sentence is irrelevant, since the clauses turn on what the offence is punishable with and on the member having been held guilty.

questions.category: Integrated - Schedule, Part, Clauses and Type
questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs the conduct with the Schedule, the Part, the number of clauses in that Part and the type of misconduct, as per the table of Schedules to the Act?
