options: A member in service accepting a part of fees by way of commission from a broker engaged by his employer - Second Schedule, Part I, 10 clauses, professional misconduct.
A member withdrawing money from a bank account, the money not belonging to him - First Schedule, Part II, 2 clauses, other misconduct.
A member, not being a fellow of the Institute, acting as a fellow of the Institute - First Schedule, Part III, 3 clauses, other misconduct.

A member in practice paying a share in the fees of his professional business to a property dealer who is not a member of any professional body - First Schedule, Part I, 12 clauses, professional misconduct.
A member held guilty by a criminal court of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months - Second Schedule, Part III, 1 clause, other misconduct.
questions.explanation: Paying a share in the fees of professional business to a property dealer contravenes clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule, which deals with professional misconduct in relation to chartered accountants in practice and contains 12 clauses, so this pairing is correct on every count. A member in service accepting commission from a broker engaged by his employer is clause (2) of Part II of the First Schedule, which contains 2 clauses, and not Part I of the Second Schedule. Withdrawing money from a bank which does not belong to the member is an illustration of bringing disrepute under clause (2) of Part IV of the First Schedule, which contains 2 clauses and deals with other misconduct, so the Part is wrongly identified although the count of 2 clauses coincidentally matches. Not being a fellow and acting as a fellow is clause (1) of Part III of the First Schedule, which contains 3 clauses but is professional misconduct, not other misconduct. Finally, an offence punishable with imprisonment not exceeding six months is clause (1) of Part IV of the First Schedule with 2 clauses, while the Second Schedule Part III clause (1), with its single clause, takes offences punishable with imprisonment exceeding six months.

questions.question:
Clause (6) of Part I of the First Schedule declares a chartered accountant in practice guilty of professional misconduct if he solicits clients or professional work either directly or indirectly by circular, advertisement, personal communication or interview or by any other means.
In the light of the Additional Points to that clause, consider the following statements:
1. A member may apply to, request, or secure professional work from another chartered accountant in practice.
2. A member may respond to a tender issued by a public sector undertaking for the statutory audit of its books, even where the tender document is silent as to the minimum fee for the assignment.
3. A member is permitted to pay a reasonable amount towards earnest money or security deposit in connection with a tender issued by an organisation.
4. A member may offer his services in a tender falling in an area of service exclusively reserved for chartered accountants, if he undertakes not to quote a fee below the recommended minimum scale of fees.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Additional Point (1) contains two express carve-outs from Clause (6): applying, requesting or securing professional work from another chartered accountant in practice, and responding to tenders or enquiries issued by organisations and securing work, with permission to pay a reasonable amount towards earnest money or security deposits; statements 1 and 3 therefore hold. Statement 2 fails because the second carve-out is subject to the sub-restriction that a member shall not respond to any tender issued by an organisation in areas of services exclusively reserved for chartered accountants, such as audit and attestation/assurance services, and statutory audit of a company's books is squarely such an area. The restriction is displaced only where the minimum fee of the assignment is prescribed in the tender document itself, or where the areas are open to other professionals along with chartered accountants. Statement 4 invents a third gateway: an undertaking to charge the minimum scale of fees is not one of them, so it does not convert an impermissible response into a permissible one.

questions.question:
CA Meera Shah, proprietor of M/s Meera Shah & Co., Ahmedabad, received two tender documents in July 2025.
Tender A: issued by Gujarat State Cooperative Urban Bank Ltd. for 'Statutory Audit and Concurrent Audit of 30 branches for FY 2025-26'. The document prescribes a minimum fee of ₹ 2,10,000 per branch audit and requires an earnest money deposit of ₹ 25,000.
Tender B: issued by Gujarat Metro Rail Corporation Ltd. for 'Transaction Audit and Revenue Verification at 40 stations'. The document states that chartered accountants, cost accountants and company secretaries are all eligible to bid, and it prescribes no fee.
Separately, having heard from a friend that the Income-tax Department may maintain a panel of chartered accountants for transfer-pricing work, she drafts a letter to twenty field authorities asking each whether such a panel exists and requesting that her name be considered.
Consider the following statements:
1. She may respond to Tender A and may pay the ₹ 25,000 earnest money deposit.
2. She may respond to Tender B.
3. Her letters to the twenty field authorities are permissible, since she is merely ascertaining whether a panel exists and is not seeking allotment of work.
4. She may not respond to Tender A, because statutory and concurrent audit are services exclusively reserved for chartered accountants and that conclusion is unaffected by anything written in the tender document.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Tender A falls in an area exclusively reserved for chartered accountants, but the restriction on responding does not apply where the minimum fee of the assignment is prescribed in the tender document itself; the ₹ 2,10,000 stipulation supplies exactly that condition, and payment of the reasonable ₹ 25,000 earnest money is separately permitted, so statement 1 is right. Tender B is open to cost accountants and company secretaries along with chartered accountants, which is the second situation in which the sub-restriction is displaced, so statement 2 is right. Statement 3 is the trap: a member is not permitted to make roving enquiries regarding the existence of such a panel, and writing indiscriminately to twenty field authorities to find out whether a panel exists is such an enquiry, notwithstanding that no allotment is asked for. Statement 4 states the general rule but ignores the decisive fact, namely that the tender document itself prescribes the minimum fee; statement 2 of the pair is unaffected by her having heard of the panel from a friend.

questions.question:
CA Meera Shah, proprietor of M/s Meera Shah & Co., Ahmedabad, received two tender documents in July 2025.
Tender A: issued by Gujarat State Cooperative Urban Bank Ltd. for 'Statutory Audit and Concurrent Audit of 30 branches for FY 2025-26'. The document prescribes a minimum fee of ₹ 2,10,000 per branch audit and requires an earnest money deposit of ₹ 25,000.
Tender B: issued by Gujarat Metro Rail Corporation Ltd. for 'Transaction Audit and Revenue Verification at 40 stations'. The document states that chartered accountants, cost accountants and company secretaries are all eligible to bid, and it prescribes no fee.
Separately, having heard from a friend that the Income-tax Department may maintain a panel of chartered accountants for transfer-pricing work, she drafts a letter to twenty field authorities asking each whether such a panel exists and requesting that her name be considered.
Assume that in Tender A the sentence prescribing the minimum fee of ₹ 2,10,000 per branch audit is deleted from the document, and every other fact remains unchanged. Which one of the following states the correct position regarding Tender A?
options: She may still respond to Tender A, because statutory and concurrent audit of a cooperative urban bank's branches is a field open to other professionals along with chartered accountants.
She may still respond to Tender A, because she is permitted to pay the earnest money deposit of ₹ 25,000 and that permission carries with it the right to make the response itself.
She may respond to the concurrent audit element of Tender A alone, statutory audit being the only service in that tender reserved exclusively for chartered accountants.
She may no longer respond to Tender A, since audit and attestation or assurance services are exclusively reserved for chartered accountants and the prescribed minimum fee has gone.
questions.explanation: The permission to respond to tenders is subject to the sub-restriction that a member shall not respond to a tender issued by an organisation in areas of services exclusively reserved for chartered accountants, such as audit and attestation/assurance services, and that restriction is displaced only where the minimum fee of the assignment is prescribed in the tender document itself or where the areas are open to other professionals along with chartered accountants. Once the fee stipulation is deleted, neither gateway is available for Tender A, so the response becomes impermissible. The entitlement to pay a reasonable earnest money or security deposit is ancillary to a response that is otherwise lawful and cannot independently legitimise the bid. Tender B is a different assignment in a different field, and its eligibility clause does not make a bank's statutory and concurrent audit open to other professionals; nor does the source split an exclusively-reserved tender into reserved and unreserved components.

questions.question:
Match the acts in Column I with their treatment under Clause (6) of Part I of the First Schedule in Column II.
Column I
A. Publishing an advertisement under a box number in a daily newspaper
B. Uploading an educational video on the standards on auditing, with no reference to the member's firm, his contact details or any website address
C. A notice in the press announcing a change in the partnership constitution and a change in the firm's telephone number
D. Forwarding the firm's profile to a person who may become a client, where that person has made no query of his own
Column II
1. Permissible
2. Not permitted unless it is in response to a specific query of the proposed client
3. Prohibited
Which of the following is the correct match?
questions.explanation: Publishing advertisements under box numbers is specifically stated to be prohibited, so A-3 and not A-2; the special condition attached to the firm profile has nothing to do with box numbers. Educational videos may be uploaded by members provided there is no reference to the CA firm, to contact details or to a website address, and since those conditions are satisfied the act is simply permissible, which rules out B-2. Press notices relating to changes in partnerships or dissolution and to change in address and telephone numbers are expressly listed as permissible advertisements, so C-1; treating it as prohibited confuses it with the general bar on advertising professional attainments. Sharing a firm profile with a prospective client is not permitted unless it is in response to a specific query of that proposed client, which is a conditional permission of its own kind and therefore D-2 rather than D-1 or D-3.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A member in practice is not permitted to make roving enquiries for the purpose of ascertaining whether an organisation maintains a panel of chartered accountants for allotment of audit or other professional work.
Reason (R): Where the existence of such a panel is within the knowledge of the member, he may request the concerned organisation to place his name on the panel, but where his name is already on the panel, a request by him for allotment of work is not permissible.
In the context of the above, which one of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
A is incorrect but R is correct
questions.explanation: Both statements reproduce the empanelment rule under Additional Point (3)(x): government departments, courts, co-operative societies and banks prepare panels of chartered accountants; where the existence of such a panel is within the knowledge of the member he may request the concerned organisation to place his name on it, roving enquiries regarding the existence of such a panel are not permissible, and once his name is on the panel a request for allotment of work is not permissible. R is therefore not the explanation of A; the two are independent limbs of the same rule, and A is in substance an application of the wider restraint in Additional Point (2) against adopting indirect methods of gaining publicity. The tempting reading that a member may canvass broadly to locate a panel and then apply formally fails, because the right to request inclusion arises only where the existence of the panel is already within his knowledge.

questions.question:
CA Harish Nair is one of three partners of M/s Nair, Balakrishnan & Menon, chartered accountants, Chennai. His daughter's marriage is fixed for 18 November 2025. He proposes to send printed invitations carrying the words 'CA Harish Nair (FCA), M/s Nair, Balakrishnan & Menon' together with a line stating that he is 'the auditor of the largest single-entity audit in the State'. The address list prepared by his wife includes his own clients, relatives and college friends, as well as the relatives and friends of his co-partner CA Menon who are resident in Coimbatore, since all of them move in the same family social circuit. The firm's new office is also to be inaugurated in December 2025 and invitations for that function are to go out on the same pattern.
Consider the following statements:
1. The mention of the designation 'Chartered Accountant' and of the firm name on the marriage invitation is permissible.
2. The mention of his professional attainments on the invitation is not permissible.
3. The invitations may be sent to the relatives and friends of CA Menon also, since they are acquaintances of the same firm.
4. The invitation for the office inauguration falls outside the permission, which covers marriage and religious ceremonies alone.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Additional Point (ix) prohibits the issue of greeting cards or invitations indicating professional attainments, but permits the designation 'Chartered Accountant' and the firm name to be mentioned in greeting cards and invitations for marriage, religious ceremonies and office inauguration, provided the cards or invitations are sent to clients, relatives and friends of the concerned member only. Statements 1 and 2 therefore follow, and the line about the largest single-entity audit is precisely a professional attainment which cannot appear. Statement 3 fails because the source expressly withholds the concession even in respect of relatives and friends of another partner of the firm; the fact that they are socially linked to the same firm or move in the same circuit is irrelevant. Statement 4 is wrong because office inauguration is one of the three occasions named, so the December invitations are not outside the permission for that reason.

questions.question:
CA Sanjay Bhatt, who holds a certificate of practice and also conducts coaching for CA Final candidates in Surat under the name 'Bhatt Academy', took the following steps during August 2025:
(P) He put up a sign board outside the coaching premises carrying the name of the institute, the subjects taught and the telephone contact details.
(Q) He gave a paid advertisement to a Surat daily announcing admissions to his classes, quoting the number of candidates who had recently cleared the examination.
(R) He uploaded a free lecture on a standard on auditing to a video platform, with no reference to his firm, to his contact details or to any website address.
(S) He inserted an advertisement in the journal of the Institute seeking to share professional work with another member.
Which of the above are permissible under Clause (6) of Part I of the First Schedule?
questions.explanation: A member is not permitted to advertise his classes or his coaching institute; what is allowed is a sign board outside the coaching premises mentioning the name of the institute, the contact details and the subjects taught, so P is within the concession and Q is outside it. The success statistics in Q do not cure the defect, because the objection is to advertising the coaching activity at all rather than to the tone of the advertisement. Educational videos may be uploaded by members without reference to the CA firm, contact details or website address, which is exactly the form described in R. Advertisement in the journal or newsletter of the Institute for sharing professional work, seeking partnership or employment is expressly listed among the permissible advertisements, so S is also permissible; that list is confined to those three purposes and cannot be stretched to cover the coaching advertisement in Q.

questions.question: M/s Kapadia & Co., chartered accountants, Pune, is considering four separate notices to be inserted in a city daily during March 2026. Which one of the following notices is permissible?
options: A notice intimating to the public the retirement of one partner, the re-constitution of the firm and its new telephone number.
A notice expressing the firm's gratitude to a client company on the firm's appointment as its statutory auditor for FY 2026-27.
A notice inviting property owners of the Kothrud locality to entrust their book-keeping and GST work to the firm at competitive rates.
A notice announcing that the firm has organised a gold jubilee function and inviting readers to attend the valedictory dinner.
questions.explanation: The permissible advertisements and press announcements listed under Additional Point (3)(i) are changes in partnerships or dissolution and changes in address and telephone numbers; recruitment of staff for his own office; advertisements on behalf of a client requiring staff or to acquire or dispose of property; advertisement for sale of property by a member acting as trustee, liquidator or receiver; and advertisement in the journal or newsletter of the Institute for sharing professional work, seeking partnership or employment. The retirement and re-constitution notice with the new telephone number falls wholly within the first of these. A gratitude announcement on appointment as statutory auditor is nowhere in the list and is publicity of the firm's professional attainments and services; the third option is direct solicitation of clients by advertisement; the fourth fails because a member is not permitted to advertise events organised by the CA firm, even silver, golden, platinum or centenary celebrations, though such an event may be published in the newspaper or newsletter, which is a different thing from a paid advertisement with an invitation to attend.

questions.question:
CA Anil Verma's firm, M/s Verma & Associates, Jamshedpur, completed twenty-five years of practice on 1 August 2025 and he is considering how the occasion may be marked publicly. He formulates the following statements:
1. The silver jubilee function organised by the firm should not be advertised by him.
2. The silver jubilee function may be published in a newspaper or in a newsletter.
3. Since publication in a newspaper is permitted, a paid advertisement carrying the same announcement may also be given to that newspaper.
4. The restriction would not reach a platinum jubilee or centenary function, because the rule speaks only of silver and golden celebrations.
Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Additional Point (3)(iii) deals expressly with advertisements for silver, golden, platinum or centenary celebrations and states that a member is not permitted to advertise events organised by the CA firm, though the event may be published in the newspaper or newsletter. Statements 1 and 2 are therefore correct descriptions of the position. Statement 3 is not correct, because the concession to have the event published is not a concession to place a paid advertisement; the prohibition operates against the advertisement of the firm's event as such, and the decisive fact is the manner in which the space is bought rather than the newspaper in which the announcement appears. Statement 4 is not correct, because the enumeration in the source expressly extends to platinum and centenary celebrations as well, so a later jubilee would be treated identically. The length of the firm's standing, twenty-five years, is immaterial to the analysis.

questions.question: A Marathi feature film released in January 2026 carries in its closing sequence a list of collaborators, every entry appearing in the same font size and for the same screen duration. M/s Deshmukh & Co. had advanced a substantial loan to the producer from the firm's funds. CA Deshmukh asks whether his firm's name may be included. A friend advises him that the name may be shown last in the credits, in a larger font and held twice as long as the other entries, so that viewers are sure to notice it. Which one of the following is the MOST appropriate advice to CA Deshmukh?
options: Television and movie credits are a form of advertisement, so neither the member's name nor the firm's name may appear in them at all.
The firm's name may be included, but only if the exhibition of the name is not made differently as compared with the other entries in the credits.
The larger and longer display is permissible, because the loan was advanced by the firm and not by the member in his personal capacity.
The name may be exhibited in any manner the producer prefers, since closing credits are the producer's own editorial record and Clause (6) does not extend to motion pictures.
questions.explanation: Additional Point (3)(vii) permits the member's or the firm's name to be included in television or movie credits subject to one condition, namely that the exhibition of the name is not made differently as compared with other entries in the credits. Inclusion on the same terms as the remaining collaborators is therefore permissible, whereas the friend's advice to place the name last, in a larger font and for twice the duration, is precisely differential exhibition and forfeits the concession. The first option overstates the prohibition, since the source does not treat credits as per se inadmissible. The source of the funds is the red herring: whether the loan came from the firm or the member is irrelevant to a rule that turns on the manner of exhibition. The fourth option ignores that credits are expressly addressed among the forms of soliciting work.

questions.question:
CA Ritu Mehra, a member in practice at Delhi, did two things during 2025-26.
(X) She published a textbook on Ind AS in which, below her name, she stated that she was a Fellow of the Institute with twenty years' standing who had audited the accounts of several large companies.
(Y) She appeared as a panellist on a business news channel's discussion on consolidation accounting, gave her name, described herself as a chartered accountant, referred to her specialised knowledge in group accounting, and the channel carried the caption 'Ritu Mehra, Chartered Accountant / Mehra & Associates'. She said nothing inviting viewers to engage her firm.
Consider the following statements:
1. X is impermissible in so far as it mentions her professional attainments.
2. X may nevertheless carry the designation 'Chartered Accountant' and her firm name.
3. Y is impermissible, because a member's firm name may not appear in connection with any electronic media programme.
4. Y is permissible, since special qualifications or specialised knowledge directly relevant to the programme may be given and the firm name may also be mentioned, provided what she says is not promotional.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Additional Point (3)(viii) makes it impermissible to mention professional attainments in a book or article published by the member, but allows him to mention the designation 'Chartered Accountant' and the firm name; statements 1 and 2 together give the correct treatment of X, the reference to twenty years' standing and to the audits of large companies being an attainment rather than a designation. Additional Point (5) stands on a different footing: members may appear on television, in films and on the internet, may give their names and describe themselves as chartered accountants, special qualifications or specialised knowledge directly relevant to the programme may also be given, and the firm name may also be mentioned, the single limiting condition being that what he says or writes must not be promotional. Statement 3 is wrong because it treats the firm name as inadmissible on electronic media, and the caption here carries no invitation to engage the firm. The contrast to note is that attainments are barred in a self-published book while programme-relevant specialisation is permitted on a media panel.

questions.question: CA Pravin Joshi of M/s Joshi & Co., Pune, is considering four separate spends during 2026-27. Which one of the following acts is permissible for him as a chartered accountant in practice?
options: Sponsoring the annual cricket tournament of a district association, with the firm's name displayed on the boundary banners.
Advertising the firm's centenary celebration function in the Sunday supplement of a Pune daily.
Sponsoring a school building under the client's corporate social responsibility framework, with a plaque carrying the firm's name and the CA logo alongside the member's name.
Sponsoring a continuing professional education programme conducted by a Programme Organizing Unit of ICAI, with the prior approval of the CPE directorate of ICAI.
questions.explanation: The general rule in Additional Point (3)(xi) is that a member is not permitted to sponsor an event; the only stated relief is where the event is conducted by a Programme Organizing Unit of ICAI and the prior approval of the CPE directorate of ICAI is obtained, which the fourth act satisfies on both counts. The first act is ordinary event sponsorship with the firm's name on banners and is outside the relief, since a district cricket association is not a POU of the Institute. The third act fails on the manner of recognition: in sponsoring activities relating to CSR a member may mention his individual name with the prefix 'CA', but mention of the firm name or of the CA logo is not permitted. The second act is separately prohibited as the advertisement of an event organised by the CA firm, centenary celebrations being expressly within that restriction, although the function may be published in the newspaper or newsletter.

questions.question:
CA Girish Iyer of M/s Iyer & Iyer, Bengaluru, met the managing director of a listed company at a business lunch on 3 February 2026. The managing director asked him to send 'whatever you have about your firm'. Iyer proposes the following four steps:
(1) Send the firm profile to that company, it being the response to the specific query of the proposed client.
(2) Send the same profile, without any query from them, to five other companies which the managing director mentioned as likely to need a tax auditor.
(3) State in the profile that the firm is empanelled by a bank, and write to that bank seeking allotment of the audit of two more branches, his name already appearing on the bank's panel.
(4) Having obtained the placement of his name on the panel of a co-operative society, whose existence was known to him, decline to make any request to that society for allotment of work.
Which combination of steps is fully appropriate under Clause (6) of Part I of the First Schedule?
questions.explanation: Additional Point (3)(xiii) permits sharing of the firm profile with a prospective client only where it is in response to a specific query of that proposed client, so step 1 is appropriate and step 2 is not, the five companies having asked nothing and a reference from a third person being no query by the proposed client. Under Additional Point (3)(x) a member may, where the existence of a panel is within his knowledge, request the organisation to place his name on the panel, but once his name is on the panel a request by him to allot work is not permissible; step 3 is therefore defective on the allotment request even though the initial placement was lawful, and step 4 correctly stops at placement. The mention of the bank empanelment in the profile does not cure the request for allotment. Nothing in the fact that tax audit is a permitted assignment converts an unsolicited profile into a permitted one.

questions.question:
M/s Chatterjee & Co., Kolkata, took the following steps during 2025-26:
(A) It caused an advertisement to be published under a box number in a daily newspaper, stating that applications relating to the audit of a deceased person's estate should be addressed to Box No. 4117, Kolkata.
(B) CA S. Chatterjee gave an interview to a financial weekly which was published with his photograph and the heading 'the city's busiest tax auditor', resulting in publicity for the firm.
(C) The firm uploaded an educational video explaining the new revenue standard to a video platform; the closing frame carried the firm's name and the firm's website address.
(D) A notice was inserted in a daily newspaper announcing the dissolution of the partnership and the change in CA Chatterjee's residential telephone number.
(E) On behalf of its client Kirti Spins Ltd., the firm inserted an advertisement requiring managers for that client's factory.
Which of these acts amount to solicitation of clients or professional work?
options: A, C, D and E only
questions.explanation: Publishing advertisements under box numbers is specifically stated to be prohibited, so A is solicitation notwithstanding that the subject matter is an estate audit. Giving public interviews which result in publicity is not permitted, and the photograph and the label 'the city's busiest tax auditor' are exactly such publicity, so B falls within the clause. Educational videos may be uploaded only without reference to the CA firm, to contact details or to a website address, and the closing frame naming the firm and displaying the website destroys that carve-out, so C is also objectionable. D and E are on the opposite side of the line: press notices regarding changes in partnerships or dissolution and changes in address and telephone numbers are expressly permissible, as is an advertisement on behalf of a client requiring staff or to acquire or dispose of property. The client's factory advertisement therefore remains within the permitted list even though it mentions the firm acting for it.

questions.question:
Match each situation in Column I with the correct consequence in Column II. Column II may be used for more than one situation.
Column I
P. A member writes to the chairman of a district cooperative bank, whose panel list he has himself seen, requesting that his name be included on that panel.
Q. The same member, his name already appearing on that bank's panel, writes to the bank seeking allotment of the audit of two branches.
R. The member, not knowing whether any panel exists, writes to forty public bodies asking each whether it maintains a panel of chartered accountants.
S. The member applies to another chartered accountant in practice for professional work to be given to him.
Column II
1. Permissible
2. Not permissible
Which of the following is the correct pairing?
questions.explanation: Under Additional Point (3)(x), where the existence of the panel is within the knowledge of the member he may request the concerned organisation to place his name on the panel, which makes P permissible because he has himself seen the bank's list. The same point expressly bars a request for allotment of work once the name is on the panel, so Q is not permissible even though the initial placement was lawful. R is a roving enquiry regarding the existence of a panel and is not permissible; the defence that no work was actually asked for fails, because the right to request inclusion arises only where the existence of the panel is already within the member's knowledge. S is squarely within Additional Point (1)(i), under which Clause (6) does not prohibit a chartered accountant from applying, requesting or securing professional work from another chartered accountant in practice.

questions.question: CA Neelam Fernandes of Mumbai was introduced to M/s Aurora Textiles Pvt. Ltd. by CA Prakash Sheth, who audits that company and handles its transfer-pricing work. In May 2026 the managing director of Aurora approached Mrs. Fernandes directly for a GST litigation assignment, which she was willing to take. CA Sheth was unaware of the approach, and no professional work of Aurora had ever been given to Mrs. Fernandes earlier. Which one of the following actions is LEAST appropriate?
options: Mrs. Fernandes asks the client that, in relation to this work also, it should come to her through CA Sheth, who deals with its original work.
Mrs. Fernandes accepts the GST assignment without a word to the client about CA Sheth, on the ground that the client came to her directly and that Sheth is not the GST auditor.
Mrs. Fernandes takes CA Sheth into confidence about the direct approach made to her, and settles the position with him before finalising her acceptance of the assignment.
Mrs. Fernandes confines herself to the GST assignment actually offered by Aurora and does not canvass that company for any other professional work of any description.
questions.explanation: Additional Point (3)(xii) covers acceptance of original professional work by a member emanating from a client introduced to him by another member, and provides that where any professional work of such a client comes to him directly he has a duty to ask the client that it should come through the other member dealing with his original work. Option 2 is the least appropriate because it denies the existence of the duty at the very moment the trigger operates: the direct approach by the introduced client is the fact that attracts the duty, not a reason for dispensing with it, and the nature of the new assignment need not match the nature of the other member's work. Option 1 is the conduct the rule requires. Options 3 and 4 do not conflict with the rule, keeping the introducing member informed and declining to canvass further work being consistent with the restraint on indirect methods of soliciting clients.

questions.question:
On 9 January 2026 CA Vikram Sethi of Nagpur addressed a seminar on the disclosure of particulars in the directors' report. No member of the audience asked him for any particulars of his firm. He nevertheless sent the firm's profile, with a covering letter, to six companies represented at the seminar. A week later the finance director of one of those companies telephoned him and asked him to send the firm profile for consideration of a possible appointment as internal auditor, and he sent a profile to that company as well.
Consider the following statements:
1. The six profiles despatched in January 2026 amount to solicitation of professional work and are not permissible.
2. The profile sent to the company whose finance director specifically asked for it is permissible.
3. Had no company asked for the profile, he could still have sent it, because internal audit is a service area open to other professionals along with chartered accountants.
4. The second despatch becomes impermissible if the profile states the firm's professional attainments, because a firm profile may in no case carry the firm's name.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Additional Point (3)(xiii) states that sharing the firm profile with a prospective client is not permitted unless it is in response to a specific query of the proposed client. The unsolicited mailing to six companies fails that test, so statement 1 is correct, and the telephone request of the finance director is precisely such a specific query, so statement 2 is correct. Statement 3 imports the wrong test: the fact that an area is open to other professionals along with chartered accountants is relevant to the restriction on responding to tenders, not to the permission to share a firm profile, and the nature of the assignment cannot supply the missing query. Statement 4 misstates the rule twice, since a firm profile may obviously carry the firm name and the condition governing the despatch is the specific query, so the correctness of the second despatch is not put in issue by that reasoning.

questions.question:
CA Anil Dubey addressed a single common application document both to CA Rakesh Pillai, seeking professional work to be given to him, and to a State Power Distribution Company Ltd., responding to its tender for 'Outsourced Internal Audit and Energy Audit of 12 divisions', the document stating that chartered accountants, cost accountants and engineers are all eligible; no fee was prescribed and he paid the earnest money deposit of ₹ 50,000. In that document he stated that his firm had twenty partners and had completed the statutory audits of forty listed companies, when in fact it had four partners and no listed-company audit. On 14 March 2026 he also responded to a second tender of the same company for 'Statutory Audit of two Zone Offices', in which the document itself prescribed a minimum fee of ₹ 4,75,000.
Which one of the following best states the position under the First Schedule?
options: He may respond to neither tender, because a member in practice is not entitled to approach a Government company or its bodies for professional work at all, and the false particulars are of no consequence in either proceeding.

He may respond to the internal audit tender only if a minimum fee is prescribed in its own document, and the false particulars are immaterial, since Clause (6) positively permits a member to invite professional work from another chartered accountant.

Both tender responses are permissible under Clause (6), and separately he is guilty of professional misconduct under Part III of the First Schedule in giving information knowing it to be false while inviting work from another chartered accountant and while responding to tenders.

He may respond to the internal audit tender but not to the statutory audit tender, audit being exclusively reserved for chartered accountants, and the false particulars attract no consequence because that area was lawfully open to him.
questions.explanation: Clause (6) does not prohibit responding to tenders or enquiries issued by organisations and securing work, subject to the bar on tenders in areas exclusively reserved for chartered accountants, which bar is displaced where the areas are open to other professionals along with chartered accountants or where the minimum fee of the assignment is prescribed in the tender document itself; the eligibility clause satisfies the first condition for the internal audit tender and the ₹ 4,75,000 stipulation satisfies the second for the statutory audit tender, and payment of a reasonable earnest money deposit is separately permitted. The solicitation analysis, however, says nothing about the truthfulness of what he wrote: Part III, Clause (3) of the First Schedule makes a member of the Institute, whether in practice or not, guilty of professional misconduct if, while inviting professional work from another chartered accountant or while responding to tenders or enquiries, he gives information knowing it to be false. The two questions are therefore distinct, and permission to seek work is not immunity from misstating facts. The first option wrongly closes both tenders on a ground that does not exist, the fourth wrongly closes the statutory audit tender, and the second wrongly treats the carve-out as neutralising the false statement.

questions.question:
CA Mahesh Gowda, a partner of M/s Gowda & Associates, Bengaluru, proposes two steps in October 2026.
(I) To mail invitations for the inauguration of his own firm's new office, carrying the designation 'Chartered Accountant' and the firm's name, to a list comprising his own clients and relatives together with the relatives of his co-partner CA Sunil Rao.
(II) To enclose the firm's profile with each such invitation, no invitee having made any query about the firm.
Which one of the following is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
options: Both steps are permissible, office inauguration being one of the covered occasions and a profile being capable of accompanying a permitted invitation.
Step I is wholly impermissible, since neither the designation 'Chartered Accountant' nor the name of the firm may appear on a greeting card or invitation in any circumstances.
Step II is permissible, because the issue of an invitation by the member is itself to be treated as a specific query by the proposed client for the firm's particulars.
Step I is permissible as to the occasion and as to the mention of the designation and the firm name, but the recipient list and Step II are each independently objectionable.
questions.explanation: Additional Point (ix) permits the designation 'Chartered Accountant' and the firm name to be mentioned in invitations for marriage, religious ceremonies and office inauguration, provided the invitations go only to clients, relatives and friends of the concerned member, and it expressly withholds that concession even as regards relatives and friends of another partner of the firm; CA Rao's relatives are therefore outside the permissible list. Additional Point (xiii) permits sharing of the firm profile with a prospective client only in response to a specific query of that proposed client, and an enclosure sent along with every invitation cannot satisfy a condition that requires the recipient to have raised the query first. The two defects are independent, so curing the distribution list would not by itself validate the bulk profile mailing. The third option inverts the logic of (xiii), and the second ignores that the firm name is expressly admissible on such invitations.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A member in practice should not adopt any indirect methods to gain publicity and thereby solicit clients or professional work.
Reason (R): Such a restraint is to be practised so that members may maintain their independence of judgment and may be able to command the respect of their prospective clients.
In the context of the above, which one of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
A is incorrect but R is correct
questions.explanation: Additional Point (2) is in precisely these words: members should not adopt any indirect methods to gain publicity and thereby solicit clients or professional work, and such a restraint must be practised so that members may maintain their independence of judgment and may be able to command the respect of their prospective clients. R is accordingly not merely a true statement but the reason expressly recorded for A, which is why the first option and not the second is correct. The point matters in application, because it is the publicity-seeking character of an act, and not its outward form, that brings it within Clause (6); this is why a member may lawfully respond to a tender of an organisation open to other professionals, yet may not buy publicity for his firm through sponsorship banners or press notices outside the permitted list. Direct solicitation by circular, advertisement, personal communication or interview is already caught by the clause itself, and R explains why the words 'indirectly' and 'by any other means' were inserted.

questions.question:
CA Pankaj Trivedi was appointed statutory auditor of M/s Meridian Steel Ltd. by the shareholders at the annual general meeting held on 28 September 2020 for a term of five years. In June 2025 the Board circulated a note stating that his continuation was undesirable, and he proposes to send a representation to the company under section 140(4) of the Companies Act, 2013. His draft contains four paragraphs:
(P) A description, in a dignified manner, of how he had been acting independently throughout his term.
(Q) A statement that he is willing to continue as auditor if he is reappointed by the shareholders.
(R) Allegations that individual members of the audit committee deserve to be suspended, with no statement of his own conduct.
(S) A paragraph setting out his professional attainments and inviting shareholders to engage him for a further term at fees lower than those currently prevailing in the market.
Which combination falls within the scope of the representation which he is entitled to make?
questions.explanation: Additional Point (4) fixes the scope of the representation which an auditor is entitled to make under section 140(4) of the Companies Act, 2013: the letter should set out in a dignified manner how he has been acting independently throughout his term and may indicate his willingness to continue as auditor if reappointed by the shareholders. P and Q reproduce both limbs, and the conditional form of Q matters because the shareholders are the body that would reappoint him. R is outside the scope, since the entitlement is to a dignified account of his own independent conduct and not an attack on individual committee members unaccompanied by any such account. S is outside it as well, because professional attainments are not a permissible subject and the paragraph is in substance an invitation to engage the firm; the low fee is a red herring, charging low fees for an assignment not constituting misconduct, the defect being the solicitation and the claim of attainments. The date of the original appointment is immaterial to this analysis.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on Clause (6) of Part I of the First Schedule and its Additional Points:
1. A member in practice is not permitted to give interviews which result in publicity.
2. A member may appear on television, in films and on the internet, may agree to broadcast in radio and may give lectures at forums, and may give his name and describe himself as a chartered accountant.
3. In such an appearance the firm's name may not be mentioned in any circumstances.
4. In such an appearance special qualifications or specialised knowledge of the member may be given where these are directly relevant to the programme.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Additional Point (3)(vi) records that a member is not permitted to give interviews which result in publicity, so statement 1 is correct. Additional Point (5) separately governs appearance of a chartered accountant on electronic media including the internet: members may appear on television, in films and on the internet, agree to broadcast in radio or give lectures at forums, and may give their names and describe themselves as chartered accountants, which makes statement 2 correct; the same point also allows special qualifications or specialised knowledge directly relevant to the programme to be given, so statement 4 is correct. Statement 3 is wrong because Additional Point (5) says in terms that the firm name may also be mentioned. The reconciling condition is that what the member says or writes must not be promotional, and that is what separates a permitted panel appearance or lecture from an interview that yields publicity for him or his firm.

questions.question:
Match each item in Column I with the correct treatment in Column II, applying the Website Guidelines forming part of the additional points to Clause (6) of Part I of the First Schedule.

Column I
(P) Year of establishment of the firm
(Q) Details of employees of the firm
(R) Number of articled assistants
(S) Names of clients and the fee charged
(T) Experience of the partners
(U) Nature of services rendered and assignments handled

Column II
(1) May be displayed on the website but not on letter heads and other professional documents
(2) May be displayed only on a specific 'pull' request
(3) May be displayed on the website without any 'pull' request
(4) Cannot be given, except where required by a regulator
(5) May be displayed on the website as well as on letter heads and visiting cards
questions.explanation: The Website Guidelines list member/firm name, year of establishment, address, telephone number, e-mail ID, details of employees and job vacancies as information which can be displayed on the website; the year of establishment is expressly 'allowed on website but not on letter heads etc.', so P matches (1) and Q matches (3). The number of articled assistants, partner experience, and the nature of services rendered and assignments handled are each subject to a specific 'pull' request, so R, T and U match (2). Names of clients and fee charged cannot be given, the only permitted case being where a regulator requires it, so S matches (4). Column II entry (5) is the trap: it wrongly assumes that what is good for the website is good for letter heads, whereas the year of establishment and partner experience are restricted.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements relating to the Website Guidelines applicable to a chartered accountant in practice and to a chartered accountants' firm:

1. A CA or a CA firm is free to create its own website; the actual format is not prescribed, no standard format is given, and there is no restriction on the colours used in the website.
2. The website should be run on a 'push' model and not on a 'pull' model, so that information reaches persons without their having to ask for it.
3. Information contained in the website should not be circulated by the member on his own or by e-mail, except on a specific 'pull' request.
4. A member may mention his website on professional stationery, letter heads, visiting cards and e-mail, but soliciting people to visit the website is not permitted.
5. The website should be befitting the CA profession, and no advertisement of any nature is permitted on the website.
6. The website address is to be filed by the member on an annual basis in the annual form to the Institute.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement 2 reverses the rule: the guidelines require the website to be run on a 'PULL' model and NOT a 'PUSH' model, which is precisely why statement 3 forbids self-circulation of website information or its sending by e-mail unless a specific pull request is received. Statements 1, 3, 5 and 6 reproduce the guidelines exactly - freedom to have a website with no prescribed format or colour restriction, no advertisement of any nature on the website, the website being befitting the profession, and annual filing of the website address in the annual form. Statement 4 is also correct, because mentioning the website on stationery, letter heads, visiting cards and e-mail is permitted while soliciting persons to visit the website is not. The decisive point is the pull/push distinction, which is the root from which the circulation prohibition flows.

questions.question:
M/s Rao & Menon, Chartered Accountants, Bengaluru, launched the firm's website on 1 April 2025. The pages are laid out in dark maroon and gold, no standard format having been prescribed. The home page shows the year of establishment '1994', a full-width banner photograph of the three partners, and a passport-size photograph of the managing partner. It also lists the names of the firm's ten largest clients together with the aggregate fee of Rs 3.40 crore received from them in FY 2024-25, and a section headed 'Our Partners' gives the names and detailed work experience of each partner. Between 15 and 20 April 2025, an office assistant, acting on a partner's instructions, e-mailed a link to the 'Our Partners' page and the firm's profile to about 800 companies and to other chartered accountants' firms in Karnataka, none of whom had asked for the information. The website carries a rotating banner advertising an accounting software vendor, for which the firm receives commission. The partners' visiting cards carry the website address, and the firm does not solicit anyone to visit the website in any other manner. The website address was filed with the Institute in the annual form for FY 2024-25.

Which one of the following correctly identifies the position under the Website Guidelines?
options: Both the display of the year of establishment and the display of the partners' names are irregular, because neither is permitted on a website though both may be printed on letter heads.

Because no standard format for a website is prescribed and there is no restriction on colours, the banner photograph and the software advertisement are matters of the firm's discretion, and only the unsolicited e-mail is irregular.

The clients' names and the aggregate fee may be shown because the fee is not disclosed client-wise, and the partners' work experience may be shown because partner details are permitted on the website.

The year of establishment and the partners' names may be shown on the website, but the full-width banner photograph, the clients' names with the fee charged, the rotating software advertisement, and the display of partners' work experience otherwise than on a specific 'pull' request each contravene the guidelines.
questions.explanation: Year of establishment is expressly allowed on the website (though not on letter heads), and partner names fall within 'partners details', so both are regular. No photograph of any sort is permitted and only the display of a passport-size photo is permitted, so the full-width banner photograph of the three partners is a breach while the managing partner's passport-size photograph is not. Names of clients and fee charged cannot be given except where required by a regulator, and aggregating Rs 3.40 crore does not cure the breach because the fee charged is itself disclosed. Partner experience may be displayed only on a specific 'pull' request, and the guidelines permit no advertisement of any nature on the website, so the software banner is irregular; the absence of a prescribed format or colour restriction does not extend to these specific prohibitions.

questions.question:
M/s Rao & Menon, Chartered Accountants, Bengaluru, launched the firm's website on 1 April 2025. The pages are laid out in dark maroon and gold, no standard format having been prescribed. The home page shows the year of establishment '1994', a full-width banner photograph of the three partners, and a passport-size photograph of the managing partner. It also lists the names of the firm's ten largest clients together with the aggregate fee of Rs 3.40 crore received from them in FY 2024-25, and a section headed 'Our Partners' gives the names and detailed work experience of each partner. Between 15 and 20 April 2025, an office assistant, acting on a partner's instructions, e-mailed a link to the 'Our Partners' page and the firm's profile to about 800 companies and to other chartered accountants' firms in Karnataka, none of whom had asked for the information. The website carries a rotating banner advertising an accounting software vendor, for which the firm receives commission. The partners' visiting cards carry the website address, and the firm does not solicit anyone to visit the website in any other manner. The website address was filed with the Institute in the annual form for FY 2024-25.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate conclusion on the model on which the website should operate and on the way the e-mail campaign was handled?
options: The e-mail campaign is regular because partner details are among the items the website may display, and the recipients' status as firms or companies is immaterial.
Since the website address was filed in the annual form, the annual filing operates as a safe harbour for the manner in which the website information was circulated.

The website should be run on a 'pull' and not a 'push' model, so website information may not be circulated by the firm on its own or by e-mail in the absence of a specific 'pull' request; the visiting cards may carry the website address, but soliciting persons to visit the website is not permitted.

A 'push' model is the correct model for a professional website, therefore e-mailing the 'Our Partners' page was appropriate; what is barred is only the mention of the website address on visiting cards.
questions.explanation: The guidelines require the website to run on a 'pull' model and not a 'push' model, and expressly bar circulation of website information by the member on his own or by e-mail except on a specific 'pull' request. None of the 800 recipients had asked for the material, so the campaign was a push and was impermissible regardless of the fact that partner details are website-permissible. The mention of the website address on professional stationery, letter heads, visiting cards and e-mail is permitted, so the visiting cards are regular; what is not permitted is soliciting people to visit the website. Annual filing of the website address is an independent compliance requirement and has no bearing on the manner of circulation, so it cannot cure the push e-mail.

questions.question: Each of the following statements relates to features which a chartered accountant's firm may or may not build into its website. Which one of them is NOT correct?
options: The website may provide a link to the websites of ICAI, its Regional Councils and Branches, and to the websites of the Government, Government Departments, regulatory authorities and other professional bodies.

Members may include articles, bulletin boards and material for professional updation on the website, and educational videos on professional topics are permissible; a firm may also provide a link to its page on a social networking site, without soliciting people to visit it.
Chat rooms may be provided which permit chatting amongst members, the firm and its clients, and members or firms may provide online advice to those clients who specifically request advice.

A firm may carry the advertisement of a mutual fund house provided the advertisement is of a nature befitting the profession, and may give online advice to any visitor who leaves a query in the chat room.
questions.explanation: No advertisement of any nature is permitted on the website, so a mutual fund advertisement is barred however respectable its content; the requirement that the website be befitting the profession is an additional general obligation and not an exception which unlocks advertising. Online advice is permitted only to clients who specifically request it, which rules out advice to any casual visitor who posts in a chat room, even though chat rooms for chatting amongst members, the firm and its clients are themselves permissible. The other three statements reproduce the guidelines correctly on links, articles, bulletin boards, professional updation, educational videos on professional topics, social networking links without solicitation, and chat rooms. The decisive words are 'no advertisement of any nature' and 'clients who specifically request'.

questions.question:
CA Nalini holds a certificate of practice and runs a sole practice at Hyderabad. During July 2025 she takes the following four decisions:
(I) She lists herself on a mobile application based service provider aggregator which carries plumbers, electricians, home tutors and chartered accountants, so that a customer searching under any of those categories may reach her.
(II) She gets registered on the e-proposal portal of a Ministry of the Government of India, that portal being operated by the Government itself, in order to bid for an audit of a public sector undertaking.
(III) She answers accounting and tax queries posted by users on an online third party platform, and signs each answer with her firm's name and the contact address of her office at Gachibowli.
(IV) She gives consultation on an online third party platform mentioning only her own name and the description 'Chartered Accountant', without giving the firm name or the contact address.

Which combination of actions is permissible under the additional points to Clause (6)?
questions.explanation: Listing oneself on an online application based service provider aggregator in which other categories are also listed is not permissible, which disposes of (I). Registration on a government portal is permissible because it does not amount to listing on an aggregator, so (II) stands. A member may provide consultation and advice through online third party platforms, but the firm name and the contact address should not be provided, which makes (III) irregular and (IV) regular. Only (II) and (IV) are therefore wholly permissible. The distinction is not between online and offline exposure but between an aggregator operated by a third party and a portal operated by the client, namely the Government.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A member in practice may get himself registered on a portal operated by a Government department for the selection of professionals, but he may not list himself on an online application based service provider aggregator in which other categories of service providers are also listed.

Reason (R): An aggregator is operated by a third party, whereas a Government portal is operated by the client, that is, the Government itself, and therefore registration on a Government portal does not amount to listing on an aggregator.

In the light of the above, choose the correct option.
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: The additional points to Clause (6) state in terms that it is not permissible for members to list themselves with online application based service provider aggregators wherein other categories are also listed, and that it is permissible to get registered on government portals since that does not amount to listing on an aggregator. The source also supplies the reason for this differential treatment in the very next sentence, namely that an aggregator is operated by a third party while a government portal is operated by the client, being the Government, itself. Because the reason is the express rationale stated for the rule, (R) is the correct explanation of (A). This is not a case of two independently correct propositions merely happening to sit together.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): CA Gobind, who is appointed internal auditor of Vajram Textiles Limited for FY 2026-27 while the statutory audit of the same company is being done by M/s Hemachandra & Co., need not communicate with Hemachandra & Co. before accepting the internal audit assignment.

Reason (R): Clause (8) of Part I of the First Schedule is applicable in a situation of replacing one auditor by another auditor, and the internal auditor and the statutory auditor are parallel positions and not replacement positions.

In the light of the above, choose the correct option.
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Clause (8) bites only where a position 'previously held' by another chartered accountant or by a certified auditor under the Restricted Certificate Rules, 1932 is accepted. The additional points explain that the clause applies to replacing one auditor by another, and that an internal auditor and a statutory auditor occupy parallel and not replacement positions, so that there is no need for communication by one to the other. Since Gobind is not succeeding Hemachandra & Co. in the same position, no communication is owed and (A) follows directly from (R). Note that the carve-out rests on the parallel nature of the two positions and not on any exemption for internal audit work as such.

questions.question:
CA Phanse holds a certificate of practice and his office is at Panaji, Goa. In January 2026 four things happen:
(a) He pays the additional charges levied by the telephone authority and his name and office telephone number are printed in the Panaji telephone directory under the category 'Chartered Accountants', the entry appearing at serial 214 in the alphabetical list.
(b) At the request of a private body which publishes a directory of the Konkani speaking business community of Mumbai, his name is printed in that Mumbai trade directory, although his office is at Panaji.
(c) He pays a higher slab of charges so that his entry in the Panaji telephone directory is printed in bold and is placed above every other entry in the 'Chartered Accountants' category.
(d) His name is printed in the social directory of a club of which he is a member.

Which one of the following correctly states the position?
options: (a) and (d) are regular, but (b) is irregular because entries may be made only in directories published by telephone authorities, and (c) is irregular because a higher payment may not be made at all.
(a), (b) and (d) are regular, but (c) is irregular, because payment of an additional amount for an entry is permitted, whereas the order of entries must be alphabetical.
All four are regular, because the guidelines permit an entry to be made either on a special request or by means of an additional payment, and the mode of presentation is not regulated.
(a) and (b) are regular, but (c) and (d) are irregular, a bold entry being a form of advertisement and a club directory being a directory for a commercial activity.
questions.explanation: A CA or a CA firm may have an entry made in a telephone directory either by making a special request or by means of an additional payment, so the payment itself in (a) and (c) is unobjectionable. What is objectionable in (c) is the displacement of alphabetical order, because the entry must appear in the CA category and the order of entries must be alphabetical. Members may also include their names in trade and social directories, which covers (b) and (d); the requirement that the CA or firm belong to the town in which the directory is published is directed at the telephone directory entry, and Phanse satisfies it for the Panaji directory. Option A is wrong in treating trade directories as impermissible and in reading the additional payment rule as a prohibition on payment.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on the publication of the name or firm name of a chartered accountant in telephone or other directories:

1. A CA or a CA firm may have entries made in a telephone directory either by making a special request or by means of an additional payment.
2. The entry should appear in the chartered accountant category and the order of entries should be alphabetical.
3. The CA or the CA firm should belong to the town in which the directory is published.
4. Members may also include their names in trade and social directories.
5. Where an additional payment is made, the member may require his entry to be printed ahead of all other entries in that category, since priority of listing is then a service purchased from the authority.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements 1 to 4 reproduce the additional points exactly: an entry may be secured by a special request or by an additional payment, it must appear in the CA category in alphabetical order, the member or firm must belong to the town in which the directory is published, and trade or social directory entries are also permitted. Statement 5 is not correct because the source permits the payment but does not permit purchased priority; the order of entries must remain alphabetical, and reading the payment provision as buying a place ahead of other CAs destroys that requirement. The two rules operate independently: how the entry is obtained is one question, in what order it appears is another.

questions.question:
M/s Deshpande & Rane, Chartered Accountants, Pune, hold the statutory audit of Wagle Motors Limited. For FY 2026-27 the members also appoint the firm as internal auditors of the company. The senior partner records in the file that no letter need be written to the firm's own statutory audit client, because the statutory audit and the internal audit are parallel positions and not replacement positions, and separately records that the internal audit engagement letter is dated 4 May 2026, one day before the statutory audit report for FY 2025-26 is signed.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate conclusion on the communication requirement under Clause (8) of Part I of the First Schedule?
options: Communication with the earlier auditor is necessary, because the appointment of a joint auditor along with an auditor already in position is expressly covered by Clause (8).
Communication is mandatorily required, because the internal auditor is accepting a position previously held by the statutory auditor.

Communication is unnecessary, because the internal auditor and the statutory auditor are parallel positions and not replacement positions, and the date of the engagement letter does not change that analysis.
Communication is unnecessary only if the firm also obtains a certificate from the company that Sections 139 to 141 have been complied with.
questions.explanation: Clause (8) applies to accepting a position as auditor previously held by another chartered accountant or by a certified auditor under the Restricted Certificate Rules, 1932, and the additional points confine it to the replacement of one auditor by another. The internal auditor and the statutory auditor occupy parallel positions, so no communication by one to the other is needed, and the partner's reasoning is sound. Option A misapplies the joint audit rule, which concerns a new auditor appointed to act along with an earlier auditor in the same position, and option B treats the two appointments as successive occupancies of one position. The date of the engagement letter is a red herring, and Clause (9)'s verification requirement is a separate obligation which does not create a communication duty under Clause (8).

questions.question:
The following four situations arise in the course of the year at the office of CA Ramanujan, who is in practice at Coimbatore:
(I) After his articled clerk clears the CA final examination in May 2026, Ramanujan gives a notice to a daily newspaper announcing the success, naming the articled clerk and describing the quality of training imparted by his firm.
(II) He writes a letter to the editor of a national newspaper on the treatment of government grants, and signs it 'CA V. Ramanujan, Chartered Accountant'.
(III) He organises a two-day training course for the staff of his firm, sends the brochure also to the staff of other chartered accountants and to his clients, and has his firm's name printed in the largest type on the cover page.
(IV) He gets a write-up of his firm's services published in a monthly journal which carries a testimonial from a long-standing client describing the firm's tax work as 'unrivalled'.

Which of the above situations do not contravene the additional points to Clause (7) of Part I of the First Schedule?
questions.explanation: A notice in the press relating to success in the examination should not contain any undesirable publicity relating to an articled clerk, audit assistant, employee, member or the firm, so (I) fails on both counts. Writing articles or letters to the press is expressly permitted and the member may give his name and use the description 'CA', so (II) is regular. Organising training courses or seminars for staff is permitted and staff of other chartered accountants and clients may even be invited, but undue prominence should not be given to the CA name in any document issued, which makes the brochure in (III) objectionable. Advertising through a write-up must not contain testimonials or endorsements, and must not contain exaggerated claims for services offered, so (IV) fails; the fact that inviting outside staff is permitted does not save (III), because it is the prominence of the name and not the invitation that offends.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I Clause (7) - Designations
questions.question:
Consider the following statements on the use of designations and titles under the additional points to Clause (7) of Part I of the First Schedule:

1. It is improper for a CA to use designations such as Cost Accountant, Company Secretary, Cost Consultant, Management Consultant, Income-tax Consultant, Advocate, Corporate Lawyer, Cybersecurity Expert, Member of Parliament or Municipal Councillor simultaneously.
2. A member who is also a member of ICSI may use the letters 'CS' along with 'CA', since titles, letters and initials indicating membership of other professional bodies or institutions such as CS, CMA, ACCA, CFA, LLB and ICAEW are permitted.
3. A member may use the initials 'CPA' where he is a member of a foreign institute of certified public accountants with which the Council has entered into an MoU or Members' Recognition Agreement.
4. A member may mention a title indicating membership of a foreign institute of accountancy recognised by the Council through an agreement, such as the South African Institute of Chartered Accountants, the Institute of Certified Public Accountants of Ireland or the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales.
5. A member who is a Director of a company, who heads a CA Cell of the Institute, or who being a member of a political party holds a position in a club, may mention that position along with his name.

Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Statement 3 is not correct because, notwithstanding a Council agreement (MoU or MRA) with a foreign institute of accountancy, members are not permitted to use the initials 'CPA'; what the agreement unlocks is the title indicating membership of that institute, as statement 4 correctly says. Statement 5 is not correct because members who are Directors in companies or CA Cells, or who are members of political parties holding positions in clubs or other organisations, are not permitted to mention any such position. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct, and the apparent tension between them is deliberate: a designation such as 'Company Secretary' may not be used simultaneously, while the letters 'CS' indicating membership of the body may be used, the two being treated differently by the source.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I Clause (7) - Issue advisory
questions.question:
CA Deepa's firm is appointed advisor to the public issue of Narayan Steels Limited, whose prospectus is issued in September 2025. Deepa issues the following four instructions to her articles:
(I) The prospectus will carry the firm's name and address under the caption 'Advisor to the Issue', followed by a paragraph listing the firm's professional attainments, including that the partners are Fellows of ICAI with 27 years' experience.
(II) New letter heads of the firm will describe the firm as 'Deepa & Associates - Merchant Bankers and Advisors to Issues'.
(III) The partners' visiting cards will carry the designation 'Advisor to Issue - Narayan Steels Limited'.
(IV) The prospectus will carry the firm's name and address under the caption 'Consultant to the Issue' and will contain no statement of the firm's professional attainments.

Which combination of instructions is permissible under the additional points to Clause (7) of Part I of the First Schedule?
questions.explanation: In a client company's offer documents such as a prospectus, and in advertisements regarding a capital issue, the name and address of the CA acting as advisor or consultant to the issue may be indicated under the caption 'Advisor/Consultant to the Issue'; (IV) conforms to that. However, the prospectus should not contain the professional attainments of the member, which offends in (I). Members should not use the designation 'Merchant Banker' or 'Advisor/Consultant to Issue' in their own letter heads, visiting cards or professional documents, which offends in (II) and (III). The distinction that decides this question is between the client's document, where the caption is permitted, and the member's own stationery, where it is not.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I Clause (7) - Designations
questions.question:
CA Farida, who holds a certificate of practice, is a Fellow of ICAI. She is also a member of a foreign institute of accountancy which is recognised by the Council through an agreement, a qualified company secretary and a member of ICSI, an advocate enrolled with the Bar Council of India, a non-executive director of Tamil Nadu Petrocarbs Limited, and a member of the Institute of Certified Public Accountants of a foreign country. She proposes to use the following five descriptions in her professional documents:
(I) 'CS' indicating her membership of ICSI
(II) 'Advocate' indicating her enrolment with the Bar Council
(III) 'FCA'
(IV) 'CPA' indicating her membership of the foreign institute of certified public accountants
(V) A title indicating her membership of the foreign institute of accountancy recognised by the Council through an agreement

Which of the above may she use?
options: (I), (III), (V) and, in addition, her directorship in Tamil Nadu Petrocarbs Limited
questions.explanation: Titles, letters and initials indicating membership of other professional bodies are permitted, which covers 'CS' in (I) and 'FCA' in (III); 'Advocate' and 'Corporate Lawyer' are, however, expressly named among the designations which are improper to use simultaneously, so (II) fails, and the fact of enrolment with the Bar Council does not help. Members are not permitted to use the initials 'CPA' even where the Council has an agreement with the foreign institute, so (IV) fails, while a title indicating membership of a foreign institute of accountancy recognised by the Council through an MoU or MRA is permitted, so (V) stands. A member who is a Director in a company is not permitted to mention that position, so the extension in option D is wrong.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I Clause (7) - Designations
questions.question: Which one of the following pairs of descriptions may a member in practice mention in his professional documents, according to the additional points to Clause (7) of Part I of the First Schedule?
questions.explanation: The additional points state in terms that a member can mention 'Insolvency Professional' or 'Registered Valuer', so the pair at option C is permissible notwithstanding that both describe roles outside pure audit practice. Cost Consultant and Management Consultant appear in the list of designations which it is improper for a CA to use simultaneously, and Merchant Banker is separately barred in letter heads, visiting cards and professional documents, so options A and B fail. Member of Parliament and Municipal Councillor are likewise in the improper list, and members holding positions in clubs or other organisations, including political ones, may not mention such positions.
