The point to note is that the insolvency and valuation descriptions are specifically carved out as mentionable.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I Clause (7) - Stationery and branding
questions.question:
Match each item in Column I with the correct position in Column II, applying the additional points headed 'Establishment Date, Firm Name, QR Code, Sign Board and Logo' under Clause (7) of Part I of the First Schedule.

Column I
(P) Date of setting up practice printed on the letter head
(Q) Names of all the firms in which the member is a partner, printed on his personal letter head
(R) A QR code printed on a visiting card
(S) A monogram of the member's initials in an interlaced design printed on file covers
(T) A sign board of a size chosen by the member
(U) The CA logo used on professional documents

Column II
(1) Should not be mentioned
(2) Permitted
(3) Permitted, provided the code does not contain information which is not permissible to be printed on a visiting card
(4) Prohibited on anything, whatever be the kind, form, style, design or colour
(5) Permitted as to size, but glow signs or lights on large sized boards as used by shopkeepers are not permissible
(6) Permissible, subject to the CA logo guidelines
questions.explanation: The date of setting up practice or of establishment of the firm should not be mentioned on letter heads and other professional documents, so P-1. A member is allowed to print the names of all firms in which he is a partner on his personal letter heads, so Q-2, and the same treatment is available to the CA logo only because it alone escapes the general prohibition, which is why U takes (6) and not (2). The QR code is expressly permitted on a visiting card subject to the content condition, so R-3; the use of a logo or monogram of any kind, form, style, design or colour on anything is prohibited, so S-4. Size of sign board is at the member's own discretion but glow signs or lights on large sized boards as used by shopkeepers are not permissible, so T-5.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I Clause (7) - Stationery and branding
questions.question: Which one of the following statements about the use of logos and sign boards by a chartered accountant in practice is NOT correct?
options: The use of a logo or monogram of any kind, form, style, design or colour on anything is prohibited, and only the use of the CA logo is permissible, subject to the CA logo guidelines.
A member may print a QR code on his visiting card, provided the code does not contain information which is not permissible to be printed on a visiting card.
Members have their own discretion regarding the size of the sign board, but the use of glow signs or lights on large sized boards as used by shopkeepers is not permissible.
The date of setting up practice or of establishment of the firm may be mentioned on letter heads and other professional documents, provided it is set in a font size not exceeding 14.
questions.explanation: The date of setting up practice or establishment of the firm should not be mentioned on letter heads and other professional documents at all; there is no font size which converts a prohibited item into a permitted one. The font size restriction of 14 belongs to a different rule, namely the Council guidelines governing advertisement of professional attainments or services through a write-up, and option D mis-transplants it. Statements A, B and C correctly state the logo prohibition with its CA logo exception, the conditional permission for a QR code on a visiting card, and the discretionary sign board size subject to the bar on glow signs or lights on large sized boards as used by shopkeepers.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I Clause (7) - Stationery and branding
questions.question:
CA Trilok's visiting card carries his name, the name of his firm, its address, telephone number, mobile number and e-mail ID, and also a QR code. Scanning the code opens a page which contains: (i) the year in which he set up practice; (ii) a passport-size photograph of CA Trilok; (iii) the names of four prominent client companies; (iv) a list of the vacancies in his office; and (v) a testimonial from a client praising his advisory work. His letter head does not carry the year of setting up practice, and the card is not used to solicit anybody.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: The card is irregular in itself, because a QR code is a monogram or design of the kind prohibited on anything.
Everything is regular, because the page opened by the code is website content governed by the Website Guidelines and not by the rules applicable to a visiting card.

The QR code may be printed on the visiting card, but the page must not carry the year of setting up practice, the names of client companies or the testimonial, because the code must not contain information which is not permissible to be printed on a visiting card.
The QR code is permissible only if the page carries the year of setting up practice, that year being permitted on a visiting card although not on a letter head.
questions.explanation: A member is allowed to print a QR code on a visiting card, but only provided the code does not contain information that may not be printed on a visiting card, so the medium is not a shelter and options A and B fail. The year of establishment is allowed on a website but not on letter heads and other professional documents, names of clients may not be given except where a regulator requires it, and a write-up must not contain testimonials or endorsements; these three items therefore offend. Items (ii), (iv) and (v) as to photographs and vacancies are not objectionable, and the absence of solicitation and the omission of the year from the letter head are background facts which do not cure the code.

questions.category: First Schedule Part I Clause (7) - Stationery and branding
questions.question: Which one of the following statements about a member's sign board, letter head or branding is NOT correct?
options: Members have their own discretion as to the size of the sign board.
A member who is in charge of a CA Cell of the Institute may mention that position on his professional documents.
A member may print on his personal letter head the names of all the firms in which he is a partner.
Glow signs or lights on large sized boards as used by shopkeepers are not permissible.
questions.explanation: The additional points expressly bar members who are Directors in companies or CA Cells, and members of political parties holding positions in clubs or other organisations, from mentioning any such position, so a CA Cell in-charge may not print that position on professional documents. Size of sign board is left to the member's own discretion, subject to the separate bar on glow signs or lights on large sized boards as used by shopkeepers, which makes options A and D correct statements. Printing the names of all firms in which he is a partner on a personal letter head is expressly allowed, so option C is also correct. The decisive words in the source are 'not permitted to mention any positions'.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on Clause (8) of Part I of the First Schedule, which deals with accepting a position as auditor previously held by another chartered accountant or by a certified auditor issued a certificate under the Restricted Certificate Rules, 1932:

1. The object of the incoming auditor in communicating with the retiring auditor is to ascertain from him whether there are any circumstances which warrant him not to accept the appointment.
2. Non-compliance with the provisions of Sections 139 and 140 of the Companies Act, 2013, and non-payment of undisputed audit fees by auditees other than in the case of sick units, are professional reasons for not accepting an audit, and an auditor who accepts the audit in either of these two cases would be guilty of professional misconduct.
3. The issuance of a qualified report is a professional reason for not accepting an audit, and consequently the incoming auditor can in no case accept the appointment.
4. Where the retiring auditor has issued a qualified report, the incoming auditor may accept the audit if the attitude of the retiring auditor was not proper, but if he feels that the retiring auditor had qualified the report for valid reasons, he should not accept the audit.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: The three professional reasons for not accepting an audit are non-compliance with Sections 139 and 140, non-payment of undisputed audit fees by auditees other than sick units, and the issuance of a qualified report; in the first two cases the auditor who accepts the audit is guilty of professional misconduct, which is what statement 2 says. Statement 3 overstates the position on the third reason, because the source gives the incoming auditor a judgement to exercise: he may accept if the retiring auditor's attitude was not proper, and should decline only if he considers the qualification to have been made for valid reasons. Statement 4 states that qualified position correctly, and statement 1 reproduces the object of the communication. The consequence therefore differs between the first two reasons and the third.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on the cases in which communication with the auditor who previously held the position is required under Clause (8) of Part I of the First Schedule:

1. Communication is mandatorily required for all types of audit where the auditor previously holding the position is a chartered accountant.
2. Where a new auditor is appointed to act jointly with an auditor already holding the appointment, the new auditor must communicate with that earlier auditor.
3. A person appointed as internal auditor of a company in which a statutory auditor is already in position need not communicate with the statutory auditor, the two being parallel positions and not replacement positions.
4. Communication is unnecessary where the person who previously held the position was a certified auditor issued a certificate under the Restricted Certificate Rules, 1932, the clause extending only to chartered accountants.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Communication is mandatorily required for all types of audit if the previous auditor is a chartered accountant, and it is equally necessary where a new auditor is appointed to act jointly with an earlier auditor, so statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is correct because the clause is confined to the replacement of one auditor by another, and an internal auditor and a statutory auditor occupy parallel positions. Statement 4 is not correct, because the clause in terms covers a position previously held by another chartered accountant or by a certified auditor who has been issued a certificate under the Restricted Certificate Rules, 1932, so the predecessor's status as a certified auditor does not remove the duty.

questions.question:
M/s Yede & Co. have been the statutory auditors of Karavali Steel Limited since 2021. For FY 2026-27 the members at the annual general meeting held on 28 September 2025 appoint M/s Zanzot & Co. as joint auditors along with Yede & Co. Zanzot & Co. do not write to Yede & Co., and record in their working papers that Clause (8) is concerned only with a case where one auditor is replaced by another, that no replacement has taken place here, and that the position of a joint auditor is therefore analogous to that of an internal auditor vis-a-vis a statutory auditor.

Which one of the following is the correct position?
options: Zanzot & Co. are right, because two firms holding a joint appointment occupy parallel positions and no replacement takes place.

Zanzot & Co. are wrong, because communication is necessary where a new auditor is appointed to act jointly with an earlier auditor, the requirement not being confined to the replacement of one auditor by another.
Zanzot & Co. are wrong, but the duty in a joint audit lies on the earlier auditor, Yede & Co., who must record their no-objection before the audit begins.
Zanzot & Co. are right, because Clause (8) applies only where the predecessor is a certified auditor under the Restricted Certificate Rules, 1932.
questions.explanation: The additional points to Clause (8) contain a specific rule for joint audits: it is necessary for a new auditor appointed to act jointly with an earlier auditor to communicate with that earlier auditor. The analogy drawn with the internal auditor fails, because the source treats internal and statutory audit as parallel positions precisely on the footing that neither replaces the other, whereas a joint appointment adds an auditor to an existing position and is expressly covered by a separate rule. Option C reverses the direction of the duty, which rests on the auditor coming in. Option D misreads the clause, which covers a predecessor who is a chartered accountant or a certified auditor under the Restricted Certificate Rules, 1932.

questions.question: CA Naveen is approached to accept the statutory audit of Bramha Roto Limited for FY 2026-27. From his written communication with the retiring auditor, CA Ghosh, he learns that: (i) Ghosh had issued a report qualified for a genuine disagreement with management about the valuation of closing inventory of Rs 3.10 crore, which management refused to rectify; (ii) Ghosh is also owed audit fees of Rs 4.50 lakh for FY 2024-25 which the company has admitted in writing, the provision for which stands sanctioned in the accounts signed by the auditee and the auditor, and which remains unpaid, the company being solvent with a net worth of Rs 60 crore and accumulated losses of Rs 9 crore; (iii) the previous auditor's five-year term had come to an end, yet the Board of Directors purported to appoint Naveen by a resolution passed on 10 April 2026, no appointment having been made at the annual general meeting; and (iv) Ghosh had also declined to sign the company's stock certificates in the year of the qualification. Naveen has filed a copy of the Registered Acknowledgement Due letter and Ghosh's written reply in his audit file. Which one of the following correctly states the effect of these facts on Naveen's decision?
options: The unpaid admitted fees at (ii), the qualification for genuine reasons at (i), and the Board appointment at (iii), each independently preclude acceptance.
Naveen may accept, because the fees at (ii) are undisputed and therefore recoverable by Ghosh independently, and an auditor is free to disagree with his predecessor on a qualification.
Naveen may accept, because only non-payment of fees by a sick unit and non-compliance with Sections 139 and 140 make acceptance a misconduct, and this company is not a sick unit.

Naveen should not accept solely because of the Board resolution at (iii), that being the only professional reason which makes acceptance a misconduct, Ghosh's refusal to sign stock certificates at (iv) being decisive on the remaining facts.
questions.explanation: The three professional reasons for not accepting an audit under Clause (8) are non-compliance with Sections 139 and 140 of the Companies Act, 2013, non-payment of undisputed audit fees by auditees other than sick units, and the issuance of a qualified report; in the first two cases an auditor who accepts the audit is guilty of professional misconduct. Here the five-year term had expired so the appointment belonged to the members and not to the Board, which is non-compliance with Sections 139 and 140, and the Rs 4.50 lakh is an undisputed fee of a company which is not a sick unit because its accumulated losses of Rs 9 crore are far below its net worth of Rs 60 crore, each of these being a complete bar. On the third reason the source gives a judgement rather than an absolute bar: Naveen could have accepted if Ghosh's attitude was not proper, but because the qualification rested on a genuine, unrectified disagreement, Naveen should not accept. Ghosh's refusal to sign stock certificates at (iv) is a red herring, being a matter under Clause (12) of Part I and not a Clause (8) reason, which rules out option D. Option B confuses the sick unit test with the undisputed nature of the fee, and option C reverses the rule, since it is payment by auditees other than sick units which is the bar.

questions.question:
M/s Kiran Kumar & Associates, Chartered Accountants, Hyderabad, are asked in March 2026 to take over the statutory audit of Trishul Alloys Limited for FY 2026-27 from M/s Praveen & Co., the retiring auditors. On 20 March 2026 the four partners of Kiran Kumar record the following four steps in their file:
(I) A letter is posted to Praveen & Co. under a certificate of posting; the letter is not received back and no reply is received.
(II) A letter is sent by hand on 24 March 2026 to the address of Praveen & Co. registered with the Institute, and the office boy obtains a signed acknowledgement on a photocopy of the letter.
(III) An e-mail is sent on 26 March 2026 to the vide/official e-mail address of a partner of Praveen & Co. registered with ICAI, and an acknowledgement is received from that address, Praveen & Co. having also been asked to quote their UDIN.
(IV) A letter is sent through Registered Acknowledgement Due on 28 March 2026 and is received back with the postal remark 'Office found Locked'.
Kiran Kumar also learn from the company's records that Praveen & Co. resigned with effect from 31 March 2026 and that the Board of Directors at its meeting of 15 March 2026 filled that casual vacancy, and they hold a certificate from the Managing Director stating that Sections 139 to 141 of the Companies Act, 2013 stand complied with.

Which one of the following combinations of steps, taken by themselves, is sufficient to establish communication with the retiring auditors under the additional points to Clause (8)?
questions.explanation: Mere posting of a letter under certificate of posting does not establish communication with the retiring auditor unless there is evidence that the letter reached him, which disposes of (I); the letter not having been returned is not such evidence. The three recognised forms of evidence are a letter sent through Registered Acknowledgement Due, delivery by hand against a written acknowledgement, and an acknowledgement from the retiring auditor's vide/official e-mail address registered with ICAI or his UDIN, which cover (II) and (III). A communication received back with the remark 'Office found Locked' is deemed to have been delivered to the retiring auditor, so (IV) is also sufficient. The combination of (II), (III) and (IV) is therefore the only one in which every step, standing alone, discharges the duty.

questions.question:
M/s Kiran Kumar & Associates, Chartered Accountants, Hyderabad, are asked in March 2026 to take over the statutory audit of Trishul Alloys Limited for FY 2026-27 from M/s Praveen & Co., the retiring auditors. On 20 March 2026 the four partners of Kiran Kumar record the following four steps in their file:
(I) A letter is posted to Praveen & Co. under a certificate of posting; the letter is not received back and no reply is received.
(II) A letter is sent by hand on 24 March 2026 to the address of Praveen & Co. registered with the Institute, and the office boy obtains a signed acknowledgement on a photocopy of the letter.
(III) An e-mail is sent on 26 March 2026 to the vide/official e-mail address of a partner of Praveen & Co. registered with ICAI, and an acknowledgement is received from that address, Praveen & Co. having also been asked to quote their UDIN.
(IV) A letter is sent through Registered Acknowledgement Due on 28 March 2026 and is received back with the postal remark 'Office found Locked'.
Kiran Kumar also learn from the company's records that Praveen & Co. resigned with effect from 31 March 2026 and that the Board of Directors at its meeting of 15 March 2026 filled that casual vacancy, and they hold a certificate from the Managing Director stating that Sections 139 to 141 of the Companies Act, 2013 stand complied with.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate conclusion on the validity of the appointment and on the material on which Kiran Kumar may rely for the purposes of Clause (9)?
options: The Managing Director's certificate discharges the duty under Clause (9), because a certificate from the management is the recognised means of ascertaining compliance, and the Board's resolution of 15 March 2026 is a matter to be verified under Clause (8) instead.

A casual vacancy arising from resignation must be filled by the members in general meeting, so Kiran Kumar should first obtain a regular resolution of the members; the Managing Director's certificate is, however, sufficient as to the remaining requirements.

A casual vacancy arising from resignation is filled by the Board of Directors, so the Board's appointment follows the correct pattern; but Kiran Kumar should not rest on the Managing Director's certificate, Clause (9) requiring them to verify from the records of the company whether Sections 139 to 141 have been duly complied with.

Since Praveen & Co. resigned, the appointment must be treated as that of a first auditor which the Board may make, and once the four steps above are completed no verification of records under Clause (9) is required.
questions.explanation: Clause (9) requires the incoming auditor of a company to ascertain from it whether the requirements of Sections 139 to 141 of the Companies Act, 2013, or of any other law pertaining to appointment of auditors, have been duly complied with. The additional points state that it is not sufficient to accept a certificate from the management that the sections have been complied with, so it is necessary to verify records; option A therefore fails even though it is correct that the Board may fill a casual vacancy arising from death, disqualification or resignation. Options B and D mis-state the allocation of the appointment power, which places the first auditor and a casual vacancy arising from death, disqualification or resignation with the Board and other cases with the members. The decisive fact is that the vacancy arose from resignation, making the Board's appointment the correct pattern while leaving the duty to verify records untouched.

questions.question:
M/s Kiran Kumar & Associates, Chartered Accountants, Hyderabad, are asked in March 2026 to take over the statutory audit of Trishul Alloys Limited for FY 2026-27 from M/s Praveen & Co., the retiring auditors. On 20 March 2026 the four partners of Kiran Kumar record the following four steps in their file:
(I) A letter is posted to Praveen & Co. under a certificate of posting; the letter is not received back and no reply is received.
(II) A letter is sent by hand on 24 March 2026 to the address of Praveen & Co. registered with the Institute, and the office boy obtains a signed acknowledgement on a photocopy of the letter.
(III) An e-mail is sent on 26 March 2026 to the vide/official e-mail address of a partner of Praveen & Co. registered with ICAI, and an acknowledgement is received from that address, Praveen & Co. having also been asked to quote their UDIN.
(IV) A letter is sent through Registered Acknowledgement Due on 28 March 2026 and is received back with the postal remark 'Office found Locked'.
Kiran Kumar also learn from the company's records that Praveen & Co. resigned with effect from 31 March 2026 and that the Board of Directors at its meeting of 15 March 2026 filled that casual vacancy, and they hold a certificate from the Managing Director stating that Sections 139 to 141 of the Companies Act, 2013 stand complied with.

Assume that step (IV) is altered as follows: the letter is despatched to the address at which Praveen & Co. were actually carrying on work, which was not the address registered with the Institute on the date of dispatch, and it is received back with the remark 'No such office exists at this address'. What is the effect of this change?
options: The communication would still be deemed delivered, because any communication returned undelivered is treated as delivered so that the incoming auditor is not held up indefinitely.

The communication would not be deemed delivered, because the deeming rule operates only where the address used is the same as the address registered with the Institute on the date of dispatch, and Kiran Kumar would have to rely on another permitted mode.
The communication would be deemed delivered unless Kiran Kumar prove that Praveen & Co. in fact received the letter, the burden being on the incoming auditor.
The position would be exactly as in the original step (IV), because 'Office found Locked' and 'No such office exists at this address' are treated alike.
questions.explanation: Where a communication is received back with the remark 'No such office exists at this address', it is deemed delivered only if the address used was the same as the address registered with the Institute on the date of dispatch, and even then the retiring auditor may prove that it was not really served. On the altered facts Kiran Kumar used an unregistered address, so the condition fails and the letter cannot be deemed delivered; steps (II) and (III) remain independent good evidence, but (IV) as altered adds nothing. This is unlike 'Office found Locked', which is deemed delivered without any condition about the address, so option D is wrong. Option A invents a general deeming rule which the source does not contain, and option C reverses the onus.

questions.question:
Match each situation in Column I with its consequence in Column II, applying the additional points to Clause (8) of Part I of the First Schedule on the mode of communication with the retiring auditor.

Column I
(P) A letter posted under certificate of posting to the retiring auditor, which is neither replied to nor received back
(Q) A letter sent through Registered Acknowledgement Due which is received back with the postal remark 'Office found Locked'
(R) A letter sent to the address of the retiring auditor registered with the Institute on the date of dispatch, received back with the remark 'No such office exists at this address'
(S) An acknowledgement received from the retiring auditor's vide/official e-mail address registered with ICAI in reply to the incoming auditor's letter
(T) A letter delivered by hand against a written acknowledgement

Column II
(1) Communication with the retiring auditor is established, this being an expressly recognised form of evidence
(2) The communication is deemed to have been delivered to the retiring auditor
(3) The communication is deemed to have been delivered unless the retiring auditor proves that it was not really served
(4) Communication is not established, there being no evidence that the letter reached the person communicated with
questions.explanation: Posting a letter under certificate of posting does not by itself establish communication unless there is evidence that the letter reached the addressee, and neither a reply nor the return of the letter supplies that evidence, so P-4. A communication received back with 'Office found Locked' is deemed delivered, giving Q-2, whereas a letter returned with 'No such office exists at this address' sent to the address registered with the Institute on the date of dispatch is deemed delivered unless the retiring auditor proves that it was not really served, giving R-3 and placing the onus on him. Acknowledgement from the vide or official e-mail address registered with ICAI, and delivery by hand against a written acknowledgement, are both expressly listed forms of evidence, so S-1 and T-1. The contrast between P and Q is the decisive one: non-return of a letter sent under certificate of posting proves nothing.

questions.question:
CA Maheshwar was appointed statutory auditor of Gokul Polymers Limited at the annual general meeting held on 30 September 2025, the previous auditors M/s Shantinath & Co. having not been re-appointed by the members. Maheshwar sent the required letter to Shantinath & Co. through Registered Acknowledgement Due on 5 October 2025. Shantinath & Co., who were upset at not being re-appointed, deliberately did not reply, and the letter was not received back. Maheshwar waited till 15 November 2025 and then accepted the appointment and commenced the audit.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: Maheshwar contravened Clause (8), because a reply from the retiring auditor and not merely a letter is required before the appointment may be accepted.
Maheshwar is in order, because non-return of a letter establishes communication, the risk of the addressee's silence being his own.

Where the retiring auditor fails to respond out of a feeling of hurt because of the change, the auditor appointed may act after waiting for a reasonable time, and communication had in any event been made through Registered Acknowledgement Due.
No communication was necessary, because a non-re-appointment by the members is not the replacement of one auditor by another.
questions.explanation: The additional points contemplate precisely this situation: if the retiring auditor fails to respond due to a feeling of hurt because of the change, the auditor appointed can act after waiting for a reasonable time, and a wait of about six weeks from 5 October to 15 November 2025 satisfies that. Communication was also made in a recognised form, a letter sent through Registered Acknowledgement Due being one of the three evidence modes, so the duty in Clause (8) is discharged. Option A wrongly converts the duty to communicate into a duty to obtain a reply, and option C's premise is right even though it is not the best answer because it rests on the wrong ground. Option D misreads the clause, a non-re-appointment followed by the appointment of another auditor in the same position being a replacement.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about Clause (8) of Part I of the First Schedule is NOT correct?
options: The clause is attracted when a chartered accountant accepts a position as auditor previously held by another chartered accountant, or by a certified auditor who has been issued a certificate under the Restricted Certificate Rules, 1932.
Communication with the auditor who previously held the position must be in writing, and is mandatorily required for all types of audit where the previous auditor is a chartered accountant.

In the audit of a Government company or a Government bank, where there is no time to wait for a reply from the outgoing auditor, the incoming auditor may give a conditional acceptance of the appointment and commence the work.

Where the new auditor is appointed to act jointly with an auditor already holding the appointment, it is the earlier auditor who must communicate his no-objection to the new auditor before the joint audit begins.
questions.explanation: The joint audit rule places the duty on the incoming side: it is necessary for the new auditor appointed to act jointly with an earlier auditor to communicate with such earlier auditor. Option D reverses the direction of the obligation, which makes it the statement that is not correct. Options A, B and C reproduce the source, the clause covering a predecessor who is a chartered accountant or a certified auditor under the Restricted Certificate Rules, 1932, the communication having to be in writing and being mandatory for all types of audit where the previous auditor is a chartered accountant, and conditional acceptance followed by commencement of work being available for Government companies and banks where there is no time to await the outgoing auditor's reply. That facility is confined to Government companies and banks and does not extend to private companies.

questions.question:
M/s Anand Krishnan & Co., Chartered Accountants, are invited on 20 March 2026 by the Board of Directors of Kaveri Gramin Bank, a banking company in which the Central Government holds the whole of the paid-up share capital, to fill a casual vacancy caused by the resignation of M/s Balasubramanian & Co. with effect from 19 March 2026, the statutory audit of FY 2025-26 having to be completed by 31 March 2026. Anand Krishnan send a letter through Registered Acknowledgement Due on 21 March 2026 to the address of Balasubramanian & Co. registered with the Institute, and receive no reply by 24 March 2026. The letter is not received back. They also obtain from the Chairman of the Bank a certificate stating that Sections 139 to 141 of the Companies Act, 2013 stand complied with.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Give a conditional acceptance of the appointment and commence the audit work, the engagement being that of a Government bank and there being no time to wait for the reply of the outgoing auditors.
Wait for a reasonable time for the reply of Balasubramanian & Co. before doing anything, since a conditional acceptance followed by commencement of work would not be available even on these facts.

Commence the work unconditionally, because the posting of a letter under Registered Acknowledgement Due which is not returned is conclusive that the letter reached the addressee and no reply is necessary.
Decline the appointment, because the letter must in any event have been received back with the remark 'Office found Locked' before the appointment can be accepted.
questions.explanation: In the case of the audit of Government companies or banks, where there is no time to wait for a reply from the outgoing auditor, the incoming auditor may give a conditional acceptance of the appointment and commence the work; Kaveri Gramin Bank is wholly government owned and the statutory deadline of 31 March 2026 leaves no time to wait, so option A is available. A letter sent through Registered Acknowledgement Due is one of the recognised modes of evidencing communication, so Anand Krishnan have also discharged the duty to communicate in writing, and nothing turns on the letter not having been received back. Option B would be the correct advice for a non-government entity, and option C overstates the evidentiary effect of posting by treating the absence of a reply as a substitute for the communication. Option D invents a precondition which the source does not contain.

questions.question:
M/s Anand Krishnan & Co., Chartered Accountants, are invited on 20 March 2026 by the Board of Directors of Kaveri Gramin Bank, a banking company in which the Central Government holds the whole of the paid-up share capital, to fill a casual vacancy caused by the resignation of M/s Balasubramanian & Co. with effect from 19 March 2026, the statutory audit of FY 2025-26 having to be completed by 31 March 2026. Anand Krishnan send a letter through Registered Acknowledgement Due on 21 March 2026 to the address of Balasubramanian & Co. registered with the Institute, and receive no reply by 24 March 2026. The letter is not received back. They also obtain from the Chairman of the Bank a certificate stating that Sections 139 to 141 of the Companies Act, 2013 stand complied with.

Assume that the engagement is instead the statutory audit of Sri Sai Spinning Mills Limited, a private company which is not a Government company, the date and all other facts remaining the same. Which one of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: Conditional acceptance followed by commencement of work remains available, because the pressure of the 31 March deadline is the same whatever the category of company.

Conditional acceptance is not available, that facility being expressly confined to the audit of Government companies and banks where there is no time to wait for the outgoing auditor's reply, so the firm must wait for a reasonable time for the reply before acting.
Communication with Balasubramanian & Co. ceases to be necessary, because a private company's certificate that Sections 139 to 141 are complied with substitutes for the retiring auditor's reply.
The firm may commence work immediately, because a casual vacancy caused by resignation is filled by the Board, and a Board appointment does not attract Clause (8).
questions.explanation: The source confines conditional acceptance of appointment and commencement of work to the audit of Government companies or banks where there is no time to wait for a reply from the outgoing auditor, so the change in the identity of the auditee removes the facility and leaves the firm to await a reply or, if the retiring auditor fails to respond out of a feeling of hurt at the change, to act after waiting a reasonable time. Option C confuses Clause (8) with Clause (9), the two being independent duties, one owed to the predecessor and the other to the company. Option D mis-states the consequences of a Board filling a casual vacancy arising from resignation: the appointment pattern is a Clause (9) question and does not affect the Clause (8) duty to communicate, which arises because the incoming auditor is accepting a position previously held by another chartered accountant.

questions.question:
Consider the following four propositions relating to Clause (9) of Part I of the First Schedule, which deals with accepting an appointment as auditor of a company without first ascertaining from it whether the requirements of Sections 139 to 141 of the Companies Act, 2013, or any other law pertaining to appointment of auditors, have been duly complied with:

(I) It is not sufficient for the incoming auditor to accept a certificate from the management of the company that the above sections have been complied with.
(II) It is necessary for the incoming auditor to verify records.
(III) In the case of the first auditor, and in the case of a casual vacancy arising from death, disqualification or resignation of an auditor, the appointment is made by the Board of Directors.
(IV) In cases other than the first auditor and a casual vacancy arising from death, disqualification or resignation, the appointment of an auditor is made by the members.

Which of these propositions are correct?
questions.explanation: The additional points to Clause (9) state in terms that accepting a management certificate that the sections have been complied with is not sufficient, and that it is therefore necessary for the incoming auditor to verify records, so (I) and (II) are both correct and are two halves of the same rule rather than alternatives. The appointment pattern set out under the head 'Appointment of Auditors (other than Government Companies)' is that the first auditor and a casual vacancy arising from death, disqualification or resignation are filled by the Board of Directors, while in other cases the appointment is by the members, which makes (III) and (IV) correct. Verification matters because it tells the auditor whether the body which appointed him was competent to do so; an appointment of a retiring auditor's successor by a Board resolution, for instance, would not fit the pattern.

questions.question:
Nandi Mines Limited has been in existence since 2009. Its auditors for five consecutive years, M/s Gupta & Iyer, resigned on 12 January 2026 and the Board of Directors of the company appointed M/s Harish & Co. as auditors by a resolution passed on 20 January 2026 to hold office till the conclusion of the ensuing annual general meeting. Harish & Co. accept the appointment after obtaining from the company a certificate signed by the Company Secretary confirming that Sections 139 to 141 have been complied with, and without looking at any record of the company.

Which one of the following correctly states the position?
options: The appointment is one the Board is competent to make, because the vacancy arose from resignation, and the certificate from the Company Secretary discharges Clause (9) because it comes from the management of the company.

The vacancy arose on the expiry of a five-year term rather than from death, disqualification or resignation, so it must be filled by the members; the Board's appointment is accordingly not in order, and the management certificate does not discharge Clause (9), which requires Harish & Co. to verify records.

The appointment is one the Board is competent to make, because any casual vacancy in the office of auditor is filled by the Board, and Harish & Co. need not verify records because the resignation of the previous auditors is itself a matter of record.
The vacancy must be filled by the members, but Harish & Co. have complied with Clause (9) because they obtained the certificate before accepting the appointment.
questions.explanation: Clause (9) requires the incoming auditor of a company to ascertain whether Sections 139 to 141 have been duly complied with, and the additional points make verification of records necessary because a certificate from the management is not sufficient. The appointment pattern is the decisive element: the Board fills the first auditor and a casual vacancy arising from death, disqualification or resignation, while in other cases the appointment is made by the members. Here the resignation of 12 January 2026 terminated a five year term which had already run its full length, so what had to be made was an appointment by the members and not a Board appointment; the resignation recited in the facts is what makes option A superficially attractive. Options C and D are wrong in treating the identity of the appointing body as immaterial or the certificate as sufficient.

questions.question:
CA Ritesh set up practice on 1 July 2013 and started the firm 'Ritesh & Co.' at Indore on the same date. In February 2026 he does the following five things:
(I) He gets his letter head printed with the words 'Established 2013' and with the names of the two firms in which he is a partner.
(II) He puts up, outside his office, a sign board of a size he himself selected, lit at night with glow lights.
(III) He gets a monogram of the interlaced initials 'RC' printed in blue on his file covers.
(IV) He prints on his visiting card a QR code which opens a page carrying the year of establishment, the names of his employees and a list of vacancies in his office.
(V) He places the year of establishment 2013 on the home page of his firm's website.

Which one of the following correctly identifies the items which contravene the additional points to Clause (7) of Part I of the First Schedule or the Website Guidelines?
questions.explanation: The date of setting up practice should not be mentioned on letter heads and other professional documents, so (I) offends even though printing the names of all firms in which he is a partner on a personal letter head is separately permitted. Size of the sign board is at the member's own discretion, but glow signs or lights on large sized boards as used by shopkeepers are not permissible, so (II) offends; a monogram of any kind, form, style, design or colour on anything is prohibited, only the CA logo being permissible, so (III) offends. The QR code on a visiting card is permitted only if it does not carry information which may not be printed on the card, and the year of establishment is such information, so (IV) offends. Item (V) is the point of difference: the year of establishment is allowed on the website though not on letter heads, which rules out option D.

questions.question:
Match the following, using the exceptions permitted by Regulation 192 read with Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule:

Column I (Assignment)
(P) Statutory audit of a Co-operative Society
(Q) Valuation of a property
(R) Function as Receiver or Liquidator
(S) Fund raising services
(T) Cost optimisation services

Column II (Permissible basis of fee)
(1) Percentage of paid-up capital / working capital / income
(2) Percentage of value of the property valued
(3) Percentage of realization or disbursement of assets
(4) Percentage of fund raised
(5) Percentage of benefit derived
(6) Percentage of the profits of the client

Choose the correct matching:
questions.explanation: Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule prohibits fees based on a percentage of profits, or contingent upon the findings or results of professional employment, except as permitted by regulations made under the Act. Regulation 192 permits the auditor of a co-operative society to charge a percentage of paid-up capital, working capital or income; a valuer a percentage of the value of the property valued; a receiver or liquidator a percentage of realization or disbursement of assets; fund raising services a percentage of the fund raised; and cost optimisation services a percentage of the benefit derived. Entry (6), percentage of the client's profits, is the very basis named in the clause as prohibited and is not rescued by any exception, so the options that use it fail. The remaining distractors fail by interchanging the valuer's basis with that of the receiver or liquidator, or the cost optimisation basis with that of fund raising.

questions.question:
Sanjay Kothari & Co., a chartered accountants firm in practice at Indore, accepts five assignments in FY 2025-26:
(1) Audit of Narmada District Co-operative Society Ltd. for a fee of 0.15% of its paid-up capital.
(2) Valuation of a warehouse of Vindhya Estates Ltd. for a fee of 0.5% of the value of the property valued.
(3) Assistance to a manufacturing client in reducing power consumption, for a fee of 20% of the benefit derived.
(4) Recovery of overdue dues from the debtors of a client, for a fee of 3% of the debt recovered.
(5) Statutory audit of Vindhya Estates Ltd., a public limited company, for a fee of 0.5% of its net profits.
A partner of the firm objects that (1) and (3) are 'as bad as' (5), being percentage-based and therefore contingent fees. Which of the following statements are correct?
(P) (1) is permitted, the fee being a percentage of paid-up capital in the case of the auditor of a co-operative society.
(Q) Each of (2), (3) and (4) falls within a Regulation 192 exception.
(R) (5) contravenes Clause (10), the fee being based on a percentage of profits of a company whose audit is accepted.
(S) (5) is permitted, because a company audit is covered by the entry for other non-assurance services.
(T) Since the client knew and agreed to the basis of fee in every case, no contravention arises.
questions.explanation: Regulation 192 saves (1), the auditor of a co-operative society being allowed a percentage of paid-up capital, working capital or income, so the partner's objection fails; it also saves (2) as valuation, (3) as cost optimisation services on the percentage of benefit derived and (4) as debt recovery services on the percentage of debt recovered. (5) is not saved, because the statutory audit of a company is an assurance function and the 'other non-assurance services' entry cannot be stretched to it, while a percentage of profits is the basis expressly named in Clause (10). (T) is wrong because the prohibition attaches to the basis of the fee and not to the client's consent, the only exceptions being those made by regulations under the Act. The decisive fact separating (1) from (5) is that the first client is a co-operative society and the fifth is a public limited company whose fee is on profits.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule is NOT correct?
options: The clause covers a fee which the member charges or offers to charge, and also a fee which he accepts or offers to accept in respect of professional employment, so an offer to charge a contingent fee is itself within the prohibition.
A member may charge a fee contingent upon the findings of an assignment, provided the amount is agreed with the client in the engagement letter and the client is fully informed of the basis.
Fees are not to be regarded as contingent if they are fixed by a court or other public authority.
The exceptions to the prohibition are those permitted under regulations made under the Act, such as Regulation 192.
A percentage basis of fee is permissible for debt recovery services, being a percentage of the debt recovered.
questions.explanation: Clause (10) prohibits charging or offering to charge, and accepting or offering to accept, fees based on a percentage of profits or contingent upon the findings or results of professional employment, and the only carve-out is what regulations made under the Act permit. Agreement of the client, disclosure in the engagement letter or full information do not cure the contingency, so the second statement is the one that is not correct. The first statement correctly notes that the clause reaches offers as well as actual charging and accepting. The third reflects the express additional point that fees fixed by a court or other public authority are not to be regarded as contingent, and the fifth reflects the Regulation 192 exception for debt recovery services.

questions.question: Which one of the following percentage-based fee arrangements is NOT covered by the exceptions in Regulation 192 read with Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule?
options: Fee of the auditor of a co-operative society, being a percentage of the working capital of the society.
Fee of a member acting as an insolvency professional, on a percentage basis, the regulation permitting an insolvency professional to charge on a percentage basis.
Fee of a member acting as a valuer, being a percentage of the value of the property valued.
Fee of a member rendering the statutory audit of a public limited company, being a percentage of the paid-up capital of the company.
Fee of a member rendering other non-assurance services, on a percentage basis.
questions.explanation: Regulation 192 confines the paid-up capital, working capital and income basis to the auditor of a co-operative society; it does not extend that basis to the auditor of a company, so a statutory audit fee computed as a percentage of the paid-up capital of a public limited company contravenes Clause (10). The other four arrangements are within the exceptions listed in the regulation, namely the co-operative society auditor, the valuer, the insolvency professional and other non-assurance services on a percentage basis. A candidate may be tempted by the second option because insolvency work is largely statutory, but the regulation expressly allows a percentage basis for an insolvency professional. The decisive fact is the status of the engagement, that is, statutory audit of a company, for which no percentage exception exists.

questions.question: CA Faizan Ahmed is appointed liquidator of Kaveri Spintex Ltd. by the National Company Law Tribunal. He considers two bases of remuneration, namely (i) 1% of the amount of assets realised, and (ii) a lump sum of ₹25 lakh fixed by the Tribunal, payable on conclusion of the winding up and depending on the amount realised. A young member of his firm advises that both are contingent upon the results of the employment and therefore contravene Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule. Which is the MOST appropriate advice to the firm?
options: Both (i) and (ii) contravene Clause (10), a fee payable only on conclusion of a winding up and varying with the amount realised being contingent upon results in any case, and Regulation 192 being unable to save a remuneration which is itself fixed by the Tribunal.
Neither contravenes Clause (10), because a member appointed by a Tribunal does not act as a chartered accountant in practice.

(i) is permitted, Regulation 192 allowing a receiver or liquidator a percentage of realization or disbursement of assets, and (ii) is not contingent, fees fixed by a court or other public authority not being regarded as contingent.
Only (ii) is permitted, since Regulation 192 saves a liquidator's fee only when it is fixed by a court or Tribunal.
Only (i) is permitted, since a lump sum dependent on the amount realised is necessarily contingent upon the findings of the employment.
questions.explanation: Regulation 192 expressly permits a receiver or a liquidator to charge fees on a percentage of realization or disbursement of assets, so arrangement (i) is saved and does not contravene Clause (10). Arrangement (ii) is saved by the different principle that fees should not be regarded as contingent if fixed by a court or other public authority, the Tribunal having itself fixed ₹25 lakh; the fact that it is payable on conclusion of the winding up does not make it a contingent fee within the clause. The young member's advice is therefore wrong on both counts. The distractor which permits only (ii) fails because it treats the court fixation as the sole source of protection, and the one which permits only (i) fails by ignoring the court-fixed fee rule.

questions.question:
Match the following activities of a chartered accountant in practice with their status under Clause (11) of Part I of the First Schedule:

Column I (Activity)
(P) Acting as a special executive magistrate
(Q) Editorship of a professional journal
(R) Holding the public elective office of M.L.A.
(S) Running a retail grocery store on his own account
(T) Part-time tutorship under an educational institution which is not an ICAI organisation

Column II (Status)
(1) Permitted by the General Resolution, no specific permission of the Council being necessary
(2) Permitted only after specific and prior approval of the Council under Regulation 190A
(3) Not permitted by either resolution, being a business other than the profession of a chartered accountant

Choose the correct matching:
questions.explanation: The General Resolution to Clause (11) permits, without specific Council permission, acting as notary public, justice of the peace or special executive magistrate, editorship of professional journals, and holding of public elective offices such as M.P., M.L.A. and M.L.C., so (P), (Q) and (R) are all status (1). Part-time or full-time tutorship under an educational institution other than an ICAI organisation is in the Specific Resolution list under Regulation 190A and needs specific and prior approval, so (T) is status (2). Running a retail grocery store appears in neither list and is a business other than the profession of a chartered accountant, so (S) is status (3). The distractors mostly fail by treating editorship of a professional journal as requiring Council permission, which is true only of editorship of journals other than professional journals.

questions.question:
Radhika Menon, a chartered accountant in practice at Kochi, is engaged in the following activities during FY 2025-26, no permission having been sought from the Council in any case:
(a) She is an ordinary (simple) director of Coromandel Seafoods Ltd., receiving sitting fees only, neither she nor any partner of her firm being interested in that company as auditor.
(b) She is honorary secretary of a non-commercial educational trust.
(c) She edits a monthly literary magazine which is not a professional journal.
(d) She holds an interest in her father's family business concern.
(e) She owns six acres of agricultural land at Wayanad and carries on agricultural activity there.
Which of the following statements are correct?
(P) (a) is permissible without Council permission, nothing in Clause (11) disentitling a chartered accountant from being a director of a company, not being a managing or whole-time director, unless he or any of his partners is interested in that company as auditor.
(Q) (b) and (e) are permitted by the General Resolution, as honorary office leadership of a non-commercial organisation and as owning agricultural land and carrying out agricultural activity.
(R) (c) requires the specific and prior approval of the Council under Regulation 190A, editorship of journals other than professional journals being a specific resolution activity.
(S) (d) needs no permission, a family business concern being outside Clause (11) because the member does not carry it on.
(T) (a) is misconduct, because every directorship accepted by a chartered accountant in practice requires the Council's permission.
questions.explanation: (a) falls within the express carve-out that nothing disentitles a chartered accountant from being a director of a company, other than a managing or whole-time director, unless he or any of his partners is interested in that company as auditor, and is also a General Resolution item as director simplicitor, so (P) is correct and (T) is wrong. Honorary office leadership of charitable, educational or other non-commercial organisations, and owning agricultural land and carrying out agricultural activity, are both General Resolution items, so (Q) is correct. Editorship of journals other than professional journals is in the Specific Resolution list under Regulation 190A, so (c) needed prior Council approval and (R) is correct. An interest in a family business concern is likewise in the Specific Resolution list, so (S) is wrong; the sitting fees only nature of (a) is immaterial to this conclusion.

questions.question:
During FY 2025-26 a chartered accountant in practice takes up the following six activities:
(i) Employment under another chartered accountant in practice
(ii) Holding a life insurance agency licence, for getting renewal commission
(iii) Acting as a recovery consultant in the banking sector
(iv) Part-time tutorship under a coaching organisation of ICAI
(v) Sale of a domain name in order to earn royalty
(vi) An interest in an educational institution
Which of these may be undertaken without any permission from the Council under Clause (11) of Part I of the First Schedule?
questions.explanation: Employment under a chartered accountant in practice or a CA firm, holding a life insurance agency licence for getting renewal commission, acting as recovery consultant in the banking sector and part-time tutorship under a coaching organisation of ICAI are all in the General Resolution list, so they need no specific permission from the Council. Sale of a domain name for earning royalty falls within the residual specific resolution item covering any other business or occupation for which the Executive Committee considers that permission may be granted, and an interest in an educational institution is itself an enumerated specific resolution activity under Regulation 190A, so (v) and (vi) require specific and prior approval. The trap is item (iv), since tutorship is generally a specific resolution matter only when it is under an educational institution other than an ICAI organisation.

questions.question: Consider the following statements on the General Resolution and the Specific Resolution framed under Clause (11) of Part I of the First Schedule. Which one of them is NOT correct?
options: A member in practice may act as surveyor and loss assessor under the Insurance Act without the specific permission of the Council, this occupation being in the General Resolution list and not in the Specific Resolution list under Regulation 190A.
Private tutorship, and attending classes and appearing for any examination, are permitted by the General Resolution without specific permission of the Council.
Teaching hours should not exceed 25 hours a week in the cases contemplated by the resolutions.
Valuation of answer books and acting as paper-setter, head-examiner or moderator for any examination require the specific and prior approval of the Council under Regulation 190A.
A member may take up an appointment made by a court or any other legal authority, provided his employment is not on a salary-cum-full-time basis.
questions.explanation: Valuation of papers and acting as paper-setter, head-examiner or moderator for any examination is expressly in the General Resolution list, so no specific or prior approval of the Council is required and the fourth statement is the one which is not correct. The other statements reproduce the position correctly, namely that surveyor and loss assessor under the Insurance Act, private tutorship, and attending classes and appearing for examinations are General Resolution activities, that teaching hours should not exceed 25 hours a week in the cases mentioned, and that appointments made by the Central or State Government, a court or any other legal authority may be taken up where the employment is not on a salary-cum-full-time basis. The specific resolution list applies to lectureship or tutorship for or under institutions other than ICAI bodies, not to examination related valuation of answer books.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A chartered accountant in practice may accept an appointment made by the State Government as Secretary of a commission of enquiry, without the Council's permission, provided the appointment is not on a salary-cum-full-time basis.
Reason (R): The General Resolution permits members in practice to hold public elective offices such as M.P., M.L.A. and M.L.C., and an appointment made by the Government is for this purpose a public elective office.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: (A) is correct because the additional points to Clause (11) permit a chartered accountant to take up an appointment made by the Central or State Government, a court or any other legal authority, or to act as Secretary, provided his employment is not on a salary-cum-full-time basis; the decisive condition is the absence of a salary-cum-full-time relationship. (R) is wrong because a Government nomination or appointment is not a public elective office, item (vi) of the General Resolution dealing only with offices filled by election such as M.P., M.L.A. and M.L.C. Since the reason misreads the two different sources of permission, it cannot be the explanation of the assertion either. Options treating (A) as wrong overlook this express permission for Government, court and other legal authority appointments.

questions.question: Suresh Iyengar, a chartered accountant in practice at Chennai, obtains the specific and prior approval of the Council for a part-time lectureship in a university, the course not being one relating to ICAI examinations. Separately, and without seeking any permission, he takes part-time tutorship in a coaching organisation of ICAI. In the week beginning 4 August 2025 he teaches for 15 hours in the ICAI coaching organisation and 12 hours in the university, while for the remaining weeks of the year his aggregate teaching is 20 hours a week. He is also honorary secretary of a non-commercial chamber of commerce. Which is the MOST appropriate conclusion under Clause (11) of Part I of the First Schedule?
options: Nothing is irregular, because the limit of 25 hours is measured on the average teaching hours for the year.

The ICAI coaching tutorship and the university lectureship are both regular, but the aggregate of 27 teaching hours in the week beginning 4 August 2025 exceeds the ceiling of 25 hours a week, so that week contravenes the clause.

Nothing is irregular, because each activity is separately either a General Resolution activity or covered by the Council's prior approval, and the honorary secretaryship of a non-commercial chamber of commerce is itself permitted without any permission.
The tutorship under an ICAI coaching organisation itself requires the specific prior approval of the Council and is therefore irregular.
The limit of 25 hours a week applies to a lectureship only, and not to tutorship under an ICAI coaching organisation.
questions.explanation: Part-time tutorship under a coaching organisation of ICAI is a General Resolution activity needing no permission, and a lectureship for courses other than those relating to ICAI examinations is a Specific Resolution activity for which Suresh has in fact obtained prior Council approval, so the permissions themselves are in order. However, teaching hours should not exceed 25 hours a week in any of the cases mentioned, and the 15 plus 12 hours in that single week, being 27 hours, breach the ceiling notwithstanding that the rest of the year is within it. The honorary secretaryship of a non-commercial chamber of commerce is a General Resolution activity and is a red herring. The distractors which rely on annual averaging or on treating the two teaching activities as separately capped read the limitation as per activity rather than per week.

questions.question:
Match the following situations of a chartered accountant in practice with the correct consequence, using Clause (11) of Part I of the First Schedule and Clause (4) of Part I of the Second Schedule:

Column I (Situation)
(P) A member accepts appointment as a director of the holding company while his firm is the auditor of the subsidiary company.
(Q) A member's firm is appointed auditor of a company of which that member has been an ordinary (simple) director since 2019.
(R) A member resigns as director of a company on 31 March 2024 and his firm is appointed its statutory auditor at the annual general meeting held on 15 October 2025.
(S) A member is appointed an ordinary director of a company in which neither he nor any of his partners is interested as auditor.
(T) A member becomes promoter and a signatory to the memorandum and articles of association of a company.

Column II (Consequence)
(1) Not permissible, the auditor of a subsidiary company cannot be a director of its holding company, this affecting the independence of the auditor
(2) Not permissible under Clause (4) of Part I of the Second Schedule, a chartered accountant who is a director of a company and the firm in which he is a partner being unable to express an opinion on its financial statements
(3) Not permissible under Clause (4) of Part I of the Second Schedule, two years not having elapsed from the date of his resignation as director
(4) Permissible, Clause (11) not disentitling a member from being a director of a company unless he or any of his partners is interested in it as auditor
(5) Permissible under the General Resolution, as promoter or signatory to the memorandum and articles of association

Choose the correct matching:
questions.explanation: (P) is barred by the rule that the auditor of a subsidiary company cannot be a director of its holding company, independence being affected. (Q) fails under Clause (4) of Part I of the Second Schedule, because where a chartered accountant is a director of a company, neither he nor the firm in which he is a partner may express an opinion on its financial statements; the fact that his directorship is only as an ordinary director does not help. (R) fails because the cooling-off period of two years runs from the date of completion of tenure or resignation as director, that is from 31 March 2024, and the appointment on 15 October 2025 is within that period. (S) and (T) are both permissible, Clause (11) allowing a directorship which is not a managing or whole-time directorship where neither the member nor any partner is interested as auditor, and the General Resolution expressly covering a promoter or signatory to the memorandum and articles.

questions.question:
Vikram Sheth, a chartered accountant in practice at Ahmedabad, proposes to authorise employees of his firm, none of them being a member of the Institute, to handle the following five matters:
(i) Issue of audit queries to the client during the course of the audit.
(ii) Issue of the firm's net worth certificate on the basis of the client's audited balance sheet.
(iii) Acknowledging and carrying on routine correspondence with clients.
(iv) Signing, on behalf of the firm, the profit and loss account of an auditee company.
(v) Issue of the memorandum of cash and other physical verification.
Which combination may be so delegated without contravening Clause (12) of Part I of the First Schedule?
questions.explanation: Clause (12) prohibits allowing a person not being a member of the Institute in practice, or a member not being his partner, to sign on his behalf or on behalf of his firm any balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements, so item (iv) is squarely within the prohibition. The non-applicability list permits delegation of routine documents such as audit queries during the audit, routine correspondence with clients and the memorandum of cash and other physical verification, which covers (i), (iii) and (v). Item (ii) fails because the signing or issuance of a stock certificate, production certificate, net worth certificate or any other certificate is expressly stated not to be routine work and cannot be delegated. The distractor including (iv) also fails because it treats the profit and loss account as an office record rather than a financial statement.

questions.question: Sunil Deshpande, a chartered accountant in practice at Nagpur, is engaged to audit the financial statements of Orange Agro Exports Ltd. for FY 2025-26. Owing to ill-health, on 20 October 2025 he allows a clerk employed in the accounts department of that client, not being a member of the Institute, to sign the balance sheet and profit and loss account which the firm is to issue on the company's behalf. Separately, on 5 November 2025, he signs and submits in his own name a report of an examination of the financial statements of another client, Green Valley Hotels Ltd., although the examination of that statement and of the related records had been made entirely by a chartered accountant in practice at Pune whom neither Sunil nor his firm had engaged. Sunil defends both acts on the ground that he had supervised the work and that in the second matter the examination was made by another chartered accountant in practice. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The first act contravenes Clause (12) of Part I of the First Schedule, but the second act does not contravene Clause (2) of Part I of the Second Schedule, because the examination was made by another chartered accountant in practice.

Both acts contravene the respective clauses, because the person who signs must in every case be the partner who personally made the examination of the statements and of the related records, supervision exercised over another person's work being irrelevant to both clauses.
The first act is permissible as routine office work, but the second contravenes Clause (2) of Part I of the Second Schedule.
Neither act contravenes, since he supervised both assignments and a partner may rely on supervision in place of personal examination.
The second act contravenes Clause (2), because the examiner was not a partner or employee in his firm, but the first act does not, the balance sheet being a document of the client.
questions.explanation: Clause (12) of Part I of the First Schedule prohibits allowing a person not being a member of the Institute in practice to sign on the member's or the firm's behalf any balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements, and the client's clerk is such a person, so the first act is misconduct. Clause (2) of Part I of the Second Schedule condemns certifying a report of examination only where the examination has not been made by the member, a partner or an employee in his firm, or by another chartered accountant in practice; since the Pune practitioner was a chartered accountant in practice, the second act is within the express permission and is not contravened. Supervision is irrelevant to both tests, and the balance sheet remains a document which the clause protects notwithstanding that it is the client's statement. The decisive facts are the identity of the signer in the first act and the status of the examiner in the second.

questions.question: Reeta Iyer, a chartered accountant in practice, permits the paid assistant in her office, not being a member of the Institute, to (a) issue acknowledgements for records produced by clients and for money receipts, and (b) sign and issue the firm's stock certificate arising from a bank stock audit. The assistant also prepares, but does not sign, the draft audit observations which Reeta signs herself. If the person signing the stock certificate were instead a partner in her firm, what changes in the position under Clause (12) of Part I of the First Schedule?
options: Nothing changes, a certificate not being a balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statement, so Clause (12) is not engaged in either case.
Both (a) and (b) become permissible in a partner's hands, a partner being an employee of the firm for the purposes of the delegation list.
(b) becomes permissible in the assistant's hands, stock verification being routine work, while (a) does not, an acknowledgement being a certificate.

(a) remains permissible either way, and (b) could not be delegated to the paid assistant, issuance of a certificate not being routine work; but a partner may sign it, Clause (12) excluding only a non-member in practice or a member not being his partner.

Nothing changes in either case, (b) remaining impermissible even in a partner's hands, since the signing or issuance of a certificate is expressly not routine work and nothing may issue over the signature of any person other than the individual member himself.
questions.explanation: Issuing acknowledgements for records produced and for money receipts is in the non-applicability list of routine documents, so (a) is permissible whoever signs it. Signing or issuance of a stock certificate, production certificate, net worth certificate or any other certificate is expressly stated not to be routine work and cannot be delegated, so (b) could not be done by the paid assistant. However, the prohibition in Clause (12) reaches only a person not being a member of the Institute in practice, or a member not being the partner, so a partner in the firm is outside the prohibition and may sign. Preparing draft observations without signing them raises no issue under the clause, and the option which treats a certificate as outside the clause ignores the express rule about certificates.

questions.question: The entire examination of the financial statements and of the related records of a client has been performed by an employee of a chartered accountant's firm, a graduate accountant who is not a member of the Institute. Partner X proposes to (i) certify in his own name the report of that examination, and (ii) allow that same employee to sign the client's balance sheet on the firm's behalf. Which is correct?
options: Both (i) and (ii) are permissible, the employee being a person in the firm.

(i) is permissible under Clause (2) of Part I of the Second Schedule, and (ii) is likewise permissible, the balance sheet being signed in the ordinary course of the firm's audit work, which the non-applicability list allows to be handled by employees.

(i) is permissible, the examination having been made by an employee in his firm, but (ii) contravenes Clause (12) of Part I of the First Schedule, a non-member in practice being unable to sign a balance sheet on the firm's behalf.
Neither is permissible, the examination as well as the signing having to be done by the certifying partner personally.
(ii) is permissible, a balance sheet being the client's own document, but (i) is not permissible, examination by an employee being outside Clause (2) of Part I of the Second Schedule.
questions.explanation: Clause (2) of Part I of the Second Schedule permits a member to certify a report of examination of financial statements where the examination of those statements and of the related records has been made by him, by a partner or an employee in his firm, or by another chartered accountant in practice, so (i) is good and the answer which says the examination by an employee is outside the clause is wrong. Clause (12) of Part I of the First Schedule is a different test, namely who may sign a balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statement on behalf of the member or firm, and it permits this only by the member, or by a member of the Institute in practice who is his partner. An employee who is not a member of the Institute therefore cannot sign the balance sheet, so (ii) is misconduct notwithstanding that the same person could perform the examination. The integration point is that permissible work and permissible signature are governed by separate clauses.

questions.question: CA Manoj Pillai wishes to delegate two matters to his office staff, none of them being a member of the Institute, namely (1) attending to routine matters in his income-tax practice, and (2) issuing the firm's production certificate for a bank stock audit. His senior advises that both are routine in nature and that both may therefore be delegated. Which is the MOST appropriate advice?
options: Both may be delegated, Clause (12) being confined to a balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statement, and a production certificate issued after physical verification being none of these but merely an incident of routine verification.
Neither may be delegated, whatever goes out over the firm's name must be signed by the member himself.
(2) may be delegated, stock verification being a routine audit procedure, but (1) may not, tax practice being personal to the member.
Neither may be delegated, because tax practice is not an activity of a chartered accountant in practice.

(1) may be delegated subject to Section 288 of the Income Tax Act, but (2) may not, the signing or issuance of a stock certificate, production certificate, net worth certificate or any other certificate not being routine work.
questions.explanation: Attending to routine matters in tax practice is one of the enumerated instances in which the non-applicability of Clause (12) is recognised, but only subject to Section 288 of the Income Tax Act, so (1) may be delegated within that limit. Issuing a production certificate is caught by the express rule that the signing or issuance of a stock certificate, production certificate, net worth certificate or any other certificate is not routine work and cannot be delegated to a person not being a member of the Institute in practice or to a member who is not the partner. The first option errs by reading the clause only through its list of financial statements and ignoring the certificate rule, while the last wrongly assumes that tax matters cannot be delegated at all.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule:
(P) The duty not to disclose information acquired in the course of a professional engagement continues even after completion of the assignment.
(Q) In the case of a partnership firm, consent to disclose may be given by any partner.
(R) In the case of a company, consent may be given by the Board of Directors, and in the case of a sole proprietary concern, by the proprietor or by his constituted attorney who is legally empowered to give such consent.
(S) Once the assignment is over, a member may disclose his former client's information at his own discretion, the clause then being spent.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: The duty of confidentiality under Clause (1) is not limited to the subsistence of the engagement, it continuing even after completion of the assignment, so (P) is correct and (S), which treats the clause as spent on completion, is wrong.
