The identity of the person who can give consent varies with the constitution of the client, being the proprietor or a legally empowered constituted attorney for a sole proprietary concern, any partner for a partnership firm, and the Board of Directors for a company, which makes (Q) and (R) correct. The distinction between an authorised representative giving consent and any employee doing so is what decides (R). Absent consent or a requirement of law, disclosure to a person other than the client engaging him is misconduct.

questions.question: Alok Vaidya, a chartered accountant in practice at Surat, is the statutory auditor of Bharuch Forgings Ltd., which has developed a specialised alloy. In October 2025 the company's finance head refuses to give him a written reply on certain inventory matters. In January 2026 he addresses a regional seminar of industry representatives and displays slides carrying the company's name, its actual plant-wise production data and its inventory valuation methodology, in order to explain how he had resolved a query. In February 2026 he also furnishes to a trade association, without the company's consent, data which he honestly believes will help Indian manufacturers compete internationally. The company has at no time given consent. What is the correct position under Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule?
options: No contravention arises in either respect, the seminar use being permissible because he was only explaining to an audience of industry representatives how an audit query had been resolved, and the trade association disclosure being protected by his honest belief that the information would help Indian manufacturers compete at the international level rather than serve any commercial interest.
Contravention as regards the trade association only, a seminar presentation falling within the performance of his professional duties.
No contravention in either respect, the company having forfeited confidentiality by refusing to reply to his queries.

Contravention in both respects, the duty not to disclose continuing after completion of the assignment, and disclosure of vital client information without consent to help the nation compete internationally, as also use at a seminar of the client's actual data with full identification displayed, being examples of misconduct under this clause.
Contravention as regards the seminar only, the trade association data having been given to an appropriate recipient.
questions.explanation: Clause (1) prohibits disclosure of information acquired in the course of professional engagement to any person other than the client, without the client's consent or otherwise than as required by law, and the duty continues even after completion of the assignment. Both of Alok's acts are the illustrations of misconduct given under this clause, namely disclosing vital client information without consent on the impression that it would help the nation compete internationally, and using actual client data at a seminar with the client fully identified to explain a query. The refusal of the finance head to reply, and his honest belief about the national interest, are red herrings, since neither consent nor a requirement of law is present. An appropriate recipient is irrelevant without consent, so the last two options fail.

questions.question: CA Neelam Bansal holds information acquired in the course of a professional engagement. She discloses: (i) information which a law for the time being in force requires her to disclose; (ii) information the disclosure of which is required as a part of the performance of her professional duties; (iii) information about her client's costing system to a friend in the trade, at the friend's request and without her client's consent. Which disclosure or disclosures is or are permissible under Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule?
options: (iii) only, the friend being an appropriate recipient of trade information
questions.explanation: Clause (1) condemns disclosure to a person other than the client where made without the client's consent and otherwise than as required by any law for the time being in force, so (i) is clearly outside the prohibition. The additional points also permit a member to disclose information where disclosure is required as a part of the performance of his professional duties, which covers (ii). (iii) fails both tests, since a friend's curiosity is neither a statutory requirement nor a professional duty, and the absence of client consent is decisive. Whether the recipient is appropriate goes to the manner of disclosure and cannot cure a disclosure that is neither consented to nor required.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A chartered accountant in practice contravenes Clause (3) of Part I of the Second Schedule merely by participating with his client in the preparation of a projected profit statement, if in his report he clearly indicates the sources of information, the basis of the forecast and the major assumptions made in arriving at the forecast.
Reason (R): SAE 3400 'The Examination of Prospective Financial Information' provides that management is responsible for the preparation and presentation of prospective financial information, and that a chartered accountant may be asked to examine and report on such information in order to enhance its credibility.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: (A) is wrong because a chartered accountant may participate in the preparation of profit or financial forecasts and may review them, provided he clearly indicates in his report the sources of information, the basis of the forecast and the major assumptions made, and does not vouch for the accuracy of the forecast; the clause bites only where his name or firm name is used in a manner which may lead to the belief that he vouches for accuracy. (R) is a correct statement of the position under SAE 3400, which places responsibility for preparation and presentation of prospective financial information on management and contemplates examination and reporting by a chartered accountant to enhance credibility. Since (A) itself is wrong, (R) cannot be its explanation. The decisive element is the absence of any vouching for accuracy.

questions.question:
Tarun Bhalla, a chartered accountant in practice at Ludhiana, is approached by Punjab Auto Parts Ltd. in connection with a five-year earnings estimate carried in its draft prospectus for a proposed expansion. Four versions of his involvement are considered:
(i) He computes the projected earnings for the board and permits the prospectus to carry the sentence 'the auditors certify that the projections are accurate and will be realised', with his firm's name below it.
(ii) He reviews projections prepared by management and reports, clearly stating the sources of information, the basis of the forecast and the major assumptions, without vouching for accuracy.
(iii) He prepares a cash-flow forecast at the client's request and adds a note that its achievement depends on assumptions which may not hold good.
(iv) He allows his firm's name to appear beside the estimate of earnings in a manner designed to make lending banks believe that the firm vouches for the forecast.
Which conclusion is correct under Clause (3) of Part I of the Second Schedule?
options: (ii) and (iii) attract Clause (3); (i) and (iv) do not.
All four attract Clause (3), the member having participated in the forecast in each case.
(i) and (iv) attract Clause (3); (ii) and (iii) do not.
Only (iv) attracts Clause (3), a certification in a prospectus not being an estimate of earnings contingent upon future transactions.
None attracts Clause (3), the clause applying only to reports issued on audited financial statements.
questions.explanation: Clause (3) is contravened where a member permits his name or his firm's name to be used in connection with an estimate of earnings contingent upon future transactions in a manner which may lead to the belief that he vouches for the accuracy of the forecast, and (i) and (iv) create precisely that belief. (ii) is the permitted course, SAE 3400 placing preparation and presentation of prospective financial information on management while allowing the member to examine and report to enhance credibility. (iii) is likewise permissible, since participation in preparation is allowed provided the sources of information, the basis of the forecast and the major assumptions are clearly indicated and accuracy is not vouched for, and the caution note achieves that result. The decisive distinction is therefore vouching for accuracy rather than participation in preparation.

questions.question: Consider the following statements on Clause (4) of Part I of the Second Schedule. Which one of them is NOT correct?
options: The clause is applicable to all types of attest and assurance functions performed by members.
The clause is contravened only where the substantial interest is held by the member personally, an interest held by his firm or by a partner in his firm being outside it.
Non-assurance functions, for example evaluation of the cost of products manufactured, can be provided even where there is an interest in the enterprise.
A member shall not express an opinion on the financial statements of a business or enterprise in which a relative of the member, as referred to in AS 18, has a substantial interest.
Where a chartered accountant is a director of a company, neither that chartered accountant nor the firm in which he is a partner shall express any opinion on the financial statements of that company.
questions.explanation: The very text of Clause (4) covers an interest held by the member, by his firm or by a partner in his firm, so the second statement is the one which is not correct. The clause is applied to all attest and assurance functions, which is wider than statutory audit alone, and the illustrations of permitted work are non-assurance functions such as evaluating the cost of products manufactured, which may be done despite an interest in the enterprise. The prohibition is also extended to a substantial interest held by a relative of the member as referred to in AS 18, and a directorship of the company disables both the member and his firm from expressing an opinion. The distinction between assurance and non-assurance work is the decisive point in the third statement.

questions.question:
Rakesh Gupta & Co., chartered accountants in practice at Jaipur, considers four assignments for FY 2025-26:
(1) Audit of a college in which Rakesh Gupta is working as a part-time lecturer.
(2) Audit of a trust in which a partner of the firm is an employee.
(3) Writing of the books of account of an auditee client.
(4) Evaluation of the cost of products manufactured by an enterprise in which the firm holds a substantial interest.
Which of these may be accepted consistently with Clause (4) of Part I of the Second Schedule?
questions.explanation: The other prohibitions recorded under Clause (4) bar a chartered accountant from accepting the audit of a college in which he works as a part-time lecturer, and from accepting the audit of a trust where his partner is an employee or trustee, so (1) and (2) are impermissible. Members are also not permitted to write the books of account of their auditee clients, so (3) fails. (4) is permissible because the clause strikes at expressing opinions and other attest or assurance functions in an enterprise of which the member, his firm or a partner has a substantial interest, while non-assurance functions such as evaluating the cost of products manufactured may be provided even where there is such an interest. The decisive fact is therefore the assurance or non-assurance character of the assignment.

questions.question: Devi Prasad, a chartered accountant in practice, resigned as a director of Sree Balaji Motors Pvt. Ltd. on 31 August 2024. In September 2025 he is offered the statutory audit of that company for FY 2025-26. The company confirms that neither he, nor his firm, nor any partner of his firm has any financial interest in it, that he has never borrowed from it, and that while a director he drew only sitting fees. Which is the MOST appropriate advice?
options: He may accept, Clause (4) addressing only a substantial interest in the enterprise held by the member, by his firm or by a partner in his firm, and the confirmation on record establishes that no interest of that kind is held by any of them here.
He may accept, because the two-year period runs only from completion of a full tenure as director and not from resignation.
He may accept, because the sitting-fees-only arrangement shows that he was never concerned with the company's financial statements.
He may accept, because the cooling-off rule concerns public companies and not the audit of a private limited company.

He may not accept the audit, a member being unable to accept the audit of a company for two years from the date of completion of his tenure or of his resignation as its director, and less than that period having elapsed.
questions.explanation: Under Clause (4) of Part I of the Second Schedule a cooling-off period of two years operates from the date of completion of tenure or of resignation as director, and here the resignation on 31 August 2024 means that the offer in September 2025 is within that period, the two years ending only on 31 August 2026. The absence of any substantial interest, and the drawing of sitting fees alone, do not attract that test, since the bar is triggered by the directorship itself and not by the existence of an interest, so the first and third options are wrong. The rule is not confined to public issues of financial statements, and it expressly covers resignation as well as completion of tenure. The decisive fact is the date of resignation read against the date of the offer of audit.

questions.question: Devi Prasad, a chartered accountant in practice, resigned as a director of Sree Balaji Motors Pvt. Ltd. on 31 August 2024. In September 2025 he is offered the statutory audit of that company for FY 2025-26. The company confirms that neither he, nor his firm, nor any partner of his firm has any financial interest in it, that he has never borrowed from it, and that while a director he drew only sitting fees. What changes if the date of his resignation had been 31 August 2023 instead of 31 August 2024?
options: Nothing, because two years would still not have elapsed in September 2025.
He may then accept the audit, the two-year period from his resignation having ended on 31 August 2025, before the offer was made.
Nothing, because once a member has been a director of the company the bar under Clause (4) becomes permanent, the two-year period being relevant only to a member who completed the full tenure.
He may then accept the audit, but only if he also ceases to be a partner of his firm.
He may then accept, but the cooling-off restriction revives for FY 2026-27.
questions.explanation: The cooling-off period under Clause (4) of Part I of the Second Schedule is a period of two years from the date of completion of tenure or of resignation as a director of the company, so shifting the resignation to 31 August 2023 makes the period expire on 31 August 2025. The offer in September 2025 would then fall outside it and the audit could be accepted, the bar having run its course. The prohibition is neither permanent nor dependent on the member later leaving his firm, and it does not revive in subsequent years once the two years have elapsed. The decisive fact is therefore the single changed date, not the absence of any financial interest in the company.

questions.question:
Vikram Sethi & Co., a firm of chartered accountant in practice at Pune, has three partners, namely Vikram Sethi, Neha Kulkarni and A. Ranganathan. The following facts are noticed in FY 2025-26:
• Vikram Sethi works as a part-time lecturer in St Xavier's College, Pune, and the firm is asked to take up the audit of the college and, in addition, to write its books of account for the year.
• Neha Kulkarni's husband holds a substantial interest in Trimbak Sugar Co-operative Ltd., whose audit the firm accepts, neither the firm nor any partner holding any share in it.
• A. Ranganathan retired as a director of Gokak Industries Ltd. on 31 March 2023, and the firm is appointed its statutory auditor at the annual general meeting held on 28 September 2025.
• The firm also accepts an assignment to evaluate the cost of products manufactured by an enterprise in which the firm holds a substantial interest, this being a non-assurance function.
Which one of the following correctly states the position under Clause (4) of Part I of the Second Schedule?
options: All four engagements may be accepted, the substantial interest rule being confined to an interest of the member personally.

The college audit may be accepted, a part-time lectureship being an occupation which the resolutions permit, and the writing of the college's books of account may not; and the Trimbak audit may also be accepted, because the client is a co-operative society and because the substantial interest is that of a relative of a partner rather than of the firm or of a partner in it.
Only the cost evaluation is impermissible, a substantial interest of the firm barring every kind of work in that enterprise.

The college audit and the writing of its books of account are both impermissible, the Trimbak audit being impermissible because a relative of a partner has a substantial interest in it, while the Gokak audit and the cost evaluation are permissible, the first because two years had run since Ranganathan's retirement as director and the second because it is a non-assurance function.
The Gokak audit is impermissible, the firm of a retired director being barred for all time from auditing that company.
questions.explanation: A chartered accountant should not accept the audit of a college in which he works as a part-time lecturer, and members are not permitted to write the books of account of their auditee clients, so both parts of the college engagement fail. The prohibition in Clause (4) is extended to a substantial interest held by a relative of the member as per AS 18, and a husband is such a relative, so the Trimbak Sugar Co-operative Ltd. audit is barred notwithstanding that neither the firm nor any partner holds shares, the client being a co-operative society making no difference as the clause speaks of any business or enterprise. The two-year cooling-off period from Ranganathan's retirement on 31 March 2023 expired on 31 March 2025, before the appointment on 28 September 2025. The cost evaluation survives because non-assurance functions may be provided even where there is an interest in the enterprise.

questions.question:
Vikram Sethi & Co., a firm of chartered accountant in practice at Pune, has three partners, namely Vikram Sethi, Neha Kulkarni and A. Ranganathan. The following facts are noticed in FY 2025-26:
• Vikram Sethi works as a part-time lecturer in St Xavier's College, Pune, and the firm is asked to take up the audit of the college and, in addition, to write its books of account for the year.
• Neha Kulkarni's husband holds a substantial interest in Trimbak Sugar Co-operative Ltd., whose audit the firm accepts, neither the firm nor any partner holding any share in it.
• A. Ranganathan retired as a director of Gokak Industries Ltd. on 31 March 2023, and the firm is appointed its statutory auditor at the annual general meeting held on 28 September 2025.
• The firm also accepts an assignment to evaluate the cost of products manufactured by an enterprise in which the firm holds a substantial interest, this being a non-assurance function.
Which one of the following statements about these facts is NOT correct?
options: A part-time lectureship for courses other than those relating to ICAI examinations is an activity requiring the specific and prior approval of the Council under Regulation 190A, and teaching hours in such cases should not exceed 25 hours a week.
A member shall not accept the audit of a company for a period of two years from the date of completion of his tenure or of his resignation as a director of that company.
The audit of Trimbak Sugar Co-operative Ltd. is permissible, because the substantial interest is that of a relative of a partner and not that of the member, his firm or a partner in his firm.
Members are not permitted to write the books of account of their auditee clients.
Non-assurance functions, such as evaluation of the cost of products manufactured, can be provided even where there is an interest in the enterprise.
questions.explanation: Clause (4) of Part I of the Second Schedule is expressly extended, a member also being unable to express an opinion on the financial statements of a business or enterprise in which a relative of the member, as per AS 18, has a substantial interest, and a husband is such a relative. The status of the client as a co-operative society does not help, since the clause speaks of any business or enterprise, so the third statement is the one which is not correct. The first statement correctly records that Vikram Sethi's university lectureship, being for a course not relating to ICAI examinations, falls in the Specific Resolution list under Regulation 190A. The remaining statements reproduce the two-year cooling-off period, the bar on writing the books of account of auditee clients, and the permitted non-assurance function.

questions.question:
Match the following situations with the provision of Part I of the Second Schedule attracted:

Column I (Situation)
(P) While auditing Udupi Ceramics Ltd., the auditor learns that the company had taken a loan from the Employees' Provident Fund which is nowhere reflected in the books of account and hence not disclosed in the financial statements; he signs without any reference to it.
(Q) The company's balance sheet shows loans and advances of ₹8 crore, though the auditor knows that ₹3 crore of that amount had become irrecoverable two years earlier; he reports the financial statements without reporting this.
(R) The auditor discovers that a charge created against a guarantee given by the company in favour of a group company has not been disclosed in the financial statements, and he signs without disclosure.
(S) A member acting as authorised representative of an assessee files with the department, on his client's instructions, a statement which he knows to be incorrect.

Column II (Provision)
(1) Clause (5), failure to disclose a material fact known to him which is not disclosed in the financial statement
(2) Clause (6), failure to report a material misstatement known to him to appear in the financial statement
(3) He is not liable for misconduct under Clauses (5) and (6)
(4) Clause (1), disclosure of information acquired in the course of professional engagement

Choose the correct matching:
questions.explanation: Clause (5) covers failure to disclose a material fact which is not disclosed in the financial statement but whose disclosure is necessary in making that statement, and the omission of an Employees' Provident Fund loan from the books and the failure to disclose a charge created against a guarantee given in favour of a group company are the illustrations given under that clause, so (P) and (R) map to (1). Clause (6) covers failure to report a material misstatement known to him to appear in the financial statement, which is what happens in (Q), where an amount already known to be irrecoverable continues to be shown as recoverable in the balance sheet. (S) attracts the express position that a chartered accountant acting as authorised representative who submits incorrect statements on the instructions of his client is not liable for misconduct under Clauses (5) and (6). Clause (1) is irrelevant, no information of the client is given to a third party in any of the four situations.

questions.question: During the audit of Rathi Spinning Mills Ltd. for FY 2025-26, CA Anil Bhatia notices three matters: (a) a loan of ₹1.20 crore taken from the Employees' Provident Fund, which is nowhere reflected in the books of account and is therefore not disclosed in the financial statements; (b) no disclosure made of a charge created against a guarantee given by the company in favour of a group company; and (c) an arithmetical difference of ₹40,000 in the printing and stationery expenses head, which is far below the materiality he has determined. He issues an unmodified report on the financial statements without referring to (a), (b) or (c). Which conclusion is correct?
options: He contravenes Clause (6) in respect of (a), (b) and (c), every known departure from the true position being a misstatement.

He contravenes Clause (5) in respect of (a), (b) and (c), the test being his knowledge of the fact and not its quantum, so that even an item below the materiality he has determined must be brought out, and this is more so where the amount is presented as a separate line in the financial statements.
He contravenes none, (a) being a matter of statutory dues of the employees of the company rather than a matter to be reflected in the company's financial statements.
He contravenes Clause (5) in respect of (b) only, (a) being an omission from the books of account and not from the financial statements.

He contravenes Clause (5) in respect of (a) and (b) only, these being material facts not disclosed in the financial statements, materiality being determined under SA 320 'Materiality in Planning and Performing Audit', so (c) falls outside.
questions.explanation: Clause (5) of Part I of the Second Schedule strikes at failure to disclose a material fact known to the member which is not disclosed in a financial statement with which he is concerned in a professional capacity, and both the Employees' Provident Fund loan which never entered the books and the undisclosed charge arising from the guarantee given to the group company are the illustrations recorded under this clause. Clause (6) is not attracted, since it deals with a material misstatement appearing in the financial statement rather than with a fact absent from it. The determination of materiality is governed by SA 320 'Materiality in Planning and Performing Audit', so the ₹40,000 printing and stationery difference, being below his determined materiality, does not attract either clause. The omission from the books of account is itself what causes the omission from the financial statements, so the fourth option's distinction fails.

questions.question: Harish Chandra, a chartered accountant in practice, is appointed authorised representative by M/s Anand Steels for its assessment proceedings. On the assessee's written instructions he files before the assessing officer a statement which has been prepared and signed by the assessee and which he knows to contain incorrect particulars of income. In a different capacity he is the statutory auditor of the same company and signs its balance sheet, although he has ascertained that stock of ₹5 crore, shown at cost, has a net realisable value materially lower and the shortfall is neither recorded nor disclosed. He contends that, as he throughout acted on his client's instructions, no misconduct under Clauses (5) and (6) of Part I of the Second Schedule is attracted. Which is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
options: Both acts are protected, a member acting on his client's instructions not being answerable under Clause (5) or Clause (6).

The filing as authorised representative on the client's instructions is protected, but as statutory auditor he was concerned with that financial statement in a professional capacity, and his failure to report the known overvaluation of stock contravenes Clause (6).
The audit act is not objectionable, an incorrect valuation being a matter of management judgement and not of a misstatement appearing in the financial statements of the company.
Only the filing before the assessing officer contravenes, a statement filed with a revenue authority being a financial statement for the purposes of Clause (6).

Neither act contravenes, the shortfall having been communicated to the management in a working note, and a member who has brought a matter to the notice of the management cannot be said either to have failed to disclose it or to have failed to report it.
questions.explanation: The additional points to Clause (6) of Part I of the Second Schedule provide that a chartered accountant acting as authorised representative who submits incorrect statements on the instructions of his client to the authorities is not liable for misconduct under Clauses (5) and (6), so the filing before the assessing officer is protected. That protection does not follow him into his capacity as statutory auditor, where he is concerned with the financial statement in a professional capacity and stock of ₹5 crore shown at cost although he has ascertained a materially lower net realisable value is a material misstatement appearing in that statement, attracting Clause (6). A working note to management is not a report of the misstatement, so it does not discharge the duty, and an ascertained overvaluation is not a mere matter of management judgement. The decisive fact is the difference in the capacity in which he acted, representative on instructions as against auditor expressing an opinion.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements relating to clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949:

I. It is a vital clause which gets attracted whenever it is necessary to judge whether the chartered accountant has honestly discharged his duties.
II. The expression 'negligence' used in the clause has a narrow meaning, being confined to gross and culpable neglect, and excludes both fraud and minor negligence.
III. A member in practice who does not exercise reasonable skill and care and performs his work in a casual manner offends against the clause.
IV. Issuing a clean report on financial statements without examining the accounts is misconduct only under clause (8), and not under clause (7).

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Clause (7) makes it misconduct for a CA in practice to not exercise due diligence, or to be grossly negligent, in the conduct of his professional duties, and it is described as a vital clause attracted whenever it is necessary to judge whether the CA has honestly discharged his duties. Statement II is not correct because the expression 'negligence' in the clause covers a wide field ranging from fraud to minor negligence, so it is not confined to gross or culpable neglect. Statement III is correct, since 'not exercising reasonable skill and care and performing work in a casual manner' is expressly listed as an instance of misconduct under this clause. Statement IV is not correct, because 'issuing clean reports on financial statements without examining the accounts' is itself one of the listed illustrations under clause (7), not clause (8). Therefore only I and III are correct.

questions.category: Second Schedule Part I - Clauses (7) to (10)
questions.question:
Match the situations in Column I with the provision of Part I of the Second Schedule most directly contravened in Column II:

Column I
P. A member in practice submits a stock audit report by relying on the client's M.I.S. report, without physically verifying the stock.
Q. A member in practice is unable to obtain the information necessary for his opinion because the client's records are defective, yet he issues an unmodified opinion without noting the exceptions.
R. A member in practice adopts a procedure involving a material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit, namely the Engagement and Quality Control Standards applicable to the circumstances, and stays silent about it.
S. A member in practice keeps moneys of his client, other than fees or remuneration, in his own savings account.

Column II
1. Clause (8)
2. Clause (7)
3. Clause (10)
4. Clause (9)

Choose the correct pairing:
questions.explanation: Reliance on an M.I.S. report for a stock audit without physical verification of stock is expressly listed as an instance of failing to exercise due diligence under clause (7), so P pairs with 2. Q concerns the failure to obtain sufficient information which is necessary for the expression of an opinion, or exceptions sufficiently material to negate the expression of an opinion, which is the subject matter of clause (8). R is a failure to invite attention to a material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit, covered by clause (9), which is a reporting failure and not a performance failure. S falls within clause (10), which requires client moneys other than fees, remuneration or money meant to be expended to be kept in a separate banking account. The boundary to note is that clause (7) tests how the work was done, clause (8) tests whether adequate information supported the opinion, and clause (9) tests whether a departure from audit procedure was disclosed.

questions.question:
CA Meenal Rathi, a partner of Rathi & Associates, Pune, was appointed statutory auditor of Virudho Structures Pvt. Ltd. on 1.7.2024 for FY 2024-25. The audit fee had been paid to the firm in full on 15.8.2024, and an experienced audit assistant had been deputed to her. She did not attend the physical verification of inventory and treated the stock statement printed from the client's M.I.S. as sufficient. She confirmed the value of the company's listed investments from stock exchange quotations for 31.3.2025, but did not confirm or verify the value of an unquoted investment of ₹ 2,40,00,000 from any proper source. The management delayed the books repeatedly and, on 30.9.2025, the audit work was still incomplete and the audit report had not been submitted.

Which provision of Part I of the Second Schedule is attracted principally by the failure to complete the audit work and to submit the audit report in due time?
options: Clause (8), because sufficient information necessary for the expression of an opinion was not obtained
Clause (9), because a material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit was not reported
Clause (10), because the delay related to moneys received from the client
Clause (7), because not completing the audit work and not submitting the audit report in due time is an instance of failing to exercise due diligence
questions.explanation: 'Not completing his audit work and not submitting his audit report in due time' is one of the illustrations expressly listed under clause (7), which deals with a member not exercising due diligence or being grossly negligent in the conduct of his professional duties. The decisive fact is therefore the chronology - appointment on 1.7.2024, financial year end 31.3.2025 and the report still outstanding on 30.9.2025 - and not the management's delays. The facts that the fee was paid in full and that an assistant was deputed are non-decisive, because neither discharges the member's own duty of diligence. Clause (8) is not the answer, since that clause turns on information necessary for the opinion rather than on timeliness, clause (9) turns on non-disclosure of a departure from audit procedure, and clause (10) governs client moneys and has no application here. Note that the unverified unquoted investment is a separate and independent instance of misconduct under clause (7).

questions.category: Second Schedule Part I - Clauses (8) and (9)
questions.question: Which one of the following statements regarding clauses (8) and (9) of Part I of the Second Schedule is NOT correct?
options: Clause (8) is attracted where the member fails to obtain sufficient information which is necessary for the expression of an opinion
Clause (8) is also attracted where the exceptions to the information obtained are sufficiently material to negate the expression of an opinion
Clause (9) obliges the member to invite attention to every departure, however minor, from the generally accepted procedure of audit
Clause (9) concerns a material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit, that is, the Engagement and Quality Control Standards applicable to the circumstances
questions.explanation: Clause (9) is confined to a material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit applicable to the circumstances, so an obligation to report 'every departure, however minor' overstates the provision and is the statement which is not correct. Clauses (8) and (9) are correctly described in the other three options. Clause (8) has two limbs, namely failure to obtain sufficient information necessary for the expression of an opinion, and exceptions which are sufficiently material to negate the expression of an opinion. Clause (9) is expressed by reference to the Engagement and Quality Control Standards, which supply the 'generally accepted procedure of audit'. The practical distinction is that clause (8) is about the adequacy of the evidence supporting the opinion, while clause (9) is about transparency regarding the procedure actually followed.

questions.question:
While auditing M/s Nakkal Traders, CA Sharmila Menon departed from the generally accepted procedure of audit by not obtaining direct external confirmation of trade debtors, which represented 42% of the turnover of the business, and instead verified only subsequent receipts up to 15.7.2025. She recorded the reasons for her approach in her working papers and prominently disclosed the departure in the 'Observations' annexure to her report. The client objected and asked her to delete that annexure. Assume that the alternative procedure was honestly and competently performed.

What is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
options: She contravenes clause (9), because omission of external confirmation of debtors is itself a prohibited procedure
She contravenes clause (7), because substituting verification of subsequent receipts for confirmation shows gross negligence
She contravenes clause (8), because she failed to obtain sufficient information about debtors
She does not contravene clause (9), because she invited attention to the material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit applicable to the circumstances
questions.explanation: Clause (9) is contravened only where the member fails to invite attention to a material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit. Here the departure was material, being in respect of debtors representing 42% of turnover, but she did invite attention to it prominently in the report, so the clause is satisfied and the client's objection does not change the position. Clause (7) is not attracted because the alternative procedure was performed honestly and with reasonable skill and care, and clause (8) is not attracted because she did obtain evidence, namely subsequent receipts, rather than leaving the opinion unsupported. The decisive fact is the disclosure in the report; had she confined the departure to her working papers, clause (9) would have been contravened.

questions.question:
Match each situation in Column I with the correct consequence under clause (10) of Part I of the Second Schedule in Column II:

Column I
P. A member in practice receives ₹ 5,00,000 from a client as an advance against professional services to be rendered.
Q. A member in practice receives ₹ 40,000 from a client specifically for payment of statutory fees and purchase of stamp papers, to be spent within ten days.
R. A member in practice receives ₹ 12,00,000 in his capacity as executor under a deceased client's will.
S. A member in practice receives ₹ 1,50,000 towards his professional fees.

Column II
1. Not covered by clause (10), being fees or remuneration
2. Must be put in a separate bank account immediately
3. Need not be put in a separate bank account, being money meant to be expended within a short time
4. Does not fall under clause (10), being an advance received against services to be rendered

Choose the correct pairing:
questions.explanation: Clause (10) carves out four categories of money, and the answer lies in identifying which category each receipt belongs to. An advance received by a CA against services to be rendered does not fall under this clause, so P pairs with 4. Moneys received for expenses such as payment of statutory fees or purchase of stamp papers, which are intended to be spent within a short time, need not be put in a separate bank account, so Q pairs with 3. Moneys received by a CA in his capacity as trustee, executor or liquidator must be put in a separate bank account immediately, so R pairs with 2. Fees or remuneration are expressly excluded from the clause by its own words, so S pairs with 1. The statutory fees receipt in Q is distinguishable from the executor money in R because the former is meant to be expended promptly while the latter is fiduciary money held for the estate.

questions.question:
CA G. Krishnan, a chartered accountant in practice at Indore, is the proprietor of G. Krishnan & Co. The following receipts and dealings in his account were noted between April and September 2025:
(a) On 4.4.2025 he received ₹ 7,20,000 from Shri Babulal Jain as advance towards a transfer pricing assignment to be taken up in October 2025.
(b) On 12.4.2025 he received ₹ 3,50,000 from Realpec Chemicals Ltd., whose statutory audit he conducts, as professional fees for FY 2024-25.
(c) On 30.4.2025 he received ₹ 22,00,000 forming part of the estate of a deceased client, in his capacity as executor under the will, and paid ₹ 15,00,000 of it into his personal savings account on 2.5.2025; it was moved to a separate bank account only on 21.8.2025.
(d) On 18.6.2025 he received ₹ 95,000 from M/s Anand Spinners for payment of Registrar of Companies fees and stamp duty, and disbursed it on 25.6.2025.
(e) On 9.7.2025 he withdrew ₹ 4,00,000 from the executor money lying in his account and repaid an overdraft which he had taken for purchasing a personal motor car.

Consider the following statements:
I. Receipt (a) does not attract clause (10) of Part I of the Second Schedule.
II. Receipt (c) required the money to be put in a separate bank account immediately.
III. Receipt (d) contravenes clause (10), because money received for Registrar of Companies fees and stamp duty must invariably be kept in a separate banking account.
IV. Event (e) is relevant only to clause (4) of Part II of the Second Schedule and is of no relevance whatever to clause (10) of Part I.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement I is correct because an advance received by a CA against services to be rendered does not fall under clause (10). Statement II is correct because moneys received by a CA in his capacity as executor must be put in a separate bank account immediately, and depositing ₹ 15,00,000 into a personal savings account on 2.5.2025 and transferring it only on 21.8.2025 is a clear failure. Statement III is not correct, because moneys received for expenses such as statutory fees and stamp papers, which are intended to be spent within a short time, need not be put in a separate bank account; the ₹ 95,000 was disbursed seven days later. Statement IV is not correct, because the member must utilise such funds only as per the instructions of the client or for the purposes intended by the client, so diverting ₹ 4,00,000 of estate money to clear a personal motor-car overdraft independently offends clause (10) of Part I even before clause (4) of Part II is reached. The decisive facts are the capacity in which each sum was received and the purpose to which it was applied.

questions.category: Second Schedule - Clause (10) with Part II Clause (4)
questions.question:
CA G. Krishnan, a chartered accountant in practice at Indore, is the proprietor of G. Krishnan & Co. The following receipts and dealings in his account were noted between April and September 2025:
(a) On 4.4.2025 he received ₹ 7,20,000 from Shri Babulal Jain as advance towards a transfer pricing assignment to be taken up in October 2025.
(b) On 12.4.2025 he received ₹ 3,50,000 from Realpec Chemicals Ltd., whose statutory audit he conducts, as professional fees for FY 2024-25.
(c) On 30.4.2025 he received ₹ 22,00,000 forming part of the estate of a deceased client, in his capacity as executor under the will, and paid ₹ 15,00,000 of it into his personal savings account on 2.5.2025; it was moved to a separate bank account only on 21.8.2025.
(d) On 18.6.2025 he received ₹ 95,000 from M/s Anand Spinners for payment of Registrar of Companies fees and stamp duty, and disbursed it on 25.6.2025.
(e) On 9.7.2025 he withdrew ₹ 4,00,000 from the executor money lying in his account and repaid an overdraft which he had taken for purchasing a personal motor car.

Which one of the following best describes the position in respect of event (e)?
options: Clause (10) of Part I alone, because Part II of the Second Schedule applies only to members who are not in practice
Clause (4) of Part II alone, because money received in the capacity of an executor is not money of a client for the purposes of clause (10) of Part I

Clause (10) of Part I for failing to use the money for the purpose for which it was intended, and clause (4) of Part II as well, if money received in his professional capacity is defalcated or embezzled
Neither clause, because the sum was earmarked for replacement within the same financial year
questions.explanation: Clause (10) of Part I requires client moneys, other than fees, remuneration or money meant to be expended, to be kept in a separate banking account and to be used for the purposes for which they are intended within a reasonable time, and the member must utilise such funds only as per the instructions or for the purposes intended by the client. Applying executor money to clear a personal motor-car overdraft defeats that purpose, so clause (10) is engaged. If the same conduct amounts to defalcation or embezzlement of money received in his professional capacity, clause (4) of Part II is separately attracted, because Part II applies to members of the Institute generally. The first option is wrong because Part II of the Second Schedule applies to members whether in practice or not, not only to members not in practice. The fourth option is wrong because neither clause excuses misuser on the strength of an intention to restore the amount later.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
I. Clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule requires every member to act within the framework of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, the regulations made thereunder and the guidelines issued by the Council, and any violation by a member amounts to misconduct.
II. Regulation 47 deals with premium, loan or deposit from an articled assistant, Regulation 48 with stipend to an articled assistant to be paid monthly, and Regulation 65 with an articled assistant not engaging in any other occupation.
III. Issuing a certificate or report as a chartered accountant in practice without even having applied for a certificate of practice is an instance of misconduct under clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule.
IV. Clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule is attracted only where a member contravenes the Act itself, contravention of regulations or of Council guidelines being outside its scope.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule covers contravention of any provision of the Act, of the regulations made thereunder and of any guidelines issued by the Council, so all three sources are within its scope. Statement IV is therefore the incorrect one, because it wrongly narrows the clause to the Act alone. Statements I and II are correct, and the three Regulations cited are precisely those under which cases of contravention have generally come to the notice of the Council. Statement III is correct and is one of the two illustrations given under this clause, the other being failure to pay stipend to an articled assistant every month; issuing a certificate without a certificate of practice violates the Act itself, whereas the stipend default violates a regulation.

questions.question:
Match each instance in Column I with the Act or Regulation contravened in Column II; each instance is professional misconduct under clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule:

Column I
P. A CA in practice accepts a deposit of ₹ 2,00,000 from his articled assistant.
Q. A CA in practice pays the consolidated amount of stipend to his articled assistant once at the end of every quarter.
R. A CA in practice allows his articled assistant to work as a part-time accounts executive in another firm during the period of articleship.
S. A member who has not even applied for a certificate of practice issues a certificate as a chartered accountant in practice.

Column II
1. The Act itself (practising without a certificate of practice)
2. Regulation 48 - stipend to articled assistant, monthly payment
3. Regulation 65 - articled assistant not to engage in any other occupation
4. Regulation 47 - premium, loan or deposit from an articled assistant

Choose the correct pairing:
questions.explanation: Regulation 47 covers taking a premium, loan or deposit from an articled assistant, so P pairs with 4. Regulation 48 requires the stipend to an articled assistant to be paid monthly, and a quarterly consolidated payment is a contravention, so Q pairs with 2. Regulation 65 prohibits an articled assistant from engaging in any other occupation, which covers the part-time accounts executive work, so R pairs with 3. Issuing a certificate as a CA in practice without even having applied for a certificate of practice is a violation of the Act itself, so S pairs with 1. Each of these is professional misconduct under clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule, because that clause reaches contravention of the Act, of the regulations made thereunder and of Council guidelines alike.

questions.category: Second Schedule Part II - UDIN and Peer Review
questions.question:
Consider the following statements made in the context of clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule:
I. As per the UDIN Guidelines (Chapter XIV) issued by the Council, a chartered accountant in practice shall generate a Unique Document Identification Number for all kinds of certification, audit reports and other audit, assurance and attestation functions undertaken or signed by him.
II. The Statement on Peer Review shall be deemed to be a guideline of the Council.
III. Audit of listed companies may be undertaken by any member in practice holding a valid certificate of practice, whether or not he has been subjected to the Peer Review process of the Institute.
IV. Failure to make payments of stipend to an articled assistant every month is an instance of contravention of a Regulation, and therefore of clause (1) of Part II.

Which of the above statements is/are NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Statement III is not correct, because audit of listed companies shall be done only by those auditors who have been subjected to the Peer Review process of the Institute; merely holding a certificate of practice is not enough. Statements I, II and IV are correct as recorded in the additional points to clause (1) of Part II. Statement I is important for its width, since the UDIN obligation under Chapter XIV applies to all kinds of certification, audit reports and other audit, assurance and attestation functions undertaken or signed by the member, and not merely to statutory audit reports. Statement II explains why a Peer Review default is reachable under clause (1), because the Statement on Peer Review is deemed to be a guideline of the Council. Statement IV is the illustration expressly given, being a violation of Regulation 48.

questions.question:
CA Farhan Qureshi, a member of the Institute who is not in practice, is employed as Finance Manager of Bramhapuri Logistics Ltd. On 9.8.2025, at a family gathering, he told his brother-in-law, who acts as a broker for a competitor, the exact pricing terms which his employer was about to offer a major customer. No law required the disclosure and the employer had not permitted it. It subsequently emerged that the competitor had already learnt the terms from another source and derived no advantage from them.

Which one of the following best describes the position under the Second Schedule?
options: Clause (2) of Part II of the Second Schedule, since being an employee of a company he disclosed confidential information acquired in the course of his employment, otherwise than as required by law and otherwise than as permitted by the employer
Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule, since a member disclosing information acquired during an engagement is governed by that clause
Clause (3) of Part II of the Second Schedule, since pricing terms are particulars which must be reported to the Institute
No misconduct, since the competitor derived no advantage from the disclosure
questions.explanation: Clause (2) of Part II of the Second Schedule makes it professional misconduct for a member, being an employee of any company, firm or person, to disclose confidential information acquired in the course of his employment, except as and when required by any law for the time being in force or except as permitted by the employer. Here the member was an employee, the information was acquired in the course of employment, no law required the disclosure and the employer did not permit it, so every ingredient is present. The absence of advantage to the competitor is a red herring, because the clause is not damage-based. Clause (1) of Part I applies to a CA in practice disclosing information acquired in the course of a professional engagement, which does not describe a salaried employee. Clause (3) of Part II concerns false particulars in documents submitted to the Institute or Council and has no application.

questions.question:
CA Pooja Deshpande and CA Ravi Salunkhe were partners of Deshpande Salunkhe & Co. up to 31.3.2025, when Ravi retired. On 20.6.2025 the firm filed an application for empanelment as auditor of branches of banks with the Institute, in which the partners of the firm were shown as 'P. Deshpande and R. Salunkhe'. Pooja believed that Ravi would rejoin the firm in September 2025, and the printed form did not call for the date of retirement.

Which one of the following is the correct position?
options: No misconduct, because Ravi was expected to rejoin the firm and the form did not call for the date of retirement
Professional misconduct under clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule, because the Act prescribes a cooling-off period before a retired partner's name may be shown in an application
Professional misconduct under clause (3) of Part II of the Second Schedule, because particulars known to be false were included in a form to be submitted to the Institute
Other misconduct under clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule, because making a false statement to the Institute is an offence punishable with imprisonment exceeding six months
questions.explanation: Clause (3) of Part II of the Second Schedule makes it professional misconduct for a member to include in any information, statement, return or form to be submitted to the Institute, Council or any of its Committees, Director (Discipline), Board of Discipline, Disciplinary Committee, Quality Review Board or the Appellate Authority any particulars knowing them to be false. The facts given are the very illustration recorded under this clause, namely showing another CA as a partner in an application for empanelment as auditor of branches of banks when that person was not a partner on the date of the application. The decisive fact is the position on the date of the application, namely 20.6.2025, when Ravi had ceased to be a partner on 31.3.2025; the expectation that he would rejoin in September 2025 and the silence of the printed form do not cure the falsity. No cooling-off provision is invoked by this clause, and clause (1) of Part III deals only with being held guilty by a civil or criminal court of an offence punishable with imprisonment exceeding six months.

questions.category: Second Schedule Part II - Clauses (4) and (5)
questions.question:
CA Ashok Behera, a chartered accountant in practice: (i) received ₹ 3,00,000 as sale proceeds collected by him on behalf of a client and applied ₹ 1,00,000 of it to pay his children's school fees, intending to replace it in four months; and (ii) accepted appointment as statutory auditor of a private company while holding the office of whole-time director of that company, contrary to the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.

Consider the following statements:
I. Item (i) amounts to professional misconduct under clause (4) of Part II of the Second Schedule, which applies to a member whether in practice or not, in respect of money received in his professional capacity.
II. Item (i) can also attract clause (10) of Part I of the Second Schedule, since the money was not used for the purpose for which it was intended.
III. Item (ii) amounts to professional misconduct under clause (5) of Part II of the Second Schedule.
IV. Item (ii) attracts clause (5) of Part II only if the company concerned is a listed company.

Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Clause (5) of Part II of the Second Schedule makes it misconduct for a member to act as an auditor of a company in contravention of the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, and it is not restricted to listed companies, so statement IV is the one which is not correct. Part II of the Second Schedule applies to members of the Institute generally, that is, whether in practice or not, which makes statement I correct; the ₹ 1,00,000 was money received in his professional capacity and its appropriation amounts to defalcation. Statement II is also correct, because clause (10) of Part I requires client moneys to be used for the purposes for which they are intended within a reasonable time, and school fees are not the client's purpose. Statement III is correct, since accepting an auditorship while holding the office of whole-time director contravenes the Companies Act, 2013, and clause (5) of Part II captures that contravention as professional misconduct.

questions.category: Second Schedule Part III with First Schedule Part IV
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
I. Clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule covers a member being held guilty by any civil or criminal court for an offence which is punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months.
II. Clause (1) of Part IV of the First Schedule covers a member being held guilty by any civil or criminal court for an offence which is punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months.
III. Both the provisions above fall within the category of 'Other Misconduct'.
IV. An offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of five months, of which a member is held guilty by a criminal court, attracts clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule and clause (1) of Part IV of the First Schedule are mirror provisions divided by the six-month line, the former dealing with offences punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months and the latter with offences punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months. Both fall in the 'Other Misconduct' category, which is why statement III is correct, and clause (1) of Part III applies to a member of the Institute whether in practice or not. Statement IV is not correct, because five months is not exceeding six months, and such an offence attracts clause (1) of Part IV of the First Schedule, not clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule. The decisive point is the punishment to which the offence is punishable, and the trap is to read the sentence actually awarded instead of the statutory exposure.

questions.question:
CA Iqbal Singh, a member of the Institute who is not in practice, was held guilty by a criminal court in 2025 of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months, and this was treated as other misconduct under clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule.

Which one of the following changes in the facts, standing alone, would move the case from clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule to clause (1) of Part IV of the First Schedule, without altering its character as other misconduct?
options: That he was held guilty by a civil court instead of a criminal court
That the offence is instead punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months
That he is a member in practice rather than a member not in practice
That the offence has no connection whatever with his professional work
questions.explanation: The single dividing line between clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule and clause (1) of Part IV of the First Schedule is whether the offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months or not exceeding six months. Both provisions are expressly framed as applying to a member of the Institute whether in practice or not, and both speak of 'any civil or criminal court', so shifting the forum, shifting the member's status, or severing the professional nexus changes nothing. The offence having no professional connection is precisely what makes 'other misconduct' meaningful, since these provisions empower the Council to inquire into misconduct even where it does not arise out of professional work. Hence only the change in the length of the punishment to which the offence is punishable transfers the case from one Schedule to the other.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements correctly contrasts Chapter II of the Council General Guidelines, 2008 with clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949?
options: Chapter II applies to a chartered accountant in practice while clause (7) applies to a chartered accountant employee, and the two never overlap
Chapter II and clause (7) apply only to members in practice, a member in service being governed solely by Part II of the Second Schedule

Chapter II requires a chartered accountant employee to exercise due diligence and not to be grossly negligent in the conduct of his duties, whereas clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule applies to a chartered accountant in practice
Chapter II merely recommends, and does not require, the exercise of due diligence by a chartered accountant employee
questions.explanation: Chapter II of the Council General Guidelines, 2008, headed 'Conduct of a Member being an Employee', provides that a CA employee shall exercise due diligence and shall not be grossly negligent in the conduct of his duties. Clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule is in identically worded substance but applies to a chartered accountant in practice, since Part I of the Second Schedule opens with 'A CA in practice is deemed to be guilty of professional misconduct if he'. The first option reverses the two, and the second wrongly assumes that a member in service has no duty of diligence. The fourth option fails because Chapter II is expressed as a requirement, and a contravention of Council guidelines is itself reachable under clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule, which applies to members generally.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on Chapter V of the Council General Guidelines, 2008 (Maintenance of Books of Account):
I. A chartered accountant in practice shall maintain and keep, in respect of his professional practice, proper books of account including a Cash Book and a Ledger.
II. The obligation extends to a chartered accountant firm in which the member is a partner.
III. The obligation arises only where the member's gross annual professional receipts exceed ₹ 50 lakh.
IV. Where the member is a sole proprietor, a Cash Book alone is sufficient and a Ledger is not required.

Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Chapter V requires a CA in practice, or a CA firm in which he is a partner, to maintain and keep in respect of his professional practice proper books of account including a Cash Book and a Ledger. Statements I and II therefore correctly restate the guideline, and no monetary threshold qualifies it, so statement III is not correct. Statement IV is also not correct, because the Cash Book and the Ledger are both expressly named and the requirement does not relax for a sole proprietor. The trap in statement III is the importation of a receipts limit which Chapter V does not contain, and the trap in statement IV is the suggestion that one of the two named books is optional.

questions.question:
Karpagam & Co., a chartered accountants' firm at Madurai, has four partners, namely CA Karpagam Raman (whole-time, holding a certificate of practice), CA Vetrivel Iyer (who is also a part-time practising partner of S. Selvam & Co., Trichy), CA Anbarasi Doss and CA Maruthu Pandian. The following facts were ascertained on 20.5.2026 for the financial year 2025-26:
(i) Karpagam & Co. has accepted 46 tax audits under section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961, nine of which relate to branch offices of four concerns whose head-office audits are also with the firm. CA Karpagam Raman individually signed all 46 tax audit reports.
(ii) CA Karpagam Raman is also a partner of Raman & Sundaram, Chennai, which has accepted 14 tax audits under section 44AB for the same financial year, none of which relates to a head office and branch offices of the same concern.
(iii) Karpagam & Co. has also conducted 17 audits under section 44AD and 5 audits under section 44ADA.
(iv) Karpagam & Co. holds, at 20.5.2026, the statutory auditorship of 28 companies under section 141 of the Companies Act, 2013, which include 6 one person companies and 2 dormant companies.
(v) The firm is the statutory auditor of Neelamegha Spinning Mills Ltd., a listed company having a turnover of ₹ 412 crore for the year, for a statutory audit fee of ₹ 18,00,000. In the same year the firm received from that company ₹ 11,00,000 for a working-capital modelling assignment, ₹ 7,50,000 for an audit under another statute and ₹ 4,00,000 for representing the company before the GST authorities.
(vi) CA Maruthu Pandian's brother borrowed ₹ 60,00,000 from Neelamegha Spinning Mills Ltd., and Maruthu Pandian gave a guarantee for ₹ 1,20,000 of that borrowing.

Consider the following statements:
I. For the purposes of Chapter VI, the 46 assignments referred to in (i) are counted as 37 tax audit assignments.
II. CA Karpagam Raman contravenes Chapter VI merely because she individually signed all 46 tax audit reports of the firm.
III. The 17 audits under section 44AD and the 5 audits under section 44ADA referred to in (iii) must be added to the count under Chapter VI.
IV. In applying the Chapter VI limit to CA Karpagam Raman, her tax audit assignments are taken as the aggregate for Karpagam & Co. and Raman & Sundaram together.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement I is correct because the audit of the head office and branch offices of a concern is taken as one tax audit assignment: the nine branch reports together with the four head-office reports represent thirteen reports but only four assignments, so 46 minus 13 plus 4 equals 37. Statement II is not correct, because one partner can individually sign all tax audit reports on behalf of all partners in the CA firm, subject to the specified limits, and 37 is within the limit of 60 per CA or per partner in a financial year. Statement III is not correct, because audits conducted under sections 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE shall not be taken for this purpose. Statement IV is correct, because where a CA is a partner in more than one firm the number of tax audit assignments in relation to that partner is taken as the aggregate for all the firms together, namely 37 plus 14, which is 51 and still within 60. Incidentally, assignments of Vetrivel Iyer, being a part-time practising partner, are not taken for the limit.

questions.question:
Karpagam & Co., a chartered accountants' firm at Madurai, has four partners, namely CA Karpagam Raman (whole-time, holding a certificate of practice), CA Vetrivel Iyer (who is also a part-time practising partner of S. Selvam & Co., Trichy), CA Anbarasi Doss and CA Maruthu Pandian. The following facts were ascertained on 20.5.2026 for the financial year 2025-26:
(i) Karpagam & Co. has accepted 46 tax audits under section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961, nine of which relate to branch offices of four concerns whose head-office audits are also with the firm. CA Karpagam Raman individually signed all 46 tax audit reports.
(ii) CA Karpagam Raman is also a partner of Raman & Sundaram, Chennai, which has accepted 14 tax audits under section 44AB for the same financial year, none of which relates to a head office and branch offices of the same concern.
(iii) Karpagam & Co. has also conducted 17 audits under section 44AD and 5 audits under section 44ADA.
(iv) Karpagam & Co. holds, at 20.5.2026, the statutory auditorship of 28 companies under section 141 of the Companies Act, 2013, which include 6 one person companies and 2 dormant companies.
(v) The firm is the statutory auditor of Neelamegha Spinning Mills Ltd., a listed company having a turnover of ₹ 412 crore for the year, for a statutory audit fee of ₹ 18,00,000. In the same year the firm received from that company ₹ 11,00,000 for a working-capital modelling assignment, ₹ 7,50,000 for an audit under another statute and ₹ 4,00,000 for representing the company before the GST authorities.
(vi) CA Maruthu Pandian's brother borrowed ₹ 60,00,000 from Neelamegha Spinning Mills Ltd., and Maruthu Pandian gave a guarantee for ₹ 1,20,000 of that borrowing.

What is the correct position under Chapter VIII of the Council General Guidelines, 2008 in respect of fact (iv)?
options: 28 assignments are held, which is within the specified number of 30, so no question of exclusion arises
26 assignments are held, the dormant companies alone being excluded, which is within the specified number of 25
22 assignments are held, the one person companies alone being excluded, so the firm may add 8 more companies
20 assignments are held, one person companies and dormant companies being excluded, which is within the specified number of 30
questions.explanation: Chapter VIII fixes the specified number of audit assignments at 30 audit assignments per CA or per partner, except one person companies and dormant companies, and it speaks of appointments held at any time of companies under section 141 of the Companies Act, 2013. Excluding the 6 one person companies and the 2 dormant companies from the 28 companies gives 20 assignments, which is comfortably within 30. The first option reaches a coincidentally similar conclusion by counting all 28, but it does so by ignoring the express exclusions and by taking the wrong figure. Options excluding only one class of company misread the exception, which covers both one person companies and dormant companies, and the reference to a limit of 25 is not to be found in Chapter VIII. The decisive facts are the 6 one person companies and 2 dormant companies, which are not to be counted at all.

questions.question:
Karpagam & Co., a chartered accountants' firm at Madurai, has four partners, namely CA Karpagam Raman (whole-time, holding a certificate of practice), CA Vetrivel Iyer (who is also a part-time practising partner of S. Selvam & Co., Trichy), CA Anbarasi Doss and CA Maruthu Pandian. The following facts were ascertained on 20.5.2026 for the financial year 2025-26:
(i) Karpagam & Co. has accepted 46 tax audits under section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961, nine of which relate to branch offices of four concerns whose head-office audits are also with the firm. CA Karpagam Raman individually signed all 46 tax audit reports.
(ii) CA Karpagam Raman is also a partner of Raman & Sundaram, Chennai, which has accepted 14 tax audits under section 44AB for the same financial year, none of which relates to a head office and branch offices of the same concern.
(iii) Karpagam & Co. has also conducted 17 audits under section 44AD and 5 audits under section 44ADA.
(iv) Karpagam & Co. holds, at 20.5.2026, the statutory auditorship of 28 companies under section 141 of the Companies Act, 2013, which include 6 one person companies and 2 dormant companies.
(v) The firm is the statutory auditor of Neelamegha Spinning Mills Ltd., a listed company having a turnover of ₹ 412 crore for the year, for a statutory audit fee of ₹ 18,00,000. In the same year the firm received from that company ₹ 11,00,000 for a working-capital modelling assignment, ₹ 7,50,000 for an audit under another statute and ₹ 4,00,000 for representing the company before the GST authorities.
(vi) CA Maruthu Pandian's brother borrowed ₹ 60,00,000 from Neelamegha Spinning Mills Ltd., and Maruthu Pandian gave a guarantee for ₹ 1,20,000 of that borrowing.

Consider the following statements on fact (v):
I. The remuneration for other work to be tested against the statutory audit fee is ₹ 11,00,000.
II. Chapter IX applies to Neelamegha Spinning Mills Ltd.
III. If the working-capital modelling fee had been ₹ 19,50,000 instead of ₹ 11,00,000, the firm could not have accepted the statutory auditorship of that company.
IV. The audit under another statute and the representation before the GST authorities are both included in the expression other work.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Chapter IX applies to a public sector undertaking, government company, listed company and other public companies having turnover of ₹ 50 crores or more in a year, so a listed company with a turnover of ₹ 412 crore is squarely within it and statement II is correct. The expression other work, service or assignment includes management consultancy and all other professional services permitted by the Council, but expressly does not include an audit under any other statute, certification work required to be done by statutory auditors, or any representation before an authority. Applying that to fact (v), only the ₹ 11,00,000 working-capital modelling assignment counts, so statement I is correct and statement IV is not. Since ₹ 11,00,000 does not exceed the statutory audit fee of ₹ 18,00,000, the appointment is permissible, but at ₹ 19,50,000 the other work remuneration would exceed the audit fee and the bar would operate, which makes statement III correct. The decisive comparison is countable other work against the statutory audit fee of the same company, not the gross sum of ₹ 22,50,000.

questions.question:
Karpagam & Co., a chartered accountants' firm at Madurai, has four partners, namely CA Karpagam Raman (whole-time, holding a certificate of practice), CA Vetrivel Iyer (who is also a part-time practising partner of S. Selvam & Co., Trichy), CA Anbarasi Doss and CA Maruthu Pandian. The following facts were ascertained on 20.5.2026 for the financial year 2025-26:
(i) Karpagam & Co. has accepted 46 tax audits under section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961, nine of which relate to branch offices of four concerns whose head-office audits are also with the firm. CA Karpagam Raman individually signed all 46 tax audit reports.
(ii) CA Karpagam Raman is also a partner of Raman & Sundaram, Chennai, which has accepted 14 tax audits under section 44AB for the same financial year, none of which relates to a head office and branch offices of the same concern.
(iii) Karpagam & Co. has also conducted 17 audits under section 44AD and 5 audits under section 44ADA.
(iv) Karpagam & Co. holds, at 20.5.2026, the statutory auditorship of 28 companies under section 141 of the Companies Act, 2013, which include 6 one person companies and 2 dormant companies.
(v) The firm is the statutory auditor of Neelamegha Spinning Mills Ltd., a listed company having a turnover of ₹ 412 crore for the year, for a statutory audit fee of ₹ 18,00,000. In the same year the firm received from that company ₹ 11,00,000 for a working-capital modelling assignment, ₹ 7,50,000 for an audit under another statute and ₹ 4,00,000 for representing the company before the GST authorities.
(vi) CA Maruthu Pandian's brother borrowed ₹ 60,00,000 from Neelamegha Spinning Mills Ltd., and Maruthu Pandian gave a guarantee for ₹ 1,20,000 of that borrowing.

Which one of the following is the correct position in respect of fact (vi)?
options: A bar arises under Chapter X, because a relative of a partner is indebted to the concern and because the guarantee of ₹ 1,20,000 exceeds the ₹ 1,00,000 limit applicable to guarantee and security
No bar arises, because ₹ 60,00,000 was borrowed by the brother and not by the firm or by a partner
No bar arises, because Chapter X applies only to a CA in practice personally and not to partners of a CA firm
A bar arises only if Maruthu Pandian is himself indebted to Neelamegha Spinning Mills Ltd. for an amount exceeding ₹ 5,00,000
questions.explanation: Chapter X prohibits a CA in practice, a CA firm, a relative of such member or a relative of such partner from accepting appointment as statutory auditor of a concern while indebted to the concern, or having given any guarantee or provided any security in connection with the indebtedness of any third person to the concern. Neelamegha Spinning Mills Ltd. is a company, so the limits fixed by the Companies Act apply, namely ₹ 5,00,000 for indebtedness and ₹ 1,00,000 for guarantee and security. The guarantee of ₹ 1,20,000 given by Maruthu Pandian for his brother's borrowing from the company exceeds ₹ 1,00,000, and independently his brother, being a relative of a partner, is indebted to the concern. The second and third options wrongly read down the words 'or relative of such member or partner'. The fourth option confuses the indebtedness limit with the separate and lower limit which governs guarantees and security.

questions.question: Which one of the following is NOT to be taken into account in computing the specified number of tax audit assignments under Chapter VI of the Council General Guidelines, 2008?
options: A tax audit under section 44AB of a partnership firm
A tax audit under section 44AB accepted by a CA who is a partner in more than one firm
The tax audit of the head office and the branch offices of a concern
Assignments of a part-time practising partner of a CA firm
questions.explanation: Chapter VI expressly provides that a part-time practising partner of a CA firm shall not be taken for the purpose of the limit, which makes option 3 the correct answer. A tax audit of a partnership firm is an ordinary assignment under section 44AB and counts fully. A tax audit accepted by a CA who is a partner in more than one firm is also taken, but the number in relation to such partner is taken as the aggregate for all the firms together, so it is not excluded from computation. The audit of the head office and branch offices of a concern is taken as one tax audit assignment, which means it is counted once and not disregarded. The distinction worth noting is that audits under sections 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE are the ones which shall not be taken at all.

questions.question:
