CA Dinesh Paliwal, a chartered accountant in practice at Bhopal, wishes to accept appointment as statutory auditor of two companies for FY 2026-27.
Raisen Agro Products Ltd. was incorporated on 12.8.2019. Its net worth at the close of FY 2025-26 is ₹ 22 crore and its accumulated losses at that date are ₹ 26 crore. The outgoing auditor's fee of ₹ 8,00,000 for FY 2025-26 has not been paid, and the accounts for FY 2025-26 carry a provision for audit fee of ₹ 8,00,000 which is signed by both the auditee and the outgoing auditor.
Bhelsi Polymers Ltd. was incorporated on 5.2.2023. Its accumulated losses at the close of FY 2025-26 are ₹ 40 crore against a net worth of ₹ 8 crore, and the outgoing auditor's undisputed fee of ₹ 3,00,000 has not been paid.

Which one of the following is the correct conclusion?
options: He may accept the auditorship of both companies, since in each case the accumulated losses exceed the net worth
He may accept neither, since the sick unit exception applies only where the unpaid fee does not exceed ₹ 5,00,000
He may accept Raisen Agro Products Ltd., which is a sick unit, but not Bhelsi Polymers Ltd., which is not registered for at least five years and therefore is not a sick unit
He may accept Bhelsi Polymers Ltd. but not Raisen Agro Products Ltd., because the unpaid fee in the latter case exceeds ₹ 5,00,000
questions.explanation: Chapter VII bars a CA in practice from accepting appointment as auditor of an entity where the undisputed audit fee of another CA for carrying out the audit has not been paid, but the prohibition does not apply in the case of a sick unit. A sick unit means a unit registered for at least 5 years which has accumulated losses greater than or equal to its net worth at the end of any financial year. Raisen Agro Products Ltd. was incorporated on 12.8.2019 and so was registered for well over five years by the close of FY 2025-26, and its accumulated losses of ₹ 26 crore exceed its net worth of ₹ 22 crore, so it is a sick unit and the unpaid ₹ 8,00,000 does not bar Dinesh. Bhelsi Polymers Ltd., incorporated on 5.2.2023, fails the five-year registration condition even though its losses far exceed its net worth, so the prohibition operates against the unpaid undisputed fee of ₹ 3,00,000. Both limbs of the definition must be satisfied, and the monetary size of the unpaid fee is irrelevant since no fee ceiling appears in Chapter VII.

questions.question:
CA Dinesh Paliwal, a chartered accountant in practice at Bhopal, wishes to accept appointment as statutory auditor of two companies for FY 2026-27.
Raisen Agro Products Ltd. was incorporated on 12.8.2019. Its net worth at the close of FY 2025-26 is ₹ 22 crore and its accumulated losses at that date are ₹ 26 crore. The outgoing auditor's fee of ₹ 8,00,000 for FY 2025-26 has not been paid, and the accounts for FY 2025-26 carry a provision for audit fee of ₹ 8,00,000 which is signed by both the auditee and the outgoing auditor.
Bhelsi Polymers Ltd. was incorporated on 5.2.2023. Its accumulated losses at the close of FY 2025-26 are ₹ 40 crore against a net worth of ₹ 8 crore, and the outgoing auditor's undisputed fee of ₹ 3,00,000 has not been paid.

Consider the following statements:
I. A provision for audit fee in the accounts signed by both the auditee and the auditor is treated as undisputed audit fees for the purposes of Chapter VII.
II. The ₹ 8,00,000 of Raisen Agro Products Ltd. is outside Chapter VII because it is only a provision carried in the accounts and not a sum separately invoiced and admitted by the company.
III. Chapter VII bars a CA in practice from accepting appointment as auditor of an entity where the undisputed audit fee of another CA for carrying out the audit has not been paid, and this bar is lifted in the case of a sick unit.
IV. A unit registered for three years with accumulated losses of ₹ 40 crore against a net worth of ₹ 8 crore satisfies the definition of a sick unit.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Chapter VII expressly provides that a provision for audit fee in the accounts signed by both the auditee and the auditor shall be considered as undisputed audit fees, which makes statement I correct and statement II incorrect. The provision being countersigned by the auditee is precisely the mechanism by which the Chapter converts a book provision into a deemed undisputed fee, so the objection in statement II fails. Statement III correctly states the prohibition and the sick unit exception. Statement IV is not correct, because the definition of a sick unit requires the unit to be registered for at least 5 years in addition to having accumulated losses greater than or equal to its net worth, and three years of registration defeats the claim even where losses are five times the net worth.

questions.question:
CA Sathish Kumar, a chartered accountant in practice at Nagercoil, was approached in June 2026 to accept appointment as the statutory auditor of Kanyakumari Cold-Storage Ltd., an unlisted public company having a turnover of ₹ 96 crore for the year, for FY 2026-27. The statutory audit fee agreed for that year is ₹ 6,00,000. The following facts emerge:
(a) Sathish Kumar borrowed ₹ 4,20,000 from the company in January 2025 to construct his house; ₹ 90,000 of this remained outstanding on 30.6.2026 and is being repaid in monthly instalments.
(b) His wife Usha stands as guarantor for ₹ 1,10,000 in connection with a loan taken by her brother from the same company.
(c) The company also proposes that Sathish Kumar should conduct its GST audit, which is required under another statute, for a fee of ₹ 3,00,000, and should represent it before the income-tax authorities for a fee of ₹ 2,50,000.
(d) Sathish Kumar's professional fees from the company are agreed to be paid on a progressive basis.

Consider the following statements on the above facts:
I. The guarantee of ₹ 1,10,000 given by Usha, a relative, in connection with a third person's indebtedness to the company exceeds the ₹ 1,00,000 limit for guarantee and security under the Companies Act, 2013, and therefore Sathish Kumar shall not accept the appointment.
II. The outstanding ₹ 90,000 is an indebtedness which exceeds the ₹ 5,00,000 limit under the Companies Act, 2013 and independently bars him.
III. Because his professional fees are payable on a progressive basis, he must be treated as indebted to the company.
IV. No bar arises under Chapter X, because Usha's guarantee relates to a loan taken by her brother and the Chapter covers only indebtedness of the member himself.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Chapter X prohibits acceptance of appointment while indebted to the concern for the limits fixed in the statute, and covers a member, a CA firm, a relative of such member or partner, and also a guarantee given or security provided in connection with the indebtedness of any third person to the concern. Under the Companies Act the limits are ₹ 5,00,000 for indebtedness and ₹ 1,00,000 for guarantee and security. The ₹ 1,10,000 guarantee by his wife in respect of her brother's loan from the company is within the Chapter and exceeds ₹ 1,00,000, so statement I is correct and statement IV is not. Statement II is not correct, because an outstanding ₹ 90,000 does not exceed the ₹ 5,00,000 indebtedness limit; the purpose of the loan for house construction is a red herring, since Chapter X does not classify loans by purpose. Statement III is not correct, because if the auditor receives fees on a progressive basis he cannot be said to be indebted to the concern.

questions.question:
CA Sathish Kumar, a chartered accountant in practice at Nagercoil, was approached in June 2026 to accept appointment as the statutory auditor of Kanyakumari Cold-Storage Ltd., an unlisted public company having a turnover of ₹ 96 crore for the year, for FY 2026-27. The statutory audit fee agreed for that year is ₹ 6,00,000. The following facts emerge:
(a) Sathish Kumar borrowed ₹ 4,20,000 from the company in January 2025 to construct his house; ₹ 90,000 of this remained outstanding on 30.6.2026 and is being repaid in monthly instalments.
(b) His wife Usha stands as guarantor for ₹ 1,10,000 in connection with a loan taken by her brother from the same company.
(c) The company also proposes that Sathish Kumar should conduct its GST audit, which is required under another statute, for a fee of ₹ 3,00,000, and should represent it before the income-tax authorities for a fee of ₹ 2,50,000.
(d) Sathish Kumar's professional fees from the company are agreed to be paid on a progressive basis.

Which one of the following changes to the above facts, standing alone, would enable Sathish Kumar to accept the statutory auditorship of Kanyakumari Cold-Storage Ltd.?
options: His own outstanding borrowing from the company is increased from ₹ 90,000 to ₹ 5,80,000
His professional fees are made payable as a single lump sum instead of on a progressive basis
He repays the ₹ 90,000 in full while Usha's guarantee of ₹ 1,10,000 continues
Usha's guarantee is reduced from ₹ 1,10,000 to ₹ 80,000
questions.explanation: The operative disqualification is the guarantee of ₹ 1,10,000 given by a relative in connection with a third person's indebtedness to the company, because it exceeds the ₹ 1,00,000 limit fixed for guarantee and security under the Companies Act. Reducing that guarantee to ₹ 80,000 brings it within the limit, and since his own indebtedness of ₹ 90,000 is well within the ₹ 5,00,000 limit, no bar survives. Increasing his own borrowing to ₹ 5,80,000 would create a fresh and larger breach of the ₹ 5,00,000 indebtedness limit. Repaying the ₹ 90,000 while retaining Usha's guarantee leaves the disqualifying limb untouched. Converting the fee arrangement from a progressive basis to a lump sum is irrelevant, because an auditor who receives fees on a progressive basis cannot be said to be indebted to the concern in the first place.

questions.question:
CA Sathish Kumar, a chartered accountant in practice at Nagercoil, was approached in June 2026 to accept appointment as the statutory auditor of Kanyakumari Cold-Storage Ltd., an unlisted public company having a turnover of ₹ 96 crore for the year, for FY 2026-27. The statutory audit fee agreed for that year is ₹ 6,00,000. The following facts emerge:
(a) Sathish Kumar borrowed ₹ 4,20,000 from the company in January 2025 to construct his house; ₹ 90,000 of this remained outstanding on 30.6.2026 and is being repaid in monthly instalments.
(b) His wife Usha stands as guarantor for ₹ 1,10,000 in connection with a loan taken by her brother from the same company.
(c) The company also proposes that Sathish Kumar should conduct its GST audit, which is required under another statute, for a fee of ₹ 3,00,000, and should represent it before the income-tax authorities for a fee of ₹ 2,50,000.
(d) Sathish Kumar's professional fees from the company are agreed to be paid on a progressive basis.

What is the MOST appropriate conclusion on Chapter IX in respect of fact (c)?
options: Chapter IX applies to this company, but neither the audit under another statute nor the representation before an authority is included in other work, so the Chapter IX bar is not attracted
Chapter IX does not apply at all, because the company is not listed and is not a public sector undertaking
Chapter IX applies and bars the appointment, because the GST audit fee and the representation fee together exceed the statutory audit fee
Chapter IX applies and bars the appointment, because any other work accepted for such a company is prohibited irrespective of remuneration
questions.explanation: Chapter IX extends to a public sector undertaking, government company, listed company and other public companies having turnover of ₹ 50 crores or more in a year, and this unlisted public company has a turnover of ₹ 96 crore, so the Chapter is engaged. The expression other work, service or assignment includes management consultancy and all other professional services permitted by the Council, but it does not include an audit under any other statute, certification work required to be done by statutory auditors, or any representation before an authority. The GST audit is an audit under another statute and the income-tax work is a representation before an authority, so neither is counted and no aggregate is tested against the audit fee of ₹ 6,00,000. The second option is wrong because the Chapter is not confined to listed companies, and the fourth is wrong because the bar operates only where the remuneration for counted other work in total exceeds the statutory audit fee of the same company.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): An auditor who receives his fees from a concern on a progressive basis cannot be said to be indebted to that concern for the purposes of Chapter X of the Council General Guidelines, 2008.
Reason (R): Chapter X prescribes one and the same monetary limit for every concern, irrespective of the statute which governs it.

Which one of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
questions.explanation: Assertion A is a direct statement of the additional point recorded under Chapter X, namely that if the auditor receives fees on a progressive basis he cannot be said to be indebted to the concern. Reason R is not correct, because Chapter X distinguishes between indebtedness or guarantees covered by limits fixed in the statute, which for the Companies Act are ₹ 5,00,000 for indebtedness and ₹ 1,00,000 for guarantee and security, and other cases where the bar arises for an amount exceeding ₹ 1,00,000. Since the reason is false, the first two options are unavailable, and the fourth option is also unavailable because the assertion is true. The two limbs of Chapter X therefore have to be kept apart: the character of the amount as progressive fees defeats the indebtedness objection altogether, while the monetary limits apply only where the Chapter is otherwise engaged.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on Chapter X of the Council General Guidelines, 2008:
I. The prohibition extends to a relative of the member in practice or of a partner, and not merely to the member or the firm itself.
II. For concerns to which the limits fixed in the statute do not apply, the bar arises where the amount exceeds ₹ 1,00,000.
III. Under the Companies Act, 2013, the limit is ₹ 5,00,000 for indebtedness and ₹ 1,00,000 for guarantee and security.
IV. A guarantee given in connection with the indebtedness of a third person to the concern is outside Chapter X, because the Chapter speaks only of indebtedness.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Chapter X covers a CA in practice or CA firm, and also a relative of such member or partner, so statement I is correct. The Chapter sets the bar at the limits fixed in the statute for companies governed by them, and in other cases at an amount exceeding ₹ 1,00,000, which makes statements II and III correct. The Companies Act limits specifically recorded are ₹ 5,00,000 for indebtedness and ₹ 1,00,000 for guarantee and security. Statement IV is not correct, because Chapter X expressly covers having given any guarantee or provided any security in connection with the indebtedness of any third person to the concern, as distinct from the auditor's own borrowing.

questions.category: Council General Guidelines - Chapters VI, IX and X
questions.question:
CA Zoya Merchant, a chartered accountant in practice at Surat, is considering four proposals as on 15.5.2026:
(1) Accepting the statutory auditorship of Vasan Insurance Brokers Ltd., a listed company having a turnover of ₹ 410 crore, for a statutory audit fee of ₹ 6,00,000, and simultaneously accepting for ₹ 9,00,000 the certification work required to be done by the statutory auditor of that company.
(2) Accepting, in the financial year 2025-26, 58 tax audits under section 44AB as a partner of one CA firm only, and signing all 58 tax audit reports herself.
(3) Accepting the statutory auditorship of Hiror Textiles Pvt. Ltd. while her brother has given a guarantee of ₹ 1,20,000 in connection with a third person's indebtedness to that company.
(4) Accepting the statutory auditorship of Sadra Estate Owners' Co-operative Association while she is indebted to that Association for ₹ 1,30,000.

Which of the above proposals may be accepted without contravening the Council General Guidelines, 2008?
questions.explanation: Proposal (1) is permissible because certification work required to be done by statutory auditors is expressly excluded from 'other work' under Chapter IX, so the ₹ 9,00,000 is never compared with the audit fee of ₹ 6,00,000 even though on its face it exceeds it. Proposal (2) is permissible because 58 is within the specified number of 60 tax audit assignments per CA or per partner in a financial year, and one partner can individually sign all tax audit reports on behalf of all partners in the firm, subject to that limit. Proposal (3) is barred under Chapter X, because a guarantee of ₹ 1,20,000 given by a relative in connection with a third person's indebtedness exceeds the ₹ 1,00,000 limit for guarantee and security. Proposal (4) is barred under Chapter X, because the Association is not governed by the statutory limits, so the residual limit of an amount exceeding ₹ 1,00,000 applies and ₹ 1,30,000 crosses it.

questions.category: Second Schedule Part II and Part III
questions.question:
Match the situations in Column I with the provision attracted or the consequence in Column II:

Column I
P. A member, being an employee of a firm, discloses confidential information acquired in the course of his employment, as permitted by his employer.
Q. A member in practice issues a certificate as a chartered accountant in practice without having applied for a certificate of practice.
R. A member includes, in a return filed with the Council, particulars which he knows to be false.
S. A member is held guilty by a civil court for an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of nine months.

Column II
1. Clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule - contravention of the Act
2. Clause (3) of Part II of the Second Schedule - false particulars in a statement or return submitted to the Institute or Council
3. No misconduct under clause (2) of Part II of the Second Schedule, the disclosure being permitted by the employer
4. Clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule - other misconduct

Choose the correct pairing:
questions.explanation: Clause (2) of Part II of the Second Schedule prohibits disclosure of confidential information acquired in the course of employment except as required by law or as permitted by the employer, so an employer-permitted disclosure falls within the exception and P pairs with 3. Issuing a certificate as a CA in practice without having applied for a certificate of practice is a violation of the Act itself and is one of the illustrations under clause (1) of Part II, so Q pairs with 1. Including particulars known to be false in a return submitted to the Institute or Council or its statutory authorities is clause (3) of Part II, so R pairs with 2. An offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of nine months exceeds six months, so it falls within clause (1) of Part III of the Second Schedule as other misconduct, and S pairs with 4. Note that clause (1) of Part III expressly reaches a civil court as well as a criminal court.

questions.question: Which one of the following is NOT one of the instances of misconduct expressly listed under clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949?
options: Submitting a stock audit report by relying on an M.I.S. report without physically verifying the stock
Certifying circulation figures on the basis of an M.I.S. report without examining the books of account
Digital signing a form without verifying its genuineness
Failing to keep moneys of a client, other than fees or remuneration, in a separate banking account
Failing to confirm or verify, from any proper source, the value of investments
questions.explanation: Failing to keep client moneys other than fees or remuneration in a separate banking account is the subject matter of clause (10) of Part I of the Second Schedule, not clause (7). The other four are all illustrations recorded under clause (7), which deals with not exercising due diligence or being grossly negligent in the conduct of professional duties, along with issuing clean reports on financial statements without examining the accounts, not exercising reasonable skill and care and performing work in a casual manner, and not completing the audit work and submitting the audit report in due time. The common thread in the clause (7) illustrations is defective performance of the work itself, whether the reliance is on an M.I.S. report, an unverified digital form or an unverified investment value. That thread distinguishes clause (7) from clause (10), which is about custody and application of client money.

questions.category: Council General Guidelines Chapter XV - Networking - Concept of Network
questions.question:
Consider the following statements on the concept of a network under Chapter XV of the Council General Guidelines, 2008:

I. Entities within a structure are deemed to be a network only if they share profit; the sharing of cost by itself is not enough.
II. Common ownership, common control or common management of the entities in a structure is by itself sufficient for the structure to be treated as a network.
III. Sharing of professional resources such as systems, staff, technical departments and training courses brings a structure within the concept of a network.
IV. A structure which shares a common brand name and a common business strategy, but does not share profit or cost, falls outside the concept of a network.

Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Chapter XV defines a network by reference to three alternative limbs - entities within a structure are deemed to be a network where they share profit or cost; or where they have common ownership, control, management, business strategy or brand name; or where they share professional resources such as systems, staff, technical departments and training courses. The limbs are disjunctive, so the presence of any single one of them is sufficient; a structure sharing only a brand name, or only a common business strategy, is still a network. Statement I is therefore not correct because sharing of cost, and not merely sharing of profit, constitutes a network. Statement IV is not correct because a common brand name and a common business strategy are independently enough, and the absence of profit or cost sharing is irrelevant. Statements II and III correctly restate the second and third limbs, which is why the option excluding them is wrong.

questions.category: Council General Guidelines Chapter XV - Networking - Forms and Name
questions.question:
Case: Seven CA firms having 46 partners between them, with offices in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Pune and Lucknow, have agreed to (a) share the profits of a common technology consulting vertical, (b) operate under one brand name 'VidSutra' and a common business strategy paper approved by an assembled committee of partners, (c) run a common training centre for articled assistants and a common data analytics technical department, with articles enrolled centrally and deputed to the firms, and (d) retain their own separate audit methodologies for statutory audit work. No entity of the structure carries out any professional practice; a mutual association called 'VidSutra Consortium Association' only collects membership subscriptions and arranges the common training. The promoters propose to name the network 'VidSutra & Co.' and applied to the Institute in the prescribed form on 4 March 2024. The Institute intimated approval of the name on 2 April 2024, and the network filed its application for registration on 12 August 2024. On 15 May 2024 the structure entered into an arrangement with an entity having its office in Singapore and filed the declaration for listing on 10 July 2024. On 1 August 2024 one member firm exited and this was communicated to the Institute on 25 September 2024. Rane & Associates, a member firm, also continues as a member of a different network formed with entities outside India. Sahay & Co., another member firm, is the statutory auditor of Nandi Infra Ltd, a listed company, for a statutory audit fee of ₹ 9 lacs for FY 2023-24; the other member firms propose to collectively take up the internal audit and book-keeping work of Nandi Infra Ltd.

Consider the following statements on the above facts:
I. The structure is a network, because entities which share profit, or which have a common brand name or common business strategy, or which share professional resources such as technical departments and training courses, are deemed to be a network, any one of these being sufficient.
II. Constituting the network through a mutual entity acting as a facilitator for the constituents, so that the network itself does not carry out any professional practice, is an accepted form of network.
III. The proposed name is acceptable, because '& Co.' is customarily appended to the name of a structure of firms and the Institute reserves an approved name for 12 months.
IV. The structure cannot be a network, because each firm retains its own audit methodology and because the constituent firms have 46 partners between them, the maximum permitted being 20.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and II are both correct. On I, the sharing of the profits of the technology vertical, the common brand name and business strategy paper, and the common training centre and data analytics department each independently satisfy the definition of a network, so the structure is a network whatever it is called. On II, Chapter XV expressly permits a network to be constituted as a mutual entity acting as a facilitator for the constituents of the network, in which case the network itself will not carry out any professional practice, which is exactly the role of the VidSutra Consortium Association. Statement III is not correct because a network's distinct name must be approved by the Institute and, to distinguish a network from a CA firm, the words '& Affiliates' shall be used after the name of the network while the words '& Co.' and '& Associates' shall not be used; further, the Institute reserves the approved name for three months, not twelve. Statement IV is not correct because the audit methodology is not one of the criteria and the cap of 20 partners applies only where the network itself is constituted as a partnership firm, not to the aggregate partners of the constituent firms - the 46 partners figure is a red herring.

questions.category: Council General Guidelines Chapter XV - Networking - Ethical Compliance
questions.question:
Case: Seven CA firms having 46 partners between them, with offices in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Pune and Lucknow, have agreed to (a) share the profits of a common technology consulting vertical, (b) operate under one brand name 'VidSutra' and a common business strategy paper approved by an assembled committee of partners, (c) run a common training centre for articled assistants and a common data analytics technical department, with articles enrolled centrally and deputed to the firms, and (d) retain their own separate audit methodologies for statutory audit work. No entity of the structure carries out any professional practice; a mutual association called 'VidSutra Consortium Association' only collects membership subscriptions and arranges the common training. The promoters propose to name the network 'VidSutra & Co.' and applied to the Institute in the prescribed form on 4 March 2024. The Institute intimated approval of the name on 2 April 2024, and the network filed its application for registration on 12 August 2024. On 15 May 2024 the structure entered into an arrangement with an entity having its office in Singapore and filed the declaration for listing on 10 July 2024. On 1 August 2024 one member firm exited and this was communicated to the Institute on 25 September 2024. Rane & Associates, a member firm, also continues as a member of a different network formed with entities outside India. Sahay & Co., another member firm, is the statutory auditor of Nandi Infra Ltd, a listed company, for a statutory audit fee of ₹ 9 lacs for FY 2023-24; the other member firms propose to collectively take up the internal audit and book-keeping work of Nandi Infra Ltd.

Consider the following statements on the ethical compliance obligations of this network:
I. Since Sahay & Co. is the statutory auditor of Nandi Infra Ltd, the network and its associate firms shall not accept the internal audit or book-keeping assignments of that company, these being assignments prohibited for such firm.
II. If the rotation of firms provision applies to Nandi Infra Ltd, another firm of the VidSutra network may accept appointment as its auditor in place of the retiring firm, because each constituent firm is a separate legal firm.
III. The network may advertise itself to the extent permitted by the Advertisement Guidelines issued by the Institute, and the firms constituting the network are permitted to use the words 'Network Firms' on their professional stationery.
IV. Because the VidSutra Consortium Association does not itself carry out any professional practice, the ethical requirements prescribed by the Institute do not extend to the firms constituting the network.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A network has to comply with all applicable ethical requirements prescribed by the Institute, and the requirement is extended to the whole network and not confined to the individual firm. Statement I is correct: where one firm of a network is the statutory auditor of an entity, the network and its associates shall not accept internal audit, book-keeping or other assignments which are prohibited for that firm, so the proposal of the other member firms to take the internal audit and book-keeping of Nandi Infra Ltd fails whatever the fee agreed. Statement III is correct, since the network may advertise itself to the extent permitted by the Advertisement Guidelines and the constituent firms are permitted to use the words 'Network Firms' on their professional stationery. Statement II is not correct because, where rotation of firms applies, no firm of the network can accept appointment as auditor in place of the retiring firm - separateness of the constituent firms does not save the appointment. Statement IV is not correct because the fact that the network entity is merely a facilitator limits the form of the network; it does not dilute the ethical obligations which bind the member firms.

questions.category: Council General Guidelines Chapter XV - Networking - Ceiling on Non-audit Fees
questions.question:
Case: Seven CA firms having 46 partners between them, with offices in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Pune and Lucknow, have agreed to (a) share the profits of a common technology consulting vertical, (b) operate under one brand name 'VidSutra' and a common business strategy paper approved by an assembled committee of partners, (c) run a common training centre for articled assistants and a common data analytics technical department, with articles enrolled centrally and deputed to the firms, and (d) retain their own separate audit methodologies for statutory audit work. No entity of the structure carries out any professional practice; a mutual association called 'VidSutra Consortium Association' only collects membership subscriptions and arranges the common training. The promoters propose to name the network 'VidSutra & Co.' and applied to the Institute in the prescribed form on 4 March 2024. The Institute intimated approval of the name on 2 April 2024, and the network filed its application for registration on 12 August 2024. On 15 May 2024 the structure entered into an arrangement with an entity having its office in Singapore and filed the declaration for listing on 10 July 2024. On 1 August 2024 one member firm exited and this was communicated to the Institute on 25 September 2024. Rane & Associates, a member firm, also continues as a member of a different network formed with entities outside India. Sahay & Co., another member firm, is the statutory auditor of Nandi Infra Ltd, a listed company, for a statutory audit fee of ₹ 9 lacs for FY 2023-24; the other member firms propose to collectively take up the internal audit and book-keeping work of Nandi Infra Ltd.

The member firms now ask, on the assumption that the non-audit work proposed is not otherwise prohibited, about the ceiling on non-audit fees in respect of Nandi Infra Ltd. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate position under the Networking Guidelines?
options: The ceiling applicable to Sahay & Co., the network firm doing the statutory audit, is the same as the limit normally applicable to it, while the other firms of the same network, taken collectively, are limited to ₹ 27 lacs, being three times the statutory audit fee of ₹ 9 lacs.

Each of the other firms of the VidSutra network is individually entitled to a ceiling of ₹ 27 lacs, so that the six firms may collectively charge up to ₹ 162 lacs, the word 'collectively' in the Guidelines being read as applying to each constituent firm separately.

The enhanced ceiling of ₹ 27 lacs is available to Sahay & Co. itself, being the firm which holds the statutory audit of Nandi Infra Ltd, while the other firms of the network are subject to no ceiling at all since they do not certify its financial statements.

No ceiling on non-audit fees applies at all, because the VidSutra Consortium Association is a mutual entity which does not carry out professional practice and because Nandi Infra Ltd is a listed company whose fees are governed by the Companies Act, 2013.
questions.explanation: Chapter XV provides that the ceiling on non-audit fees applies to a network as follows: for the network firm which is doing the statutory audit it is the same as the limit normally mentioned, and for the other firms of the same network, collectively, it is three times the statutory audit fee. Applying that here, the aggregate available to the other member firms is 3 x ₹ 9 lacs = ₹ 27 lacs, while Sahay & Co. gets no enhancement merely because a network exists. The second option misreads 'collectively' as 'individually', which would multiply the ceiling six times over; the third option reverses the rule, giving the enhanced ceiling to the audit firm itself. The fourth option is wrong on both counts, since the facilitator form of the network and the listed status of the client do not displace the ceiling. The decisive fact is that the ₹ 9 lacs is the statutory audit fee of Nandi Infra Ltd and the six other firms are treated as one collective basket.

questions.category: Council General Guidelines Chapter XV - Networking - Registration and Reporting
questions.question:
Case: Seven CA firms having 46 partners between them, with offices in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Pune and Lucknow, have agreed to (a) share the profits of a common technology consulting vertical, (b) operate under one brand name 'VidSutra' and a common business strategy paper approved by an assembled committee of partners, (c) run a common training centre for articled assistants and a common data analytics technical department, with articles enrolled centrally and deputed to the firms, and (d) retain their own separate audit methodologies for statutory audit work. No entity of the structure carries out any professional practice; a mutual association called 'VidSutra Consortium Association' only collects membership subscriptions and arranges the common training. The promoters propose to name the network 'VidSutra & Co.' and applied to the Institute in the prescribed form on 4 March 2024. The Institute intimated approval of the name on 2 April 2024, and the network filed its application for registration on 12 August 2024. On 15 May 2024 the structure entered into an arrangement with an entity having its office in Singapore and filed the declaration for listing on 10 July 2024. On 1 August 2024 one member firm exited and this was communicated to the Institute on 25 September 2024. Rane & Associates, a member firm, also continues as a member of a different network formed with entities outside India. Sahay & Co., another member firm, is the statutory auditor of Nandi Infra Ltd, a listed company, for a statutory audit fee of ₹ 9 lacs for FY 2023-24; the other member firms propose to collectively take up the internal audit and book-keeping work of Nandi Infra Ltd.

Which one of the following is the MOST appropriate conclusion on the three procedural steps followed by the VidSutra network?
options: All three steps were regular, because each period runs from the date on which the Institute receives the network's application or communication and not from the date of approval or of the underlying event, the date stamp of the Institute's office being the operative one.

Only the listing declaration is irregular, because an approved name may be reserved afresh on a second application within a further three months, and because a change in constitution need be reported only when the registration of the network is renewed.

Only the two communications are irregular, because the name continues to stand approved until the Institute expressly cancels it, and because registration of a network which does not itself carry on professional practice is optional rather than mandatory.

The name stood cancelled on expiry of three months from 2 April 2024 because registration was not completed within that period; the declaration for listing was due within 30 days of 15 May 2024 and is late; and the exit of the member firm was to be communicated within 30 days of 1 August 2024 and is also late.
questions.explanation: Three separate clocks run here. First, after the name is approved the Institute reserves it for three months from the date of approval, the network must get itself registered within three months, and registration is mandatory; on approval intimated on 2 April 2024 the period expired on 2 July 2024, yet the registration application was made only on 12 August 2024, so the assigned name stood cancelled on expiry of that period. Second, where a network enters into an arrangement with entities outside India it must file a declaration with the Institute for listing within 30 days of entering into the arrangement, that is by 14 June 2024 for the arrangement of 15 May 2024, and it was filed on 10 July 2024. Third, a change in constitution due to any entry or exit from the network must be communicated to the Institute within 30 days of the change, that is by 31 August 2024 for the exit of 1 August 2024, and it was communicated on 25 September 2024. Options 1 to 3 all fail because they relocate the starting date of these periods or treat mandatory registration as optional.

questions.category: Council General Guidelines Chapter XV - Networking - Sequence of Name Approval and Registration
questions.question: A group of firms proposes to constitute a registered network and wants to know the order in which things must happen. Which of the following represents the correct sequence of events, together with the time limits prescribed by the Networking Guidelines?
options: Form received by the Institute, name reserved for three months from that date, Institute then intimates approval or rejection within 30 days of the reservation, registration to follow within 30 days of that intimation; a name once assigned cannot be cancelled.

Form received by the Institute, Institute approves or rejects the name and intimates the same within 30 days of receipt of the form, approved name reserved for three months from the date of approval, network gets itself registered within three months, failing which the assigned name stands cancelled on expiry of that period.

Form received by the Institute, registration completed within three months of the date of the form, the Institute then approving the name within 30 days of registration, and the approved name being reserved for a further 30 days after registration.

Form received by the Institute, Institute intimates its approval within three months of receipt, name reserved for 30 days from the intimation, registration to be completed within three months of the date of the form, registration being recommendatory rather than mandatory.
questions.explanation: The Networking Guidelines lay down a definite order. The Institute shall approve or reject the name of the network and intimate the same to the network within 30 days from the date of receipt of the form. After the name is approved, the Institute reserves that name for three months from the date of approval, and the network shall get itself registered with the Institute within three months; if it does not, the assigned name shall be cancelled on the expiry of that period, registration being mandatory. Option 0 puts the reservation before approval and wrongly denies cancellation. Option 2 reverses approval and registration, which would mean registering before a name exists. Option 3 swaps the 30-day and three-month periods and treats registration as recommendatory; the recommendatory character belongs to the Self-Regulatory Measures, not to network registration.

questions.category: Council General Guidelines Chapter XV - Networking - One Network Rule and Common Partners
questions.question: Case: 'Sanjeevini & Affiliates' is a registered network of nine CA firms in Bengaluru, constituted as a mutual association which acts only as a facilitator. On 1 February 2025 two of its constituent firms, Rao & Sons and Sona & Company, admitted a common partner, CA Vikram Rao, who continues as a partner of both firms. The network entered into an arrangement on 20 August 2025 with an entity having its office in Dubai, and filed the declaration with the Institute for listing on 3 October 2025. CA Vikram Rao's third firm, Rao & Velan, has been since 2022 a member of a different network, 'Kaveri & Affiliates'. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate advice?
options: The listing declaration is irregular, but the common partnership and the membership of two networks are permissible, because a firm may join one network constituted in India and one additional network formed with entities outside India, the two restrictions operating separately.

Every arrangement described is regular, because a network constituted as a mutual association acting only as a facilitator for its constituents is exempt from the listing requirement and from the restriction on joining more than one network.

Rao & Sons and Sona & Company, having a common partner, shall join one network; the declaration for listing was due within 30 days of 20 August 2025 and is late; and Rao & Velan cannot continue as a member of two networks, since a firm is allowed to join only one network.

The only irregularity is the membership of two networks by Rao & Velan, because the admission of a common partner is a change in constitution reportable within three months rather than 30 days, and because no time limit is fixed for the listing declaration.
questions.explanation: Three rules bite on these facts. A firm is allowed to join only one network, and firms having common partners shall join one network, so the admission of CA Vikram Rao as a partner of both Rao & Sons and Sona & Company cannot leave the two firms as separately identified constituents of the same structure; it also means that Rao & Velan, which is already in the Kaveri & Affiliates network, cannot simultaneously belong to the Sanjeevini network. The rule that members and firms are allowed to join only one network with entities outside India is an additional restriction on such networks; it is not a permission to hold one India network plus one outside-India network, which is why option 0 is wrong. The listing declaration for a network with entities outside India is due within 30 days from the date of entering into the arrangement, so the declaration for the 20 August 2025 Dubai arrangement was due by 19 September 2025 and the filing on 3 October 2025 is late; option 3's claim that a change in constitution is reportable within three months is also wrong, that period being 30 days. Option 1 invents an exemption for facilitator networks, which does not exist.

questions.category: Council General Guidelines Chapter XV - Networking - Framework of Internal Bye-laws
questions.question:
A newly registered network proposes the following clauses for its internal bye-laws, on which the affiliates may enter into a written agreement among themselves:
I. Appointment of the Managing Committee and administration of the network.
II. Contribution of membership fees to meet the administration cost of the network.
III. Identifying a partner responsible for an assignment, that is the engagement partner, and dispute settlement procedures through arbitration and conciliation.
IV. Fixing the maximum number of tax audit assignments which each member firm may sign in a financial year and the allocation of clients among the member firms.
V. Development of training materials, and determining the methodology and compensation for drawing resources from each member firm.

Which of the above are matters which the bye-laws of a network may contain?
options: I, II, III, IV and V
I, III, IV and V only
I, II, III and V only
questions.explanation: To streamline networking, the network shall formulate bye-laws which may contain clauses on which the affiliates may enter into a written agreement among themselves, namely appointment of the Managing Committee, administration of the network, contribution of membership fees to meet the administration cost of the network, identifying a partner responsible for the assignment (the engagement partner), dispute settlement procedures through arbitration and conciliation, development of training materials, and determining the methodology and compensation for drawing resources from each member firm. Statements I, II, III and V each reproduce items from that list, III combining the engagement partner item with the arbitration and conciliation item and V combining training materials with the resource and compensation item. Statement IV is not a matter contemplated by the framework: the cap on the number of tax audit assignments is a Council General Guidelines limit fixed by the Institute for each member or partner and is not something a network bye-law may redistribute, and allocation of clients among member firms is not one of the listed clauses. Any option which includes IV is therefore bound to be wrong.

questions.category: Council General Guidelines Chapter XVI - Logo Guidelines
questions.question:
The marketing executive of 'Goemala & Co.' proposes four uses of the new 'CA India' logo:
(i) the letters 'CA' in blue colour with a tri-colour tick mark placed upside down, on a white background, with the font, spacing and dimensions exactly as prescribed.
(ii) the same logo reduced to one-fourth of its prescribed size in a newspaper supplement, with the spacing and dimensions otherwise unchanged.
(iii) the logo tilted through 15 degrees on a hoarding so that it fits alongside a client's logo.
(iv) the tick mark printed in a single colour and the white background replaced by a light grey one in a presentation deck.

Which of these uses are NOT in conformity with the Logo Guidelines?
questions.explanation: The prescribed logo consists of the letters 'CA' in blue colour with a tri-colour tick mark, upside down, on a white background, so use (i) is the correct rendering and is conforming. The Guidelines require that there should be no alteration of the font, that is of colour, bold or unbold and size, and no change in spacing and dimensions; they also state that the logo should not be shrunk or distorted. Use (ii) is therefore non-conforming despite preserving proportions, because shrinking the logo is itself prohibited - the size of the reproduction is a font attribute that may not be altered. Use (iii) offends the direction to refrain from rotating or tilting the logo, and use (iv) offends the direction not to change the design and colours, including the background. Hence (ii), (iii) and (iv) are non-conforming and only (i) may be retained; the options which include (i) wrongly treat the correct rendering as a breach.

questions.category: Council General Guidelines Chapter XVII - Corporate Form of Practice
questions.question:
Consider the following statements on the Guidelines for Corporate Form of Practice under Chapter XVII:
I. A member in practice may hold the office of Managing Director of a body corporate which renders management consultancy services along with the concurrent audits of two public companies.
II. A member in practice may hold the office of Wholetime Director or Manager of a body corporate engaged exclusively in rendering Management Consultancy and Other Services, and may retain his full-time certificate of practice.
III. A member's equity holding in such a management consultancy company is subject to the same ceiling as the share of a partner in an audit firm.
IV. No audit practice can be done in the corporate form, and the name of the management consultancy company must be approved by the Institute and the company must be registered with the Institute.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: The Council has allowed members in practice to hold the office of MD, WTD or Manager of a body corporate engaged exclusively in rendering Management Consultancy and Other Services, and a member can retain a full-time CoP along with holding such an office, so statement II is correct. Statement IV is correct: no audit practice can be done in the corporate form, and the name of the management consultancy company is required to be approved by the Institute while the company has to be registered with the Institute. Statement I fails because the exclusivity condition is breached the moment the body corporate also takes concurrent audits, which is audit practice. Statement III is the mirror image of the rule: the Guidelines expressly provide that there is no restriction on equity holding of members in such a company, so importing a partner-wise ceiling is wrong. Options including either I or III are therefore unusable.

questions.category: Council General Guidelines Chapter XVII - Corporate Form of Practice - Permissible Actions
questions.question:
Case: CA Iqbal Nadeem holds a full-time certificate of practice. He accepts the office of Wholetime Director of Meridian Advisory Services Pvt Ltd, a company rendering management consultancy, systems design and cost management assignments, and which also holds the statutory audits of two small public companies. Iqbal holds 74% of its equity. Nadeem & Co., the firm in which Iqbal is a partner, is the statutory auditor of Kaveri Steels Ltd, and Meridian proposes to accept the internal audit of Kaveri Steels Ltd for a fee which is only half of Nadeem & Co.'s audit fee. Meridian has adopted its name without applying to the Institute and is not registered with it. The partners propose to circulate a brochure advertising their professional attainments and to approach a list of prospective clients for work. Consider the following actions:
1. Meridian must confine itself exclusively to Management Consultancy and Other Services, must give up the statutory audits it holds, must get its name approved by the Institute and must get itself registered with the Institute.
2. Iqbal may continue to hold his full-time CoP along with the office of Wholetime Director, and his 74% equity is not objectionable, since there is no restriction on equity holding of members in such a company.
3. Meridian may accept the internal audit of Kaveri Steels Ltd, because the fee for that assignment is less than the statutory audit fee charged by Nadeem & Co.
4. Meridian must desist from the proposed brochure and from approaching prospective clients, since it is required to comply with clauses (6) and (7) of Part I of the First Schedule of the CA Act, 1949.

Which combination of actions is fully appropriate?
questions.explanation: Actions 1, 2 and 4 are correct and action 3 is not. On 1, the body corporate must be engaged exclusively in rendering Management Consultancy and Other Services and no audit practice can be done in the corporate form, so the two statutory audits cannot be retained; the name must be approved by the Institute and the company must be registered with it. On 2, a member may hold the office of WTD and retain a full-time CoP, and the Guidelines impose no restriction on equity holding, so the 74% figure is a red herring. On 4, the management consultancy company must comply with clauses (6) and (7) of Part I of the First Schedule, which deal with soliciting clients and advertising professional attainments or services, so the brochure and the approach to prospective clients offend. Action 3 is wrong because where a member of the management consultancy company is the statutory auditor of an entity, that company shall not accept internal audit, book-keeping or other assignments from that entity which are prohibited for a statutory auditor; the comparison of fees, drawn from a different provision, does not create permission.

questions.category: Council General Guidelines Chapter XVII - Corporate Form of Practice - Ethical Compliance
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Where a member of a management consultancy company is the statutory auditor of an entity, that company shall not accept the internal audit or the book-keeping work of that entity.

Reason (R): A management consultancy company formed under Chapter XVII of the Council General Guidelines is required to comply with clauses (6) and (7) of Part I of the First Schedule of the CA Act, 1949.

In the light of the above, choose the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true but they are two separate ethical-compliance requirements of Chapter XVII. A is true because the Guidelines specifically provide that if a member of the management consultancy company is the statutory auditor of an entity, then such company shall not accept internal audit, book-keeping or other assignments from that entity which are prohibited for a statutory auditor; the prohibition therefore flows from that independence-based requirement, not from the advertising rules. R is also true, because Chapter XVII separately requires the management consultancy company to comply with clauses (6) and (7) of Part I of the First Schedule of the CA Act, 1949, which are the clauses dealing with soliciting clients or professional work and with advertising professional attainments or services. Since clauses (6) and (7) say nothing about internal audit or book-keeping assignments of audit clients, R cannot be the explanation of A, so the first option is wrong. The third and fourth options wrongly deny the literal text of one of the two requirements.

questions.category: Recommended Self-Regulatory Measures - Nature, Branch Audits and Fees
questions.question:
Consider the following statements on the Recommended Self-Regulatory Measures issued by the Council:
I. The measures are recommendatory in nature and have been given to ensure the healthy growth of the profession.
II. Branch audits of a company should not be conducted by its statutory auditors consisting of 10 or more members, but should be conducted by local firms of auditors consisting of fewer than 10 members.
III. The restriction in statement II does not apply where the accounting records of the branches are maintained at the head office, or where significant operations are carried out at the branch office.
IV. Charging an excessive fee, or charging a low fee, for an assignment constitutes professional misconduct.
V. The Institute has issued a minimum scale of fees for professional assignments and the recommended scale of fees is to be charged for such assignments.

Which of the above statements are correct?
options: I, II, III and V only
I, II, III, IV and V
questions.explanation: Statements I, II, III and V correctly reproduce the measures. The Self-Regulatory Measures are recommendatory, which is why failure to observe them is not by itself misconduct. The branch audit measure bars a statutory audit firm of 10 or more members from doing branch audits and asks that these be given to local firms of fewer than 10 members, subject to the two exceptions that the accounting records of the branches are maintained at the head office, or significant operations are carried out at the branch office. The minimum scale of fees has been issued by the Institute and the recommended scale is to be charged. Statement IV is not correct, because the measure expressly states that charging an excessive fee or low fees for an assignment does not constitute any misconduct; it follows that options containing IV must be rejected even though the recommended scale in statement V remains the standard to be followed.

questions.question: Case: Virat Textiles Ltd has 112 branches. Its statutory auditor, Mehta & Shah LLP, has 14 partners. The accounting records of 40 branches are prepared and kept at the head office at Surat, the branch offices merely executing purchase and sale transactions on approvals and data sent from Surat; in the case of 12 other branches, all records are kept at the branch offices but significant operations are carried out at those branches; for the balance 60 branches, the entire accounting records are prepared and maintained at the branch offices and no significant operations are carried out there. Mehta & Shah LLP proposes to conduct all 112 branch audits with teams of its own paid assistants. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate position under the Recommended Self-Regulatory Measures?
options: Since the LLP has 10 or more members it may conduct all the branch audits, because this measure is directed only at a statutory auditor who is a sole practitioner or a firm of two partners and does not bind a large LLP.

The branch audits of all 112 branches should be given to local firms of auditors consisting of fewer than 10 members, the measure being one of general application and admitting of no exception based on where the accounting records are prepared or where operations are carried on.

The branch audits of all 112 branches should be given to a firm consisting of fewer than 5 members, that being the number fixed by the measures for a firm to be associated as joint auditor in large companies, and the same figure governing branch audit work.

The branch audits of the 40 branches whose records are maintained at the head office and of the 12 branches where significant operations are carried out may be conducted by Mehta & Shah LLP notwithstanding its size, while the branch audits of the remaining 60 branches should, consistently with the measures, be given to local firms of auditors consisting of fewer than 10 members.
questions.explanation: The measure recommends that branch audits of a company should not be conducted by its statutory auditors consisting of 10 or more members, but should be conducted by local firms of auditors consisting of fewer than 10 members, and with 14 partners Mehta & Shah LLP prima facie falls within the restriction. The two stated exceptions apply here to two identifiable groups: the 40 branches whose accounting records are maintained at the head office at Surat, and the 12 branches at which significant operations are carried out, so for those 52 branches the statutory auditor may itself conduct the branch audit. For the remaining 60 branches neither exception is available, since the records are kept at the branch and no significant operations are carried out there, and the local firm route is the one consistent with the measures. Option 0 invents a sole practitioner limitation, option 1 ignores the exceptions, and option 3 borrows the fewer than 5 members figure from the joint audit measure, which is a different matter altogether.

questions.category: Recommended Self-Regulatory Measures - Joint Audit, Staff Ratio and Disclosure
questions.question:
Match each situation in Column I with the Recommended Self-Regulatory Measure most directly relevant to it in Column II:

Column I
P. The partners of a listed company with a turnover of ₹ 4,200 crores propose to appoint a large firm as auditor and the senior partner is considering associating another firm.
Q. For the audit of a large manufacturing company, the firm has deployed one partner and 22 non-qualified members of staff.
R. In addition to his audit fee, an auditor has received ₹ 6 lacs from the same client for implementing an ERP system.
S. A newly qualified CA quotes one-third of the Institute's minimum scale of fees to win a statutory audit assignment.

Column II
1. Ratio between qualified and unqualified staff
2. Disclosure of interest by auditors in other firms, that is disclosure of payments received for other services
3. Joint audit, that is associating a firm with fewer than 5 members in large companies
4. Recommended minimum scale of fees
5. Branch audits by local firms of fewer than 10 members

Choose the correct pairing:
questions.explanation: P relates to joint audit: in large companies the measure recommends that a firm with fewer than 5 members should be associated as joint auditors, which is the point the senior partner is weighing. Q relates to the qualified to unqualified staff ratio, a CA firm being expected to have at least 1 member for every 5 non-qualified members of staff in every audit, so 22 non-qualified staff would call for a larger qualified presence than one partner. R relates to disclosure of interest, auditors being expected to make a disclosure of payments received by them for other services, here the ₹ 6 lacs ERP fee alongside the audit fee. S relates to the recommended minimum scale of fees, which is the scale to be charged, although charging low or excessive fees does not by itself constitute misconduct. The measure in column 1, item 5, about branch audits by local firms, is not engaged by any of the four situations and is correctly left unused; the other pairings shift these items between the wrong situations.

questions.category: Recommended Self-Regulatory Measures - Disclosure of Fees
questions.question:
Case: The total fees of the firm Nadarajah & Co. were ₹ 62 lacs in FY 2023-24 and ₹ 71 lacs in FY 2024-25. The gross annual professional fees received by it from its client Karpagam Polymers Pvt Ltd, an unlisted company which is not a public interest entity and whose auditor is appointed by its shareholders, were ₹ 26 lacs in FY 2023-24 and ₹ 29.5 lacs in FY 2024-25. The firm made no disclosure regarding these fees. Consider the following statements:
I. Disclosure was required, because the gross annual professional fees from this audit client for two consecutive years were more than 40% of the total fees of the firm.
II. Disclosure was not required, because the threshold applicable to such a client is more than 20% of the total fees of the firm and the firm's fees from it did not cross that figure.
III. If Karpagam Polymers were a public interest entity, disclosure would be required whenever the gross annual professional fees from it for two consecutive years exceed 20% of the total fees of the firm.
IV. Disclosure would have been unnecessary irrespective of the percentages, if the total fees received by the firm did not exceed ₹ 20 lacs, or if the client were a government company, a public undertaking, a nationalised bank, a public financial institution or a regulator, or where the appointment is made by the Government.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: For non-public interest entities disclosure is required where gross annual professional fees from an audit client for two consecutive years exceed 40% of the total fees of the firm. Here ₹ 26 lacs on total fees of ₹ 62 lacs is about 42% and ₹ 29.5 lacs on ₹ 71 lacs is about 41.5%, so the threshold is crossed in two consecutive years and statement I is correct. Statement II is wrong because 20% is the threshold for public interest entities, not for a non-PIE such as Karpagam Polymers, and it is in any event a lower, not a higher, bar, so the fees certainly exceeded 20%. Statement III correctly states the PIE threshold, and statement IV reproduces the two exemptions from applicability, namely total fees of the firm not exceeding ₹ 20 lacs and audits of government companies, public undertakings, nationalised banks, public financial institutions, regulators or appointments made by the Government; the ₹ 20 lacs test looks at the firm's total fees, not at the fees from the client.

questions.category: Integrated - Networking Ceiling on Non-audit Fees with Disclosure of Fees
questions.question:
Case: Deshpande & Iyer is a constituent firm of a registered network and is the statutory auditor of Kalyani Cements Ltd, a public interest entity, for a statutory audit fee of ₹ 10 lacs for FY 2024-25. The other constituent firms of the same network collectively charge Kalyani Cements ₹ 28 lacs for consultancy in that year. The total fees of Deshpande & Iyer were ₹ 62 lacs in FY 2023-24 and ₹ 58 lacs in FY 2024-25, of which gross professional fees of ₹ 26 lacs and ₹ 25 lacs respectively were received from Kalyani Cements. Consider the statements:
I. The consultancy taken by the other firms of the network from Kalyani Cements exceeds the ceiling applicable to them, because any amount above the statutory audit fee is impermissible.
II. Disclosure of the fees is required, because the gross annual professional fees from this audit client exceeded 20% of the total fees of the firm for two consecutive years and Kalyani Cements is a public interest entity.
III. If Kalyani Cements were not a public interest entity, no disclosure would be required, because the 40% threshold would not be crossed in either year.
IV. No disclosure is required in any event, because the fees received from Kalyani Cements are less than ₹ 20 lacs in the aggregate sense contemplated by the exemption.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Only statement II holds. On I, the ceiling for the other firms of the same network, collectively, is three times the statutory audit fee, that is 3 x ₹ 10 lacs = ₹ 30 lacs, so consultancy of ₹ 28 lacs is within the limit; the statement wrongly equates the ceiling with the statutory audit fee itself. On II, Kalyani Cements is a public interest entity, so the disclosure threshold is more than 20% of the total fees of the firm for two consecutive years: ₹ 26 lacs on ₹ 62 lacs is about 42% and ₹ 25 lacs on ₹ 58 lacs is about 43%, and disclosure was therefore required. On III, the same percentages comfortably exceed the 40% non-PIE threshold in both years, so reclassification as a non-PIE would not have removed the disclosure obligation, making the statement wrong. On IV, the ₹ 20 lacs exemption applies where the total fees received by the firm do not exceed ₹ 20 lacs; Deshpande & Iyer's total fees are ₹ 58 to ₹ 62 lacs, so the exemption is unavailable.

questions.category: Recent Decisions of Ethical Standards Board - Permissible and Not Permissible
questions.question:
Match each activity in Column I with its status in Column II according to the recent decisions of the Ethical Standards Board:

Column I
P. A member in practice is appointed a financial adviser and receives commission from financial institutions.
Q. A member in practice acts as a mediator in a dispute between two companies before a court.
R. A member in practice holds a credit card issued by a bank of which he is the auditor.
S. A member in practice takes the agencies of UTI, GIC or NSDL and also holds a customs broker's licence.
T. A member in practice accepts the assignment of a mystery audit for a retail chain.

Column II
1. Not permissible for a CA in practice
2. Permissible for a CA in practice
3. Permissible for a CA in practice subject to a condition

Choose the correct pairing:
questions.explanation: P and S are on the not permissible list: a CA in practice cannot become a financial adviser and receive commission from financial institutions, cannot take the agencies of UTI, GIC or NSDL, and cannot hold a customs broker's licence, so both pair with 1. Q pairs with 2 without condition, because acting as a mediator or arbitrator in court is expressly permissible. T also pairs with 2, the Board having held that accepting the assignment of a mystery audit is permissible. R alone pairs with 3, because holding a credit card when he is the auditor of a bank is permissible provided the outstanding balance does not exceed ₹ 1 lac - the activity is lawful only so long as that figure is observed. The other options misplace R as unconditional, treat the barred agencies and licence as permissible, or convert Q and T into conditional permissions which the decisions do not impose.

questions.category: Recent Decisions of Ethical Standards Board - Statutory Auditor's Other Work
questions.question:
Consider the following statements on the recent decisions of the Ethical Standards Board:
I. A statutory auditor may prepare a BRSR study for his audit clients and may also be the assurance provider of BRSR for the same client.
II. A statutory auditor shall not engage in a compilation engagement as per SRS 4410 in respect of that entity.
III. The statutory auditor of a bank may simultaneously accept the ASM assignment of a customer of that bank, provided the ASM work is completed before the audit of the bank commences.
IV. Where a member is the statutory auditor of a bank, he may accept the stock audit or inspection audit of a branch of the same bank for the same financial year, if the branch is located outside his own city.
V. A statutory auditor or tax auditor shall not be the valuer of the unquoted equity shares of the same entity where the law prohibits it.

Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
options: II, III, IV and V only
questions.explanation: Statement I is not correct, because a statutory auditor cannot prepare a BRSR study for audit clients; what the Board permits is that he may provide advisory services on the same and can be the assurance provider of BRSR for the same client, so the two halves of the statement are not equally admissible. Statement III is not correct, because the statutory auditor of a bank cannot accept an ASM assignment of a customer of that bank simultaneously; the sequence in which the two assignments are completed does not cure the bar. Statement IV is not correct, because the restriction on the statutory auditor of a bank taking the stock audit or inspection audit of any branch or sister concern of the same bank is fixed for the same financial year, and the location of the branch is not the operative condition; the words 'outside his own city' are the red herring. Statements II and V correctly restate the decisions, the SRS 4410 compilation engagement being impermissible for the statutory auditor of the entity and valuation of unquoted equity shares of the same entity being impermissible where the law prohibits it, which also shows that the prohibition in V is conditional on the legal bar.

questions.category: Recent Decisions of Ethical Standards Board - Bank Audit Independence
questions.question: Case: CA Nitin Bhandari has accepted the statutory audit of Indus Grande Bank Ltd for FY 2024-25. He holds a credit card issued by that bank with an outstanding balance of ₹ 82,000, and he had taken a housing loan of ₹ 48 lacs from the bank against a fixed deposit held by him in that bank. During the same year four further proposals arise: (i) he accepts the inspection audit of the Pune branch of the bank for FY 2024-25; (ii) he accepts the ASM assignment of Kabira Steels Ltd, a borrowing customer of the bank; (iii) he continues as the concurrent auditor of Indus Grande Bank and accepts appointment as statutory auditor of Meridian Bank, which was sponsored by Indus Grande Bank; (iv) he declines to exercise a lien over a client's records for fees which that client owes him. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The statutory audit appointment is regular, because a loan secured against his own fixed deposit exposes the bank to no credit risk; proposals (i) and (ii) are equally regular, while only proposal (iii) offends the decisions of the Board.

The statutory audit appointment itself is not permissible because he had taken a loan against the fixed deposit held by him in that bank; proposals (i), (ii) and (iii) are each separately impermissible; while the credit card with an outstanding balance within ₹ 1 lac and the declining of the lien are the only two things in the case that are in order.

Proposals (i) to (iv) are all regular, because a branch, a borrowing customer and a sponsored bank are each distinct reporting entities from the bank whose statutory audit he holds, and the lien question concerns a different client entirely.
Only proposal (iv) calls for scrutiny, because a member in practice may lawfully exercise a lien over his client's documents and records to enforce payment of fees which are overdue and undisputed.
questions.explanation: The decisive fact is the housing loan taken against the fixed deposit held by him in the same bank: a CA is not permitted to accept the audit of a bank if he took a loan against an FD held by him in that bank, so the appointment itself fails irrespective of the other proposals. Proposal (i) is impermissible because the statutory auditor of a bank cannot accept the stock audit or inspection audit of any branch or sister concern of the same bank for the same financial year. Proposal (ii) is impermissible because the statutory auditor of a bank cannot accept an ASM assignment of a customer of that bank simultaneously, and proposal (iii) is impermissible because the concurrent auditor of bank 'X' cannot be appointed as statutory auditor of bank 'Y' sponsored by 'X'. Against this, holding a credit card issued by an audited bank is permissible provided the outstanding balance does not exceed ₹ 1 lac, which is satisfied at ₹ 82,000, and a CA cannot exercise a lien over client documents or records for non-payment of his fees, so his refusal in (iv) is correct conduct; option 3 therefore states the position on the lien backwards.

questions.category: Recent Decisions of Ethical Standards Board - Co-operative Banks
questions.question:
CA Prakash Kudalcar is a member in practice. He receives four offers relating to co-operative banks:
I. Appointment as an independent director of a district central co-operative bank, given that he is not involved in its day-to-day activities and neither he nor his partners are interested as an auditor.
II. Appointment as a professional director on the management board of a co-operative bank.
III. Appointment as a member of the management board of a primary (urban) co-operative bank, where he has no involvement in day-to-day operations and is provided only sitting fees for his services.
IV. Appointment as an executive director of an urban co-operative bank to supervise its credit and recovery department, on the assurance that he will not be given the audit of that bank.

Which of the above are permissible for a CA in practice under the decisions of the Ethical Standards Board?
questions.explanation: The Board has permitted a member to become a non-executive or independent director in a co-operative bank provided he is not involved in day-to-day activities and neither he nor his partners are interested as an auditor, which is exactly the shape of offer I, so I is permissible and the two conditions are satisfied on the facts. Becoming a professional director on the management board of a co-operative bank is separately shown as permissible, so II stands. Becoming a member of the management board of primary (urban) co-operative banks is permissible where there is no involvement of the member in day-to-day operations and only sitting fees are provided for the services, which fits III. Offer IV is different in kind: it is an executive role supervising the credit and recovery department, that is day-to-day operations, and the assurance that he will not audit that bank does not substitute for the condition which the decisions actually impose; hence any option including IV is wrong.

questions.category: Recent Decisions of Ethical Standards Board - Publicity, Stationery and Fee Structure
questions.question:
Consider the following five activities proposed by CA firms:
I. A firm prints its values, vision and mission statements on its letterheads and visiting cards to project a professional image.
II. A firm includes the same values, vision and mission statements in its firm profile, which is provided only on specific request.
III. A partner sends periodic messages about his practice and the services he offers to a contact list through a messaging application.
IV. A CA certifies the amount spent by an institute out of a grant received by it and charges fees as a percentage of the utilisation amount.
V. A CA's name appears on a company's portal as its promoter or director, with no mention of his professional attainments or of his firm's name.

Which of the above are permissible for a CA in practice?
options: I, III, IV and V only
questions.explanation: A CA cannot publish or print values, vision or mission statements on letterheads, visiting cards and the like, which makes I impermissible; the decisions expressly leave room for them to be printed in the firm profile and provided on specific request, which is the shape of II and makes it permissible. Using messaging applications to send messages about one's practice and services is on the not permissible list, so III fails even though the recipients volunteered their numbers. Charging fees on a percentage of the utilisation amount for certifying the amount spent by an institute from a grant is permissible, so IV stands, and being mentioned as promoter or director on a company portal without professional attainments and firm name is likewise permissible, so V stands. The pairing options that retain I or III, or that drop IV or V, cannot be correct.

questions.category: Recent Decisions of Ethical Standards Board - IFSC, Kiosk and Digital Services
questions.question:
Consider the following statements on the activities of a CA in practice:
I. A member may set up his practice in an IFSC or GIFT city, and he may also render services to IFSC units from an office situated outside the IFSC.
II. A CA firm may register itself on Udyog Aadhaar, the web portal of the MSME Ministry, and a member may engage as a registration authority for obtaining digital signatures for his clients.
III. A member may act as the authorised representative of a foreign company even if he is also the auditor of that company, since representation is not an assurance service.
IV. Two or more CAs may collectively take a joint GST training session for their clients and share the fees.
